## of the Revelation
## that is,
# THE REVELATION
## of Saint John clearly opened,
### with a logical analysis <term>original: Resolution; the process of breaking a complex text down into its component parts to understand its structure</term>
### and exposition.
## WHEREIN THE MEANING <note>original: sense</note>
### is clarified from the scriptures; the fulfillment <note>original: event</note> of things foretold is also discussed based on church histories.
## By Thomas Brightman

## To the Holy Reformed Churches of
# BRITAIN, GERMANY & FRANCE,
### Grace and peace from God the Father, and
### our Lord JESUS CHRIST.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'T' containing floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>
*You cannot wonder at all (most Holy Spouse of Christ <note>The "Spouse of Christ" is a traditional theological metaphor for the Christian Church.</note>) that a new interpretation of this Book of Revelation is offered to you here. Seeing as there is such a great variety of interpretations, both old and new, it is a matter universally acknowledged that the Revelation still necessarily requires a "revelation" <note>The author is making a wordplay: though the book is titled "Revelation," its meaning remains hidden without further divine uncovering.</note> to be understood. This voice of the Lord sounds continually in your ears: "The Lord has spoken; who can but prophesy?" (Amos 3:8). For the Lord has not only spoken through dreams and visions in the past, but He also speaks every day—specifically, as often as He enlightens the minds of His servants so they may be able to search out the hidden truth of His Word and bring it forth into the open world <note>original: "champion world," referring to "champaign" or open, public land.</note>.* 

*Now, anyone with whom the Lord communicates His counsels in this manner cannot help but feel a necessity laid upon him to declare to others what he has received. For should a candle be lit only to be put under a basket? Or should a common danger be revealed to any one man in private for his own sake alone? Should it not rather be for this end: that he, being placed as if in a watchtower, should give warning to all others so they might avoid and prevent, with all speed, the evil and*

<summary>In this dedication, the author argues that interpreting the Book of Revelation is an ongoing divine duty, comparing the interpreter to a watchman who must share God's revealed truths to warn the Church of coming dangers.</summary>
<keywords>Reformed Churches, Britain, Germany, France, Book of Revelation, Amos 3:8, prophecy, biblical commentary, watchtower, divine enlightenment</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the author's dedication to the Reformed Churches, comparing his duty to share his interpretation of Revelation to the duty of the four lepers in the Bible who felt compelled to share news of relief during a famine.</meta>

## To the Holy Reformed Churches of

*destruction that is rushing in upon them? The four lepers wisely concluded that they would be culpable and liable to some punishment if they had concealed that joyful news even until the morning (2 Kings 7:9) <note>In 2 Kings 7, four lepers discover that the Syrian army besieging Samaria has fled, leaving behind food and riches. They realize they must share this news with the starving city or face divine punishment.</note>. If someone should conceal an imminent destruction, what punishment would he be worthy of? One that is even more grievous, by as much as it is worse for one to be utterly ruined than to be deprived of joy for a few hours.*

*Therefore, when I had learned from this Book of Revelation both that a most grievous trial was immediately <note>original: "straightwayes"</note> to come upon the whole Christian world—so that the sword of the Lord was to be made drunk with blood in the heavens, and all their host was to be shaken—and also that you, the Christian churches of Germany, France, and Britain <note>original: "Britany," referring here to Great Britain</note>, were most mercifully warned about this storm by letters addressed to you by name, I, having by God’s providence found these letters cast abroad and understanding from their inscriptions to which churches they were sent, dared not do anything but give them to you. I feared that by intercepting them and keeping them to myself, I would both treacherously endanger your safety and also make myself deservedly guilty of high treason against God's Majesty.*

*There is no godly person living, or who has lived for a long time, whose mind does not tell him—judging by the contempt for God's worship, the mocking of His Holy Word, the extreme carelessness and ambition of pastors, and the altogether dissolute and wicked lives of all men of every rank and condition seen everywhere—that some horrible calamity will immediately follow. But these letters do not guess at the matter by doubtful conjecture; rather, they teach in express terms that there is an immeasurable gulf, as if full of miseries, already prepared, and that we who live today stand on the very brink of it. You (O Spouse <note>The Church.</note>), I pray you, look upon the seal; take notice of the words, the handwriting, and the style of the Writer.*

*You know the voice of your husband best. If these are letters sent to you from Him, as they openly appear to be, it is more than*

<summary>The author explains his moral obligation to publish his findings, warning the Reformed Churches of Europe that the Book of Revelation contains specific, urgent warnings of an impending calamity intended for them.</summary>
<keywords>Reformed Churches, Book of Revelation, 2 Kings 7:9, divine judgment, Britain, Germany, France, Spouse of Christ, prophecy</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's address to the Reformed Churches of Britain, Germany, and France, urging them to prepare for God's impending judgment on the Roman Church and the subsequent era of peace.</meta>

->Britain, Germany, and France.<-

It is time for you to cast away all that filth which, through far too long a period of complacency <note>original: "securitie"</note>, you have gathered; otherwise, if you continue to be overly negligent in this, you will soon be purged with the fire of the metal-worker <note>original: "founder"; i.e., a refiner of metal</note> to your great risk and harm. Yet do not think that I bring only mournful and tearful subjects; behold, I also bring you matters of exceeding joy and of a most glorious triumph. For after this storm has blown over, there shall immediately follow bright and festive days <note>original: "gawdy dayes"</note> that are most greatly to be desired. 

For what can be more joyful to a most chaste spouse—who has been thrust out of doors by the whore of Rome (who yet boasts of herself as if she were Christ’s true wife) and has been for so many ages harassed with all manner of injuries and insults by her—than to see this shameless prostitute finally have her nose slit <note>A historical physical punishment for adultery intended to brand the offender with shame</note>, be stripped of her garments and head-dresses <note>original: "tires"</note>, besmeared with dirt and rotten eggs, and at last burned up and consumed with fire? Listen diligently, therefore, for a while, and receive from this prophecy not some obscure signs, but most evident proofs <note>original: "arguments"</note> that your husband is about to arise even now to avenge your grief, and that he may deliver this whore into your hands so you may pour out upon her the full rage of your jealousy. 

And so that you may rejoice more fully, receive as well news of the final destruction of the Turks <note>Referring to the Ottoman Empire</note> immediately after the overthrow of Rome. For she [Rome] must first be destroyed as being the only substance and fuel of their barbarous tyranny; their strength <note>original: "sinewes"</note> shall be quite cut to pieces and their power brought to nothing once the Christian world is purged from the wicked abominations of Rome by its final and universal slaughter.

And lest anything should yet be lacking to complete your joy, you may know here that the calling of the Jews to become a Christian nation is joined to this, along with a most happy tranquility from that time until the end of the world. These are indeed matters exceedingly great and wonderful, of which one part was in some way published to the Christian Church long ago, as far as was appropriate for those times, which were so distant...

<summary>The author calls the Reformed Churches to repentance while promising the imminent and violent downfall of the Roman Church, the defeat of the Ottoman Empire, and the eventual conversion of the Jews.</summary>
<keywords>Reformation, Rome, anti-Catholicism, Ottoman Empire, Jewish conversion, eschatology, Thomas Brightman, Apocalypse</keywords>

# To the Holy Reformed Churches of

*...from the outcome of this prophecy. For the Church, as she draws nearer to these events, a more full knowledge is reserved. The other part is so strange and unexpected that I could never find even a probable suspicion of it gathered from this Revelation by any man. All these effects—which this new century <note>original: "hundred of the ages"</note> we have entered into shall bring to us—our interpretation makes plain, if I am not mistaken. For now the last act of a very long and mournful tragedy has begun, which shall completely overflow with scourges, slaughters, and destructions. But after this theater is once removed, there shall come in its place a most delightful spectacle of perpetual peace, joined with an abundance of all good things.*

*And thus you have (most dear Spouse of Christ <note>A traditional metaphor for the Christian Church</note>) the whole remainder of the race of your warfare. Stand now upon the deck <note>original: "hatches"</note> and, after being long tossed up and down, finally behold the land. Until now, the cloud beheld from afar has deceived you, but now see the shore and take notice of the mouth of the harbor. Whether I am worthy or not to have the reward of a bringer of good news, I leave to the judgment of your own eyes. For I am so far from thinking I should submit to the judgment and arbitration <note>original: "umpirage"</note> of Rome alone, that I hope I shall demonstrate by necessary arguments that she is quite blind <note>original: "destitute of eyes"</note> by God’s just judgment, so that she might unexpectedly fall into everlasting destruction.*

*Let her, therefore, think and judge what she pleases; she shall shortly know what it is to deceive herself and others with her deceptive tricks <note>original: "iuglinge conueyances"</note>. You, in the meantime (O true and right-hearted Spouse), think upon this storm hanging over your head and prepare yourself before it comes. Lower your sails so that the wind may have less force over them; labor hard at the rudder <note>original: "sterne"</note> and the ship's pump, lest you are shipwrecked at the very entrance into the harbor—which God forbid.*

*And now see how exceedingly welcome this Book of Revelation ought to be to you, not only because of these events of great importance which are to come, but also in respect to the history of things past; for if you will cast your eyes upon it, you shall see the perpetual...*

<summary>The author frames the Book of Revelation as a navigational guide for the Reformed Church, predicting a final period of "tragedy" and conflict before a lasting era of peace and the destruction of the Roman Church.</summary>
<keywords>Reformed Churches, Spouse of Christ, Rome, Book of Revelation, prophecy, maritime metaphor, apocalypse, church history</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the author's preface to the Reformed Churches of Europe, specifically addressing those in Britain, Germany, and France. He is explaining his motivations for writing this commentary on the Book of Revelation.</meta>

# Britain, Germany, and France.

*...track in which you have set your footsteps even from the Apostles' times, so vividly described that you could require no clearer or more notable history; and at the same time, you may enjoy a most pleasant memory of those dangers you have escaped, which will provide you with so many clear arguments of God's incomprehensible providence, wisdom, love, and truth, keeping you safe in the most extreme hardships <note>original: "streights"</note> and dangers. Surely this addition [the Book of Revelation], along with the rest of the Apostolic writings being joined to the Old Testament, sufficiently provides you with the histories of the world from its first beginning to its final end. In this regard, this invaluable treasure ought to be most dear to everyone. And these were the reasons on your behalf (O Christian Churches) why I have published this work. There are also some reasons on the part of the Roman Catholic Church <note>original: "Popish Church"</note> which moved me to do this: namely, pity and indignation <note>original: "repine"</note>. Pity, because I saw that many people—being unrefined and ignorant of the sacred truth—still worshiped the Antichrist [the Pope] as a God. These people needed to be rescued from the jaws of hell, if it seemed good to God. For this purpose, we carry such a clear torchlight of truth before them that they must see (if they will only open their eyes) that the Pope of Rome is that "man of sin," unto whom if they continue to cling in this way, they cannot be saved. But my anger and indignation <note>original: "repine"</note> burst out against the Jesuits. For I happened by chance to come across Francisco Ribera <note>Francisco Ribera (1537–1591) was a Jesuit theologian who wrote a commentary on Revelation to prove that the Antichrist was a future individual, not the Pope.</note>, who had written a commentary upon this same Holy Revelation. "Is it really so?" I said. "Do the Catholics <note>original: "Papists"</note> take heart again, so that they now dare to handle and fully discuss that Book which for a long time they would hardly allow anyone to touch? What? Was it only a hollow image or a bogeyman <note>original: "Bugge"</note> that they used to tremble at a few years ago, even in the dim light? Do they now dare to be so bold as to look intently <note>original: "wishly"</note> into this mirror <note>original: "glasse"</note> in the clear sunshine, and dare to proclaim to the world that anything else is pointed at in it rather than their Pope of Rome?" O, what sluggish and lazy creatures we are if we allow that! I thought it appropriate, therefore, that the croaking of these fellows should be...*

<summary>The author explains that the Book of Revelation completes the history of the world and was published to help lead people away from the "Antichrist" (the Pope). He expresses particular outrage that Jesuit scholars like Francisco Ribera are now writing their own interpretations of Revelation to deflect these accusations.</summary>
<keywords>Reformed Churches, Church History, Providence, Antichrist, Pope of Rome, Jesuits, Francisco Ribera, Book of Revelation, Counter-Reformation</keywords>

--- Page 19 ---
<meta>This page concludes Thomas Brightman’s dedication to the Reformed Churches of Europe. He has been discussing his reasons for writing this commentary on Revelation, specifically as a response to Jesuit theologians like Francisco Ribera.</meta>

## To the holy Reformed churches of Britain, Germany, etc.

*...somewhat repressed, thinking it worth my labor to make the Jesuits see how wickedly they rage, how foolishly they trifle, how they understand nothing of these mysteries, and how it cannot be possible that they should have any wit or insight <note>original: "reach"</note> at all in this matter. This way, if they truly desire the truth, as they hypocritically <note>original: "dissemblingly"</note> pretend, they might accept me as a helper at least in searching it out. But if they shall still stubbornly despise it when it is offered to them, I will be a helper in advancing their condemnation with my support <note>original: "suffrage"</note>. and regardless of the fact that they will not remain silent—for I know they will continue to fill heaven and earth for a while longer with their boastful <note>original: "ruffling"</note> and rustling noise—yet I hope I have brought such powerful evidence of light and truth here that, being left without even the appearance of an argument, they shall henceforth do nothing but vomit <note>original: "belch"</note> out mere blasphemies against God and men.*

*You (O Holy Mother <note>Brightman is addressing the collective Reformed Church here</note>), for the sake of your kindness and tenderness toward all your own, please pardon my weakness in whatever I have offended. Above all, do not regard or care for the coarseness <note>original: "rudeness"</note> of my speech. The truth alone is what you and I set before ourselves; allow me, in my stammering fashion, to speak with you, my Mother. Here I bring such mandrakes <note>A reference to Genesis 30:14–16; mandrakes were often associated with fertility or love-charms, here representing the "fruits" of his labor</note> as I could find in the field. There are no herbs in my basket for those fussy people who value fine words more than sound substance—unless, perhaps, their heads ache from the smell of so many elegant phrases and they might choose to take from here the scent of brimstone and goat's-beard <note>A plant (*Tragopogon*), used here metaphorically for something sharp or pungent to contrast with "dainty" perfumes</note>. With these, like the Sabeans <note>The Sabeans were an ancient people of South Arabia, often associated in classical literature with perfumes and luxury, but sometimes also with spiritual lethargy</note>, they may be roused from their deadly sleep and awaken their dull senses. I pray to Jesus Christ that you (O Christian Churches) may grow in godliness through understanding, and that through true and earnest repentance, you may either completely turn away the evil hanging over you, or at length be so defended by His power that you may stand invincible in all storms and troubles whatsoever.*

-> Your most unworthy Countryman <-
-> and Foster-child, <-

-> **Thomas Brightman.** <-

<summary>In this concluding dedication, Thomas Brightman expresses his hope that his work will expose the errors of the Jesuits and strengthen the Reformed Churches through truth and repentance.</summary>
<keywords>Thomas Brightman, Jesuits, Reformed Churches, polemic, Mandrakes, Sabeans, repentance, ecclesiastical mother</keywords>

# GENERAL
## VIEW
->Of the whole<-
# REVELATION.

Chapter 1. 1. *The Preface declares the theme <note>original: "Argument"</note> of the Book. 4. An Epistle given in common to the seven Churches, after the title <note>original: "Inscription"</note>, declares who gave the Prophecy, who received it, and the things heard and seen, by which he confirms his authority.*

<margin>A specific <note>original: "particuler"</note> Prophecy</margin>
Chapter 2. *The Epistles are given individually <note>original: "severally"</note>. 1. The spiritual decline <note>original: "decaying"</note> of the Ephesians is described. 8. The Smyrnaeans are strengthened against the assault of their enemies. 12. Those of Pergamus are reproved for permitting Balaam and the Nicolaitans. 18. Those of Thyatira are criticized <note>original: "found fault with"</note> for tolerating Jezebel.*

Chapter 3. 1. *The hypocrisy of the Sardians is briefly and sharply condemned <note>original: "taxed"</note>. 7. The piety of the Philadelphians is commended. 14. The lukewarmness and boasting of the Laodiceans is vehemently rebuked.*

<margin>A common Prophecy</margin>
Chapter 4. *The common Prophecy sets down a general symbolic representation <note>original: "Type"</note> of the holy Church, which is distinguished <note>original: "remarkable"</note> by its Center: God (verses 2–3); its Circumference: the faithful (verse 4); God's protection (verse 5); gifts, doctrine, and rites (verses 5–6); Ministers (verses 6, 7, 8); and finally, by the purity of God's public worship (verses 9, 10, 11).*

*Chapter 5. A Prophecy of things specifically declared, where first its dignity is shown: 1. By the weakness of the creature. 6. By the worthiness of the Lamb. 8. By his exaltation <note>original: "extollinge"</note> by them all.*

<margin>The seals from John to Constantine.</margin>
*Chapter 6. The first specific events are the seals. 1. The truth is first of all opened and overcomes under Trajan, Hadrian, and Antoninus Pius. At the voice of the first beast, Quadratus, Aristides, and Justin Martyr <note>Early Christian apologists who wrote defenses of the faith to Roman Emperors</note> speak. 3. At the voice of the second beast (namely <note>original: "viz," short for the Latin "videlicet"</note> the same Justin, Melito of Sardis, and Apollinaris), the red horse comes forth under Marcus Aurelius <note>original: "Marcus Antonius verus"</note>, throwing everything into confusion with wars. 5. The third seal being opened, the third beast, Tertullian, cries out under Severus the Emperor, when the black horse scourges the world with famine and barrenness. 7. The fourth seal is opened and then speaks the fourth beast, Cyprian, while Decius was Emperor, when the pale horse wasted everything with war, famine, pestilence, and wild beasts. 9. The fifth is opened, and some intermission from public persecution is given under Claudius, Quintillus, Aurelian, and the rest until the 19th year of Diocletian. 12. The sixth is opened, when Diocletian and Maximian Herculius rage until at length they were cast out of their Empire by the power of the Lamb, for fear of whom those tyrants fled and hid themselves.*

*Chapter 7. The seventh seal offers, first, a general representation <note>original: "Type"</note> of all the ages following. 1. When wicked men were ready to trouble all the world with contention, ambition, heresy, and war, they are restrained by Constantine the Great, until he had sealed the elect by providing for the faithful (who were few and living in obscurity) during that great calamity of the Church which immediately followed. 9. This sorrowful <note>original: "ruful"</note> time being at last over, the prosperity and happiness of the faithful grew great.*

*Chapter 8. Secondly, to this seventh seal belongs the silence that was in Heaven, that is, the peace procured by Constantine. 2. The*

<margin>The Trumpets from Constantine to the year 1558.</margin>
The Trumpets are prepared, and Constantine calls the **Council of Nicaea** to put an end to troubles, which are nonetheless increased by it. 6. The Angels sound the Trumpets. At the sound of the first, the contention of the **Arians** <note>Arianism: a theological belief that Jesus was a created being, not co-equal with God the Father</note> about the word *Coessential* <note>original: "Coessentiall"; the term "homoousios" used to describe Jesus being of the same substance as God the Father</note> arose. 8. At the second, the burning mountain of Ambition is cast into the Sea by the decree concerning the primacy and dignity of **Bishops**. 10. At the third, the star falls from heaven, as the **Arian** heresy is defended by **Constantius** and **Valens** <note>Roman Emperors who supported Arianism</note>. 12. At the fourth, the third part of the sun (the **Church of Africa**) is struck by the **Vandals** <note>A Germanic tribe that established a kingdom in North Africa and persecuted orthodox Christians</note>. 13. The world is warned by **Gregory the Great** <note>Pope Gregory I (c. 540–604), whom the author sees as a herald of coming woes</note> concerning more grievous Trumpets to follow.

**Chapter 9.** 1. At the fifth sounding, the bottomless Pit is opened and swarms of locusts crawl out; that is, of **Religious persons** <note>In this context, Catholic monks, friars, and clergy</note> in the West, and of **Saracens** <note>Arab Muslims</note> in the East. 13. At the sixth, the **Turks** invade the world, which is punished for **Roman Catholic Idolatry**.

**Chapter 10.** 1. At the same time that the **Turks** rise up, the study of the truth is kindled in many in the **Western regions**. Through their efforts, the interpretation of **Scripture** is restored again to the earth.

**Chapter 11.** 1. Once prophecy was restored, there was a fuller knowledge of the ages past—namely, that the **Church** from the time of **Constantine**, for 1,260 years, was hidden in the secret part of the **Temple**. Meanwhile, the **Romans** boasted of the **Holy City** and the **outer court** <note>The author distinguishes between the true, "hidden" Church and the visible, institutional Roman Church</note>. 7. And at the end of those years, the **Bishop of Rome** <note>The Pope</note> would wage war against the **Church** and would "cut the throat" of the **Scriptures** with his **Council of Trent** <note>The Roman Catholic council (1545–1563) held to counter the Reformation</note>; indeed, he would make mere carcasses of them and triumph over them for three and a half years. He would also, by the help of force and arms from **Charles V** <note>The Holy Roman Emperor who fought against the Protestant princes</note>, tread upon the **Saints in Germany**. Yet after three and a half years, these Saints lived again in the men of **Magdeburg** and **Maurice** <note>Maurice, Elector of Saxony (original: "Mauritius"), who led a successful revolt against Charles V in 1552</note>, and struck the

enemies <note>catchword for the next page</note>

<meta>This page continues the "General View of the Whole Revelation," concluding the summary of the seventh trumpet's effects in the 16th century (Protestant Reformation) before pivoting to a detailed historical recap in Chapters 12 and 13. A VIEW of the whole

...enemies with a great fear, and overthrew the tenth part of the *Empire of Rome*. 15. *The seventh Angel sounds, and around the year 1558, Christ gains for himself new Kingdoms—England, Ireland, and Scotland—which embrace the Gospel.*

<margin>The first part of the seventh Trumpet concerning things past.</margin>
**Chapter 12.** *The first part of the seventh Trumpet gives an even fuller light into the state of the past age, as the **Magdeburg Centuries** <note>original: "Century-Writers of Magdeburgh"; a massive 16th-century Protestant history of the Church organized by centuries, which the author believes was divinely inspired to reveal historical truth</note> were raised up by God. The whole matter is repeated from the beginning, and we are taught: 1. That the first Church of the Apostles was most pure, yet most of all afflicted by the Dragon—that is, the pagan Roman Emperors. They endeavored with all their might to ensure that no path was given to any Christian to reach the supreme power of the Empire. 5. At length, **Constantine the Great** was born as the "male child" of the Church. At his birth, although the Church's original purity fled into the wilderness <note>A reference to the Church losing its spiritual simplicity as it gained worldly power</note> away from the eyes of men, Constantine threw down the Dragon from heaven. The pagan Emperors were driven out and prevented from ever reigning again in or against the Church. 13. Once all hostile power was taken from the Dragon, he persecuted the Church under the cover of the Christian name through **Constantius** and **Valens** <note>Roman Emperors who supported the Arian heresy, which the author sees as a form of persecution</note>. 15. And he sought to overwhelm the Church as she fled from him with a flood of **Barbarians** <note>The Germanic tribes whose migrations and invasions destabilized the Western Roman Empire</note> rushing into the West. 17. When that flood was dried up, he stirred up the war of the **Saracens** <note>Early Islamic conquests</note>.*

# A PRAYER.

> Since I am about to take in hand a matter that is beyond the power of man <note>original: "mā"</note>, I beseech you (O Father of lights <note>A biblical title for God from James 1:17</note>, together with your Son, the chief Prophet, and the Holy Spirit, the guide of truth) to make plain and manifest before my face the way which, to this day, was never sufficiently known by mortal men. Our mind is half blind in things that are even before our feet; how little—or rather, nothing at all—does it understand of high and hidden mysteries? Because of this, how great a danger is there, either to thrust ourselves rashly into your secrets, or else to pass by things that are true and add from our own imagination <note>original: "own head"</note> things that are absurd and contrary to the truth? Nevertheless, you who have given your word as a lamp <note>original: "lanterne"</note> for our feet, you who call the most simple to search your hidden mysteries and commonly choose fishermen before the wise of this world, please <note>original: "vouchsafe"</note> assist me in my poverty and weakness. Grant me a successful <note>original: "happie"</note> passage through these difficult, rocky matters; keep me from running at any time upon the steep rocks of pride, nor let me get stuck in the shallow fords of blind ignorance. Instead, let me, by your guidance, go straight forward until I reach the truth. Then, after I have found it, let me so holily and religiously love, honor, and keep it, that I may neither conceal it through dishonest fear, nor corrupt or distort <note>original: "sophisticate"</note> it for the sake of hatred or the favor of any man; but let me purely and sincerely bring it forth into the light for the glory of your most great name, and for the comfort <note>original: "consolation"</note> of your Church, which to this day mourns grievously, through Jesus Christ our Lord, Amen.

<meta>This page begins the formal analysis of the Book of Revelation, transitioning from the introductory prayer into a structured breakdown (or "logical resolving") of the first chapter's contents.</meta>

<image-desc>A rectangular ornamental headpiece featuring intricate symmetrical scrollwork and floral motifs.</image-desc>

# THE FIRST CHAPTER.

## *The logical analysis <note>original: "resolvinge"</note> of the chapter into its parts.*

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap initial 'T' featuring floral and scrollwork ornamentation.</image-desc>

The Book of Revelation, after the Preface, is entirely contained within an Epistle <note>An "Epistle" is a formal letter. The author argues that the entire book is framed as a letter sent by John.</note>. The preface is found in the first three verses and declares the Argument <note>The "Argument" refers to the main theme or subject matter of the text.</note>, the authors (both principal and ministerial <note>God is the "principal" author, while John is the "ministerial" or servant author</note>), and the fruit <note>The spiritual benefit or outcome</note> of the book. The Epistle is divided into an inscription, a prophetic narration, and a conclusion. 

The inscription is notable for the person of the writer and those to whom it is written, but especially for Him from whom health <note>In this context, "health" refers to spiritual well-being or salvation</note> is requested. In this section, the eternal truth of God the Father and the manifold grace of the Holy Spirit are described (verse 4). The Son’s threefold office (verse 5) is also described, along with the exceedingly great benefits overflowing <note>original: "redoundinge"</note> to the elect, both in the present (verse 6) and in what is to be expected at His glorious coming. This coming of Christ is described and greatly extolled; the tribes of the earth shall receive <note>original: "intertayne"</note> Him with exceedingly great lamentation, while the saints vehemently wish for it, as is expressed in those words, "*Even so, Amen*" (verse 7). 

The prophetic narration concerns either particular churches or the whole Church, addressing them either collectively in the rest of this chapter, or else individually in the next two. The matters which are declared together serve this end: that the seven churches might know that John did not undertake to write this book of his own accord <note>original: "upon his owne head & pleasure"</note>, but was called and commanded to do so by God. To establish full credibility, the text identifies the Person calling him—who can be none other than God (verse 8)—as well as the person called (verses 9–10). Lastly, it describes the manner of his calling: through hearing (verse 11) and through seeing (verse 12). A vision is set before us (verses 12–16), and a certain consequence of it is declared: astonishment on John’s part and consolation on Christ’s part (verses 17–18). This is followed by a commandment to write (verse 19) and an interpretation of the vision (verse 20).

<meta>This page begins the line-by-line commentary (the "Exposition") of the first chapter, focusing specifically on the first few words of verse 1: "A Revelation of Jesus Christ."</meta>

# A REVELATION: The Exposition.

*Verse 1. A Revelation.* The Argument <note>The "Argument" refers to the main theme or subject matter of the text.</note> of the book, signifying a revelation made by God from which all the veils of obscurity are taken away, which previously kept it from the sight of mortal men. This kind of matter was accustomed to be called of old *visions and prophecies*, but in the writings of the Apostles, the word *Revelation* is more frequently used. *I will come (says Paul) to visions and revelations of the Lord,* 2 Corinthians 12:1. And again, *lest I should be exalted above measure by the excellence of revelations,* verse 7. *So every one of you has a psalm, has a doctrine, has a tongue, has a revelation,* 1 Corinthians 14:26. 

Besides this, the knowledge of the Gospel is attributed to a revelation; for we have no more power to understand it until it is opened to us than we have to understand things yet to come. *I give you thanks, O Father, that you have hidden these things from the wise and have revealed them to babes, says Christ,* Matthew 11:25. Now then, is this the meaning of this word—that no new thing is introduced in the preaching of the Gospel, but rather that the Gospel is an unsealed and disclosed law? That when the veils are removed, it only points out clearly what previously lay hidden under the old coverings? Indeed, it might seem so, unless this word were also used in and belonging to the Old Testament. *The saying (says Balaam) of him who hears the words of God, who sees the vision of the Almighty, falling into a trance, yet whose eyes were opened <note>original: "revealed"</note>,* Numbers 24:4. So the man of God says to Eli in the name of the Lord: *I have revealed myself to the house of your father,* 1 Samuel 2:27. 

Therefore, no single argument can be drawn from this word alone to settle the matter. This much may be certain: this manner of speaking, used here and there, shows that it was not at the beginning, nor is it yet, within the power of mortal wit <note>In this context, "wit" refers to human intellect or reason.</note> to attain to such mysteries as these by searching alone. And yet, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, all things are made easy to be passed through, so far as may be beneficial for His Church. You therefore, most excellent Morning Star <note>original: "day-starre"</note> and Light-bringer, open our eyes that we may behold your marvelous things.

*Of Jesus Christ:* Who is one of the principal authors of the Revelation, and the Mediator between God and men. From this same Christ have always proceeded all the old prophecies, but in these last days, God has spoken to us in His Son after a certain singular and peculiar man-

# OF THE APOCALYPSE.

...manner, Hebrews 1:1. From this, there is a difference between the ancient titles of the prophecies and the title of this one. In those cases, we have *the vision of Isaiah*, *the vision of Obadiah*, *the Book of the vision of Nahum*, or *the prophecy which Habakkuk saw*; but never until now have we had *the vision, or Revelation of Jesus Christ*. It must necessarily be a prophecy full of majesty, as it is so distinguished by its title above all others. Nor should it be doubted that, according to the nature of the light of the Gospel, all things are delivered here more clearly and precisely than ever before.

**Which God gave him;** namely the Father, the author and fountainhead <note>original: "head-springe"</note> of all things. Now, he gave these things to Jesus Christ in his role as Mediator, not as his co-essential Son <note>In traditional theology, as the "co-essential Son" (fully God), Jesus is all-knowing. However, as the "Mediator" (the bridge between God and humanity), he receives knowledge from the Father to pass it on to the Church.</note>. For these things teach the order in which God shares knowledge with his Church, rather than the beginning of knowledge for his Son, as Theodore Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605) was a prominent French Protestant theologian and successor to John Calvin.</note> most learnedly explains. He is the pipe through which whatever is for our benefit <note>original: "behoufe"</note> is channeled to us from that endless depth of goodness. Although the word "to give" followed by an infinitive verb often signifies "to permit," as in:

> You shall not **give** your Holy One to see corruption, that is, you shall not **suffer** him. <note>Psalm 16:10</note>

And:

> Edom refused to **give** passage by him, that is, to **permit**. <note>Numbers 21:21</note>

In this same way Demosthenes <note>A famous ancient Greek orator.</note> speaks, joining the word for "permitting" with it:

> **Give and permit** me to discourse of these things before you. <note>original: "δὸς καὶ ἐπίτρεψόν μοι"</note>

But it all amounts to the same thing, whether we judge it to signify the beginning of knowledge or the beginning of power. Therefore, I think it is best to rely on the first answer.

**To declare it unto his servants.** The understanding of these things, therefore, is specifically reserved for these men. Stay far enough away, you profane-minded men! What right do you have (O Jesuits) to even touch this book? These are mysteries sealed and closed off from you, no matter how much diligence you show in trying to interpret them. There is nothing to do here for the sworn subjects <note>original: "vassalle"</note> of Antichrist. Stop troubling yourselves and deceiving others. If you truly desire to understand these things, renounce that Lord you serve, so that the one whose name you now misuse may share these secrets with you—returning again into his family after you have been strangers from it for so long, like a company of dead men.

**Which must shortly come to passe.** This is a declaration of what things the Revelation consists of: not of things that have happened in the past, but which are to be done from now on. Now, he says the time is at hand because the matters were to begin immediately and would flow from then on in a perpetual course without interruption, although the final con-

# A REVELATION,

...fully the way to escape them.

<margin>+</margin> *John to the seven Churches.* Thus far the Preface. The Epistle follows, whose writer's identity is sufficiently known by the things already spoken. The persons to whom it is written are the seven Churches in Asia; namely, all Churches in general that are in all places whatsoever, as Aretas and Bede <note>Aretas of Caesarea (c. 860–935) and the Venerable Bede (c. 672–735) were influential early and medieval commentators on the Book of Revelation.</note>, and all interpreters, I suppose, do with one consent determine—and rightly so. For the matters recounted here do not allow us to focus only on these seven. We shall hear in the individual Epistles frequent admonitions that everyone should listen to such things as are written to the Churches. 

Besides, it belongs to these seven to take notice of things to come as well as things present, both of which things (as he declares below in verse 19) he had a commandment to write and to send to them. And the last clause of the whole Book, which wishes the grace of Christ to them all, shows that this whole Prophecy was sent in the form of an Epistle to the seven Churches (Chapter 22:21). Now, how would it have concerned or benefited <note>original: "profited"</note> these seven Churches—which would remain in safety for only a short time afterward—to understand matters to come many ages later, which would not belong to them at all? 

Moreover, the number seven is a universal number, by whose revolution all times are framed; all ages are in a similar way whirled around this pole, just as the whole frame of heaven is turned around the seven stars of the Big Dipper <note>original: "Charles-wayne." This is an archaic name for the constellation Ursa Major.</note>. For this reason, this number, being full of mystery, is used throughout the Book afterward in the description of everything. And yet, all Churches are not to be included as if nothing at all were actually sent to those specific Churches that are named below; rather, together with the symbolic meaning of the mystery, the historical truth is to be retained. 

Seeing, therefore, that these seven Churches extend further than their names show, should the condition of all times until the final coming of Christ be considered in them? No, truly, but only that age in which the Church lived among the Gentiles; this shall be made plain from the things that follow. In the meantime, such express mention of the Churches of Asia seems to suggest that the congregations of the Jews are not to be mixed with these. This has led me in my general survey to distinguish the whole Prophecy into that which is specific to the particular Churches, and that which is common to them all.

> *Grace be with you and peace from him who is, etc.* 

Now he comes to the salutation, in which the third person of the inscription is declared. This fountain of grace and peace he makes one true God, three in...

<meta>This page continues the detailed commentary on the opening of the Book of Revelation, specifically focusing on the greeting from "him who is, and who was, and who is to come" (Revelation 1:4), and identifying this description with God the Father.</meta>

# OF THE APOCALYPSE.

These words describe the first of these persons. Aretas <note>Aretas of Caesarea (c. 860–935), an influential Byzantine commentator on the Book of Revelation.</note> thinks that these three times belong specifically to the three persons of the Trinity. He says that the Father is called "he who is" (as in Exodus 3:14), the Son "he who was" (as in John 1:1), and the Holy Spirit "he who comes" (as in John 16:8, 13). 

But the very clear distinction that follows immediately after contradicts this view. That later passage claims this phrasing—this <term>circumlocution</term> <note>a roundabout way of speaking</note> of the name *Ehyeh* <note>original: "Ebei"; the Hebrew name for God, "I AM," from Exodus 3:14.</note>—as belonging to the person of the Father alone. While this description is indeed common to the entire Godhead, it is used here specifically for the Father. 

From this, we are given to understand that this threefold difference in time refers to the unchangeable and constant truth of God in his promises. This phrasing carries the same weight as that concise description of God in Exodus 3:14, which we know was used then to teach Moses that the time had finally arrived to fulfill the ancient promise made to Abraham regarding the deliverance of his offspring <note>original: "seede"</note> out of Egypt. This is also why God was not known to the patriarchs by the name *Jehovah*: because they had not yet reached the fulfillment of the promise. 

Some others argue that this is the name of God’s essence, of which a created mind can perceive no part—as if God would take such names for his own sake alone, and not for ours. If that were the case, the meaning would be: "from God the Father, who is most true and constant in all his dealings." He gives abundant present proof of his truth by finally sending his Son into the world; he never failed in any of the things he promised in ancient times; and lastly, he has given us such hope of fulfilling things yet to come that he is diligent every day to perform them, thus hastening the full perfection of his entire truth. 

This is the power of the words: *Who comes*, or *is in the process of coming*, as if they signify a "present-future" thing, if I may call it that. For that which is "coming" is not yet fully present, yet it is not altogether absent either. It is, therefore, far more significant than if he had said "he who is about to come," as it is commonly translated. This phrase "he who comes" declares that he will no longer postpone his promises, but that he is even now working to fulfill them. This is a significant comfort to those who are ready to grow faint because of the weariness of the delay. 

But some might ask: is truth only attributed to the Father? Indeed, it is common to all three persons of the Trinity; however, since the roles of the Son and the Holy Spirit are exercised in executing divine decrees, it is spoken of as if it were proper to the Father alone. In the order of divine work, the Father is the Author of promises and the Fountain of benefits and mercies. Even the impiety of the pagans <note>original: "Gentiles"</note> imitated this three-part distribution in their oracle from a tripod <note>original: "Trivet"; the three-legged stand used by the priestess of Apollo at Delphi to deliver prophecies.</note>, which they say Apollo used, because of...

<meta>catchword: those</meta>

<summary>This page analyzes the divine title "him who is, and who was, and who is to come," arguing that it refers specifically to God the Father's constancy in fulfilling His promises, similar to the name revealed to Moses in Exodus.</summary>
<keywords>Trinity, Aretas, Exodus 3:14, Jehovah, God the Father, divine promises, Apollo's tripod, biblical commentary</keywords>

...those three periods of time <note>original: "opportunityes of matters"; referring to the past, present, and future.</note>, which he was very skillful in, as one who knew things present, things to be, and those that have been before—as it is described by the commentator on *Aristophanes* in the play *Plutus* <note>original: "Pluto"; referring to the Greek comedy by Aristophanes.</note>.

*And from the seven Spirits.* The second fountain of peace is the Holy Spirit, who most plentifully enriches and furnishes the Church with all kinds of gifts; for this reason, this <term>circumlocution</term> <note>a roundabout way of speaking</note> is used. For he can be no created being <note>original: "creature"</note> who, together with the Father and the Son, is a giver and an author of peace and grace. Regarding this point, see what the learned Iunius <note>Francis Iunius (1545–1602), a prominent Reformed theologian.</note> has written. Nor can this position argue that he is a created being—as the Jesuit <note>Likely referring to Francisco Ribera or other Catholic commentators who argued the "seven spirits" were created angels.</note> would have it—simply because he is said to "stand in the sight of the Throne," in the manner of those who are ministering spirits to God rather than being God himself. For by this logic, the Son would not be God either, since he, being the Lamb, "came and took the book out of the right hand of him who sits upon the Throne," as seen below in Chapter 5:7. And it is even more plain in Daniel 7:13: "And before him" (*namely, the one sitting upon the Throne*) "came the Son of Man." Is the Son, therefore, to be excluded from the <term>Deity</term> <note>the state of being God</note>? 

Therefore, we must understand that throughout this book, mention is made both here and elsewhere of God in general as the highest and chief governor (which is why he is given a Throne), and also of the Son and Holy Spirit as ministering unto him, because all things are made and done through their closely joined help. Therefore, they are said to stand before the Throne as if in readiness, and as though they waited for the command <note>original: "becke and biddinge"</note> of their highest governor. So the Revelation was given to the Son above in verse 1; and therefore the Holy Spirit in this place seems to be identified by the gifts he works in the saints, rather than by his proper name. However, matters that serve only to show the order of their roles are not to be used to abolish their divine natures.

5. *And from Jesus Christ, who is that faithful witness.* The missing relative pronoun is supplied here <note>The author is noting a grammatical adjustment from the original Greek/Hebrew style into English.</note>, which is very common in this book, following the manner of the Hebrews. These words belong to the third fountain of peace, which is Christ. We call him the third according to the place he holds here in the text, not according to the order of his person within the Trinity. He was placed last here because a longer pause was required for his description, and the thanksgiving was meant to begin with him, as it is by his merit alone that we are made partakers of all good things. Now, first, the author mentions Christ's <term>prophetical office</term> <note>Christ's role as the supreme teacher and revealer of God's will.</note>, calling him a "faithful witness"—that is, one who has taught the whole will of God faithfully, truly, and plainly, as far as is necessary for human salvation. For the entire doctrine of the Gospel is usually called...

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Revelation 1:5, focusing on the three titles of Jesus Christ: "the faithful witness," "the firstborn from the dead," and "the prince of the kings of the earth."</meta>

# OF THE APOCALYPSE.

...called a witness, as it is in John 3:11, 5:31-32, 18:37, and 1 Timothy 6:13. Now, can there be any vain or false matter within that testimony which flows from so faithful a witness? Or does it agree with his faithfulness to conceal anything from us, as if it were not to be fetched from any other place but from the closet of the Bishop of Rome’s breast? <note>original: "closset of the Bishop of Romes brest"; a reference to the Catholic doctrine of *in scrinio pectoris*, the claim that the Pope carries all laws and truths within the "shrine of his heart."</note> Especially seeing he has nowhere, not in even one word, suggested any such storehouse from which to fetch it? But these are the delusions <note>original: "dotages"</note> of witnesses as vain and as little to be trusted as this heavenly and most true witness is true.

*The firstborn from the dead:* These words belong to his Priesthood, wherein he overcame death by death and made a full satisfaction for sins. For this is what it means to be the firstborn from the dead: he himself was the first of all to rise again after he had vanquished death. Death would never have let him go if it had had even the slightest right to keep him still. For this reason, the Apostle says that *he rose again for our justification* (Romans 4:25).

Now, he seems to be called *the firstborn from the dead* in a concise manner of speech and by way of distribution, which should more fully be set down like this: *the firstborn of those who rise again from the dead*. In these words, two things are signified: 

First, that he is the Prince and head of those who rise again, as the Apostle explains in Colossians 1:18: *And he is the beginning and the firstborn from the dead, that he might be chief among them all*. Therefore, he is also called *the firstfruits of those who slept* (1 Corinthians 15:20). 

Second, that he shall at last raise up others also from the grave by his own power, even as he himself speaks: *I will raise him up at the last day* (John 6:39-40). 

These two things belong to the elect <note>the "elect" refers to those chosen by God for salvation</note> alone. For he is not the head of the reprobates <note>original: "reprobates"; those rejected by God and destined for damnation</note>, nor will he raise them up at the last day—that is, in glory, as he does the elect. Instead, the force of that curse—*on the day you eat of it you shall certainly die* (Genesis 2:17)—shall restore their bodies to them, in which they shall suffer everlasting torments. Because of this, seeing that this kind of restoring is only for and toward death, the Scriptures hardly even give it the name of a "resurrection." And therefore, the Holy Spirit seems to speak not collectively ("the firstborn of the dead") but distributively ("the firstborn from the dead")—that is, of those who rise from the dead, as was said before, with a clear distinction between the dead who are the elect and the dead who are the reprobate.

*And the Prince over the Kings of the earth:* The Kingly office of Christ...

# A REVELATION,

is now brought down, as one to whom whatever is either in heaven or earth is subjected, according to the passage, *all power is given unto me in heaven and earth, Matthew 28:18.* <note>The original text cites Psalm 28:18, but the quote "All power is given unto me..." is actually from Matthew 28:18.</note> But it was enough for him in this place to mention only his dominion over kings; he is now infinitely greater and higher than any and every one of them, though when he was living on the earth, he seemed to be lower than the lowliest of servants. He can pull them in as he pleases, so that they cannot move themselves except as he allows, even though he once long ago gave himself over to their lawless lust.

*Who loved us:* So much for his office; the present benefit which the saints enjoy is set down and declared in and with a thanksgiving. The lack of a relative pronoun <note>original: "relative"</note> makes the sentence feel incomplete <note>original: "gape"</note> and not fit closely together; if it were complete, it would read: *To him who loved us, etc.* This relative pronoun is expressed in the next verse: *to him be glory, etc.* But seeing that repeating it would be so necessary in such a long string of words, he omitted it in the beginning so that he might not strike the same note twice. Since it must be spoken of eventually, he often conceals it where it would otherwise appear more than once.

# OF THE APOCALYPSE.

Will one reject a virgin for a single blemish, and shall a hand be given to another who is ill-favored and misshapen over her entire body? But "our Interpreter," <note>original: "Interpreter"; referring to the traditional translator of the Latin Vulgate, often identified as St. Jerome.</note> he says, has always followed true and corrected copies, as he is always accustomed to do. No doubt he did so in that place also where he translates:

* *And he stood* for *and I stood* (Chapter 12:17).
* *And no man could speak of the song* for *and no man could learn the song* (Chapter 14:3).
* *And the King of Ages* for *the King of Saints* (Chapter 15:3).
* In the same place, *clothed in clean stone* for *in clean or pure linen* (Verse 6). <note>A famous error in the Vulgate where the Greek word for linen, "linon," was likely mistaken for "lithon," meaning stone.</note>
* *Thou that art, and which wast holy* for *thou that art, and which wast, and which shalt be* (Chapter 16:5).
* In the same place, *I heard another saying* for *another out of the Altar* (Verse 7).
* *One hour after the Beast* for *one hour with the Beast* (Chapter 17:12).
* *Vessels of precious stone* for *of costly wood* (Chapter 18:12).

Let these few examples give a taste of many others. Did the Jesuit see these things and yet not blush to affirm that the old Interpreter had always followed corrected copies? But it may be that these are faults of the printer; perhaps some of them are. But what do we have to do with the printers? It is as if the dispute were not about the Greek and Latin copies now in existence, but about the first edition of the Latin translation, which today is nowhere to be found. 

Besides, these faults are ancient, and they are also now confirmed by the authority of the Council of Trent, <note>The Council of Trent (1545–1563) was a major ecumenical council of the Catholic Church that declared the Latin Vulgate the only "authentic" version of the Bible for public use.</note> which has ordained and decreed that among many Latin translations, this very same old and common <note>original: "vulgar"</note> one—which has been allowed in the Church by the long custom of so many ages—should be accounted authentic, and should not be rejected under any pretense whatsoever. It would have been easy to evade the authority of the Council if, by blaming the printers, it had been lawful to depart from the common edition. You see then that you must defend these faults, and that the credit of the old Interpreter is very indiscreetly—not to say impudently—boasted of. Though indeed, it was necessary for you to act in this manner, considering that humble service to which you are bound to Rome.

**And hath made:** That is, *who has also made*, due to the missing relative pronoun <note>original: "relative"</note> as we mentioned just now. All these things aim to teach us that Christ does not keep all those good things (which we heard in the previous words that he possesses) for himself alone, but that he pours them out upon the elect, so that they might be made happy by sharing in them.

# A REVELATION.

***Kings and Priests unto God.*** Some read "kingdom and priests," as does the Vulgate <note>original: "voulgar", referring to the Latin Vulgate Bible</note>. It does not matter much for the sense, yet the conjoining of people among themselves is more likely than the joining of things and people. The elect are kings by participating in the kingdom of Christ, through which we have overcome the law, death, and sin. We also triumph daily over the world by trampling it underfoot through faith. <margin>1 John 5:4–5</margin> Through Him, we are likewise priests; as those who are dead in Him, we find God favorable toward us and have an entrance made and laid open to speak boldly to Him. But he carefully adds that we are made kings and priests *to God*, lest we should think that this honor is given to us either to disturb the civil state or to intermingle Church government with civil government.

***To Him be glory:*** This is all that we can offer for His exceedingly great benefits: to desire that He may be most renowned among all people with His own just praises. <meta>This page continues the commentary on Revelation 1:7, focusing on the identity of "those who pierced him" and the significance of the dual Greek and Hebrew affirmation "Even so, Amen."</meta>

<page-num>14</page-num>
# A REVELATION,

But the tribes consist of those who mourn, and therefore of those who pierced him—namely, the Jews, to whom this wicked deed <note>original: "fact"</note> properly belonged. Therefore, these words of the Apostle carry this sense, as if he should say: behold, he comes with clouds, and all men of every kind shall see him, even those who pierced him, that is, the Jews. Their ancestors lifted up Christ upon the Cross and gored his side with a spear; these men, being dispersed everywhere among all nations, shall at last be converted to the true faith. They shall mourn with an earnest sorrow, both for their forefathers' horrible wickedness and for their own long-standing obstinacy. Even so, Amen. 

And so the sum of all is this: the benefit coming by Christ is celebrated here, partly in the present, in the calling of the Gentiles (for what he spoke before regarding Kings and Priests refers to the seven Churches of Asia, that is, to all nations of the Gentiles that embrace Christ for the present, for which cause he gives him the praise of glory and power); and partly in the future, in the calling of the Jews, which is declared to us here, both in their repentance and in the desire and wish of all the godly.

*Even so, Amen.* The fervent desire of the godly wishing for this coming is expressed in Greek and Hebrew <note>The "Even so" (Nai) is Greek and "Amen" is Hebrew, representing a universal prayer across different languages.</note> because this shall be the wish of all nations. The former particle <note>original: "particle," referring to the word "Even so."</note> belongs properly to one who affirms, signifying the certainty of a matter, though there may still be understood a verb of wishing: "Let it be done," or some other such word. For so at the end of this Book, "Even so, come Lord Jesus"; it is as if he should say, "I beseech you to come as you have promised" (Chapter 22:20). It is likely that both particles are used in the same sense; otherwise, the diversity of both the languages and the meanings would not indicate a joint desire of all people, for which end this double property of speech <note>original: "proprietie of speech"</note> seems to be adopted. *Amen* is a word not only used by one who confirms a matter, but also by one who prays and strives vehemently through prayer for the fulfillment and success of a matter, as in Jeremiah 28:6: "*Amen, the Lord do so*"; the latter words serve as an explanation of the former.

8. *I am Alpha and Omega:* Thus far the inscription of the Epistle; now he begins the narration itself. To give authority to the writing he has undertaken, the threefold property of the person who calls is set down: his very great power of creating, his truth in

--- Page 50 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on Revelation 1:8, explaining the titles of Christ ("Alpha and Omega") and his attributes, then transitions to verse 9 to establish the authority and context of the Apostle John's writing from the island of Patmos.</meta>

<page-num>15</page-num>

## OF THE APOCALYPSE. 15

... his promises and his sovereignty of governing. This power is first expressed metaphorically, then with literal words. For *the beginning and the end* interpret the meaning of **A** and **O** <note>Alpha and Omega</note>, of which the former is the first letter of the Greek Alphabet, and the latter is the last. By a figurative speech, they are applied to any beginning and end. These are words that plainly signify a certain order and relation of Christ to his creatures. For this reason, they cannot properly denote an eternity—which is an absolute matter and not to be measured by the creature in any respect. 

Therefore, this is the meaning: *I am Alpha and Omega*, that is, the efficient cause <term>the primary source or agent that brings something into being</term> of all things, and also the end toward which all things are directed; I have created all things at the beginning, and I have done so for my own glory alone. It is a concise expressing of what the wise man says: *The Lord has made all things for himself, even the wicked man for the day of evil* (Proverbs 16:4). 

The constant truth of God in his promises is declared by the distribution of the threefold time, as we have shown in verse 4. His omnipotence <note>all-encompassing power</note> mentioned at the end of the verse seems to belong to that supreme power of governing all things at his pleasure, wherein his incomprehensible Majesty shines forth no less than it did in the first framing of all things. For this shows that his strength was not quite spent in his first work, but that it continues in its full vigor forever without any impairment. It never grows faint with any weariness, nor is it oppressed by any overwhelming weight of business; rather, beyond all the capacity of a created mind, his strength holds out infinitely more than enough for the management of all matters. Such is he from whom the <gloss>commandment</gloss> to write proceeds, being the most powerful creator, the most faithful promiser, and the highest Governor of all things.

9. **I John:** The person of him who is called also carries great weight for the credibility of this book. I, John the Apostle, brother, and fellow in affliction, being banished to Patmos <note>original: "Pathmus," a small Greek island where John was exiled</note> for the word of God, was inspired by God in spirit on the Lord's day. What would this man relate that was not of the most certain truth?

*And in the suffering of Jesus Christ.* The Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible</note> and Montanus <note>Benito Arias Montano, a 16th-century Spanish orientalist and editor of the Antwerp Polyglot</note> read, *and in the patience of Jesus Christ*. The translator of Aretas <note>Aretas of Caesarea, a 10th-century commentator on Revelation</note> reads, *by Christ Jesus*. The sense is little or nothing changed by this, whether we read it as a grammatical construction (as Theodore Beza <note>A major Protestant reformer and scholar</note> does) or as these other men do using a preposition. All these interpretations point toward the same goal: that the communion of the faithful...

But we must take care that, like the Jesuit <note>The author likely refers to contemporary Catholic commentators like Francisco Ribera who interpreted the text through a Scholastic lens</note>, we do not interpret these words "in Christ Jesus" to mean "for Christ Jesus" or "because of Christ Jesus" merely to express the final cause <term>the ultimate purpose or goal for which something is done</term> of the sufferings. For if we do, the sharing of the Kingdom among the faithful would be thought of as existing outside of Christ—as if they did not all grow together in him, but were joined together among themselves into some outward thing separate from him.

<margin>Patmos</margin> It is an island in the Icarian Sea, about 30 miles in circumference, called *Palmosa* today as the more recent geographers claim. However, in the works of Strabo <note>Strabo (c. 64 BC – AD 24) was a famous Greek geographer and historian</note>, there is nothing notable about it besides the name. He usually provides diligent accounts and descriptions of even the groves where palms grow, if there are any; surely he would have recorded such a great abundance of them as would have made an island famous. Therefore, we may rightly suspect that name, unless perhaps a later age made it more prosperous through such fertility. Münster <note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552), a German cartographer and scholar</note> thinks that Patmos is the *Possidium* mentioned by Ptolemy in his *Geographical Tables*, Book 5, Chapter 2. But *Possidium* there is a promontory of the island of Chios, very near the city of Chios, from which they sail around the island; these locations are situated on its right hand, according to *Strabo in his 14th Book.* Now Patmos, along with the Korassiai islands, lies to the west of Icaria, which are themselves to the west of Samos, according to *Strabo in his 10th Book.* You may observe that John has not expressly mentioned his banishment to this island, but only his being there—as one who would show his modesty in enduring suffering, rather than boasting or exaggerating his calamity in a proud manner.

*For the Word of God:* That is, the word which had already been preached by him, not that he went there to preach it. For John did not go there of his own accord to preach; rather, because he had preached at Ephesus and elsewhere in Asia, he was exiled there by the tyranny of Domitian <note>Roman Emperor, reigned 81–96 AD, known in Christian tradition for persecuting the church</note>, as Irenaeus <note>A 2nd-century bishop and theologian who provided early accounts of the apostles</note> reports, along with others. The island itself seems to be almost a desert and without inhabitants, especially since Icaria, which it borders and which is of much more importance, yielded the use and fruit of its pastures to strangers because of the scarcity of inhabitants, as Strabo declares.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the nature of the Apostle John's exile and the spiritual state required to receive divine revelation, specifically contrasting the influence of the Holy Spirit with that of unclean spirits.</meta>

# OF THE APOCALYPSE.

The old Prophets, being guided by this very same Spirit, spoke no less certainly of things to come than of things either present or past. In the same way, Saint Mark speaks of a different kind of spirit: *And there was in their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit (Mark 1:23). And again, there met him a man out of the graves with an unclean spirit (Mark 5:2).* 

But this works in a completely opposite way—not only regarding the holiness and purity of God’s Spirit, but also because of its sweet and mild movement. In contrast, the tossings and shakes with which the most wicked spirits torment men are violent and horrible. Because of this, those who are possessed and driven by such a spirit are mostly harmed in all or some of their senses. But those whom the Holy Ghost instructs in an extraordinary way are further strengthened in all the powers of the soul. Both kinds of spirits make those they enter obedient, but one does so by bending them most gently, while the other does so by compelling them most cruelly, as examples of both clearly show.

*On the Lord's day.* <note>Revelation 1:10</note> See what Theodore Beza <note>original: "Th. Beza"; Beza (1519–1605) was a major Protestant reformer and successor to John Calvin</note> has to say on this point. It is very likely that there was no holy meeting <note>a church service or assembly of believers</note> on the island on that day; otherwise, John would never have walked up and down alone on the shore and so completely given his mind to receiving heavenly visions, as we see later in chapter 12:18. 

Nor is it recorded here that these visions were received at separate intervals of time, as the other Prophets used to do whenever the occasion arose. Instead, they all seem to have been given to him on the same day, flowing in a continuous order so that there was no interruption once he had been given the permission and power to see them. This is also suggested by the commandment to write to the Churches. For if any time had passed in between, he would have written to the Churches about these matters piece by piece, rather than waiting for the things that were to follow—unless, perhaps, he had been specifically told otherwise, which we do not read was done in this prophecy. Instead, all things are gathered into one Epistle <term>a formal letter</term> and are not divided into several separate letters. 

Now we see here how John’s solitary and helpless condition is exceptionally well-compensated. In his situation, where he perhaps lacked others whom he himself might teach, he gained God Himself as his teacher. Thus, after he had finished these matters, he moves on to describing the manner of his calling, which makes it even more obvious that this office was assigned to him by God.

<meta>This page continues a commentary on the Apostle John’s vision in the Book of Revelation, specifically discussing how divine revelation is a gift of God's mercy rather than a result of human effort, and beginning the analysis of Revelation 1:11.</meta>

## A REVELATION,

...out of the free mercy of God, which calls us when we are secure, passing by, negligent, and not once thinking of any such matter, to receive and perceive most worthy things. In the Prophet Isaiah <note>original: "Esay"</note>, there is mention made—among other proofs of God’s favor—of this as a principal one: *And your ears,* he says, *shall hear a word behind you, saying, "This is the way, walk in it"* (Chapter 30:21). Therefore, John—although wholly attending to divine contemplations—did not anticipate the heavenly grace. Instead, as if he had been one of the common people, he hears a voice behind him, as if it were admonishing him of the common lack of consideration in us all. We are all unfit to comprehend heavenly things until, unexpectedly, we are endowed from above with the power to understand them; this is not obtained by any worthiness of ours, but given to us by God’s mere mercy. Now it was *a great voice, as if it had been of a trumpet*, lest we should think that something muttered with a lower voice might perhaps escape John's hearing or knowledge. Here, nothing could be concealed from him or pass by his ears, which rang through with such a loud, high, and shrill voice; this is a great argument for the certainty of those things that are to be related.

<margin>11.</margin> *Saying, I am Alpha and Omega.* We had these words above in the 8th verse, but there they were the words of John describing the person whose authority he followed in writing this prophecy. Here, they are the words of Christ himself, pronouncing the same things with his own voice. Therefore, John, using this manner of speech above, did not draw it out of the shop of his own brain but learned it from God, from whom nothing that is not most holy can come. Aretas <note>A 10th-century Greek commentator on Revelation</note>, the Vulgate <note>original: "the vulgar"; the standard Latin Bible of the time</note>, and the Complutensian Polyglot <note>original: "Complutensis"; the first printed multilingual edition of the entire Bible, produced in Spain in the early 1500s</note> do not include these words; yet they seem to have been rashly struck out by some man, perhaps because they were repeated after the intervention of so few things. Nevertheless, there ought to have been a distinction made between John and Christ; nor should those words have been thought superfluous, which teach who the original Author was for using them previously.

*Write what you see in a book.* That is, that which you are straight away to see, and likewise also to hear. This express commandment to write, along with naming to whom he should write, shows that this mission <note>original: "Embaſſage"</note> was not voluntary, but deputed and assigned to him from God.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Revelation 1:11, transitioning from Christ’s self-identification as the "Alpha and Omega" to a geographical and historical description of the seven cities in Asia—Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamus, and Thyatira—where the seven churches were located.</meta>

# OF THE APOCALYPSE.
<page-num>19</page-num>
<sig>E 2</sig>

Which are in *Asia*: *Ephesus*, and so forth. Above in the 4th verse, it was mentioned only in general terms as being in *Asia*; but now, seeing these cities are named, we understand that it does not mean the whole continent known by that name (which is often spoken of as a third of the world), but only a small part of it, which is correctly called Asia by the common people. This region, situated almost like an island surrounded by the *Euxine* <note>original: "Euxine," the Black Sea</note>, *Aegean*, and *Pamphylian* seas, is bounded on the north side by *Bithynia*, on the west by the *Hellespont* and the *Aegean Sea*, on the south by *Lycia*, and on the east partly by *Lycia* and partly by *Pamphylia* and *Galatia*. In this part of the world once flourished these seven most renowned cities, which are placed here to represent the entire Church among the Gentiles. 

Regarding *Ephesus*, it is a most noble city lying on the shore of the *Icarian Sea*, not far from a river in *Lydia* called *Cayster*. It is the capital city <note>original: "head-Citie"</note> of *Ionia* and the greatest marketplace <note>original: "martinge place"</note> of all *Asia* within the *Taurus* Mountains, much praised and famous for the Temple of *Diana*. It is most renowned among Christians for *Paul’s* three years of holy labor there (Acts 19:20 and 20:31); for that divine Epistle of his written to those people; for *Timothy*, who was given to them to be their pastor; and for the most blessed spiritual care <note>original: "watering"</note> it received in later years from the Apostle St. *John*. 

*Smyrna* is also a city of *Ionia* by the seaside, located on the north side of *Ephesus* and 320 furlongs distant from it. It was once a subordinate city to the *Ephesians*, with whom they lived together in ancient times. It was once a place of great wealth and power, and it holds jurisdiction over certain nearby cities, just as *Ephesus* does. In Smyrna, the administrative meetings of the cities that are subject to it were held, as *Pliny* writes in *Book 5, Chapter 29*. 

*Pergamus* is a city of *Aeolia* to the north of *Smyrna*. It is very renowned and holds the chief position among the inland <note>original: "Mediterranean," here meaning inland rather than coastal</note> cities. It was formerly the seat of the Kings of the Attalid dynasty <note>original: "Attalia"</note>, which eventually came into the hands of the *Romans*. They were made heirs to it by the will of *Attalus* <note>Attalus III, the last king of Pergamum, who bequeathed his kingdom to Rome in 133 BC</note>, the last of that name and line. The Romans turned the country into a province and named it *Asia* after the continent—doubtless hoping to devour that whole part of the world starting from this small beginning, as if *Attalus* had bequeathed not only *Pergamus* but all of *Asia* to them by his will. From this, if I am not mistaken, came the first distinction of "Lesser Asia" <note>Asia Minor</note>. 

*Thyatira* is the furthest city of the *Mysians*, a colony of the *Macedonians* located to the west of *Pergamus*, to whose jurisdiction it also belongs.
