In ancient times, it was called *Thyatira* by *Seleucus* (the son of *Nicator*), because of the joyful news brought to him of a daughter being born to him. *Lydia* the purple-seller, who is mentioned in Acts 16:14, was a citizen of this city, though she seems to have been a resident of *Philippi* at that time.

*Sardis* is located about six hundred furlongs <note>approximately 75 miles</note> westward from *Pergamus*. It was once the royal court of the *Lydians* and was made prosperous by the rich Mountain *Tmolus* and the gold-bearing river *Pactolus*, which flows through its territories. In later ages, it held great power and dignity, being made the capital city of its jurisdiction, which took its name from the city and was called *Sardiana* (Pliny, Book 5, Chapter 29).

*Philadelphia*, which is mentioned in this place (for there are three cities of this name), belongs to *Lydia*, or rather to that country called *Cecaumena*—which means "burnt up" <note>original: "Cecaumena," from the Greek *kekauménē*</note>—on the borders of *Lydia* and *Mysia*. Even when it flourished most in ancient times, it was a city that had very few citizens because of the dangerous living conditions caused by frequent earthquakes. Most of the people lived in the countryside. Yet, one may rightly marvel at these few, says *Strabo*, who—because of the love they bear for the place—remain indifferent to danger and careless of their own safety; or rather, one might wonder what the builders of the city were thinking when they founded it in such a place.

*Laodicea*, located by the river *Lycus*, was one of the greatest cities of *Phrygia*, which borders *Caria*. It is near the *Colossians*, to whom *Paul* wrote while he was a prisoner in *Rome*, commanding that his letter should be publicly read in the church of *Laodicea*, and that the letters to that church should likewise be read by the *Colossians* (Colossians 4:16). It was once a city of great riches, partly through the generosity of its citizens, who had voluntarily given it a great abundance of wealth, and partly through the sale of wool, which was excellent for both its softness and its raven-black color <note>original: "crowe-like blacknes"</note>; for these reasons, it was in high demand among the neighboring countries.

Such are these seven cities to which this prophecy was specifically given, as summarized here. 12. *Then I turned to see, etc.* "To see" is sometimes taken for "perceiving," by that figure of speech <note>synecdoche</note> where a specific type is put for the general; as in the phrase, *The whole people saw the thunders and lightnings and the sound of the trumpet, etc.* That is, they perceived them. But yet the word remains here in its proper meaning <note>original: "signification"</note>, seeing that he had perceived the matter enough before by hearing, he now turned himself to use the benefit of the other sense, seeing. Therefore, the other word is transferred from its natural meaning, using "voice" to indicate the man whose voice he thought it was. *And when I was turned, I saw seven golden candlesticks.* 

So much for his hearing. The things seen are partly objects and partly persons. The objects are seven golden candlesticks, the interpretation of which we shall learn afterward in verse 20. In the meantime, let us observe that every godly endeavor receives some fruit greater than a man can hope for. John turned himself to behold the man, and behold, over and above that, there were seven candlesticks, which he had not the least suspicion of.

13. *And in the midst of the candlesticks.* The person that he saw was Christ himself, as we understand from verses 17 and 18. He is said to be "like the Son of Man" because he made himself able to be seen, having assumed a new form—not that natural one which he took from the Virgin, and in which he sits full of glory at the right hand of the Father. This may be the reason why the articles <note>the grammatical definite articles, such as "the"</note> are not prefixed here as is the manner in other places, according to the observation of Theodore Beza <note>a major 16th-century French Protestant theologian and scholar</note>. 

This form is taken upon him in agreement with the present condition of the Church. Therefore, a form other than this is taken where another state of the Spouse <note>the Church</note> is described, as in chapter 19, verses 11, 12, etc., just as it is commonly done elsewhere. For Christ is always one and the same unchangeably; nor does he change his figure so often for his own sake, being such a one in whom no "variation or shadow of turning" falls. But seeing that, according to his various administrations, it fares as diversely with him as it does with his Spouse, he takes upon himself a shape agreeing with the circumstances themselves—both to testify to his fellowship and familiarity with her, as also to show that he is not unmindful of her, however times change. He suffers when she suffers, and together with her, he triumphs. What marvel is it then if, in so close a society, he fashions himself like her? To explain these things one by one: The garment reaching down to the feet represents the perfect righteousness of Christ imputed to us, with which the Spouse is covered completely from head to heel, so that no "filthy nakedness" of hers can be seen. This clothing is not necessary for Christ himself, but serves to cover his Spouse; yet Christ wears it on his own body to show how beautiful she should be at these times in this respect. The "righteousness of faith" is often and significantly symbolized by a garment. *Blessed is the man, says the Psalmist, whose sin is covered (Psalm 32:1).* And *the guest who lacks this garment is cast into outer darkness (Matthew 22:12).* And later in this book, *they are pronounced blessed who watch and keep their garments, lest they walk naked and their filthiness be seen (Chapter 16:15).* The same is found elsewhere many times. Now, what can more fitly represent the righteousness of faith—which rejects our own inherent righteousness as a "menstruous cloth" <note>original: "menstruous cloth"; an archaic term from Isaiah 64:6 referring to "filthy rags" or ritual impurity, used here to describe human efforts compared to divine grace</note> and can find rest in nothing else—except only in this clothing of Christ’s righteousness?

Surely the Priest’s girdle was made of needlework, decorated <note>original: "pictured"</note> with red-purple, violet, and silk flowers (Exodus 28:39). Therefore, this girdle is called "golden," not because it is made entirely of gold, but because the High Priest’s girdle was notably distinguished by this...

14. *His head and hairs.* Garments and the girdle are common to all the members, but in the head and the hair there is a certain distribution of parts. The hairs represent the common people, who depend on the holy teachers, drawing nourishment and adornment <note>original: "garnishinge"</note> from them, while also giving them comeliness and defense. 

Both of them are white—that is, flourishing in the seven churches (or rather, in the first of the seven churches) with a singular purity. For we shall see that this order of the members refers in a way to the order of the churches. Although those things which are spoken of here in the last place are given in the Epistles to the first church. This inverting of the order teaches that these properties agree so chiefly to some of them that they may be applied to others as well as occasion serves.

It is like snow because this purity and whiteness is not natural, but is something she receives from another. So much depends on this—seeking for righteousness not in ourselves but in another—that the Holy Spirit is not satisfied with the comparison of a garment alone, but he adds to it this image of snow. He has many other ways to express it in other places, showing how much he desires, and how much it concerns us, that our ears should ring with this doctrine.

*And his eyes as a flame of fire.* Piercing the darkness, as from which no mist can take away sight; these kinds of eyes shone out chiefly in the first of the seven Churches, in which we shall see the truth has glistened so clearly that no fraud of the heretics could obscure it. All their vain shows were consumed like stubble with these fiery eyes, or else like waxen veils, they immediately melted and exposed <note>original: "beray"</note> their hidden deceit.

15. *His feet like unto fine brass.* Why does he pass so quickly from the head and eyes to the feet, especially seeing as his voice, hands, mouth, and face follow later? It is not done carelessly, but the body parts are described in the order that best fits the Churches. Now, therefore, he teaches in a way that corresponds to the first, what the condition of the next churches is, where the faithful are the feet, and those are like fine brass; in another way and manner were the head, hair, and eyes. One body part could not signify the whole state of the Spouse <note>The Church is the "Spouse" of Christ.</note>, which is why more are added, and especially because he who appeared to John was like the Son of Man. 

Regarding "fine brass," <term>Theodore Beza</term> <note>A prominent 16th-century French Protestant theologian.</note> does well to retain the Greek word in his translation. The word <term>Orichalcum</term> <note>original: "Orichalcum" — a Latin term for a gold-colored alloy, likely brass or "mountain copper."</note> among the Latins has an obvious meaning, but it cannot, in my opinion, sufficiently express the singular elegance of this brass dug out of Mount Lebanon; for <term>Aretas</term> <note>A 10th-century bishop and commentator on the Book of Revelation.</note> gives this reason for why it is so called. And we know that the territory of a country fruitful in metals fell to the share of the <term>Tribe of Asher</term>, which had its seat at the bottom of this hill. For so <term>Moses</term>, speaking of that coast where this Tribe had its home, says, "Iron and brass shall be your shoe" (<term>Deuteronomy 33:25</term>). There are some who would rather have the meaning of frankincense take place here, an opinion which <term>Aretas</term> also holds, being doubtful which of the two to choose; although he does not establish these meanings as being drawn from the common usage of the word or taken from any reliable author, but only as if the compounding...

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological debate regarding the description of Christ’s feet in Revelation 1:15, specifically the meaning of the rare word "chalcolibanus."</meta>

<page-num>25</page-num>

-># OF THE APOCALYPSE.<-

The interpretation of the word suggested some such thing. Yet Antonio de Nebrija <note>original: *Anthonius Nebriffenfis*; a Spanish Renaissance scholar</note> brings up something of importance that relates to this, writing (as he is cited by Francisco de Ribera <note>A Jesuit commentator on the Apocalypse</note>) that it is a common title which Orpheus uses in his hymns; *chalcolibanus* for Apollo and to the honor of Latona and other gods—that is, as he interprets it, male frankincense, or a sacrifice of male frankincense. It is as it appears in Virgil’s *Bucolics* <note>Eclogue 8.65: *Verbenasque adole pinguis, et mascula thura*</note>: "Burn for a sacrifice: fat vervain and male frankincense." 

But I think the words that follow argue against this: "burning as it were in a furnace." Similes are usually drawn from things commonly in use among men. Now, we read nowhere of such a lavish pouring out of frankincense—not even when Alexander the Great himself offered sacrifice—that it should be burnt in a furnace or a fireplace, when it is usually only offered upon an altar. The previous meaning of metal, therefore, seems to be the better one, especially seeing that visions are recorded to have been made in this manner in earlier times. In Ezekiel, the feet are "like shining brass" (Chapter 1, verse 7). There is also "glistening brass" in Daniel (Chapter 10, verse 6). 

As for the passage in the poet Orpheus, let scholars consider whether *chalcolibanus* addressed to Apollo might not be an image made of the "brass of Lebanon" to the honor of Apollo—as if he were saying that he would, with this verse, create a statue to Apollo made of the most precious brass. In ancient times, they used to consecrate other things besides frankincense to their gods; according to this custom, Synesius, a Christian poet, calls his hymns "garlands" and "nosegays." *I here make you this garland, picked from these open and wholesome meadows* <note>original Greek: *Σοὶ τόνδε πλέκω τὸν ἀκήρατον στέφανον, ἐξ ἀκηράτου λειμῶνος*</note>. 

Such, therefore, is this fine brass. Now, the feet burning in the furnace show the Spouse <note>The Church</note> to be afflicted in the churches of Smyrna, Pergamum, and Thyatira; yet, they should receive no damage from this affliction, but should continue invincible with a firmness like brass, and should even shine more brightly because of the fire. The Latin Vulgate reads *aurichalcum* <note>mountain copper or brass</note> for *chalcolibanus*. The Jesuit <note>Ribera</note>, as is his habit, tries to cover up the error with some plausible reason; he thinks the old translator first rendered it *chalcolibanus* as it is in the Greek, and that the word was later corrupted by printers or some unrefined people with a slight knowledge of languages. But what is the need for this defense? Why did the old translator not follow the best copies here, as he always does? And were the Greek copies corrupted instead? It is foolish to try to correct something by a standard that is less accurate than the thing itself. But the force of truth makes the man who argues against it speak contraries, like someone who has lost his wits.

# A REVELATION,

*And his voice like the voice of many waters.* This simile is common and indicates a mighty tumult almost everywhere it appears in scripture. In this book, it has a fuller significance; besides declaring the greatness of the noise, it suggests a certain imperceptible quality of things, if I may call it that. It is like the disordered and confused roaring of waters that—beating together with opposing waves and rushing in upon the shore or the rocks—make a mighty noise, yet one cannot distinctly perceive what all that noise means. 

By means of Christ's government, his voice would be like this in those churches where his feet were like burning fine brass. The truth would be an unappetizing thing, lacking any pleasant taste of wisdom to the heathens who lived even in the most pure church of Ephesus; nor would it sound like anything other than harsh and barbarous in their ears. 

Cornelius Tacitus calls the doctrine of the Gospel a "certain pestilent superstition" <note>original: *exitiabilis superstitio*; from Tacitus’s *Annals*, Book 15, Chapter 44</note>. By this impious blasphemy, he declares not so much his own hatred as the common hatred of all the heathens against it. Suetonius tells how the Christians were afflicted and punished, whom he describes as a "kind of men of a strange and harmful superstition" in his *Life of Nero*, Chapter 16. 

Pliny, a very prudent and learned man, sings the same song in a certain letter to Trajan <note>Pliny the Younger, *Epistulae* 10.96</note>. He writes that after he had used torture to inquire into the truth from two young women who were said to be servants to certain Christians, he found "nothing but a wicked and excessive superstition, the contagion of which had overrun not only the cities but the villages and country territories as well." 

How much like a crude crashing of waves, void of any sensible meaning, did the sound of the truth seem to these men? Their ears were filled with a sound of which they understood no meaning. Nevertheless, we shall see in the next chapter how these men, though heathens, belonged to Ephesus <note>The author is likely referring to the historical and geographic context of the Ephesian church addressed in Revelation 2</note>. 

But it was not only this kind of man who regarded the saving truth as a barbarous thing; many so-called Christians in the churches of Smyrna, Pergamum, and those that followed did so as well. Errors and perverse opinions so possessed many of them that they grew deaf to sound doctrine, nor did they perceive any sweetness in it, as will be made clearer in the next chapter.

16. **He had in his right hand seven stars.** The teachers of the truth (for these are the stars, as is taught below in verse 20), though tossed and troubled by many evils, would be so defended by his—

...his powerful right hand, so that they should be made able to prevail against all calamities. Although this is common to all the Churches, it is seen chiefly in those where the "feet burn in the furnace" <note>See Revelation 1:15; a reference to the Church suffering through fiery trials</note> and the truth is either not heard or not understood. There we shall see many put to death, yet in the place of one, many more spring up. The power of this right hand defending them appears not only in this, but also by making them able to escape those snares which the wicked ones laid to trap his ambassadors <note>ministers or messengers of the Gospel</note>.

*And a two-edged sword out of his mouth.* This word is the most powerful word of God, more piercing than any two-edged sword; it searches the reins <note>original: "reines"; a biblical term for the kidneys, then believed to be the seat of emotions and secret thoughts</note> and gives sentence against the ungodly and unbelievers. Not even a single jot or the smallest title of it vanishes away. It wounds and kills, bringing those calamities upon sinners which it denounces against them. Now, it proceeds out of his mouth because in the Church of Pergamum <note>original: "Pergamus"</note>, Christ would demonstrate his most holy severity to the world by avenging their sins: *Unless, he says, they repent, I will fight against them with the sword of my mouth (Chapter 2:16)*, as will be discussed more fully later.

*And his face as the sun that shineth in his strength.* The face or countenance of Christ is his worship ordained by God, in which he is as clearly beheld by his servants as those things which we behold directly in front of us. This is the purpose of those exhortations: *Seek ye my face (Psalm 27:8)* and *Seek ye the Lord and his strength, seek his face evermore (Psalm 105:4)*. It is as if he should say: "Always trust in the Lord and take earnest pains in the study of those things by which he has taught us to worship him." As long as we are engaged in this endeavor, we are present in the sight of the Lord; but as soon as the power to worship him publicly is taken away, we are exiled from his face. Similarly, Cain—cast out from the Church for killing his brother—complains that he is shut out from the face of God (*Genesis 4:14*). Therefore, the whole religion of Christ, pertaining either to doctrine, prayers, sacraments, or discipline, should shine most purely in these Churches. For the natural order requires that his shining face, being mentioned last, should signify that the last of the seven Churches should be famous for the clear beholding of Christ. Among these (as we shall see), Philadelphia is the chief; the rest behold the open face of Christ in such a way that they perceive he is angry with them, rather than enjoying any part of...

of his favorable countenance. The entire vision, therefore, can be summarized this way: the first of the seven churches is notable for Christ’s righteousness, the faith and holiness of its people, and the marvelous quickness of understanding in its teachers, whose fiery eyes drive the mists of error far away. Those churches in the middle burn through great affliction, yet they make a great noise like the waterfall of the Nile <note>original: "Nilus"</note>, even though to most it seemed like a vain crashing of waves. Finally, the last churches have teachers who are competent and safely protected, a truth powerful enough to subdue enemies, and great purity in their whole religion. For now, it will be sufficient to distinguish the churches into three categories <note>original: "rankes"</note> for the sake of clarity; we will follow a more precise classification when we come to discuss them individually.

*17. I fell down as if dead at his feet.* This was the symbolic pattern <term>Type: a person, event, or thing that foreshadows or represents something else, often a biblical prophecy</term>. Among the things that followed, John’s astonishment is the first thing we see, which is the same as what has happened to other holy men in similar situations. Human nature is so weak, and the conscience is so guilty of its own corruption, that it cannot endure even the slightest display of God’s majesty.

*Do not be afraid.* This was a very necessary comfort for John; otherwise, he would not have been in a condition to perceive the things he saw or heard, unless he had first been refreshed and strengthened against fear. This is common in all holy appearances. By contrast, wicked spirits increase fear in people as much as they can, desiring to overwhelm them with terror and despair. The reasons for comfort are drawn from Christ’s universal power over all creatures in this verse, and specifically from his victory and power over death in the text that follows. Those words *first and last* have great power to comfort; for why shouldn't John take heart, seeing that he is told not to fear by the one who made all things at the beginning and can bring all things to nothing again as he pleases? Unless perhaps "first and last" refers to his glory and humility: he is now "first" among all created things—or rather above all things in honor and majesty—though while he lived <note>original: "was conversant"</note> on earth, he seemed to be the most lowly. It is as if he were saying, "Do not be afraid to look upon my glory, which has increased beyond anything you can imagine; it is not for your destruction, but for your salvation." And just as you once knew me to be the most humble of men, so in this infinite glory of mine, I still keep

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Christ’s comforting words to John in Revelation 1:17-18, specifically interpreting the title "the First and the Last" and Christ’s authority over death.</meta>

### OF THE REVELATION <note>original: "APOCALYPSE"</note>

...my former purpose <note>original: "old minde"</note>, nor do I either despise or neglect you who are but dust and earth. These are words full of comfort; but in this sense, the order should be reversed: *I am last and first*, because his humility came before his glory. His humility should not be placed last, as it was swallowed up by the majesty that followed—unless perhaps these words carry this meaning: *I am now the first, who once was last*. Or else, keeping the order of the words: *I who was first, existing in the beginning with God and equal to the Father, at last took the form of a servant and became the last in the estimation of the world.* Both of these meanings support the second interpretation and make it more probable.

18. *And who live.* In a special manner, he remembers his victory over death so that he might steady John’s mind against the greatest fear in life. These words confirm that the person appearing to John was Christ. Nothing is ever spoken in Scripture by any creature speaking in the person of God without some indication of their subordinate role <note>original: "signification of his ministery"</note>, lest men might think the creature to be God and give to a created being what belongs only to God.

*Amen.* What I say is most certain: that I live forever and ever. To confirm this, do not take it as a mere statement, but as a solemn word of sealing: *Amen*. The Vulgate <note>The "Vulgar" refers to the Latin Vulgate, the standard Bible of the Catholic Church at the time.</note> does not include the word *Amen*. Yet it is found in all the Greek books and is repeated later in chapter 3, verse 14. We must listen to those sources rather than the Fathers of the Council of Trent, who decreed that only their Latin edition is authentic.

*And I have the keys of Hell and Death.* There is a transposition <term>Transposition: a reversal or rearrangement of the normal order</term> of the words in the commentaries of Aretas <note>Aretas of Caesarea, an early commentator on Revelation</note>, the Complutensian Polyglot <note>original: "Complutensis"; the first printed polyglot (multilingual) Bible</note>, and the Vulgate, which read: *And I have the keys of death and Hell.* In the pairing of these words, "Hell" is usually placed after "Death," as in *death and Hell followed her* (Chapter 6:8). Likewise, *death and Hell were cast into the lake of fire* (Chapter 20:14). The natural order of things requires this, seeing as Hell is the final sting of death. However, since these keys serve to open as well as to shut (for because he lives after being dead, he has the power to bring others to life from the dead), this "Hell" is not the place of the damned. That place is never opened to fetch anyone out, nor is the "Hell" mentioned later in chapter 20:13-14.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the vision of Christ in Revelation 1, specifically explaining the distinction between death and Hell (Hades) and the meaning of the command to write to the seven churches.</meta>

For how could the Hell of the damned be cast into the lake of fire? <note>This refers to Revelation 20:14: "And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire."</note> Therefore, these two seem to be distinguished in this way: death is the separating and parting of the soul and the body; Hell is that state and condition in which the body exists after this parting.

19. ***Write what you have seen, and which are.*** Here the commandment to write is repeated, but it is more fully explained. In the 11th verse, the command was simply, *write what you see in a book*; now he teaches how far the vision reached—namely, to things both present and to come. For these two joined together explain those words, *which you have seen*. In the various Epistles to which the parts of this vision are applied, we shall find predictions of future things according to their different conditions. Therefore, those words, *which you have seen*, cannot be restricted only to present things. Since the seven Epistles to the seven Churches contain things to come as well as things present, the whole prophecy is not correctly divided into "present things" and "future things" as separate categories. These parts overlap <note>original: "meete together"</note>, as we shall see later in the opening of each point one by one. Let us hold to this, then, which the words openly teach: that this vision, which specifically concerns the seven Churches, is about things both present and to come. Observing this small matter has opened a way for me to understand these particular Epistles, I believe, and I leave this to the judgment of the godly.

20. ***The Mystery of the seven stars:*** Finally, we have the interpretation, which only teaches concerning two things: the stars and the lampstands <note>original: "Candlestickes"</note>. Why does he give no explanation of the other parts? Because these few were enough to reveal his purpose for the whole. The rest are to be applied to the state of the Church in the same manner. The Holy Spirit intended to help our weakness in such a way that he would leave some parts of it to be searched out by our own diligence. Although those parts of the vision that remain unexplained will be easily understood through the Epistles—which teach us, through the condition of the various churches, what meaning the rest have that are now passed over in silence—as shall be shown in their places. Regarding the wording: the word *mystery* is in the accusative case <note>original: "fourth case"</note>, following the word *write*, which is understood to apply to both clauses. It is as if he said, *write the mystery of the seven Stars, and likewise in the following clause, write the seven Lampstands.* It is written shorthand <note>original: "Defectively"</note> for: *write the mystery of the seven golden Lampstands.*

Now he interprets the stars to be angels. ***The seven stars (he says) are the angels of the seven churches.*** That is, they signify the seven angels. I would like those who stubbornly cling to the literal meaning elsewhere to take note of this. These "angels" are not spiritual beings <note>original: "spirituall substances"; referring to supernatural angels</note>, but men who are pastors and bishops, to whom the Scriptures give this name. For example, we read that the *angel of the Lord had ascended up out of Gilgal to Bochim* (Judges 2:1). So also in the Prophet Haggai: *Then spoke Haggai, the angel of the Lord* (Haggai 1:13). And Malachi, speaking of the priests, says: *For he is the angel of the Lord of hosts* (Malachi 2:7). 

How great then is the worth of true pastors? They are both stars fixed in no other <term>firmament</term> <note>The sphere of the heavens; here used metaphorically for Christ’s authority.</note> than Christ’s right hand, and they are also called angels. What does it matter what insulting names the wicked use to mock them, seeing that they hold this position and status with God?

And ***those seven lampstands are the seven churches.*** They are excellently compared to lampstands, as the light of the truth shines in them forever, being lit by Christ the High Priest morning and evening continually. This <term>similitude</term> <note>A comparison or symbolic likeness.</note> is taken from the lampstand of the Tabernacle, which was made of pure gold. It was a single piece of work whose parts were joined firmly together without any separation, consisting of one main shaft <note>original: "shanke"</note> and seven branches. 

The multitude of the branches signifies the multitude of the particular churches, consisting of both Jews and Gentiles. Their common origin from one shaft signifies the very close joining of all particular churches. All of these come forth from that one church of the Jews, as if out of the main stem. This stem was more decorated than the rest of the branches, having a bowl, an almond shape, and a small flower. This was because, as it seems, the church of the Jews is eventually to be more abundantly filled with the gifts of the Holy Spirit than our church of the Gentiles (Exodus 25:31). The lampstands, then, are the churches; their costly material symbolizes their excellent worth. The beauty of every member has been individually represented by Christ himself in that figure in which he was seen by John.

### Of the Church of Ephesus.

We spoke of the city of Ephesus in a few words at the eleventh verse of the first chapter. To that, we must now add the reason for the order in which it appears, the meaning of its name, and its spiritual <term>counterpart</term> <note>original: "Counterpayne"; a duplicate or corresponding part of a document, used here to mean a symbolic parallel.</note>, so that the purpose of the Holy Spirit may be better understood. 

The reason for its placement in the order may be twofold. First, because this city sets before our eyes the Church of the Gentiles more clearly than all the rest. It is most like that Prodigal Son who went away to live a life of sin and wasted his inheritance riotously in a far country (Luke 15:13). We know that Christ offered that parable as a resemblance of the conversion and calling of the Gentiles. For this city—besides the horrible idolatry in which it was, so to speak, a torchbearer to the other cities—was luxurious beyond all measure or hope of recovery. They were so corrupt that they banished one Hermodorus for no other crime than being a trustworthy and honest man. To justify their action, they added this saying: *“Let none of us ever be good for anything; if he is, let him go to another place and find himself other companions.”* 

This was a speech fit for beasts, even in the opinion of the pagans, and worthy to be punished with death, as Cicero notes in his *Tusculan Disputations*, book 5 <note>original: "Tusculan quest: booke 5."</note>. Indeed, that death was specified as hanging; for as Strabo says: *“All the Ephesians, young and old, were worthy to be hanged for saying such a thing.”* 

Yet, behold here this riotous son returning again to his father’s house, and his father running to meet him, falling upon his neck and kissing him. How greatly the grace of God is to be magnified! It has converted us Gentiles—who were once a gulf and dungeon of wickedness (the nature of which we see in this city)—into a most glorious palace of salvation. We were formerly princes and captains of mischief, but now we are made chief leaders of holiness, just as this city was among the seven churches. It came to excel in piety just as much as it was previously famous for detestable acts. Certainly, this is that father in the Gospel who has caused the finest robe to be brought out and has killed his fatted calf for our sake.

The second reason for the order is that this city was the principal one in that entire region for embracing the faith, from which it was then spread to the neighboring places. For when Paul came to Ephesus, he disputed daily in the school of a man named Tyrannus for two years, so that everyone who lived in Asia—both Jews and Greeks—heard the word of the Lord Jesus (Acts 19:9–10). Therefore, the beginning of the cities is rightly counted from there,

...where the beginning of the faith was. Now we are to explain the force of the name. For it will be clear in each of these Churches that the Holy Spirit has deliberately chosen these specific Churches so that by their very names—as if by certain marks written upon their foreheads—they should declare their whole condition. We will pass over that warlike woman, one of the Amazons, from whom they say the city drew its name. That which follows afterward in verse 4—*“That you have abandoned or let go your first love”*—sufficiently teaches what the Spirit respected in this city. Namely, that Ephesus was, as it were, *Aphesus*, from the Greek word *aphesis* <note>original: "Aphesis"; meaning omission, letting go, or remission.</note>, meaning "omission." Because of this, we call it "languishing Ephesus," as its piety grows cold little by little until at length it is quite extinguished. How much is it to be feared that it bears the image of the <term>Gentiles</term> <note>Non-Jewish people or nations; here referring to the pagan world.</note> in this thing also?

As for its counterpart <note>original: "Counterpayne"; a corresponding part or duplicate, used here to mean a symbolic parallel.</note>, since these seven cities contain the universal condition of the Church among the Gentiles (as is evident enough by those things which have been said about the first chapter), we must consider not only the city itself in each case, but we must likewise join it to some fellow-Church which may answer directly to it. But what kind of counterparts shall we call these? Are these seven cities appointed as patterns for all Churches at the same time, or for different times? 

If we say the first—that the Church dispersed in every age throughout the whole world should agree with these seven (one being the Ephesian Church, another the Smyrnean, a third like the Church of Pergamum, and so on)—then the Church would always be uniform. It would carry the same face today as it did in the first times, which is contrary to what the experience of all history teaches. It is necessary, therefore, to make them individually <term>types</term> <note>A "type" is a person, thing, or event that represents or foreshadows something else to come.</note> one by one, and in the order in which they are numbered. Those Churches are the counterparts which, being divided either by different periods of time or by distances of place, agree with each of them in their order. The correspondence of events will show clearly enough how their boundaries are limited. 

According to this rule, we hold that the counterpart <note>original: "Counter copie"</note> of the city of Ephesus is the first Christian Church, which took its beginning from the preaching of the Apostles and endured until the time of Constantine the Great, as the things taught afterward will plainly show. This is the primary Church of all others, just as Ephesus is the first of the seven cities.

<header>A REVELATION,</header>

**“These things says he who holds the seven stars.”** This is a description of the one who sends the letter, which is different in each of the seven letters; yet it is taken from the vision seen above in the previous chapter. The various parts of that vision are applied according to the different conditions of things, which teaches abundantly two things: first, that the entire vision laid out before only foreshadowed the administration of things; and second, that it was, in a sense, specifically suited to these seven churches. The seven stars in his right hand declare the remarkable power of Christ in defending the ministers of this church. He is indeed just as powerful a keeper and as faithful a supporter of all his faithful servants, in whatever part of the world or in whatever age they may be. Yet, in certain times and places, he makes himself more clearly known to the world as the advocate <note>original: "Proctour"; a legal representative or agent.</note> and protector of his church, and a redeemer of their wrongs, more than he commonly does in other cases. This appears both in this city and also in its counterpart <note>original: "Counterpayne"; here referring to the symbolic historical period the Ephesian church represents.</note>.

Regarding the city: how many adversaries did Paul find there, who was the first to plant the faith in that place? *“I will stay,”* he says, *“at Ephesus until Pentecost, for a great and effective door has opened to me, and there are many adversaries”* (1 Corinthians 16:9). And yet we do not read that any calamity happened to him there. In other places, he was beaten, stoned, and left for dead; but here, when Demetrius raised up trouble against him, he who holds the stars in his right hand not only kept Paul free from all harm, but Gaius, Aristarchus, and Alexander as well, quieting the uproar through the prudence of the Town Clerk (Acts 19). The same hand protected Tychicus and Timothy, and the rest of the <term>Angels</term> <note>In the context of Revelation, "Angels" refers to the ministers or leaders of the individual churches.</note> of that church who followed them (Ephesians 6:21, 1 Timothy 1:3). 

And it no less protected the ordinary elders of that church, whom Paul called to Miletus when he was about to give them his final farewell. At last John came there, and he remained there many years, establishing all the surrounding churches. Nor did the tyrant’s rage proceed to the point of putting him to death; instead, having finally returned from exile, he died peacefully in this city. Such great safety did the power of this mighty, star-bearing hand provide for his servants. A similar power shone forth in the preservation of the pastors throughout the entire era of the <term>Primitive Church</term> <note>The early Christian church during the first few centuries.</note>. There was indeed a great number of the faithful killed daily, but it was remarkable that—

...that when men believed the name of "Christian" must necessarily be completely wiped out—especially regarding the pastors of Christ, against whom the tyrants were most violent—even then there was such daily growth that it was commonly and truly said that "the blood of the martyrs was the seed of the church" <note>original: *Sanguis martyrum semen ecclesiae*; a famous observation by the early Christian writer Tertullian (c. 155–220 AD).</note>. Now, Christ walks among the candlesticks <note>In the Book of Revelation, the seven golden candlesticks represent the seven churches.</note> whenever he gives open proof that he is present and diligently caring for all things that lead to the salvation and safety of the faithful. In what city did he provide an experience of more plentiful grace and favor than in *Ephesus*? To this city, he gave teachers such as *Paul*, *Apollos*, *Tychicus*, *Timothy*, and *John* the Apostle, besides many other apostolic men. And where or when, since his ascension into heaven, did Christ more clearly dwell <note>original: "conuerse"; in this context, it means to live among or have close interaction with people.</note> on earth than in those early times, until around the time of *Constantine*? He enriched his church so abundantly with gifts of all kinds; he prodded their dullness, corrected their negligence, and rewarded their virtue, so that he himself seemed to make his rounds about every one of the faithful and to view their labor closely with his own eyes. In the same way, he is always among the candlesticks; he does not sit idly but continually travels about and watches everything that is done, so that he has no need for a vicar <note>original: "vicar"; a substitute or deputy. The author is likely arguing that because Christ is spiritually present, there is no need for a central human authority like the Pope to act as his "Vicar" on earth.</note>. Yet, because this often does not appear the same way to the world through outward evidence, it is described here as if it were a unique privilege granted to one city and time.

<margin>verse 2.</margin>
**I know your works.** Here begins the main account, and first, it begins with praise. It is common in all the letters <note>original: "Epistles"; referring to the seven letters in Revelation chapters 2 and 3.</note> to declare at the start of the account that he knows the works of every "angel" <note>The "angel" of the church is generally understood to be its lead pastor or bishop.</note> and has searched them out thoroughly, as if they were kept by him in his books of remembrance. Therefore, there can be neither a lack of reward for virtue nor a lack of just punishment for wickedness. And as I mentioned just now regarding a vicar, how impiously and presumptuously over-diligent are those who—as if they were absolute lords—claim for themselves power over their fellow servants? This is despite the fact that Christ knows and perceives everything thoroughly, and his presence among the candlesticks is not in vain. The praise of the Ephesian pastor concerns either his office (in this verse) or the strength he had against outward evils.

<header>A REVELATION,</header>

I know **your labor and your long patience.** For since the labor spent in preaching the word is toilsome and full of troubles, it is usually called in the Scriptures *toil* <note>original: *Kopos*, meaning a wearying or toilsome labor</note>, as in: *We beseech you, brethren, to acknowledge those who labor among you, etc. (1 Thessalonians 5:12).* And: *Those who labor in the word and doctrine are worthy of double honor (1 Timothy 5:17).* Now, patience must be joined to the labor of teaching as a necessary companion, which the Holy Spirit declares here by saying, **and your patience.** As Paul also says: *The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all people, able to teach, patient, in humility correcting those who are in opposition (2 Timothy 2:24-25).* 

This Church, then, was notable for its faithfulness and diligence in teaching. Look at the example of Paul, who for **three years together did not cease, day and night, to warn everyone with tears (Acts 20:31).** Consider also those godly Bishops who loved Paul so greatly and dearly, whom he also loved in return with no less affection **(Acts 20:37–38).** Consider also John and the rest; but a matter so clear does not need many words. 

As for the counterpart <note>original: "Counterpayne"; here meaning the historical fulfillment or the matching record of these events.</note> to this, the matter is just as clear. There was never a time when there was more faithful diligence and earnest endeavor in teaching. That monstrous wickedness had not yet been hatched—where someone could be a "Pastor" who did not feed the flock at all, or where someone could sit in the "Doctor’s chair" while remaining silent and lazy, distracted by other business. No man was then a Bishop with the office of teaching who did not teach most diligently. 

Even in Rome, where the mystery of iniquity <note>original: "misterye of iniquity"; a reference to 2 Thessalonians 2:7, which many Protestant commentators interpreted as the hidden rise of the Papacy.</note> was to bud forth more quickly, there was as yet no stopping this duty. The Pastor of the Church, at least every Lord's day, plainly and clearly explained the things that were read from the Books of the Apostles or Prophets; he also warned and encouraged them to imitate those holy and good things they had heard read <note>original: *Justin. Apologie 2*; Justin Martyr (c. 100–165 AD) provided one of the earliest descriptions of Christian worship.</note>. Clement, Origen, Tertullian, and Cyprian <note>Significant early Christian theologians and leaders from the 2nd and 3rd centuries.</note> all testify to the same thing. But the matter is as clear and manifest as it is clear that the opposite is done today.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the church in Ephesus, moving from their labor and patience to their exercise of church discipline against false apostles and sinners.</meta>

<header>OF THE APOCALYPSE.</header>

The clergy itself, if I may call it that, is addressed in the following words: *And you have tested those who say they are Apostles, etc.* <note>Reference to Revelation 2:2: "and you have tested those who say they are apostles and are not, and have found them liars."</note> General discipline did not tolerate in the least those who lived in any detestable way that caused offense to others. According to the nature of their crime, the church reproved them either privately or before many, if private admonition had been of no use. Afterward, it also kept them back from holy things <note>Meaning the sacraments, particularly the Lord's Supper.</note> if they would not listen to those who tried to persuade them toward what was good and right. 

As for Ephesus, it cannot be doubted that this holy course was kept constantly there, seeing as Paul taught there for three years and also commanded Timothy very precisely and diligently regarding everything that belonged to this matter. The observation of this practice was also famous in the primitive Church, as even Pliny the Heathen <note>original: "Pliny the Heathen"; referring to Pliny the Younger, a Roman governor who wrote to Emperor Trajan about the early Christians.</note> witnesses in an Epistle of his to Trajan the Emperor. *The Christians* (he says) *are accustomed to rise early and to magnify Christ as if he were their God; and for the preserving of their religion, they forbid murder, adultery, greed, deceit, and things like these* (Eusebius, in the 3rd book, 34th chapter of his *Ecclesiastical History*, quoting Tertullian). <note>original: "Euseb. in his 3. booke 33. Chap." The author likely refers to Eusebius’s summary of Pliny's letter.</note> 

Without doubt, they did not only forbid these sins in word by teaching, but they also suppressed them by holy discipline. They judged well and wisely that religion could not otherwise be preserved unless vices were cut down with this spiritual sword. Justin Martyr witnesses that *no man was admitted to the Sacrament of the Supper, but he whose life answered to his profession of godliness* (in his 2nd *Apology*). 

But Tertullian writes even more clearly: 
> *In the same place, exhortations, corrections, and divine censures are used; for it is proclaimed with great gravity and earnestness by the Church that if anyone offends, he should be banished from participating with the Church in prayer and in every one of their holy assemblies and meetings, whether public or private. Every one of the elders who are most approved are made the Presidents in these censures, an honor they have obtained not by their money but by their good report.* (Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chapter 39).

Origen, in his 35th treatise on Matthew, says: 
> *In the churches of Christ, such a custom prevailed that those who were caught manifest in foul offenses should be cast out from common prayer, lest a little leaven of those who do not pray out of a pure heart should corrupt the whole lump and the consensus of truth.* 

So, in his 7th Homily upon Joshua, he says: 
> *Christ commands that he who is admonished for the third time, and yet will not repent, should be cut off from the body of the Church by the...*

Leaders of the Church; where he also shows that the priests who spare any one man and so neglect priestly severity actually bring about the destruction of the whole Church. Cyprian's *Epistles* are most clear and notable witnesses of how devoutly and religiously he observed this discipline in his Church. Indeed, they show how intact this discipline remained in Rome at that time, as is clear from the letters of Cyprian to the clergy of Rome and to Cornelius, as well as their replies back to Cyprian. Great indeed was the praise for that era, which joined purity of doctrine with holiness of behavior by the help of this most beneficial discipline.

*And you have tested those who say they are Apostles.* Here is the other part of the discipline directed against churchmen, who were not only rebuked for their moral offenses, but also if they introduced any new thing contrary to the truth. If, after a lawful examination, such things were found to deviate from the "square of the Sanctuary" <note>original: "fquire of the Sanctuary"; a metaphor for the standard of the Holy Scriptures</note>, they suffered punishment answerable to their impiety. And the courage of the Angel <note>Refers to the "Angel of the Church" mentioned in Revelation 2:1, traditionally interpreted as the bishop or presiding pastor.</note> in this point was very great; he would not be frightened from doing his duty by impressive titles, but instead called back to the "holy balance" <note>A metaphor for testing or weighing something against the truth.</note> even those men who bragged and boasted of themselves as if they were Apostles. It is clear that there were men of this kind at Ephesus, based on the charge given to Timothy: *To remain at Ephesus and charge certain men that they should not teach different doctrines, nor pay attention to myths and endless genealogies, which breed questions rather than godly edification (1 Timothy 1:3-4).* And the same Paul warned the bishops of Ephesus, *To look to themselves and to the whole flock; for I know this (he says), that after my departure, vicious wolves will break in upon you, not sparing the flock; and from among yourselves shall arise those who speak perverse things to draw disciples after them (Acts 20:28-30).* 

But the diligence of the pastors stripped away these disguises and masks from the hypocrites, and would not allow the deceitful and poisonous doctrines of these crafty "Apostles" to invade the flock to their destruction. Thus, this Church remained uncorrupted until the coming of John, who governed it for many years. After he was later removed for a time, the church grew somewhat slack and retreated from its ancient diligence, as we shall soon discuss. In the same way, in the primitive Church, there was such a large troop of heretics that the like was scarcely seen in any other time. There arose the Simonians, Menandrians, Ebionites, and Cerinthians,

false Apostles, Gnostics, Sabellians, Samosatenians, Manicheans, etc. Of whom some were thrust through with the dart of truth by the Apostles themselves; Paul gave over Hymeneus and Alexander to Satan; he dealt similarly with Phygellus, Hermogenes, and Philetus, as it seems. And he commanded Titus that he should avoid a heretic after one or two admonitions (Titus 3:10). But after they had gone to be with Christ, there arose many other worthy lights who diligently drove away all the fog of heresy. Among these were Agrippa Castor (as Eusebius reports), Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Cyprian, and others. They all fought stoutly for the truth against these counterfeit Apostles. Therefore, just as both that city and that first age were in great danger because of the impudence of those who made a show of themselves through false titles—as if they had been Apostles—they were also no less fortunate through the faithfulness and diligence <note>original: "painfullnes"</note> of such champions. These leaders would not be deceived by their vain show, but by bringing the matter to the true touchstone, they made the whole Church see plainly that these men—who wanted to be accounted as the highest and most principal masters—were actually most filthy and vile scoundrels <note>original: "Varletts"</note>.

3. **And you have been pressed with a burden, etc.** Hitherto he has spoken of their faithfulness in executing their function; now he speaks of their virtue of patience in overcoming outward evils. These were very many and mighty, coming both against the city and also against the whole Christian world. The skirmishes of Paul against "beasts at Ephesus" are renowned (1 Corinthians 15:32). And what rest from troubles could there be for the Angels <note>In the context of Revelation, "Angels" usually refers to the bishops or presiding pastors of the churches.</note> who followed him, who had to grapple with "grievous wolves" that would not spare the flock (Acts 20:29-30)? It was, therefore, to the praise of this Angel that he endured calamity valiantly. This is declared in a threefold degree: that he bore a burden, that he labored under the burden, and that yet for all that he was not tired out. It is as if he were saying, "Indeed, a great load of calamity lay upon you, under the burden of which you have groaned; yet, nonetheless, you have not lost heart <note>original: "cast away thy hart"</note>, so as to be driven to withdraw your neck from the yoke and betray the truth." It is a manly courage to endure anguish and pains like a man. Many bear the yoke cheerfully when they feel but little trouble; but to go on constantly amidst the stings of grief is the part of a stout mind and of a heavenly fortitude. Such was this Angel; so also was the primitive Church. Nero and Domitian had vehemently afflicted it before John wrote these things.

<insert>Bn A</insert>

And besides Nero and Domitian, it had endured the rage of Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus, Severus, Decius, and Diocletian. There were never such times so full of calamity, when the Emperors sold themselves and became hired slaves to the devil to shed Christian blood, which he thirsts after always unsatiably—just as people suffering from dropsy <term>dropsy: an old medical term for edema, or swelling caused by fluid retention, which was often associated with extreme thirst</term> thirst for drink. Yet notwithstanding, the faithful did not turn back from God, but constantly held out even to the most extreme combat, and at last became conquerors and triumphed over the devil and all their enemies. 

For what else were those many scars and marks of wounds and maiming—with which most of the bishops were notably marked when they gathered at the Council of Nicaea <note>The First Council of Nicaea in 325 AD, where many survivors of the Great Persecution gathered</note> after the storm of tyrannical persecution had blown over—than so many triumphal arches <note>original: "bowes"</note> and other ensigns of the victory which they had won against their enemies? Paul of Neocaesarea was deprived of the use of both his hands, their tendons having been shrunken and cut by the persecutors with burning irons. Others had their right eyes dug out; others had their right hands cut off at the elbow, among whom was Paphnutius of Egypt. In brief, there was to be seen a company of famous and most glorious martyrs gathered together (Theodoret <note>A 5th-century Christian historian</note>, Book 1, Chapter 7). 

That Angel <note>referring to the presiding bishop or leader of the church</note> possessed an invincible courage, which such great miseries could not break, nor even bend in the slightest manner. Now, therefore, if we gather all these things together into one main summary, we shall see a most beautiful portrait of an excellent Church. For look upon the Angel in his labor of teaching, sparing no personal effort, exercising discipline most religiously, and tolerating no one who would offend the Church with his wickedness <note>original: "naughtines"</note>. He either drove far away the leaven of the heretics or else, with all speed, most earnestly labored to remove it entirely. To conclude, above all these things, he undauntedly underwent whatever the wicked enemies could inflict. 

Does anything here need any repair or perfect completion? Truly, nothing—had things only remained in this perfect purity. But godliness languishes little by little unless it is continually fanned and kindled; and oftentimes a certain hollow profession remains where all the force of faith is stone-dead and lies completely extinguished, as we shall presently see happened with this Church. 4. *But I have something against you.* Hitherto has been the praise of this Church; the reprehension is because she had cast off her first love. He suffered some of his flock to perish through ignorance and others to be carried away into destruction through the weakness of their flesh, not setting upon the right and speedy way to recover them. commandment unto Peter: *If you love me, feed my sheep* (John 21:16–17). But in this Church, after some process of time, this heat of love grew cold, or rather vanished away altogether, as is plain by this reproof. Such is the weakness of our minds, always no less ready to rush into the destruction of spiritual life than our bodies are hastening every moment toward our graves. Why then do we take such excessive care for our bodies, and so little, or rather none at all, for our spiritual life? The Ephesians retained their outward profession of faith, and no calamities could take it away from them, as the former verse has shown; yet in the meantime, they grew careless little by little of those things without which true piety cannot stand. 

Now it seems that this abandoning of their love occurred at the time when John was banished to Patmos. Doubtless, as long as he remained at Ephesus, he would not endure for either the doctrine or the discipline to decay; but being at last deprived of such a vigilant watchman, they fell into this hateful slothfulness. We may take as an example of this that Bishop—though not of this city, yet of a place adjoining it—who, having a certain young man committed to his custody by John, suffered him to become a notorious roadside robber through the neglecting of holy discipline. For this cause John, and not unworthily, upbraids him for his dishonesty in being so careless of his charge (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 3, chapter 23). 

But however silent the histories are in revealing to us the decay of Ephesus, it is certain that the Angels <note>The "Angels" refer to the bishops or presiding leaders of the church</note> of Ephesus fell into foul negligence about this time; this is the kind of carelessness which we find prevailing more and more, little by little, in and against the primitive Church. In the first times, while it had the Apostles themselves to rule it and to be eyewitnesses of all things that were done, the diligence of the elders was fervent; they both faithfully preached the word and also earnestly promoted the godliness of their flock by means of discipline. 

But eventually, about 200 years after Christ's birth, they allowed all things to grow worse and worse, with a manifest decline. How did discipline begin to be loosened and corrupted when the martyrs and confessors <note>original: "confessours"—those who suffered for the faith under persecution but were not killed</note> gave leave <note>In the early church, martyrs often granted "libelli pacis" (letters of peace) to those who had lapsed, bypassing the formal penance required by bishops.</note> to those who had fallen <note>original: "those that had fallen"—the 'Lapsi', or Christians who had renounced their faith during Roman persecution to avoid death</note>, not only without consulting those Bishops to whose charge those who fell belonged, but even against their wills? How greatly this unreasonable perversion of the heavenly ordinance grieved the heart of Cyprian <note>St. Cyprian (c. 210–258 AD), Bishop of Carthage, who wrote extensively on church discipline and the treatment of the lapsed.</note>, we may see from his Epistles. For this reason, among many other causes for the persecution that then lay heavily upon the church, which he recounts...

And not many years later, Eusebius, describing the condition of the Church shortly before Diocletian <note>Roman Emperor from 284–305 AD, famous for the "Great Persecution" of Christians.</note> began his persecution, said: "Those who seemed to be our pastors, rejecting the bond of piety, boiled with the heat of mutual contention among themselves. They piled up measureless controversies to quarrel over—threats, envy, mutual grudges, and hatred—aspiring to and pursuing positions of power <note>original: "principalities"</note> as if they were worldly kingdoms with all their might" (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book 8, chapter 1). It must necessarily be that the edge of holy discipline was marvelously blunted, which could do nothing to cut down such harmful weeds. 

But most clearly of all, Ambrose shows this, telling us that this divine ordinance was worn away long before his time. Speaking of elders, he finally brings in these words: "From which both the Synagogue <note>Ambrose refers to the Jewish assembly structure, which the early Christian church adopted as a model for its own eldership.</note> and after that the Church had elders, without whose counsel nothing was done in the Church. I cannot tell by whose negligence this has grown out of fashion, unless perhaps it has been through the slothfulness, or rather the pride of the teachers, while they alone wanted to seem important" (Commentary on 1 Timothy, chapter 5). Ambrose was not far removed from what we call the Primitive Church; yet he speaks as if this saving custom had been abolished some ages before his day. These things clearly teach us how this first love was utterly diminished in its intensity, and at last came to nothing.

5. **Remember, therefore, from where you have fallen.** This explains their sin. The remedy consists of three parts: 1. A due consideration of their fall. 2. Repentance. 3. A renewing of discipline. These things are all required together for an amendment, and in the same order in which they are laid down here. Because we do not fall all at once, but step by step, we almost do not realize how deep a ditch we have been plunged into. But let us once cast our eyes upon that high top of the hill from which we have slipped down, and we shall wonder at the gulf as deep as hell in which we lie tumbling. For this reason, he warns the person to rethink from where he has fallen. Neither is it enough to know that we have fallen, but we must struggle up as soon as we can out of this whirlpool of destruction by repentance. He adds, therefore, "Repent." But many deceive themselves and think they have repented very well, when in truth

He knew that the order he himself instituted would apply as well to provinces as to cities, and that it did not hinder the government of the commonwealth at all, but rather furthered and adorned it above all other things. 

Let us therefore learn from this that the first government of the Church is common to all times and places. It must not be left to the whims <term>original: "arbitrement"; the power to decide or judge according to one's will</term> of men to follow whatever way they please. Instead, whenever we reform a church, we must return to its first beginnings. As our only rule, we must call back whatever strays from it; these principles are not to be twisted or "tuned" to match the crookedness and jarring sounds of the churches that followed.

But what need is there for him to "come," he who walks in the midst of the lampstands? He does not dwell among his servants as an avenger, but as a brother and defender. I am not referring to the name "Church," which I know it kept for many centuries, but I mean that it lost its primitive purity. For as the leaders continued in their negligence—as we have learned from what was said above—Christ took away the first and principal golden lampstand from the sight of men. He did this by removing those most holy ordinances <note>original: "ordināces"</note>, of which the world was most unworthy, by which the primitive Church was founded in the beginning by himself and his Apostles. 

For there was a new fashion of things upon Constantine's <note>Roman Emperor Constantine the Great (r. 306–337 AD)</note> arrival. Indeed, some care and desire for preaching remained among the Bishops, but the doctrine was shamefully defiled in many of its key points <note>original: "heades"</note>. Relics began to be highly valued, the temples were over-sumptuously decorated, and all kinds of superstition began to grow. Furthermore, the pride of the teachers—as *Ambrose* <note>Saint Ambrose, Bishop of Milan (c. 340–397 AD)</note> just taught us—robbed the Church of its necessary help for overseeing and governing the behavior <note>original: "manners"</note> of the people. In its place, church dignities were increased, with everything being diligently sought out that might serve for pomp rather than for the truth.

7. *He that has an ear, etc.* This is the concluding proclamation common to all the Epistles. By this, He teaches that all people, regardless of who they are, ought to apply their minds to listening to these admonitions of the Spirit. These messages do indeed properly belong to the Angels <note>the bishops</note>, but it concerns us all very deeply what kind of men they are. They do not commit offenses or perform their duties for themselves alone; rather, their condition is tied to the great benefit or harm of their entire flock. 

But how do these things, done so long ago, apply to us? The nature of all churches, and of every individual in private, is the same. Therefore, it greatly concerns our own well-being—no matter what age we live in—to take warning for ourselves from the evils they committed. Yet all people will not listen and take warning; only those whose ears the Holy Spirit opens will do so. For those who "have ears" are the ones commanded to hear. Therefore, it is not surprising if we see many people despise these threats and think that these praises and rebukes are unsuitable for them or do not concern them.

There, was one river, but it divided itself from the Garden into four heads; here, is one voice of truth among all the Apostles, which, taking its beginning from Jerusalem, was divided into the four quarters of the world, filling all lands wherever it flowed with the waters of peace and salvation. ## The Analysis or Resolution of the Letter to those of Smyrna.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial letter 'T' decorated with scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>

*So much for the first letter. The second is sent to the Smyrneans, but addressed, as is the custom, to the Angel <note>original: "Angell"; referring to the pastor or leader of the local church</note>. It then describes the one who sends it: that he is the first and the last, and also that he was once dead but is now alive (verse 8). The narration partly commends them for their patient endurance of affliction, which the blasphemous Jews caused (verse 9). It also partly prepares them against a new calamity, both by showing the author, the nature <note>original: "kinde"</note>, the purpose <note>original: "end"</note>, and the duration <note>original: "continuance"</note> of it, and also by promising them a crown (verse 10). The conclusion contains both the usual call to listen <note>original: "Acclamation"</note> and also a promise of freedom from the "second death" as a reward (verse 11).*

# THE EXPOSITION.

8. **To the Angel of the Smyrneans.** We have said that Smyrna was a colony belonging to the Ephesians; it was also named after Smyrna, one of the Amazons <note>In Greek mythology, the Amazons were a race of formidable female warriors; various cities in Asia Minor claimed to be founded by them</note>. Yet the Holy Spirit respects a different meaning of the name <note>original: "notation"; the etymological significance</note>. For this reason, she is called "sweet-smelling Smyrna"—that is, *Myrrh*—or she who is far more delightful than any pleasant and sweet spices. This is evident because Christ rebukes no fault in her, but shows her to be most dear to himself, even though there was nothing more contemptible or despised by the world at that time.

Neither should we think that the second place was given to this Church after Ephesus by chance. For the Holy Spirit does not list the Churches at random <note>original: "by leapes, without order"</note>, joining either Sardis or Philadelphia next, or any of the others, but follows the order in which they are situated. First, then, he moves to the North, on which side Smyrna is placed on the shore, about one hundred and twenty fathoms <note>original: "fadomes"; the author likely refers to a much larger distance, perhaps "stadia" (furlongs), as 120 fathoms is only about 720 feet</note> away. From there, the path to Pergamum turns again further Northward; and from Pergamum, the rest turn in...

their order southward. No doubt this order demonstrates a similar progression for the Church. In that part of the world where we are, the further we go northward, the further we go back from the sun, which is the fountain of light. Smyrna, following Ephesus, teaches us that after the primitive purity, the Church would daily grow into and proceed toward greater darkness, until at length it came to Pergamus, the last boundary of it; from there it should betake itself again toward the south, to be enlightened with a more plentiful beam every day more and more. We shall see in those things that follow that the event so corresponds, that no fair judge will condemn these things as vain witchcraft and subtleties, but will rather admire with me the greatness of the mystery.

If we will reform our judgments until we have thoroughly viewed the whole matter, we shall be able to judge more sincerely what shall be most beneficial for ourselves and for the truth; which is the only thing I propose to myself (God is my witness), not any desire for either faction or novelty. 

But (some will say) how can the Church of Smyrna be such delightful Myrrh <note>original: "Mirrhe"; the name Smyrna is etymologically related to the Greek word for myrrh, a fragrant resin used in incense and embalming</note> in God's account, when her state was worse than that of Ephesus? It is indeed far more deformed in regard to her outward appearance <note>original: "hewe"</note>, as not being beautified with any ornament of lawful government; in this regard, the Northern decline applies to her. Yet the ardent desire of the godly, who fought most valiantly for the truth in that miserable and rueful state of things, made a most sweet-smelling favor in the nostrils of God. 

Besides, the more grievous the trouble and trial that lies upon God's servants, the more kindly God is accustomed to deal with them. He does not then show rigor against them with threatenings, but he comforts them as much as he can, so that he might strengthen those who are feeble-hearted and not add affliction to affliction. The primitive Church did indeed endure most grievous calamities, but at the hands of heathen men, which was some mitigation of their sorrow. But Smyrna was to suffer every extremity at the hands of those who professed Christianity. Lest she should then fall down under the burden of such great griefs, she hears nothing but that which might put heart into her. For this cause, reproofs are omitted, even though it had more dregs in it than the former Church. The counterpart <note>original: "Counterpaine"; meaning a parallel or a corresponding historical period</note> is the Church succeeding the first—an "under-church" of it, just as Smyrna was an "under-city" of Ephesus—often also having the same...

This church has the same name as the first Church, just as those two cities had, because of the very great closeness of their origins, as Strabo <note>Strabo (c. 64 BC – 24 AD) was a Greek geographer and historian</note> shows. This Counter-Church <note>The author uses "Counter-Church" to mean the historical period that corresponds to or "counters" the biblical description</note> begins with Constantine (until which time the primitive Church, the era of Ephesus, extended) and continues until Gratian, about the year of our Lord 382, according to Eusebius.

**These things says he who is the first and the last.** This is a description of him who sends the letter, and it is taken from the 17th and 18th verses of the first chapter. In those words, we showed that Christ is said to be the Creator and Governor of all things, at whose command alone all things are made, and that for his own glory. Or rather, by this honorable testimonial, that wonderful joining of his majesty and his humility is exalted. This interpretation is indeed confirmed here because the condition of the Smyrneans was similar: *You are afflicted and poor (he says) but indeed you are rich.* What is this else but to say, "though you are accounted by the world as one of the last and lowest, yet in truth you are first and chief"? 

At the same time, he shows that changeable state of the Smyrneans, by which it happened that the truth—which at first flourished among them and was in highest honor—was afterward despised and trodden underfoot by wicked hypocrites. Similarly, Christ was in the beginning God with God, of incomprehensible glory, but afterward, taking upon himself the form of a servant, he emptied himself and became like men. He takes titles for himself which agree with the present condition of things. From this, he scatters various beams of his glory in each letter, as the different conditions of the Church gave occasion. By this, he teaches that the part of his divine, infinite majesty to be chiefly considered is that which best serves the present purpose. 

But lest they should think they should lie always in this dejected state, he adds the other title: *who was dead (he says) but lives.* It is as if he should say: "though, being at first chief of all, I was after that last and lowest, yet I did not stay any long time in this most base condition. Having vanquished death within three days, I attained to my former dignity, in which I now live forever." These things, therefore, declare that notable change which befell Smyrna, and no less to that Church of which it is a type <note>In biblical interpretation, a "type" is a person, event, or institution that foreshadows a future reality</note>. Here, the first truth, which had been for 300 years founded and spread abroad with much blood, at length came to be hated by the Christians themselves and received extremely harsh treatment <note>original catchword: offered</note>...

9. **I know your works, and your affliction.** Here is the account of their condition, which he says is known to himself, just as in the other Epistles, lest perhaps they should think that because of his long patience, he did not care about their miseries. The persecutions from open enemies were hushed and gone, but quarrels and brawls among the citizens themselves immediately grew very fierce and hot. This happened not only in the whole Church in general, but in this city as well: Theodosius the Younger, boiling with envy against a man named Cyrus—whom he saw was very popular with the people—sent him to Smyrna under the pretense <note>original: "vnder a colour"</note> of making him Bishop of that city, but with the firm intention of having him killed. For the people of Smyrna had recently killed four of their bishops; this barbarous cruelty shows us how severely this "Angel" <note>In the Book of Revelation, the "Angel" of the church is often interpreted as its bishop or presiding leader</note> was afflicted. This is recorded in the *Abridgment of the Chronicles* <note>original: "Epitome of the Chronicl."</note> published with the *Chronicle of Eusebius* by that excellent man Joseph Scaliger, page 293. 

But if we slightly enlarge the scope of this "Smyrna" to include those contentions among Christians I mentioned, Arius soon arrived. He kindled such a fire that everything, both divine and human, was set ablaze. The bishops sought nothing but to thrust one another out of their seats <note>original: "Chayres," referring to the bishop's throne or cathedra</note> and to deprive each other of their church dignities. Eustathius of Antioch was exiled along with a large company of priests and deacons, as recorded by Athanasius in his *Letter to the Solitaries* <note>original: "Epiſtle to them that lived a ſolitary life"</note>. This Athanasius himself—almost the only fortress the truth had left—was not only assaulted but even overwhelmed with all kinds of false accusations. His enemies did not cease their wicked opposition against him until they had succeeded in getting him banished to Trier <note>original: "Treuirs"</note> in France. Those times were truly lamentable, as the Emperor meanwhile did not sufficiently perceive the purposes of those most wicked bishops and did not know the source of those troubles.

**But you are rich.** That is, you are not left naked and forlorn as people think; rather, through my help and in my estimation, you abound with a full supply of all necessary things. These words also suggest what defense and respect Christ provided for his servants, even in spite of the world. 

Their authority would increase along with their affliction, as we know happened to Athanasius. Though he was harassed with all kinds of reproachful wrongs in the East, he was held in great honor in the West. Constantine the son, Constans the brother, Julius the Bishop of Rome, and the Bishop of Trier <note>original: "Treuirs"</note> (who sheltered him for two years and entertained him very kindly and generously) all honored this man as he deserved. Indeed, even Constantine the Great himself, after investigating the slanders of his enemies, gave honorable testimony of his innocence and virtue, and saw fit to recall him from his banishment.

Say, those who boast that they worship God by the ancient ordinance of the law, according to the manner in which their ancestors worshiped him of old—and as they thought all men ought to worship him always.
