These were men who were not heathens, nor entirely lacking in the knowledge of God—just as the Jews were not—but they were Christians in name only. They were the standard-bearers of the "Christian" military, or so they wished to be thought. Yet no less than that stubborn nation of the Jews, they held stiffly to their errors and struggled to establish their own decrees alone. They harassed in every way those who opposed them, and—while boasting of themselves as the only orthodox men—condemned all others for impiety and blasphemy. But whatever this wicked group boasted, as if God dwelt in their congregations alone, they gathered assemblies together not for God but for the Devil, whose synagogues they ruled.

> 10. *Fear none of those things which you shall suffer.*

Here, it also includes heretics: those who are Christians in name but are, in truth, wolves...

...devouring the flock. The type of punishment is imprisonment, which in this context includes proscriptions <note>legal seizure of property or the declaration of someone as an outlaw</note>, confiscation of goods, banishment, killings, fires, torture on the rack, or whatever other extreme torment besides, as history shows. By all these means, the Devil would outrageously labor to draw men away from the truth. 

But this persecution was to endure for only ten days. Now, a "day" in this book is often taken to represent a year. The number ten sometimes signifies a literal ten; however, it also often signifies an uncertain or general number by a *synecdoche* <note>original: "Synechdoche"; a figure of speech where a specific number represents a general quantity</note>. I suppose both meanings are used here: that the specific number (ten years) belongs to the historical "Type" (the early church in Smyrna), and the general, uncertain number belongs to the later "Counterpart." 

Regarding Smyrna specifically, this persecution occurred in the time of the Emperor Trajan. He acted as a "devil"—that is, an open enemy of the truth—and reigned shortly after this book was written. He was very cruel toward the Christians, delivering them over to prison and death to drive them through fear away from their profession of Christ. Smyrna could not escape this common calamity, especially since Bithynia (which borders it) was completely overflowing with the massacres of Christians, as the letter from Pliny the Younger <note>original: "Pliny the second"</note> to Trajan describes. 

From this, we can somewhat gather how long this persecution lasted. For in the fourteenth year of Trajan's reign, Pliny reported to him the vast number of those who had been killed, which provided an opportunity to halt that rage and obtain some relief <note>original: "breathing"</note>. Historians do not clearly state which year the persecution began. Some think it began as soon as he took control of the Empire. However, in his fourth year, he was triumphing over the Dacians and Scythians; the beginning of his reign seems to have been so troubled that he did not have the leisure to afflict the Christians. But it is certain that he exercised his cruelty for at least ten years. It is likely that the end of that war was the beginning of this torment of the Christians. 

Nor is it necessary to think that this affliction was limited to Smyrna alone. Rather, it was that universal persecution which was to come upon the whole world, as mentioned in the Letter to the Church of Philadelphia (Chapter 3:10). 

As for the counterpart of the Church of Smyrna, the Emperors Constantius <note>original: "Constans"; the author likely refers to Constantius II, known for his support of Arianism and persecution of Nicene Christians</note> and Valens—though Christians in name—were in fact no less terribly cruel toward truly godly men of sound belief than the heathen "devils" of old had been. Among that number, the inferior instruments of their wickedness are also counted. Among the laity were Syrianus the governor and Sebastian...

# Chapter 2. A REVELATION,
<page-num>60</page-num>

<margin>
*Sweet-smelling Smyrna.*

As well as to the Pastors, comfort is provided to the people by name, serving the same purpose as the former encouragement, but in a different manner. For there are two things that usually ignite our desires to undertake any worthy achievement: the hope of reward and a disregard for danger. 

The former [hope of reward] was set before the Pastors, whose minds, being more filled with knowledge and more noble, are usually led by reward. The latter [disregard for danger] is laid before the people, whom the fear of danger primarily frightens away from their duty and will not allow them to do anything worthy of praise. He shows, therefore, that they ought not to fear losing their lives if it were necessary. For there can be no fear of the "second death," through which the body and soul perish forever, according to the words of Christ: *“Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Hell” (Matthew 10:28).* This Hell is that "second death" of which he speaks here, whereby the whole person shall be as much deprived of all comfort in God as the body is destitute of all help coming from the soul once it is severed from it by the first [physical] death. 

This is that horrible death which is truly to be feared, and from which He—who has overcome death—delivers His servants. He promises them freedom from this second death, and not from the first death, which is a much lighter matter than such a mighty Master of the prizes <term>Master of the prizes: original 'Master of the prizes,' a metaphor comparing Christ to the official who awarded prizes to victors in ancient Greek athletic games</term> would grant, or His soldiers would expect. Now, what need is there to be defended from the first death, which the necessity of nature would bring at last anyway? However, to face that necessity early for the sake of the truth paves the way to obtaining a more magnificent crown. He promises, therefore, that which is best, and does not deceive us with a hollow display of a lesser and lighter good.

# Chapter 2. OF THE REVELATION

## The Analysis or Outline of the Letter to those in Pergamus.

<margin>High and Haughty Pergamus</margin>
<image-desc>An ornamental drop cap 'S' featuring intricate floral and foliage patterns within a square border.</image-desc>
So much for the Letter to the people of Smyrna. The one addressed to the people of Pergamus is likewise addressed to the Angel <note>The "Angel" refers to the bishop or lead pastor of the church.</note>. He who sends it has a two-edged sword. The narration commends their constancy, which is highlighted by the presence of "Satan’s Throne" and those common times of danger in which Antipas suffered (verse 13). After that, he reproves their sin, showing partly what kind of sin it is—in that they tolerated the Balaamites (verse 14) and the Nicolaitans (verse 15). He also shows the remedy for it, which is repentance; he emphasizes this by the danger they face if they despise it (verse 16). Finally, he concludes with his solemn call to listen and sets down the reward: the hidden Manna, the white stone, and the unknown name written upon it (verse 17).

# THE EXPOSITION.

**12. And to the Angel of the Church of Pergamus.** As far as the Holy Spirit seems to aim at the etymology <note>original: "notation," referring to the linguistic origin and significance</note> of the word in this place, Pergamus is essentially the Greek *Pergamos*—that is, the "Tower of Troy," as Hesychius <note>an ancient Greek grammarian and lexicographer</note> interprets it. For it is a towered city, high and proud, which agrees with what follows in the next verse: *where Satan's Throne is*. It is distant from Smyrna toward the North by about 540 furlongs—further from Smyrna than Smyrna is from Ephesus—located at the furthest boundary of the northern latitude among these seven cities. 

There was a great reduction of the light during the decline of Smyrna under Constantine, Constantius, and Valens. This occurred even in that first and smallest turning away from Ephesus, which represented the primitive purity of the church. But now there is a passage from Smyrna to Pergamus, into the uttermost darkness. The Church is now destined to suffer a more grievous eclipse of the light than ever before since the birth of Christ. The counterpart <note>original: "counterpaine," meaning the historical parallel or matching period</note> of this is of a larger extent in time than...

<margin>Sweet-smelling Smyrna</margin>
...Just as it was for the pastors, comfort is administered to the people by name, serving the same purpose as before but in a different manner. For there are two things that usually spark our desire to take on any worthy task: the hope of reward and a lack of concern for danger. The hope of reward was set before the pastors, whose minds—being better furnished with knowledge and more noble—are usually led by such incentives.

This [disregard for danger] is presented to the people, whom the fear of danger primarily frightens <note>original: "fray"</note> from their duty and prevents from doing anything worthy of praise. He shows, therefore, that they should not fear losing their lives if necessary; for there is no need to fear the "second death," by which both body and soul perish forever. This is according to the words of Christ: *Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Hell (Matthew 10:28).*

This Hell is the "second death" he speaks of here. Through it, the whole man <note>The OCR "mã" uses a tilde to indicate a missing "n," a common shorthand in early printing.</note> shall be as much deprived of all comfort in God as the body is stripped of all help from the soul once it is severed by the first death [physical death]. This is that horrible death that is truly to be feared. He who has overcome death delivers his servants from it. This is the freedom he promises them—not freedom from the first death, which is a far lighter matter than what such a mighty "Master of the Prizes" <note>original: "Master of the prizes"; this refers to Christ as the judge and awarder of crowns in the spiritual "games" or struggle of life.</note> would give, or what his soldiers should expect. 

After all, what need is there to be defended from the first death, which the necessity of nature would eventually bring anyway? But to face that necessity early for the sake of the truth paves the way to receive a more magnificent <note>original: "ample"</note> crown. Therefore, he promises that which is best and does not deceive us with a hollow display of a lesser and more trivial good.

## The Analysis or Resolution of the Letter <note>original: "Epistle"</note> to those of Pergamus.

<margin>High and Haughty Pergamus</margin>

So much for the letter to those of Smyrna. The letter to the people of Pergamus is likewise addressed to the Angel <note>Commonly interpreted as the bishop or pastor of the church</note>. He who sends it has a two-edged sword. The narration commends their constancy, which is illustrated by the "Throne of Satan" and those common times of danger in which Antipas suffered (verse 13). After that, he reproves their sin, showing partly what kind it is: they tolerated the Balaamites <note>Followers of the false prophet Balaam, associated with compromise</note> (verse 14) and the Nicolaitans (verse 15). He also shows the remedy for it: repentance. He emphasizes this by the danger they face if they despise it (verse 16). Last of all, he concludes with his solemn proclamation and sets down the reward: the hidden manna, the white stone, and the unknown name written upon it (verse 17).

# THE EXPOSITION.

12. **And to the Angel of the church of Pergamus.** As far as the Holy Spirit seems to aim at the meaning <note>original: "notation"</note> of the word in this place, *Pergamus* is essentially the Greek word *Pergamos*, which means the "Tower of Troy," as Hesychius <note>A 5th-century Greek lexicographer who compiled a dictionary of difficult Greek words</note> interprets it. For it is a towered city, high and proud, which agrees with what follows in the next verse, where "Satan's Throne" is located. It is distant from Smyrna toward the north by about 540 furlongs <note>Approximately 67 miles</note>—further from Smyrna than Smyrna is from Ephesus. It sits at the outermost boundary of the northern latitude regarding these seven cities.

There was a great dimming of the light during the decline of Smyrna under the emperors Constantine, Constantius, and Valens. This occurred even in that first and smallest turning away from Ephesus, where the primitive purity was found. But now there is a passage from Smyrna to Pergamus—into the outermost darkness. The church was now to suffer a more grievous eclipse of the light than ever before since the birth of Christ. The counterpart <note>original: "Counterpaine"</note> of this period covers a larger extent of time than...

Therefore, he would inveigle <note>original: "inueigle"; to entice or deceive by flattery</note> men with matters as small and as fair in appearance as he could. In words, he would detest idols as much as any other, and would cry out that this honor he commanded to be given to holy images is far from such impiety. With these kinds of speeches, he would deceive the simple and draw them into this snare which the Holy Ghost speaks of here.

15. *Even so, you have them.* Here is the latter part of a comparison; the former part is concealed. It should be fully stated thus: "As once the Israelites had those who held the doctrine of Balaam, so you have those who hold the doctrine of the Nicolaitans." Instead of stating this former part directly, he attributes the doctrine of Balaam to the Church of Pergamus because it is suited to its counterpart <note>original: "Counterpaine"; meaning a parallel or a matching historical era</note>, but in such a way that the first part of the comparison may be gathered from it. Now, this poison of the Nicolaitans had without doubt infected Pergamus.

*Which I hate.* As mentioned before, the Vulgate <note>original: "the vulgar"; referring to the Latin Vulgate translation of the Bible</note> likewise says, "Repent." And so it begins the next verse to this effect: "As I have admonished the Church of Ephesus, so do I admonish you." But this is weaker than if he should simply command, saying, *Repent.*

16. *I will come quickly against you, and will fight with them.* He threatens a double punishment: one against the Church, against which he says he will come quickly; and another against the corrupters of it, whom he will fight with the sword of his mouth. For it is not to be thought that he would come against that Church only to take away those plagues and destroyers of mankind—this would not be something to be afraid of, but rather something to be greatly desired. Instead, even the Church herself should suffer for her negligence, just as they should for their wickedness. This invasion into the Church was some chastisement by war, or some such calamity, as is more manifest in the counterpart <note>original: "Counterpaine"</note>. The times of this counterpart were very lamentable, partly due to the breaking in of the Northern Barbarians <note>referring to the Germanic tribes like the Goths and Vandals who invaded the Roman Empire</note>, and partly by the Saracens <note>referring to the early Arab Muslim conquests</note>, whom the devil armed against the "seed of the woman" after she fled into the wilderness, as we shall show in Chapter 12. These things belong to that time, though they are only generally and obscurely pointed at here because this was not the place to give further light. The other punishment is for the Balaamites, against whom he will draw the sword of his mouth. # OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chapter 2.

The Pontifical Pope is a most cursed, cursing <term>Balaam</term> <note>original: "Balaam"; a biblical figure who led the Israelites into sin through idolatry and immorality. The author uses him as a symbol for the Pope.</note>. That city, which is praised by the foolish boasting of vain men as if it were the gate of heaven, is the very palace and throne where the Devil keeps his court. No one should think that malice drives a declared adversary of the Pope to speak this way; rather, let him compare the prophecy with its fulfillment in these times without any partiality. Then, if he perceives that everything has turned out exactly as foretold, let him realize that he is being warned of the coming danger, not so much by the words of any man, but by the Holy Spirit himself.

*To him who overcomes, I will give to eat.* The reward is threefold: *hidden Manna, a white stone, and an unknown name written on it.* All of these things align with these times remarkably well. Concerning the Manna: it was food which God gave the people abundantly in the wilderness, when there was no possibility of obtaining any other. Now, in this condition of the Church of Pergamus—when that sink of filthiness which came from the <term>Nicolaitans</term> <note>A group mentioned in Revelation 2:6 and 2:15, accused of teaching compromise with paganism.</note> and the successors of Balaam (that is, the Roman idolaters) overspread everything—the Church was hiding, as if in a wasted, woeful, and hideous wilderness. We shall see the "woman" taking refuge there when she fled from the Dragon in Chapter 12. 

But Christ nourishes her with the food of the wilderness, just as he fed the children of Israel in ancient times. For he will not fail his servants in the most distressing times, but will abundantly pour out the joy of his Spirit, by which they may not only be kept alive but may also rejoice exceedingly, as having a very great cause and reason for joy. This Manna is the same food as the fruit of the Tree of Life in Paradise, as we noted on verse 7, but here it is given in a different manner. There, in a most chaste, pure, and flourishing Church, it was the fruit of the Tree in the middle of the Paradise of God; here, when the truth was rejected, despised, trodden underfoot, and completely overwhelmed with darkness, it is Manna: the food of the wilderness. This food would not be seen by the world, who would think that those who had fled into this wilderness were dying of hunger because of the scarcity of provisions <note>original: "vitailes"; victuals or food supplies</note>—just as the Egyptians thought the Israelites would immediately perish in the wilderness. But God sustained his people extraordinarily with this "bread of Angels." Yet, this is the difference between the Manna of the people of Pergamus and that of the Israelites:

For this manna was scattered in every direction around the tents; it was distributed privately to each of the Saints, who did not live as close together as the Israelites did in their tents. It is truly like that Manna which was gathered by the collective work of the whole people, and was by God’s commandment hidden and laid up within the golden pot, which the people were no longer permitted to see <note>Exodus 16:33-34; Hebrews 9:4</note>. This prefigured the heavenly food in a more magnificent way. For while the other manna bred worms if kept for more than one day, this manna remained whole and uncorrupt through all ages, being a living and clear resemblance of immortal food. This Manna, therefore, does not lie in plain view around the tents, ready for anyone who wants it to pick it up. Indeed, unless Christ had provided for his servants in those most corrupt times in some hidden manner, they might have said farewell forever to both safety and salvation.

> **And I will give him a white stone.**

The second reward. <term>Aretas</term> <note>Aretas of Caesarea, a prominent 10th-century commentator on the Apocalypse.</note> tells us that such a stone was usually given to wrestlers who competed in the theaters. However, it is unlikely that this custom is being referred to here. That stone was only given when the battle was just beginning, not when it was ended and the conqueror was to be rewarded. In the <term>Olympic games</term> <note>original: "games of Olympus"</note>, to prevent the champions from competing at random, they drew stones out of a silver pot. Those who drew stones marked with the same letter (for there were two stones engraved with each character) were paired together by the judges as opponents. I believe there was no other use for these stones in the games. In legal judgments, they were used for a different purpose: namely, to cast a vote <note>original: "suffrage by voices"</note>. These stones were of various types, according to the different customs of people. Many times they were hollow or bored through, which were used to give a sentence of condemnation; sometimes they were solid, which were used to grant acquittal. There was also a time when they were distinguished by their color only, with the black stone condemning and the white stone, on the contrary, acquitting. So says <term>Ulpian</term> <note>A famous Roman jurist (c. 170–223 AD).</note> in his commentary on <term>Demosthenes</term> <note>The famous Greek orator of Athens.</note>.

In the speech *Against Timocrates*, stones used for <term>suffrages</term> <note>original: "suffrages"; here meaning votes or ballots</note> (he says) were sometimes pierced through, and sometimes unpierced; sometimes also black and white. This is therefore an allusion to the custom of acquitting people in legal judgments. 

But why should there be a second and third reward here, when there was only one for the former churches? It was because the situation of the godly in this Church required it. Since the faithful were few and scattered thinly among such a large company of the wicked, they were hated by all men and condemned for schism, error, heresy, and every other kind of wickedness. Therefore, a ballot of acquittal is promised to them. Even if they are declared guilty on earth by the voices of all men, they should know with absolute certainty that they are judged guiltless before the heavenly tribunal of God. How great a comfort is this against the insults and reproaches of the world! Be of good cheer: *If God justifies, who shall condemn?* (Romans 8:33).

**And in that stone a new name written.** The third reward. He continues with the same custom of legal judgments. On some of those stones, the names of those who came into judgment were written and engraved. Plutarch, in his account of the wise sayings of Aristides, tells how Aristides was once approached by an unlearned man who did not know who he was. The man asked him to write the name "Aristides" upon a shell <note>original: *ostrakon*, used in the Athenian practice of ostracism to vote for banishment</note> that he had in his hand so he could vote to condemn him. Aristides wrote his own name upon it, even though it led to his own banishment. 

The same custom is pointed to here. Now, the "new name" that is to be written upon the white stone is "child of God." The faithful shall know and acknowledge themselves to be children of God by the testimony of the Spirit (Romans 8:16). This also serves as a defense against the reproaches of the world, who would regard them as the <term>offscouring</term> <note>original: "of-skouringe"; meaning the scum, refuse, or lowest form of filth</note> and filth of all things. But why do you upset yourself by thinking about how much the world despises you, when you are honorable in God’s sight as one of his children? This name is also unknown to all men except to him who has received it; for "the world has not known us" (1 John 3:1-2). Therefore, their testimony is worth nothing, whether it is for us or against us. But behold

### The Analysis or Logical Breakdown of the Letter to the Church of Thyatira.

<margin>Growing Thyatira.</margin>
*This concludes the letter to the Church of Pergamus.* This letter to those in Thyatira is also addressed to the Angel. It describes the one who sends it as the Son of God, with eyes like fire and feet like fine brass (verse 18). The narrative praises their increase in piety (verse 19). However, it rebukes them for tolerating Jezebel, whose wickedness the author describes: first by the type of sin (verse 20); then by her stubbornness (verse 21); and finally by her punishment (verse 22). This punishment is notable because it varies according to the specific condition of the offenders: Jezebel herself is punished in her bed, while those who commit adultery with her face great affliction. Finally, her "sons" <note>In this context, "sons" refers to her followers or those produced by her teachings</note> are punished with death (verse 23). This section ends with the solemn witness of all the Churches, confirming that God's judgment against her is both just and rigorous. To this, he eventually adds counsel against this wickedness, showing a path of mercy (verse 24) and requiring the Church to remain constant (verse 25). He encourages them to do so with the promise of a reward: power over the nations (verses 26–27) and the "morning star" (verse 28). The conclusion follows in verse 29.

...to the thing itself. For the piety of this Church is growing, like a newborn daughter who always increases in age and size until she reaches her full maturity. In this regard, this Church is contrasted with Ephesus; while Ephesus was at her full strength on the first day (or shortly after), the further she progressed, the more she weakened and decayed every day. She was like someone hastening toward old age until, at length, the natural and original heat being extinguished, she fell into the coldness of death itself. Now, this is the first turn from the North—namely, from Pergamus—toward the South, but further toward the East, being distant from it by about eighty English miles, according to Ptolemy. Its historical counterpart <note>original: "Counterpaine"</note> is the time from the year 1300 until the year 1520 (which is 520 years beyond the first 1000 years).

**18.** *These things says the Son of God.* Now Christ makes himself known by his name, his eyes, and his feet. All of these things appear more clearly through the historical counterpart. Regarding the name, it now presents itself to us for the first time, not having been explicitly stated among the things that were either seen or heard in the first chapter. There, mention was made of the "Son of Man" (verse 13), but the whole vision sufficiently declared him to be the Son of God. It seems to be named here as if he were now returning out of Egypt. He had been in exile for a long time, but in the renewing of the Church, he returns home again, as it were, beginning to make himself known in a more familiar way to his servants, from whom he seemed to have been absent for so long before. His fiery eyes (of which he spoke in chapter 1:14–15) are those through which he reveals himself to the Thyatirians in brilliance. This is because that flourishing time was now coming in which the light of the truth would scatter the darkness, just as darkness flees from the light of a fire. This occurred around the year 1300, when a new company of scholars <note>original: "Doctours"</note> arose. By the judgments of these men, the Pope's authority was fatally wounded <note>original: "the Popes throate was cut"</note> and he began to be stripped of the honor he had craftily acquired and held for a long time. For they earnestly strove to prove that the Imperial Majesty <note>the authority of the Holy Roman Emperor</note> ought to have the chief place and influence, and that the Pope had no power at all over it. Among these scholars were William of Ockham, Marsilius of Padua, Dante, John of Jandun, and many others. His feet, like fine brass, show what kind of torments that "Balaam of Rome" <note>a reference to the Pope, comparing him to the corrupt biblical prophet Balaam</note> used in his cruelty against the faithful, who were the "feet" of Christ. He gave them over to be consumed in the flames of fire, endeavoring to put out one...

# Chap. 2. A REVELATION,

<margin>Growing Thyatira.</margin>
...burning fire with another. Indeed, he did not use this cruelty for the first time now, but he made it more notorious through more frequent graves and more blazing fires than he had ever done before. These fires shone throughout all Europe, as many martyrs were burned every day. But among all the rest, these were of special note: John Hus and Jerome of Prague. Being a noble pair of feet, they glistened like fine brass in the furnace of Constance <note>Referring to the Council of Constance (1414–1418), where Hus and Jerome were burned at the stake for heresy</note>, in the eyes of the whole world. But the Antichrist was deceived, thinking he could consume these feet with fire. For now, at last, he has found by experience that these feet are not stubble, but fine brass of Lebanon <note>original: "Libanus"</note>, which shines more and more in the fire and is not consumed.

**19.** *I know your works.* The works which are recounted are love, service, faith, and patience. These belong more to the private duty of every saint than to the public function of men, as if this Church were lurking in some hidden members and was not renowned through any magnificent outward government. Doubtless, such was the state of the city of Thyatira; and as for its historical counterpart <note>original: "Counter-paine"</note>, it is very plain that it was the same. For though there were many excellent men everywhere who defended the truth with their writings and speeches, there were yet no public meetings appointed. Or, if there were any (as they did indeed begin to assemble more freely towards the end of this period <note>original: "cõpasse"</note> of years), they still did not achieve any proper reformation. The chief praise was for their love toward one another—not that fake love by which large promises are made but nothing is performed, but a love by which they helped one another in deed and truth when there was need. This is why he joins "service" to "love"—that is, ministering to the necessities of the saints. Their mutual faith was also excellent, devoid of all hypocrisy and treachery. For this "faith" seems to be a fruit of that other virtue properly called "faithfulness," by which everyone had a hearty and sincere care for the good of another. When "faith" signifies trust in God through Christ, it is usually placed first, as the fountain and spring-head of all other virtues. This perhaps deceived the old translator <note>referring to the Latin Vulgate</note> and made him place this word before the rest, contrary to the authority of all the Greek copies; for he reads, *and faith, and charity, and ministering, and patience.* Their patience was seen in enduring those...

# OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chap. 2.

<margin>Growing Thyatira.</margin>
...calamities with which they were afflicted by means of the hatred and subtle policy of the Pope of Rome. The last commendation is for their "last works," which were more than the first. For so read the Vulgate <note>original: "the Vulgar," referring to the common Latin translation of the Bible</note>, the Complutensian Polyglot <note>original: "Complutensis," the first multi-language printed Bible</note>, and a certain royal manuscript which Robert Estienne <note>original: "Robert Stephen," a famous 16th-century printer and scholar</note> used in his edition: *“And your last works are more than your first.”* In this version, the second mention of the word *works* is removed. Indeed, the sentence runs better this way, especially since "works" are mentioned at the beginning of the verse; if they were repeated here by themselves and not read together with the other words, the repetition might perhaps be superfluous.

As for the matter itself, it is an excellent commendation to grow in godliness and to exceed the earlier times of our life in the fruitfulness of good works as we grow toward our later days. This is the habit of all who are planted in the house of God: they abound with fruit in their old age and are healthy and flourishing (Psalm 92:15). Their journey toward heaven proceeds like the light of the morning, *“that shines more and more until the perfect day”* (Proverbs 4:18).

So this Church, always increasing with a more ample progress, daily grew great and strong from small beginnings. Around the year 1300, many bold champions and faithful patrons of the truth showed themselves. But about 70 years later, John Wycliffe <note>original: "Iohn Wicklefe"</note> greatly helped their beginnings; he cleared and laid open the doctrine in many of its main points, and what they had only partially discovered, he confirmed with more formidable <note>original: "doughtie"</note> arguments.

After forty years, John Hus and Jerome of Prague succeeded this man. Through their preaching and martyrdom, the Church grew much larger. After these followed the people of Bohemia <note>original: "Boemia"</note>, who openly revolted from that Antichrist of Rome and set up a more reformed worship of God in their assemblies. Then the hearts of the godly were raised up to much greater strength and courage throughout all Europe; they professed the truth with more freedom of spirit, even though they knew they did so at the risk of their lives.

Thyatira did not stop here, either. In her old age, around the year 1500 <note>original: "a thousand and a halfe"</note>, she poured out into the world a new supply of most learned men. These indeed gave great hope that the light would soon break forth into its full brightness. These are the "last works" that were "more than the first." She is therefore worthily called "Daughter" <note>original: "Thugateira"</note>, for she grew so notably, even like those waters that came out...

For this **Jezebel** is **Rome**: that Queen, that idolater, that sorceress, that harlot, that killer of martyrs, that Prophetess, the head of all...

That infant **Rome** abused the help of Kings to bring in and to establish her idolatry; this **Rome**, in her pride and peak <note>original: "ruffe"; a state of display or the height of one's power</note>, commands men by her own authority to eat things offered to idols, by strictly requiring the worship of statues and images. Who can sufficiently admire the singular workmanship of the Holy Spirit, who has set forth the matter in such a lifelike manner? This, then, is that *Jezebel*. 

The holy men of this time, challenging <note>original: "rowzinge vp"</note> this deadly creature more mildly and moderately than they should, did not fully please Christ (the Archbishop of our souls) for that reason. He would have us spare no intensity of zeal and indignation in curbing such shameless insolence from wicked seducers. The learned men of that time indeed dealt more bluntly <note>original: "roundly"</note> than they had in former times, yet not with that vehemence that was required in a cause such as this.

22. **Behold, I will cast her upon a bed.** Here is the punishment of Jezebel. A bed is sometimes for luxury <note>original: "deliciousness"</note> and wantonness, as in the Prophet: *They stretch themselves upon their ivory beds* (Amos 6:4). Sometimes it is for diseases and sickness, as: *The Lord shall strengthen him upon the bed of his sickness; you shall turn his bed in his disease* (Psalm 41:3 <note>original: Ps. 41.4</note>). Which of these does it serve to express in this place? Not luxury—though that is a grievous punishment, to be given over to an occasion for sinning—but languishing, as it appears by what follows immediately after, where *those that commit adultery with her shall be cast into great affliction.* 

The woman of Thyatira, therefore, began to languish. Rome was also in a languishing state from the year 1300, wasting away more and more like one who is sick with consumption <term>consumption: a wasting disease, historically often referring to tuberculosis</term>. For from that time, her face began to grow pale, her stomach grew weaker, her life was painful, and her flesh was consumed away. Indeed, her weakness has prevailed so far that if a man looks at her as she is today, he will say that she is but a dry corpse <note>original: "carrion"</note> compared to her former health and vitality <note>original: "good liking"</note>. 

Oh, infinite wisdom of God! Which even with one word has drawn for us such a lifelike portrait of so long a time. Could the lingering destruction of Rome be noted for us more elegantly or significantly? God would not have her perish with a swift disease, lest his people should forget it, but rather that she should rot piecemeal with a wasting consumption <term>Ptisicke: an archaic term (phthisis) for a wasting lung disease or tuberculosis</term>. This was both so that this lingering punishment should, by its long duration, be an image of her eternal punishment, and also so that she might be a spectacle to many ages, having drawn many ages into error. Certainly, unless Rome feels and acknowledges this consumption of hers, her disease is not only a wasting sickness but a madness <term>Phrensie: a state of mental derangement or delirium</term> as well.

**26. For if anyone should overcome, etc. Or, And he who overcomes and keeps my works until the end, I will give to him, etc.** For I will give to him who overcomes and observes, etc. It is an Hebraism <note>A grammatical structure characteristic of the Hebrew language, often preserved in the Greek of the New Testament.</note>, similar to what follows in the next chapter, verses 12 and 21. In these cases, the nominative case is used absolutely due to the absence of the preposition "to," "of," or "for." For example, **Psalm 11:4: The Lord, His throne is in heaven**—meaning "As for the Lord, His throne is in heaven," or "The throne of the Lord is in heaven." Likewise, **Psalm 18:30: As for God, His way is perfect**—meaning "the way of God is perfect." A similar instance is found in Paul’s writing: **that which was impossible for the law, etc. (Romans 8:3).** This passage troubles many interpreters because they do not recognize this Hebraism; for "That which is impossible" <note>original Greek: "Τὸ ἀδύνατον" (To adynaton)</note> is an absolute nominative case, the meaning of which is, "As for the impossibility of the law, etc." The "end" mentioned here is not the end of their lives, but the end of this period of hundreds of years, which would then cease, being replaced by a more complete reformation.

**I will give him power over the nations.** Here is a double reward: power over the nations and the morning star. This "power over the nations" is a power over the enemies of the Church. This name was once common to all those who were not of the people of Israel but were strangers to their covenant and commonwealth. But now among these "Gentiles," all who sincerely profess Christ are accounted and reckoned among the true Israelites. The rest of the profane and hypocritical crowd—who either openly despise the truth or embrace it only in outward show—remain stuck in the old mire and are called by the ancient name of "Gentiles." The "nations" among the people of Thyatira were Jezebel and her followers. Among us, they...

# OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chap. 2.

<margin>The growth of Thyatira.</margin>

For once Luther had risen up, certain princes of Germany departed from the obedience of the Romish Harlot [the Roman Catholic Church], whom at length, after some wrestling, they threw down to the ground and trampled under their feet. The same thing happened by God’s mercy in many other places. This promised power, then, is a joint participation of the Church in the victory against the Papists, which all reformed churches enjoy today; the full and glorious triumph of this will come shortly, as we shall show later in its proper place, by the help of God.

27. *And he shall rule them.* These are the characteristics of the previously mentioned power. To rule them with an iron scepter is to subdue their power fully and to compel them to obedience, whether they want to or not. This was accomplished by the Protestant princes of Germany and elsewhere. They drove the Papists out of their monasteries, colleges, temples, lands, and other of their goods, and bestowed them on better uses—namely, toward the maintenance of godly teachers, widows, orphans, schools, or finally whatever else might help advance Christianity. But the Papist cries out against this as being sacrilegious and tyrannical. Let him cry until he bursts; the more he groans with pangs at the heart to see this, the more we take notice of this hard and iron rod that makes his shoulders ache. Therefore, as many of the "Thyatirians" <note>The author uses this term to refer to the faithful reformers across history</note> as kept alive the light (or fire) of the truth once kindled until the end would see this joyful day with their own eyes and share in the victory. This does not mean it was necessary for those who were raised up to stand for the truth around the year 1300 to still be alive at that time. Rather, it is because what happened to some of them—namely, those who survived and were living at the end of this period—is customarily attributed to all who share the same condition. For the Communion of Saints requires that what belongs to a few should be shared by all.

*And they shall be bruised like earthen vessels.* That is, easily and without any hope of restoration, made like potsherds <note>fragments of broken pottery</note> which are of no use. Let the Pope of Rome sweat, therefore, and turn over every stone, using all the ways he can to regain his former authority; he strives in vain. His fall is beyond repair; he shall find no binding...

The full restoration of the Jews follows closely behind it, just as the sun follows the morning star. This point is only briefly asserted here as far as it serves to illustrate this passage; the treatise following shall provide the proofs. Shortly after this communion with Christ, the full happiness of the Saints—such as can be experienced on earth—shall follow.

For to what end is the reward set after the epilogue in the first three Epistles, while in the four last this acclamatory sentence <note>The phrase "He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches."</note> always holds the final place? First, the Holy Spirit teaches us that there is an undoubted difference between the first three and these four latter Epistles. We observed this before, distinguishing all seven churches into the three foremost—which grow worse and worse—and the four latter—which begin to return to health again after their sickness is over, and to do better and better. 

Besides, there may be another reason which I gather from the outcome: that the rewards in the first three Epistles (such as eating the fruit of the tree of life in Paradise, etc.) were not fulfilled suddenly and in a moment. Instead, they were being fulfilled over a long period with a lengthy delay. Therefore, the rewards follow these conclusions as if, after the admonition, they would give time for deliberation. 

But in the four latter letters, the acclamation comes after the rewards, as if once the warning is given, there should be no place or time for taking counsel. Instead, the matter should immediately reach its conclusion beyond all expectation, being no sooner said than done. 

We know this happened in the Reformation begun by Luther, which we have shown to be the reward corresponding to <note>original: "Counterpaine"—a counterpart or duplicate</note> the state of Thyatira. Who would have thought that the matter would eventually lead to such proof, having had such small beginnings? Certainly, Luther himself expected nothing less than a total change or a break from Rome. Or who could have expected such a metamorphosis <note>original: "Metamorphosis"—a complete transformation</note> in the whole Church in such a short time? But now was the time when the Church should have power over the nations. Therefore, once matters were begun, they proceeded of their own accord. In a moment, such an interchangeable transformation occurred that the world at that time was astonished—and not without cause. Even today, our adversaries behold it with such resentment that it is an eyesore to them. 

The same quick dispatch seems likely to follow in the fulfillment of the rewards that come next. A person shall see them bestowed before even hearing that they are to be bestowed; therefore, they precede the admonishing conclusion, just as they shall also precede it in time.

## *The Analysis or Explanation <note>original: "Resolution"</note> of the Chapter, as*
### *also of the Letter <note>original: "Epistle"</note> to those of Sardis.*

<image-desc>Decorative ornamental woodcut initial letter 'T' featuring scrolling floral and vine motifs.</image-desc>
There are three letters in this chapter: one to those of *Sardis*; another to those of *Philadelphia*; and the last to those of *Laodicea*. Nor are they included in one chapter without cause, seeing that they have a condition somewhat different from the previous ones. For the earlier ones, as they were at a greater distance from one another, so they had counterparts <note>original: "Counterpaines"; here meaning historical parallels or matching parts</note> separated by larger spans of time. But these churches are both separated by smaller distances of place from one another, and we shall also find the corresponding <note>original: "counter-answering"</note> churches for each of them to be more closely joined together in time.

*The letter <note>original: "Epistle"</note> to the Church of Sardis, after the address to the Angel, describes the sender by seven Spirits and seven Stars. After that, he adds the narration: which reproves him because, while he carries the name and makes the show of one who lives spiritually, he is in truth dead nonetheless (verse 1). Yet it also teaches the remedy, which is twofold: the first consists of strengthening the remainder who are about to die. For it would happen that many would die by the just judgment of God, who would thus avenge himself for their carelessness regarding the right and proper reformation (verse 2). The second consists of remembering the things which he had received and repenting. Lest this warning be weakened by their negligence, it is sharpened by a threat of his unexpected coming (verse 3). Then after this, he praises some of them for their pure garments; this praise also contains a reward specific to them and common to all conquerors (verses 4 and 5). This reward is threefold: white clothing, a name remaining in the Book of Life, and a confession of him before his Father and his Angels. All these things conclude with the usual call to listen <note>original: "Acclamation"</note>.*

# THE EXPOSITION.

1. **Now to the Angel of the Church which is at Sardis.** Sardis is the second of the newly emerging <note>original: "newe-springinge"</note> churches tending further southward, and growing in strength through the fuller light of the Truth. The counterpart <note>original: "Counterpaine"; meaning the historical parallel</note> is the first reformed Church, begun by the special providence of godly Martin Luther at Wittenberg, which is a town of Saxony by the River Elbe <note>original: "Albis"</note>, in the year 1517. At that time, that holy man resisted the Roman tax-collectors <note>original: "Romish Publicanes"</note>, the gatherers and farmers of the Pope's revenues, who sold pardons <note>indulgences</note> for sins to the people. The truth began to be revived under the state of Thyatira <note>referring to the period of the church of Thyatira discussed in the previous chapter</note>; but no reformation followed from it. This reformation was first taken in hand at the time I speak of. For this reason, we shall find no mention made either...

Therefore, let not this office of an interpreter cause me any displeasure, or bring any reputation but a good one upon me, while I make mention—either here or elsewhere—of present things, perhaps differently than many men would either want or expect. It is a shameful thing to make merchandise of God’s word by speaking to fit the pleasure of men rather than to set forth the truth. Therefore, laying aside both hatred and favor toward men, if what is spoken appears to us to agree with the truth, let us tremble at the threats of the most just God rather than be angry with Him. He has endeavored with all His power to disclose to us the truth that is hidden and hard to know, so that we should not be surprised unawares by such evils as hang over our heads. I hope I shall easily obtain this request from all the godly, who will be far from picking quarrels against my labors. Upon this hope, I will go forward, God assisting me, with what I have in hand.

In the description of the one who sends the letter in the vision of the first chapter, there was no mention at all made of these Spirits spoken of here. They are taken from the description of the general <note>original: "common"</note> greeting in Chapter 1:4. There are seven of them to represent the abundance of all gifts, which this number usually signifies. Christ has these in his power because, as the keeper and distributor of heavenly grace, he gives his Spirit to whomever he sees fit. This is why he says that he will send the Comforter from the Father (John 15:26), who would receive from Christ what he declares to us (John 16:14). 

The stars are in his right hand, just as they were in the letter to the Church of Ephesus. We have already heard that this represents the safety of the ministers, whom Christ carries in his hands (Chapter 2:1). To what end, then, is this same thing repeated again? Was there no other title <note>original: "ornament"</note> left for Christ but this? Was everything already used up in the previous letters? Not at all; it is because a proper order of things is sought, rather than some pointless novelty. 

Because Sardis was to experience Christ’s protection in defending its pastors—similar to the protection he showed in Ephesus—he uses that same comparison for a specific purpose, as there is a great similarity between the two situations. History is silent on how this was proven true for the literal city of Sardis, yet it is very clear in its historical counterpart <note>The author interprets Sardis as a symbol for the Church in Germany during the Reformation era.</note>. For he who gives his Spirit generously to whom and when he wills, poured out such a rich store of all gifts during those times as he never did elsewhere in these latter days. 

For a long time before this, proper learning lay neglected <note>original: "nought set by"</note>. Because of the crude methods <note>original: "barbarousness"</note> of the Schoolmen <note>The "Schoolmen" were medieval scholastic philosophers whose complex logic the Reformers often criticized as being far removed from the simple truth of the Bible.</note>, true learning was driven away for many centuries. This continued until at last, after the wonderful art of printing was invented—a clever device that flowed from this same spring of the Holy Spirit—many excellent minds were raised up to search for the truth. Among these were *Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Angelo Poliziano, Bartolomeo Platina, George of Trebizond, Theodorus Gaza, Ermolao Barbaro, Marsilio Ficino, Georg von Peuerbach, Johannes Regiomontanus, Aldus Manutius, Rodolphus Agricola, Giovanni Gioviano Pontano, Filippo Beroaldo, Johannes Reuchlin*, and many other most learned men. Their chief labor was indeed in bringing light to the study of languages, the arts, and other liberal learning. However, the times that followed closely after these men made it clear how much this paved the way to finding out the mysteries of salvation. For immediately after this, came

Martin Luther, Philip Melanchthon, Erasmus of Rotterdam, Huldrych Zwingli, Johannes Oecolampadius, Wolfgang Capito, Ambrosius Blaurer, Martin Bucer, Wolfgang Musculus, John Calvin, and many other men of singular knowledge were many great and worthy lights of the Christian world. Being helped by the labors of those men who came before them, they brought forth the truth into the light again through their own hard work. This truth had been for a long time overwhelmed with filth and overgrown with moss for want of husbandry <note>original: "husbandinge"; meaning cultivation, management, or careful tending</note>. They drove away the foggy mist of Rome and made all the deceptive <note>original: "sophisticall"</note> subtleties of the adversaries utterly vanish like smoke.

Does not Christ worthily now take to himself this emblem <note>original: "ensigne"</note> of seven Spirits, seeing that he enriched this season with such a great plenty of gifts? And his power is no less notable—together with his favor—in securing the safety of the pastors. Who would not have thought that Luther should have died a thousand deaths? He was so greatly hated and envied by all men, and almost the whole world watched for an opportunity to do him mischief. He even defied the one <note>A reference to the Pope</note> under whose feet Emperors were of old compelled to put their shoulders.

But it may be said that although troubles were raised against him, he was perhaps hard to reach and so could not be brought into their hands. On the contrary, he stood out for almost thirty years in pitched battle against them, safe from all their assaults—even from those that were secretive and treacherous. These are the methods by which the Pope is accustomed to dispatch those men whom he cannot subdue in open fight. Yet at last, lying sick in his bed and giving up his life to him who gave it, he slept quietly in the Lord.

What should I say of Melanchthon, Peter Martyr, John Calvin, and the rest of those stout worthies? Indeed, Martin Bucer—after he had been buried for some years—was finally turned to dust and dug out of his grave (or rather, some other man in his place who had been lately buried there), so that they might rage against his ashes with flames of fire. They did this to him whom they neither could nor dared to hurt while he was alive.

Who was it then who did not see the stars in the right hand of Christ, so marvelously defending his servants against all the violence of the adversaries? Or who is there for whom the fresh remembrance of these things ought not to provide constancy and a heart that cannot be dismayed? By these means, one might wholly rest himself upon that same protection <note>original: "Patronage"</note> and go on confidently in standing up for the truth according to the nature of his calling. Indeed, there is not the same promise made in express words to other times; yet there is always the same crown laid up

### OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chapter 3.

for them that fight lawfully.

<margin>Hypocritical Sardis.</margin>
*I know your works, that you are said to live, but you are dead.* Here is the rebuke, because of that counterfeit godly life which the Angel puts on as a show while being void of all truth; for this reason, it may be called "hypocritical Sardis." The force of this description appears by the very name itself. For *Sardis* is like the *Sardian Speech* <note>original Greek: *Zardianos Legos*</note>, a "Sardian laughter," which in the Greek proverb is a laughter that is more a show than a reality. It is named after the city of Sardis, just as "Sardonic laughter" <note>original Latin: *Sardonius risus*</note> is named after the island of Sardinia, as Erasmus notes from Plutarch. For that kind of herb called *Ramunculus* <note>original: *Ranunculus*; a type of buttercup believed to cause facial spasms that looked like a grin</note>—by the eating of which the mind is distracted—may grow as well in Lydia as on that island. This Church was considered as if it were alive, but it was dead; it was like this laughter, which fakes a smile while in the meantime being full of deadly grief. 

And from this it may now appear how Sardis may be compared as an opposite to Smyrna. That Church, regarding outward matters, was in very great affliction, so that it was held for dead by almost all men, yet in the meantime it lived the true life and was most acceptable to God himself. This Church, outwardly and in the opinion of men, lives and flourishes in a handsome manner, yet within, death reigns, true piety having been banished from it. This forms the second pair of opposites, as we observed in the general breakdown of the seven Epistles into their parts. 

But where did this counterfeiting lie? Regarding the city of Sardis, we have little to see or show for it from history. Not long after, the famous Melito flourished there, who was greatly praised by Eusebius in Book 4, Chapter 26. But it appears that the matter had come to such a pass when John wrote that although the Angel seemed to himself—and perhaps to others—to be notably furnished with all things required for salvation, he yet lacked many necessities and abounded in the contrary evils. 

We know that those who appear alive outwardly may be dead either through ignorance or corruptness of doctrine, or through neglect and carelessness regarding godly duties. Similarly, Christ calls those "dead" who were void of faith and knowledge of salvation in John 5:25. And the Apostle calls the promiscuous woman "dead while she lives," even though she had given her name to Christ in 1 Timothy 5:6. For this reason also, works are said to be "dead" in Hebrews 6:2, as they reveal those who give themselves to the study of such works to be truly dead. It may be that this Angel of Sardis fell into this state partly by means of his neglect of piety and partly through his corrupt teaching.

### OF THE REVELATION. Chapter 3.

<margin>Hypocritical Sardis.</margin>
...this death-like life. If the doctrine had been completely extinct—which is the very life and soul of a Church—it could not have had even the name of life. We have said that the counterpart <note>original: "Counterpaine"; referring to the historical fulfillment of the prophecy</note>, based on the order and sequence of events, is the first reformed Church rising up in Saxony when Luther began to teach. 

The Church of Thyatira bore the blame for tolerating the Roman "Jezebel" <note>The Roman Catholic Church</note>. This Church, however, was the first—acting like a new Jehu <note>The biblical king of Israel who executed Queen Jezebel</note>—to take charge of casting down this painted and shameless harlot out of the window, dashing her brains out against the earth. For this reason, she is not rebuked, not even in a single word, for that specific fault. This Church, therefore, has a reputation for being alive because of the truth that was restored within her. She brought light to the world in a marvelous way, and in no small measure because of her notable courage, by which she broke and trampled the Roman tyranny underfoot. She shook it off not only from her own shoulders but also exposed it to the ridicule of the whole world. 

Yet she is "dead" because she is dangerously infected with significant errors and corruptions. Above and before all else is the doctrine of <term>Consubstantiation</term> <note>The Lutheran belief that the physical body and blood of Christ coexist in, with, and under the bread and wine of the Eucharist</note>—the presence of the Body of Christ in the Sacrament of the Supper. Many other absurdities follow from this, which creep like a leprosy and utterly destroy the life of those members who were otherwise alive. However, these things are not to be understood as applying to every individual person, but to the overall government and form of the Church as it appeared to the world. This is the sketch that the Holy Spirit portrays for us, which is also to be observed in the rest of the Churches.

2. *Be vigilant and strengthen the things that are ready to die.* 

Here is the first remedy: diligence in confirming the remaining things; for unless care was taken for them in time, they were ready to rush into deadly destruction. By these words, we are taught that if the teachers would bestow their efforts faithfully and diligently in thoroughly purging all doctrine and piety, they might prevent many from falling. But if they carry themselves too negligently in this matter, the ruin of many would be lamentable. In the historical counterpart, this matter is so clear that one might do better to describe it with tears than with words. For how many excellent men has that monster of <term>Ubiquity</term> <note>The doctrine that Christ's human nature/body is present everywhere at once</note> tumbled headlong into death? Indeed, Luther sowed the seeds of this in the years 1526 and 1528, in his disputations against Zwingli and Oecolampadius.

How did it happen that he did not take care to keep himself from that error, which dragged with it such a company of wicked opinions? Why did he not fear what might happen to others, having experienced for himself the difficulties he was driven to in debate? But his eyes were blinded, so that he could not foresee and avoid this severe judgment that was to come upon those who were on his side. Therefore, their works were not "full" because there was no full reformation made; instead, one error was merely exchanged for another no less dangerous. Now, God is accustomed to punish sin with sin.

He admonishes the Sardians, therefore, that they should return to the first Institution <note>the original founding or principles of the church</note> and that they should amend the things that were decayed by that rule alone. In the same way, he also admonishes the Church of Germany that they should think about what Luther proposed to them at the beginning and that they should undertake a reformation according to that rule.

Now, at the beginning, he aimed at nothing else than that all human devices being put to flight, the truth of God alone—manifested in the Scriptures inspired by God—might have dominion. For so, in the preface of the *Assertion of the Articles* condemned by the Bull of Leo X <note>The 1520 Papal Bull *Exsurge Domine*, which condemned Martin Luther’s teachings</note>, he says: *"First, I call them to witness this my protestation: that I will be urged to yield by no man's authority—even if he is a most holy Father <note>a reference to the Pope or a Church Father</note>—except as far as he shall be approved by the judgment of the divine Scriptures."* Again: *"Therefore, let the first principles of Christians be nothing other than the Word of God. As for the words of all men, let them be as conclusions deduced from this, to be brought back there again and proved from there. Those words <note>the Scriptures</note> ought, first of all, to be most familiarly known to everyone; they are not to be sought and learned from men, but rather men are to be judged by them."*

Upon which occasion he cites that speech of Augustine, from Book 3 of *The Trinity*, saying: *"Do not enthrall yourself to my writings as if they were canonical Scripture, etc."* <note>original: "Doe not thou enthrall thy ſelfe vnto my vvritings, as if they vvere Canonicall..."</note> We must not, therefore, rest in the books of Luther, as the Ubiquitaries <note>A faction of Lutherans who argued that Christ's physical body was "ubiquitous" (present everywhere), used to justify his presence in the bread and wine</note> and those do who corrupt the Sacrament with that late-invented word *Consubstantiation* <note>original: "Zunuſiom. Conſubſtantiation." The former is likely a garbled Greek term for "union of substance"</note>. But as he [Luther] thought it fit to be wise from the Scriptures alone, so all his writings are to be brought back to this holy balance <note>the standard of Scripture</note>. Why should we give more authority to his books than he himself would have given either to other men's books or even to his own? It is truly a matter of great importance, and in this alone lies the turning away of the looming mischief. Unless men turn their eyes toward this and bend their ears to listen to the voice...

*Who have not defiled their garments.* This garment is Christ himself, the common clothing of all the faithful. We read of this in the parable: *'Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?'* (Matthew 22:12). In respect to God, it is the garment of <term>justification</term> <note>justification: the act of being declared righteous before God through faith</note>; in respect to other men, it is the garment of <term>sanctification</term> <note>sanctification: the process of being made holy and living a life that reflects one's faith</note> and profession; in respect to ourselves, it is the garment of glory, honor, triumph, and joy. Therefore, these Sardians kept their profession of Christ pure and spotless from all the filth and pollution of these monstrous opinions. This is true even though those who wake from their errors through repentance are also said to keep their garments pure. For those who are in Christ are not judged by their former foulness, but by their present clothing, with which all their past filthiness is covered.

*And therefore they shall walk with me in white.* That is, in garments. These are the same garments mentioned previously, but of a slightly different nature. For those earlier garments were of profession, through which they appeared to others to be bold soldiers of Jesus Christ; these are garments of glory, triumph, and joy. These they shall enjoy both within themselves—from the sense of God’s love poured into their hearts—and also through the open and public speech of others, who shall magnify God for their sake because He gave them such courage and victory. 

The white and pure gown is in great use and demand at solemnities <note>religious ceremonies or formal celebrations</note>, both among the heathens and among the people of God. It is for this reason that the wise man, alluding to this custom, says: *Let your garments be white at all times* (Ecclesiastes 9:8). But above all, I believe that the passage in Mark is referenced here, where there was a certain glimpse <note>original: "footesteppe"</note> of this heavenly glory: He appeared in a *shining garment, very white, such as no launderer <note>original: "fuller"</note> on earth could whiten* (Mark 9:3). At the sight of this, Peter, being overwhelmed with immeasurable joy, thought of only one thing: how he might enjoy it forever. Thus, this reward of the Saints shall be most ample; they shall so rest themselves within it with their whole hearts that they shall desire nothing greater in this world. Indeed, if anyone should ask the brethren who wear these garments, I have no doubt they would answer that the joy they have through Christ in holding fast to the truth is greater and of more value to them than if they were to exchange it for all the delights of this present life. Certainly, their glory is great among all the godly, and we pray with our whole hearts that it may be perpetual for them.

*For they are worthy.* The Roman Catholic faction <note>original: "Popish sort"</note> finds much satisfaction and joyful matter in this word *worthy*, as if it were a strong defender of their <term>Merit of Condignity</term> <note>The medieval theological doctrine that a person’s good works can be inherently worthy of a reward from God.</note>. 5. *He that overcomes, he shall be clothed.* Some copies and the Vulgate <note>the 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> read this with the word *so*: *He that overcomes, he shall be clothed so.* But the rendering of a comparison <note>original: "reddition of a similitude"</note> is unusual where there is no comparison proposed before it. # Chapter 3. A REVELATION

<margin>Hypocritical Sardis.</margin>

*And therefore they shall walk with me in white.* That is, in white garments. These are the same garments mentioned previously, but they represent a slightly different condition. Those were garments of profession, by which they appeared to others to be brave soldiers of Jesus Christ; these are garments of glory, triumph, and joy. They shall enjoy this joy within themselves from the sense of God’s love poured into their hearts; they shall also receive it from the public and common words of others, who shall magnify God for their sake, because he gave them such courage and victory. The white and pure robe is commonly used and requested at solemnities, both among the Pagans <note>original: "Heathen"</note> and among the people of God. Because of this, the wise man, alluding to this custom, says: *Let your garments be white at all times* (Ecclesiastes 9:8). 

But above all, I think that the passage in the Gospel of Mark is being referenced here, where there was a certain glimpse of this heavenly glory: *He appeared in a shining garment, very white, such as no fuller* <term>a person who cleans, shrinks, and thickens cloth</term> *on earth can whiten like it* (Mark 9:3). At the sight of this, Peter, being overwhelmed with immeasurable joy, thought only of how he might enjoy it forever. So this reward for the Saints shall be most ample; they shall so rest themselves within it with their whole hearts that they shall desire no greater thing in this world. Indeed, if anyone should ask the brethren who wear these garments, I do not doubt they would answer that this joy—which they have through Christ in holding fast to the truth—is greater and of more account to them than anything else, and they would not exchange it for all the delights of this present life. Certainly, their glory is great among all the godly, and we pray with our whole hearts that it may remain with them forever.

*For they are worthy.* The Roman Catholic side <note>original: "Popish sort"</note> takes much delight and finds cheerful evidence in this word "worthy," as if it were a strong supporter of their doctrine of the **Merit of Condignity** <term>the theological idea that a person's good works, performed through grace, inherently deserve a reward from God</term>. But let them consider this: this merit is attributed to the garment, not to the body. That is, it is attributed to the **imputation of Christ’s righteousness** <note>the Protestant doctrine that Christ's holiness is credited to the believer</note>, which we put on as if it were a garment, and not to our own inherent holiness. For the act of not defiling the garment cannot be of more value than the garment itself. 

As we have taught, there are different meanings for "garments," but this worthiness does not arise from one's profession, nor from the care to do good works (by which we seem holy to others), nor even from the joy of the Spirit which we feel within ourselves. Instead, it arises only from the fact that the Father counts us as righteous when we are clothed with his Son.

# Chap. 3. A REVELATION,

In the year [15]91, when Christian, the Duke of Saxony, had died, Paul Crell <note>original: "Paulus Creilius"</note> the Chancellor, being suspected of Calvinism (as they call it), was thrown into prison. Urbanus Pierius, a Professor at Wittenberg, was led away captive into prison. Gundermann was imprisoned at Leipzig <note>original: "Lypsia"</note>. The next year, a new religious inspection <term>visitation: an official inquiry by church authorities to ensure everyone follows the approved doctrine</term> was conducted, and it swept through all of Saxony like a scouring wind. Those who would not subscribe to the Articles of faith were removed from their positions. Why should I speak of the riot at Leipzig the year after that, when the university men flocked together from all places to break down the houses of the Calvinists? Or of that savage cruelty shown by those in Dresden <note>original: "Dresda"</note> toward the dead body of Jakob Lossius? They would not allow him to be buried—not even among criminals <note>original: "malefactours"</note>—because while he was alive, he favored the more pure truth.

I relate these few things here against my will, and I would be ashamed to mention them if the brethren had not been unashamed to commit such acts. But how much better is it for you to hear of these things from your friends than from your enemies? Your enemies do as much as they can to exaggerate your sinful deeds with words, to your eternal disgrace and even to the shame of our whole religion. I only show how this matches the Prophecy so that you, seeing how God regards you, might seriously think about reforming your errors and making peace with your brethren. God grant that you may take such a course so that agreeing together in one truth may remove that judgment from your shoulders which otherwise hangs over you, and will most certainly fall upon you.

In the meantime, if I achieve no good with you (and I pray God that such a rejection of me and my words is far from you), it will still do me good to encourage the brethren who endure many troubles and miseries among you for the sake of the truth to be of good cheer and courage. Christ will not be ashamed of them before his Father if they will constantly continue in their profession of faith. Do not, therefore, fear the stern and haughty looks of men, but trusting in this hope, bring out into the open light and the eyes of men that which you have previously maintained and loved in the dark out of fear.

## The Analysis or Outline of the Epistle to Philadelphia.

<margin>Godly Philadelphia.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'S' featuring scrolling floral and vine motifs.</image-desc>
*So much for the Letter to the Sardians. This one to the Philadelphians is also addressed to the Angel <note>original: "Angell"; referring to the pastor or leader of the church</note>. The one who sends it is remarkable for holiness, truth, and the key of David. He does not carry this key idly, but opens and shuts with it, as it is part of the highest sovereignty that he possesses (verse 7). The narration first recounts his good qualities, both present—namely, the open door, which is explained by its cause: his little strength and his constant keeping of God’s word (verse 8)—and also what is to come. This includes both the subduing of his enemies (verse 9) and the promise of providing help to him during a common trial <note>original: "common triall"; referring to a time of universal testing or tribulation</note>, the reason for which is stated to be his constancy in professing the Gospel (verse 10). Then he inspires him with a desire to preserve that good, because his coming is swift, and there may be danger of having their crown taken from them (verse 11). Finally, there is a very great reward, as he shall be made a pillar and shall have written upon it the name of God, the name of the New Jerusalem, and also the new name of a Son (verse 12). To all these things, the usual conclusion is added at the end (verse 13).*

### OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chapter 3.

If he were to exhort us to all piety in general, could he find anything that might more fitly recommend it to us than brotherly love, void of hypocrisy <note>original: "dissimulatioñ"; see 1 Peter 1:22</note>? How notably does this name agree with this Church, which is not openly convicted of any crime? But as it is truly godly because of its brotherly love, so it is lowly and obscure, both because of the perpetual fear of danger and its desolateness <note>emptiness or lack of population</note>, due to the lack of citizens. These people lived here and there in solitary places where they could find safer dwellings. 

In this way, it is set in direct opposition to *Pergamus*, that towered and proud city—just as *Sardis* was set against *Smyrna*, and *Thyatira* against *Ephesus*. And so, the third pair of opposites is formed. It lies south of *Sardis*, having an increase of greater light, as is appropriate for a reformed church. It is placed in the second position, next after *Sardis* (for that is the first church after *Jezebel* is defeated). By this, it is declared that its fulfillment <note>original: "Antitype"</note> is the second reformed church, which would spring up after the one in *Germany*.

And this is the Church of *Helvetia* <note>Switzerland</note>, *Swabia* <note>original: "Sueuia"</note>, *Geneva*, *France*, *Holland*, and *Scotland*. I join all these together into one Church because they live by almost the same laws and manner of government regarding any matter of importance. Nor does the distance of place break that society which the joining of minds and goodwill couples together. Indeed, this dispersal chiefly agrees with the *Philadelphians*, whom we said lived more densely in the fields than in the city. Consequently, this scarcity of citizens takes up a great deal of territory, even though the citizens themselves are not so many. 

We shall find that this Church I speak of arose after the church in *Germany*, when *Ulrich Zwingli* <note>original: "Ulrich Zuinglius"</note> began to teach at *Zürich* among the *Swiss*, in the year 1519. The reformation began in the fourth year after that—that is, 1523—when none of the popish party dared in the least to dispute against *Zwingli*, who committed the whole controversy to be decided by the judgment <note>original: "arbitrement"</note> of the Holy Scriptures. Those of *Constance*, *Basel* <note>original: "Basill"</note>, *Strasbourg*, *Geneva*, and others followed in the footsteps of these men. Here we must observe that the former counterparts <note>original: "Counterpaines"</note> were distinguished by longer intervals of time, but these later ones—just as their original types were less distant from each other in space—are joined together more closely in time. They are not as separated by ages and spans of many years as they are by laws and customs. For after they came to their beginning—which was somewhat slower in some than in others—we...
