### CHAPTER 3. A REVELATION

"These things says he who is holy and true, who has," etc. <note>A reference to Revelation 3:7: "These things saith he that is holy, he that is true, he that hath the key of David."</note> These words contain a description of him who sends the letter <note>original: "Epistle"</note>, whose first two properties are taken from the nature of the Son of God. These properties are not explicitly mentioned in the vision in the first chapter, but they serve very well to reveal the government of this Church to us.

<margin>Godly Philadelphia</margin>
Regarding the city of Philadelphia, we have no further information in the histories <note>original: "stories"</note> except that there remained a famous company of the faithful there in the following age. Their governor was Damas <note>original: "Danias"; the author refers to the Bishop of Philadelphia mentioned in the letters of Ignatius of Antioch</note>, as we gather from the letters of Ignatius. In the counterpart <note>original: "Counterpayne"; the prophetic fulfillment of the ancient city</note>, the divine power of Christ shines forth in a special way, sanctifying the Church by kindling in it a careful love of piety and by making it fit and cheerful in Christ Jesus for every good work.

I would be loath to provoke anyone to envy or to grieve anyone with my words, yet I must say this: there is no place where doctrine sounds out more purely or where the worship of God is practiced with less corruption. There is no place where the faithful diligence of the pastors flourishes more, where more free and willing obedience is given by the people, or where there is greater reverence for the whole of religion among all social ranks. 

But this holiness seems chiefly to concern their conduct <note>original: "manners"</note>. For this purpose, we should not overlook the notable testimony of Jean Bodin <note>a famous 16th-century French jurist and political philosopher</note> speaking of the men of Geneva. "Among them," he says, "is something praiseworthy—if such a thing exists among any people—and it is that which makes their commonwealth flourish. It flourishes not perhaps with wealth or the greatness of command and dominion, but indeed with virtues and godliness. Specifically, it is that 'censure' <note>the system of moral correction and discipline</note> of their pastors—whom he calls *pontifices* <note>original: "Pontifices"; literally "high priests," here referring to the senior clergy or the Consistory</note>—than which nothing more divine or powerful can be devised to bridle the lusts of men. It restrains such vices as cannot be reformed in any way by the laws and judgments of men. 

Yet this bridling is directed by the rule of Christ: first secretly and in a friendly manner, then a little more sharply. Then, unless you obey, there follows a grave and effective forbidding from participating in the holy things <note>the sacraments, specifically the Lord's Supper; this is the process of excommunication</note>. After that prohibition follows a punishment inflicted by the civil magistrates. So it happens that those things which laws elsewhere do not punish (or only keep in check by punishing) are there kept in check without force or social unrest. Therefore, there is no prostitute haunting the streets, no drunkenness, no dancing, no beggar, and no idle person to be found in that city."

As Jean Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (c. 1530–1596) was a French jurist and political philosopher.</note> said, as we heard before: *the punishment inflicted by the Magistrate follows the prohibition from holy things.* <note>original: "poena a magistratu inflicta, sequitur interdictionem sacrorum"</note> Therefore, both swords <note>The "Two Swords" is a medieval doctrine representing spiritual and secular power.</note> are drawn in this Church, but separately by those to whom each office properly belongs. 

This is indeed a most harmonious partnership, seeing as the entire effort and labor of the civil Magistrate ought to aim toward this: that men might live in all godliness and honesty (1 Timothy 2:2). Now, these words seem to be taken from Isaiah 22:22: *And I will lay (he says) the Key of the house of David upon his shoulder; he shall shut and no man shall open; when he opens, no man shall shut.* However, the word *house* seems to be omitted on purpose. For he does not say, "He who has the Key of the house of David," but "he who has the Key of David." The difference is that the former seems to belong to an inferior minister, like a steward, and only within the family of David; but the latter belongs to the highest governor, and extends through his whole kingdom. Thus, the omission of one word distinguishes the <term>Type</term> <note>A "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament seen as a symbolic foreshadowing of Christ.</note> from the Truth—Eliakim from Christ. (See also Isaiah 9:6-7). The Complutensian Polyglot <note>A famous multilingual Bible printed in Spain in the early 1500s.</note> and the "King’s Copy" <note>Likely referring to a specific royal manuscript or the Robert Estienne Greek edition.</note> read somewhat differently: *He who opens, and no man shall shut it; he who does not open, and no man shall open.* Aretas <note>A 10th-century bishop and commentator on the Apocalypse.</note> reads it this way: *If he does not open, etc.*

It may rightly be called a door, since through the Word a door is opened into heaven; once that Word is taken away, the gate is shut and locked so that no man can enter (Luke 13:25). The power of the Ministers is not the only "door," but the readiness of the hearers is as well, as seen in Paul’s words: *For a great and effective door is opened to me, and there are many adversaries* (1 Corinthians 16:9). # Chapter 3. A REVELATION,

It is a Hebraism <term>Hebraism: A Hebrew idiom or grammatical structure used in another language</term> of a nominative case put absolutely <note>An "absolute nominative" occurs when a noun is placed at the start of a sentence for emphasis but isn't the direct subject of the main verb, such as "He that overcomes, I will make him a pillar."</note>, such as we observed in Chapter 2, verse 26. He shall not fear any ruin or slipping <note>original: "slidinge"</note>, no matter how the tempestuous rain falls, the floods arise, the winds blow, and all things rush together against him in a single assault. He alludes to those two bronze <note>original: "brasen"</note> pillars placed in the Temple by Solomon, which represented the stability of the sons of God (1 Kings 7:15). And so this Church is, by God’s mercy, not defiled with any schism or filthy revolt, as we have seen the Church of Sardis to be. Because Sardis took no care to establish a full and thorough reformation, she lost many of her citizens by God’s just judgment—just as a fig tree loses her green figs—so far were they from being pillars. But Philadelphia would be without this grief; not that it would lack some renegades <note>original: "runnagates"</note> from their holy profession (which they might pretend to follow for a time), but because these few false-hearted ones would actually cause the faith and diligence of this Church to shine more brightly as it examines and casts out these hypocrites, rather than staining the church with any blot of schism or apostasy.

*Neither shall he go forth any more.* This pillar is described by two properties: the first is perpetuity, and the second is having a name written upon it. Perpetuity is signified in these words, *neither shall he go forth any more*. The force of these words seems to be an answer to a hidden doubt which might perhaps trouble someone's mind: because those pillars in the ancient Temple were broken when the city was taken by Nebuchadnezzar, and their bronze was carried into Babylon (Jeremiah 52:17). Lest anyone should fear that the same might happen here—namely, that though a person might be settled for a time in this Temple, he might eventually be banished from it—Christ tells them to be of good cheer. For he promises that he shall be such a pillar that no Nebuchadnezzar shall ever break it in pieces or carry it away by force to any place. "The Son stays in the house forever" (John 8:35). The handmaid with her son is cast out, but the heir <note>original: "aire" – an archaic spelling of heir</note> shall live always in his father's sight (Galatians 4:30, etc.).

<page-num>121</page-num>

# OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chapter 3.

The Temple, whose design the Holy Spirit points toward and explains here, teaches us along the way that nothing in that ancient Temple was ordained in vain, even if it seemed to be of no importance at all. Solomon called the two pillars he erected by two notable names: the one on the right hand he called *Jachin* <note>original: "Iachim"</note>, which means *He will establish*; the one on the left hand he called *Boaz*, which means *In it is strength* (1 Kings 7:21). He showed—not only by the material they were made of, but also by their names—the steadfastness in which the elect stand before God, both for the present and for the time to come. For the present, the children of God have strength within themselves; for the time to come, God will establish them with His grace so firmly that they shall never wholly depart from Him.

Furthermore, if I may briefly touch upon this point, these two names also seem to signify the two Churches of the Jews and the Gentiles. The Jewish Church is represented by *Jachin* on the right hand, as it is the one God would eventually establish in His own time, though it had not yet attained this stability due to the stubbornness of their minds, by which they would reject Christ when He arrived. The Gentile Church is represented by *Boaz* on the left hand, because of the immediate strength that would be found in her when she embraced Christ at the first hearing. 

Thus, Christ shall write better names upon these pillars than those of *Jachin* and *Boaz*. For first, He shall write upon them the name of His God, so that it may be made plain to all men that these people are chosen from among the rest to be God’s special possession. This is similar to the common practice of marking items openly with titles to declare to everyone whom they belong to. In this sense, it was said, *And they shall know that I have loved you (verse 9)*. For this reason also, *Holiness to the Lord* was written upon the little bells that hung upon the horses in the Prophet Zechariah (Chapter 14:20). 

The second name is that of the *New Jerusalem*, discussed in Chapter 21:2, etc. This reward belongs to that future time. From this, it is clear that these seven letters <note>original: "Epistles"</note> concerned not only the current condition of the seven cities but also, in the manner of "types" <term>types: Historical events or people that serve as prophetic symbols or patterns for the future</term>, encompass the ages following for a long period of time, just as we have interpreted them. Regarding this *New Jerusalem*, we shall show in the proper place that it is not the city which the saints shall enjoy in the heavens after this life, but rather a Church that is to be expected on earth—the most noble and pure of all others that have ever existed up to that time.

# Chapter 3. A REVELATION,

The rewards do, in a particular way, serve the specific times described; for if *this* happiness were only to occur after the final resurrection, it would be common to all the Saints, not unique to this church of Philadelphia. This signifies two things: first, that the Philadelphians would endure until that restoration of the Church when the new Jerusalem shall come down from heaven and dwell <note>original: "converse"</note> with men; and second, that they shall be joined with it in covenant and society, to be endowed with the gifts of that heavenly Jerusalem and to enjoy the same rights and happiness with it. At that time, all men shall acknowledge that your reformation is not a device of man's brain (as contentious brawlers <note>original: "brablers" – those who argue loudly and pointlessly</note> insist it is) when they see those same ordinances <note>established religious laws or forms of worship</note> flourishing in the new Jerusalem. 

The third name is the "new name" of a son. What do you think <note>original: "trowe ye"</note> can be new in this name? Undoubtedly, it is that it is not yet acknowledged by the world. Hitherto, Christ has allowed tyrants to dominate and to tread the Christian name underfoot, as if Christ were only a titular King—someone who has the right to reign, but lacks the power. But at last, he shall arise and take his scepter <note>original: "the clubbe"</note> into his hands; he shall crush all his enemies and give his Spouse <note>the Church</note> the victory. He shall be magnified by all men throughout the whole world as this King of Kings. He shall take his servants into the fellowship of this glory and deliver them from those calamities that currently oppress them. He shall give them power over their enemies and grant them the full honor of his kingdom, as far as mortal men are capable of receiving it. 

Now, there is some difference between a "new name" used by itself (as in chapter 2:17) and the "new name" of a son mentioned here. The former refers to the certainty of adoption by Christ—a faith that was very weak during the state of the church at Pergamus. This latter name refers to the fellowship of that kingdom, which shall be shared with his servants in the latter times.

**13. He who has an ear.** Hear therefore, O Philadelphia, and rejoice! You are small and lovely, but God shall exalt you. Only go forward constantly, and apply your study and care more earnestly. Do not give back even one bit <note>original: "one whitt"</note>, nor care for the scoffs of the wicked. By their mocking, they shall pull woeful plagues upon themselves, but they shall bring you a crown of glory. The end of your warfare is coming shortly; in the meantime, we will pray for your peace and prosperity. Join your own mutual wishes and prayers...

## The Analysis or Resolution <note>A logical breakdown or summary of the text's structure</note> of the Letter to the Laodiceans.

<image-desc>A large, ornate woodcut drop cap 'S' decorated with vine and floral motifs.</image-desc>
*So much for the Letter to the Philadelphians. The last of all, written to the Laodiceans, remains; the address <note>original: "Inscription"</note> of which is to the Angel, just like those of the previous letters. The description of him by whom it is sent is taken from two attributes: first, his truth—partly in his promises, in that he is "Amen," and partly in his doctrine, in that he is a "faithful and true witness"; second, his power, by which he is the "beginning of the creation <note>original: "creatures"</note> of God" (verse 14). The narrative first reproves him and shows the seriousness of his sin, both indirectly <note>original: "closely"</note> by omitting the mention of any good thing in him (contrary to the course he took with all the former churches), and also openly, both by comparing his state with coldness as a lesser evil (verse 15) and by establishing the punishment that is to be inflicted, which is being vomited out of his mouth (verse 16). After that, he shows the way to heal this disease, both by revealing the cause of it—which is a false belief <note>original: "persuasion"</note> in his own worth and excellence and ignorance of his own misery (verse 17)—as well as by prescribing the remedy, which is to be obtained from Christ alone (verse 18). And not only this, but also by persuading him to use it, both by threatening a punishment <note>original: "chastisement"</note> fit for sons if they should neglect it (verse 19) and by explaining the ease of applying it (verse 20) and the reward (verse 21). The final conclusion is the usual epilogue of hearing what the Spirit says to the churches (verse 22).*

## THE EXPOSITION.

<margin>Lukewarm, vainglorious Laodicea.</margin>
14. *And to the Angel of the Laodiceans.* Laodicea, situated by the River Lycus, was in ancient times a great and renowned city, rich in citizens, wealth, and all things, as we have shown in Chapter 1, verse 11. It was built by Antiochus, the son of Stratonice, and was named Laodicea as a favor to his wife, Laodice—a name which signifies a "princess of the people" to whom she gave laws and among whom she administered justice. Because of this, we call it "glorious" or "boasting" Laodicea, as it was a great city both in name and in its own estimation, bragging that it is rich and lacks nothing (verse 17). According to Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Greco-Roman geographer and astronomer</note>, it is located more to the east than the south of Philadelphia, no more than ten "scruples" <note>A small unit of geographic measurement used in ancient maps</note> of ground away. It is the third city mentioned since the reference to Jezebel <note>Referring to the corrupt influence mentioned in the letter to Thyatira</note> was last made, whose infamy and wickedness the Church of Sardis removed from the churches. This church has a unique characteristic: it has no counterpart set against it, unlike the previous churches.

Thyatira was paired against Ephesus, Sardis against Smyrna, and Philadelphia against Pergamus; however, Laodicea, the seventh city, lacks a parallel to match it, standing as a peerless paragon. Its counterpart <note>original: "Counterpaine," meaning a matching part or duplicate</note> is the third Reformed Church. Before I identify this church by name, I must earnestly request that readers set aside any unjust suspicions they might harbor against me or any offense they might take at my words. Truly, it was no disordered emotion of my heart that led me to seek out such an unpleasant application for this letter. God is my witness that I am not troubled by envy regarding any man's wealth or honors. The small estate I own fully satisfies me. Nor have I ever considered anything more foolish than for a man to try to please himself by displeasing others. Indeed, how foul and shameful it is for someone to lie there, raking through the sores of his brothers like a fly? My mind and disposition have always been such that I could never tolerate such behavior. But when I perceived that these seven cities were presented as a type <note>A symbolic model or prophetic pattern</note> of all the churches among the Gentiles, and when I further saw...

Having seen clearly both the order of time and the marvelous agreement of all things together, I did not dare to treacherously bury the truth in silence, lest I should make myself an accessory to so bloody a sin as the damnation of other men's souls.

God forbid that I should willingly stain that Church with even the smallest blot of infamy—the Church which, by the mercy of God, gave me birth, raised me, and continues to sustain me. For that reason, I desire with my daily wishes and efforts for it to be, and to remain, a most blessed Church. But since a boil <note>original: "Bile"</note> cannot be healed unless it is handled, nor handled without some pain and smarting grief, I thought it my duty to subject myself to whatever troubles might arise rather than betray the salvation of that Church, whose state ought to be of more account to every one of us than his own. Truly, he who gathers the tears of his children into his bottle knows right well that I have not surveyed this Laodicea with dry eyes. I could not help but pour forth tears and sighs from the bottom of my heart when I beheld Christ himself loathing us and provoked to extreme anger against us.

Therefore, let no man blame me for speaking what not so much my own mind, but the duty of a faithful Interpreter compels me to utter. I hope that those who love the truth will not disdain and reject so fair a petition. Relying on that hope—but chiefly on the help of him who is the guide of my way and my life—I will immediately prepare myself to address the matter. The counterpart <note>original: "Counterpaine"</note> of Laodicea is the third reformed Church, namely: Our Church of England. For all the purer <note>Meaning the Protestant or Reformed churches</note> Churches are to be considered in three categories. Either they follow the steps that Luther first walked—such as the Churches of Germany (especially Saxony), Sweden <note>original: "Sueueland"</note>, and Denmark—or else they reject the error of Consubstantiation <term>The Lutheran doctrine that the body and blood of Christ coexist "in, with, and under" the substance of the bread and wine in the Eucharist.</term> as all the rest do by common consent. Yet these others do not agree in all things, but follow a different manner of government: the French Churches and those allied with them follow one way, and our Church of England follows another—a specific and peculiar one, standing as it were, unique and alone <note>original: "A, per se A," a Latin-based idiom indicating something that stands by itself or is incomparable</note> in its system of government.

### Chapter 3. A REVELATION

From this, three distinct groups arise which correspond to three types: Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea. These appeared after the overthrow of Jezebel—that is, after the yoke of Roman tyranny was shaken off. Our own Church of England corresponds most closely to Laodicea, the last of them, as its beginning was the most recent, starting in the year 1547. This was when King Edward <note>King Edward VI</note>, of most noble memory, came to the throne. At that time, the Church was finally confirmed and established, and eleven years later, our most gracious Queen <note>Queen Elizabeth I</note> began her reign. 

Her father, the most mighty King Henry <note>King Henry VIII</note>, had cast out the Pope, but he retained the superstitions of the Catholic Church. Before he even began to move against the Pope, the churches of Germany and Switzerland had already been founded. The Scottish Church was born and rose up after ours. However, it is rightly numbered among these Reformed churches because it agrees with them in its form of church government. Therefore, it is considered to have the same origin, which should be judged more by its agreement on essential matters than by differences in timing alone. Therefore, our own Church of England is the only one that serves as a precise counterpart <term>original: "Counterpaine point-uice"; a duplicate that matches perfectly</term> to Laodicea, as it was the last of those churches in which a significant difference is visible.

"These things says the *Amen*." *Amen* is used here as if it were a proper name that does not change its form. "The Amen" <note>original: *ho Amēn*</note> is used in the same way as "The One Who Is" <note>original: *ho ōn*</note>—"He who is, who was, and who is to come"—mentioned previously in the first chapter. This threefold property given to Christ in this passage is intended to teach us what kind of Governor Christ would show himself to be within this Church of England. 

The first property is taken from the first chapter, verse 18. Although the word *Amen* lacks the Greek article "the" <note>original: *ho*</note> that usually accompanies nouns there, and it is not included at all by the Latin translator <note>original: "the vulgar Interpreter," referring to the Vulgate Bible</note>, this current passage suggests that it ought to be read there as well. The second property is taken not from the vision in the first chapter, but from the opening of the general letter in verse 5. The third property is not found there in those exact words, but in the eighth verse he is called "the beginning and the end," from which this phrase seems to be derived: "the beginning of the creation of God." These first two properties serve to express his double truth: one in his promises, and the other in his teaching. Regarding the first, he is called *Amen*, according to the words of the Apostle: "In him all the promises of God are 'Yes' and 'Amen'" (2 Corinthians 1:20).

# ON THE APOCALYPSE. Chapter 3.

In respect of this, he is called the faithful and true witness. Regarding that, Christ takes this name upon himself at this time because he would demonstrate his truth most notably in these days, by keeping his word with this Church to fulfill his promises. 

But what are those promises? They are all the blessings of heaven, earth, livestock, children, peace, war, good health, and such like, which are promised in the Law to those who will listen to the voice of the Lord; whereas all contrary curses are threatened against those who disobey it (*Deuteronomy 28*). How these were performed for the *Laodiceans* is not so clearly seen by us because we lack the light of *history* to inform us about this. 

But for our *England*, nothing can be clearer than the extraordinary goodness of God toward us in this matter. For during these forty-two years and more, what great abundance of all good things has he poured upon this island of ours? He has given us a most gracious *Queen* <note>Queen Elizabeth I, who had reigned for 42 years by 1600</note>, so excellent in all things that are praiseworthy that no other age has ever seen her equal; and together with her, he has granted us peace. 

What good things have not flowed from that peace? By means of it, laws are in force, justice is executed, every man enjoys his own property, injuries are repressed, and all shameful conduct in word or deed is restrained. The nobility are honored, the common people work hard at their trades, scholarship flourishes, handicrafts are practiced, cities are beautifully adorned, wealth is increased, our youth grows up in great numbers, the fields abound with grain <note>original: "corne"; in this period, "corn" referred to any cereal crop like wheat or barley</note>, the pastures with livestock, and the mountains with sheep. 

Why say more? It is from this peace that this land has been a haven and a harbor lying open to those who were exiled for *Christ's* cause. Those who have been oppressed by tyrants have had aid and relief from here; indeed, it is our chief—if not our only—work to help those who are distressed by poverty. 

Besides, we enjoy all these things while, in the meantime, our ears ring on almost every side with news of the nations that are in an uproar around us—as much as they are beaten by the waves of the sea that surrounds us <note>The author is contrasting England's internal peace with the violent religious conflicts occurring in 16th-century France and the Netherlands</note>. Never had *England* such long and quiet *halcyon days* <term>original: "Halcyon dayes"; a mythical period of calm and prosperity</term>. Foreign countries are astonished at our good fortune; our enemies gnash their teeth against it with envy; and (which is the only thing that makes us miserable) we ourselves hardly know or acknowledge what it is and where it comes from. But blessed be your name, O *Amen* <note>The name "Amen" is used here for Christ, representing his role as the ultimate truth</note>, you who are most true—indeed, Truth itself—who have been the author and sustainer of this...

...looks upon it with eyes that are impartial and objective, it may seem to him—and rightly so—to be void of all virtue whatsoever. It is a horrible evil that, as it were, says to all goodness: "What have I to do with you? Get far enough away from me!" And though we may well conjecture by this kind of silence which the Holy Spirit uses here how desperate the disease of this Church is, yet in the next words following, its quality is described to us in a more plain and vivid manner. 

And first, for the sake of clarity, it is described by a denial of opposites. *I know* (he says) *that you are neither cold nor hot*, but some odd, strange thing molten and compacted together from them both. So this evil consists of certain opposites strangely tempered and blended together. Now, he calls that person "cold" who can well endure that the duties of godliness should lie dead and out of esteem, caring little or nothing at all what way he himself or others take to worship God. He calls him "hot" who boils with heat and fervor of spirit in his due and full regard for God's worship, being like boiling water that seethes and bubbles over <note>original: "plaweth" — an archaic term for boiling or bubbling up</note> (as we say) in the pot with a certain restless motion. For that is what the word *hot* in the Greek signifies: namely, such a person who can by no means endure superstitious and impious religions, but will hazard all he has, as far as possible, to bring about a reformation. For we must not think that being "hot" is a vice in this place—as if it were an unthinking zeal, as is the case with the habits of moral virtues, where both extremes (straying from the middle ground <note>original: "mediocritie" — referring to the Aristotelian concept of virtue as a "golden mean" between two extremes</note> toward either excess or deficiency) are faults and vices, as we see in generosity, courage, temperance, and the rest. Instead, it is a matter of commendation, being the only virtue from which both coldness and lukewarmness deviate.

This we see in that Apollos is said to have been *fervent in the Spirit* <margin>Acts 18:25</margin>. And Paul exhorts men *to be fervent in the Spirit* <margin>Romans 12:11</margin>. Again, if being "hot" were in this place to deviate from the right state of mind through an excess, then being "lukewarm" would be the nature of virtue, which keeps the middle ground between two extremes. But heat or zeal here is an affection that pursues the love of holiness with a great intensity of mind, which is, as it were, a certain holy violence, such as is described in <margin>Matthew 11:12</margin>. The deficiency of this—either that of coldness, which is more distant, or this of lukewarmness, which is nearer—is here found fault

16. *Therefore because you are lukewarm.* The sharpness of the punishment also reveals the foulness of the sin, which seems to be confirmed with an oath. Now, this kind of concealing part of the statement in imprecations <note>An imprecation is a formal curse or a spoken oath calling for a specific punishment.</note> is often used: *“Therefore I swore in my wrath, if they shall enter into my rest”* (Hebrews 3:11).

It will happen that *I shall spew you out.* As it goes with food, those things that are either hot or cold are retained by the stomach because of their intense quality, which makes them felt and provokes the stomach to receive them gladly. But that which is lukewarm—because it has a heat close to the stomach's own heat and is something the stomach is well acquainted with—is neither perceived nor felt when it goes in. Therefore, when it has entered, it is not digested <note>original: "concocted"</note>, but remains without being processed; at last, becoming troublesome because of its long stay, it is cast out of doors with loathing, like an unprofitable guest. <meta>This page continues the interpretation of the "lukewarm" state of the Church of Laodicea, specifically addressing the pride that stems from material wealth and how this applies to the contemporary Church of England.</meta>

<page-num>137</page-num>
<header>OF THE REVELATION. Chap. 3.</header>

He would have been lukewarm if he had looked for spiritual riches from anyone other than Christ alone; but rather, he would be stone cold and altogether estranged from grace, being cut off and fallen from Christ and His grace <note>original: "abolished and fallen from Christ"; see Galatians 5:4</note>. Now, he seems to have abounded with earthly riches because of the wealthiness of the city which we spoke of in Chapter 1:11. This was perhaps the cause that made Archippus more negligent in his ministry; it was for this reason that Paul wanted him to be admonished in Colossians 4:17. Yet, it seems little fruit followed afterward, seeing that even until these days when this Revelation was written, there was such great matter for boasting—and that not recently, but acquired and provided long ago. 

The plenty of all things for the maintaining of this life therefore birthed this lukewarmness. It is not strange that prosperity should secretly steal away the minds of men and draw them away from God. It is often commanded in the Law that they should take heed to themselves, lest when they were full and satisfied with God’s blessings, they should forget the Lord. Now, here is a threefold boasting: first, of his present abundance; second, of his long-continuing abundance; and third, of his full and all-sufficient abundance. For the words require that those words, *I am rich*, should be referred to his present riches; those, *I have been rich* <note>original: "I haue bene rich"; most modern translations render this as "I have become wealthy"</note>, to those that are past; and those, *I want nothing*, to the full contentment he had in them. From this, there must necessarily arise an undoubted persuasion that the durability of his estate and happiness would remain constant forever after. 

Now it is to be observed that he represents this Angel boasting in his own words, differently than has been done until now. This was not in vain, seeing nothing can be spoken rashly by the Holy Ghost. But yet, regarding the Angel of Laodicea, no such evident application of these words offers itself. In a base and filthy manner, they use swelling words to proclaim the happiness of our Church, governed as it is and thereby made so "happy," as they say; they do this both in their printed books and in their sermons. It was not for nothing, therefore, that the Holy Spirit presents this Angel <note>The "Angel" refers to the leadership or personification of the church being addressed in Revelation.</note> boasting of himself; in this, He sets before our eyes our notorious vainglory. 

Now, the first boast is, as we have said, of our present riches. How our Angel triumphs in this regard, and lifts up his head above all other Reformed Churches! "In other places," he says, "the pastors of the churches are poor and of low degree, ranked almost among the common and base kind of people; they have no greater authority than what their piety and their learning can acquire for them. But our Bishops are the Peers of the Realm, ranked above many noblemen in honor—yes, and equal to any of the highest and greatest earls in wealth, attendance, the stateliness of their palaces, and all other worldly pomp." 

As for the next ranks of the clergy, how mighty, massive, and "thick-pocketed" have they grown with wealth? The Deans, the Archdeacons, the Prebendaries, and the Queen’s Chaplains—who have their <term>tot-quots</term> <note>original: "Tot-quots of Benefices"; a legal dispensation (from the Latin *tot quot*, meaning "as many as") allowing a clergyman to hold as many church positions or income-generating "benefices" as they could obtain.</note> of benefices heaped up one upon another—match esquires at least in yearly revenues. Do you think this does not greatly amplify the honor of our Church, to have our fine silk-clad ministers glitter as they go, and strut through the streets with entourages like noblemen, and by this means drive away contempt from the ministry? 

Where can you see any church or churchmen, since the Pope was turned out, so fat and flourishing in worldly prosperity? Nowhere indeed; nor do I envy this; only this vainglory of ours is not good. And I would to God that our wealth served rather to promote God’s glory than to hinder and deface it. But of this I am sure: our riches have brought in this woeful lukewarmness, while we make no account of true piety in order to hold onto them. 

The second boast is of the long duration that our prosperity has had. For it is not some "yesterday-abundance" that came in like a flash flood, which is suddenly here and gone, but such as has now been established among us for these whole forty-two years <note>The author is likely writing around 1600, measuring from the beginning of Queen Elizabeth I's reign in 1558.</note>; and that with such great peace and plenty of all things! <header>OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chapter 3.</header>

...experience of so long a time has proved to be absolutely happy? Truly, I would not be the man to accept this challenge unless I had this truth to use as a strong battering-piece to beat down all this flourish: namely, that worldly prosperity—and especially that of such long continuance—is an argument for God's patience and long-suffering toward the wicked, rather than for man's righteousness and acceptance with God.

In the third place, he boasts of himself that he lacks <note>original: "wanteth"</note> nothing. "Why do you tell me," he says, "of other Reformed Churches? I see no reason why other Reformed Churches should not rather imitate ours, than we theirs, seeing we are in no way inferior to them." *In the Answer to the Admonition made to the Parliament, Page 226.* Yes, why do you call me back to the primitive <note>Referring to the early, original church of the Apostles.</note> Church? As if we are to be tied to the first beginnings of things, as you would bind little infants in their blankets with swaddling bands? And as if it were not lawful for us to change those primitive rudiments, which were not as profitable in their first origin as they seem to be harmful <note>original: "pernicious"</note> today. *In a certain Apology made for our Church Government, Page 81.* 

This is a bold assertion—to say nothing more and call it impious—for a man to claim and avow that something ordained by the Apostles is now no less hurtful for our churches than it was beneficial <note>original: "behoofull"</note> for those to whom it was first appointed. But I willingly pardon the offense of these words, spoken more in the heat of contention than in deliberate malice. In the meantime, let such a person who speaks this way know that the Church which the Apostles founded was the most perfect of all, and that it is not to be perfected with the inventions of those who come after. Rather, all other churches are to be examined and measured by its rule, according to that solemn decree of the First Council of Nicaea: *Let ancient customs prevail* <note>original Latin: "Ta archaia ethe krateito"</note>. And that of Tertullian in *Against Praxeas*: *Whatever is first is true, and whatever is later is false.* 

Neither is it to be doubted that Paul taught Timothy most fully *how he ought to conduct himself in the house of God* (1 Timothy 3:15). What, are all those precepts now worn out of fashion and outdated with age? Shall time, the mistress of things, teach us better and surer things to which the things we received from the Apostles must give way? Certainly, the Church is like Adam: best and most whole in her first origin; the further it goes from that, the more corrupt matter it gathers.

Regardless, it is all the same fault to creep in, whether it be by bribery and **simony** <term>the illegal buying or selling of church offices</term>, or by fawning and flattery. In every place and point, they play the parts of miserable beggars. 

Some beg more craftily, like those who sit by the highways or at crossroads and offer peeled <note>original: "pilled"</note> sticks to travelers to get a piece of money, as if exchanging a pennyworth for a penny. In the same way, these men clear the path for their petitions by giving large sums of money upfront, or else by agreeing to give away some of their yearly **tithes** <term>a tenth of one's income paid to the church</term> as a bribe <note>original: "gratification"</note>.

But some will say all this is not the corruption of the laws, but the corruptness of men. No, surely, as long as that method of granting ecclesiastical <term>church-related</term> positions continues, as has been the practice among us to this day, no remedy can be applied to cure or prevent this "beggarliness." Do we not find this to be true enough in our experience? In the recent Parliament, laws were enacted severely against it; but what came of that? Nothing, truly, except that it made men act more secretly and cunningly to cheat <note>original: "cosen"</note> the law. We must not think we can do any good with our laws where Christ’s laws are not observed. 

But to proceed: once the **living** <term>a church office that provided a salary</term> is obtained from the patron through begging, what a great deal of "begging work" remains for those ***Sir John Lack-latines*** <note>A derisive name for uneducated priests who knew no Latin, the language then required for scholarship and liturgy.</note> so that they might be officially instituted by the **Bishops** <note>original: "B b," an abbreviation for Bishops.</note>. Here he must petition not only the Right Reverend Lord **Bishop**, but also the Master Examiner, his Lordship's Groom of the Chamber, his Registrar, the Yeoman of his Buttery and Larder <note>The servants in charge of the Bishop's food and wine storage.</note>—yes, even the lowliest person who belongs to him. 

It is not that a lack of Latin and learning will keep him from entering his **benefice** <term>a church office providing an income</term>, but rather that he who needs extra favor for a quick result, or an audience with my Lord Bishop, or the like, must pay the servants better, whose profit comes rolling <note>original: "trowlinge"</note> in this way. There is no castle so well-defended that a Latin-less ass laden with gold may not scale and conquer it. Neither is there almost anyone so unfit that they are rejected; but as for what schemes <note>original: "engines"</note> they use to prevail, let them look to it. The same is the condition of **Prebendaries**, **Archdeacons**, and **Deans** <note>These are higher administrative or honorary offices within the cathedral or diocesan hierarchy.</note>.

This shameful way of obtaining benefices <note>original: "beggarly coming to Benefices." A benefice was a church office, such as a rector or vicar, that provided a living through land or tithes.</note> and ecclesiastical functions must end. By this method, it comes to pass that pastors do not beg for positions, but are instead sought after; they are promoted not because of their money, but because of their integrity <note>original: "honestie"</note>; not by favor, but by learning; not at the whim of any one man, but by the voices and consent of their own flock. 

Christ insists that this "gold" be bought from him because he is the one who has clearly described this entire order, and he has not left men free to do as they please in this matter. As long as the power remains solely with the patron <note>A person, often a local landowner, who held the right to appoint a member of the clergy to a particular church.</note> and the bishop, there will never be a lack of those who give and take bribes, allowing themselves to be corrupted with gifts. *But if Christ’s rule is followed, this begging poverty will flee away and never return. For this gold is tested in the fire, frequently approved, and thoroughly refined. We see its excellence in the early church <note>original: "primitiue Church"</note>, and even today in our neighboring churches <note>Likely referring to the Reformed or Presbyterian churches in Scotland or continental Europe, which practiced congregational election of ministers.</note>. It fears no touchstone; it does not flee for fear of any fire; it does not burst apart under the strike of any hammer. Instead, it stands to this day—just as it stood of old—invincible, to the great glory of those who have grown rich by it.*

The *white garments* are contrasted with the previously mentioned "honors" and "nakedness"—that is, the contempt they received. Christ insists that these also be bought from him, as he alone possesses them, and they are most precious and praiseworthy. For how can contempt hurt those whom their own worthiness has chosen, their learning has ordained, and their sanctified heart and conduct have preferred? These are men whom many have earnestly desired for their proven piety, whom they admire for their diligence in teaching, whom they stand in awe of because the truth has free passage in their ministry, and whom they reverence as examples of all virtue and goodness. 

*Be an example to the believers,* says Paul, *in word, in conduct, in love, in spirit, in faith, in purity; let no one despise your youth (1 Timothy 4:12).* Behold, here is the way to deliver a minister from contempt. These garments are indeed full of majesty; when even the young are clothed and covered by them, they do not become lowly or disregarded. ### 19. *As many as I love, etc.* 

These words contain an exhortation to use the remedy, beginning with the chastising of those whom He loves. This is truly a reason of great importance. Whoever a person may be, he is either among the sons of God or the reprobates <note>those rejected by God</note>. If He receives no son whom He does not also reprove and chasten, what will become of the rest of the crowd? A horrible judgment awaits these men; for He who will not pamper <note>original: "cocker"; to indulge or spoil</note> His own sons will surely not spare the others in the slightest degree. 

Therefore, a chastisement hangs over them unless they repent in time—and a very grievous and woeful one at that, as the very words suggest. Such words are usually used as comfort in any affliction that is sharper than ordinary, where the mind is so beaten down that it feels as if the person were forsaken by God. For this reason, He tells them that those He is accustomed to strike with such sharp punishments are His sons, lest they should despair of His fatherly goodness because of the severity of the punishment. 

Therefore, it is now no time to bicker <note>original: "brabble"</note> and contend with one another, hating and railing against each other. Instead, we must listen diligently to Christ’s alarm and either immediately consider the remedy or else expect some great and lamentable calamity shortly. Now we must observe here that He "reproves" and "chastens"—that is, He convicts and He strikes. For both of these things are to be joined together. It is a useless punishment where words are silenced <note>original: "whisht"</note> and only blows are active. This is why a chastisement is rightly called discipline <note>original: "displinge"; an archaic term for discipline or physical correction</note>, through which the offender feels pain and finds a lesson to learn at the same time. But such trivial points of yours as these easily fall apart on their own, so I do not need to trouble myself with refuting them.

19. > *As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten.*
These words contain an exhortation to use the remedy, starting first with the chastising of those whom he loves. This is truly a reason of great importance. Whoever he may be, he is either among the children of God or the reprobates <term>Reprobates: those rejected by God and destined for damnation.</term>. If he receives no son whom he does not reprove and discipline, what will become of the rest of the crowd? <note>original: "rout"</note> A horrible judgment awaits these men; for he who will not pamper <term>Cocker: to indulge or spoil a child.</term> his own sons will certainly not spare them in the slightest. There hangs, therefore, a punishment over them unless they repent in time—and a very grievous and sorrowful one—as the very words suggest. These words are usually used as a comfort in any sharper-than-ordinary affliction where the mind is so beaten down it feels as if a person were forsaken by God. For this reason, he tells them they are sons whom he is accustomed to strike with such sharp punishments, lest they should despair of his fatherly goodness because of the severity of the punishment.

It is now, therefore, no time to bicker <term>Brabble: to argue or squabble over petty matters.</term> and fight with each other, or to hate and insult one another; rather, we must listen carefully to Christ’s alarm and either immediately think of the remedy or else expect some great and lamentable disaster shortly. Now we must observe here that he does "reprove and chasten"—that is, convict and strike. For both these things are to be joined together. It is a useless punishment where words are silenced <term>Whisht: hushed or kept silent.</term> and only blows are dealt. Because of this, a chastisement is rightly called "discipline" or a "displing" <note>original: "displinge," an archaic term for disciplining or physical penance.</note>, by which the offender feels pain and finds something to learn all at once. But what fruit shall there be then from this long-lasting and harmful conflict, when the son being—

But most of all, this is because the true use of excommunication <note>The author argues that church discipline (excommunication) is the "key" that opens the doors of the conscience to Christ.</note> is restored, whereby the gates of heaven are both shut and opened, and the doors of every man's conscience are unsealed, so that Christ may come in easily without any delay. For where a watch is kept over the behavior of every person—and men are admonished, reproved, cut off, or received back in as the occasion requires, and other things are faithfully and diligently performed which the salvation of everyone requires—there all the bars and bolts of the heart are removed.

He can find no other way into the heart than what he can win with words. We read that the force of these words was indeed great in the past, when three thousand souls were converted by one sermon (Acts 2:41). 

Nor is it any less powerful today in itself; yet there is a difference between a Church that is being gathered for the first time and one that is already established. God shows himself extraordinarily generous when he first invites a people. However, once he has gathered them into one flock, he expects them to grow through the ordinary means he has appointed. Therefore, regarding the fruit of the Gospel, the people feel the loss of such a notable ordinance <note>Here referring to the "censures" or formal church discipline mentioned earlier.</note> just as much as the Angel <note>The "Angel" represents the church leadership or bishop.</note> should acknowledge himself to be maimed and lame when deprived of his lawful power and authority. 

This key is missing from our Church, so it is no wonder that Christ is prevented from entering easily while the doors are shut against him. But what then? Are we left completely destitute of all good things? Not at all; we still enjoy a double benefit that works toward the salvation of the elect. The first of these is Christ’s entrance among those who open to him. The second is the sweet sitting of these men at Christ’s supper. That is the delightful comfort the Saints enjoy by receiving Christ whenever they feel their hearts opened through faith by the help of the Holy Spirit during the preaching of the Word. 

For then he enters in and sups with us, sharing himself most lovingly and comfortingly, just as he told Zacchaeus—who longed to see him and had climbed a sycamore tree—to come down and prepare a place to host him (Luke 19:5). In both of these, Christ communicates himself to his members, keeping a mutual feast with them; he is first entertained by us through our hearing, and then he entertains us in return with the supper of his body.

### *The Analysis or Explanation <note>original: "Resolution"; in this context, it refers to the logical breaking down of a text into its component parts.</note> of Chapter 4.*

*Until now we have spoken of the prophecy of the individual <note>original: "particuler"</note> churches. The prophecy of the whole Church follows, which first presents the matter in summary in this chapter, and then in detail in the rest. This contains a new calling of John, consisting of the thing that was seen—a door opened in heaven—and in the first voice of the trumpet that was heard, verse 1. And lastly, it contains the effect, by which he immediately became "in the Spirit" at the beginning of verse 2. It also contains a universal model <note>original: "Type"; a person, thing, or event that represents or symbolizes a future reality.</note> of the future Church, which is described throughout the rest of the chapter.*

*The Prince of this Church, who is, as it were, the center, is most glorious by means of his throne, most beautiful <note>original: "amiable"</note> to look upon, and shining all around with heavenly brightness, verses 2 and 3. The members, who are like the circumference around this center, are the twenty-four elders, full of majesty and honorable by reason of their thrones, age, holiness, and crowns of gold, verse 4.*

*The things that accompany these persons are partly the gifts which God bestows on this holy company, and partly that worship which the company of the faithful renders back to him. The gifts are, first, protection, whereby great flashes of lightning, thunders, and voices come forth from the throne for the punishment <note>original: "vengeance"</note> of the wicked world because of their attacks <note>original: "attempts"</note> against the congregation of the saints, verse 5. Besides, it will appear no less in those things that follow, that John tells of things that are nearly joined to his own time, so that the words can by no means be so understood. Therefore, that is no firm distribution <note>division or categorization</note>, by which some distinguish the whole prophecy into things present and things to come. The Holy Spirit follows no such division, but mingles many things to come among things present, as they come to hand. For this reason, these words, "after these things," are not referred—in regard to their origin—to the end of the former prophecy, but to the present time of John's age; indeed, to that very moment in time wherein the Holy Spirit revealed these things unto him. Taking a new beginning from that point, he describes the continuous race of the whole Church and annexes those things which could not be sufficiently understood from the former types. Theodore Beza <note>A prominent French Protestant reformer and scholar (1519–1605) known for his Latin translation of the New Testament.</note> rightly translates the words "after these things" with the adverb "hereafter." But in regard to the end, this second prophecy is worthily recorded after the first, as it covers a much longer period of time, reaching even to the final coming of Christ, whereas that former one is limited within far narrower bounds.

From these things, therefore, we gather two points that are very greatly to be observed. The first is that speech is made from this place concerning only such things as follow after the time that this Revelation was made. For he speaks plainly: *And I will show you what things must come to pass hereafter*. Since this was perceived by some of the interpreters, I marvel that it was not observed by them in their exposition, but that they should rather confound the times as if by a violent whirling of them about throughout the whole treatise, so that all things are covered over with most gross darkness. We, being better taught by their example, will borrow light from here for the commentary following. The second point is this: that this prophecy is common to the whole Church, being neither tied to any particular congregations, nor yet bounded with any other limits than those of the whole universal world. The Holy Spirit has set that particular prophecy in the first place so that he might relate common things in common, and not interrupt the order of the narration.

The whole Revelation seems to have been finished on that Lord’s day <note>Sunday</note> alone (Chapter 1:10), and therefore it did not have any intermission after it once began to be shown.

*And behold, there was a throne set in heaven.* So much for the preparation by a new calling. Now he comes to the common type <note>original: "Type"; a symbolic representation or prophetic pattern</note> of the Holy Church. The description of this was necessary before he should set upon the rest of the prophecy. For inasmuch as the manifold chances and notable changes of it were to be related—its flight, its return, its pretended friends, its open enemies, the counterfeit and crafty apostles who would present themselves under the colors <note>pretense</note> of the Church, and many other things of the like nature by which it would be sorely harassed <note>original: "annoyed"; in this period, the word meant to be seriously harmed or troubled</note>—it was necessary that first of all a certain portrait and resemblance should be drawn of that Church. To know this is the principal thing in the whole treatise following, lest perhaps in such great troubles and disturbances, we should either think that it were quite extinguished, or at least, through ignorance of her right form and figure, we should be less able to know which one she is. Therefore, we shall see that this type is common to all ages, as mention is made of it in Chapter 14:3, where the companions and followers of the Lamb sing a new song before the four beasts and the elders. And again, nearer to the consummation <note>completion or end</note> of the whole prophecy, the twenty-four elders and the four beasts fall down and adore God (Chapter 19:4). So elsewhere, as often as speech is made about the true Church, insofar as anything is to be done in the public assembly, it is always noted according to the manner of this type. God, who reigns in the Christian congregations, is the same God whom the ancient Church worshipped from the beginning. And seeing that in the infancy of the Church he gave them no portrait of himself, much less is any likeness to be expected now that she has grown to her ripe and full age. Indeed, this manifestation is more familiar and more ample, seeing that besides one and the same essence—which his common glory expresses—the incomprehensible distinction of the three persons is, in a way, revealed by the three precious stones: the Jasper, the Sardine, and the Emerald. For it pleases the Holy Spirit <note>original: "holy Ghost"</note> to use these delightful creatures for declaring these mysteries, because the grace and beauty that these gems have in this lower world excel above all other things. Because of this, they may be the most fitting images of that delightfulness which surpasses all created understanding, especially since this is a representation of their virtue <note>inner power or essential quality</note> rather than any physical form. 

The first appearance of a Jasper stone resembles the person of the Father. This gem is green and is aptly called the "mother of pearl," as there are so many kinds of it, and the honor given to it is so ancient. Now, what among all gems could more fittingly represent the Father, who is first in order, of an eternity always flourishing, and from whom the rest of the persons have their origin <note>original: "of springe"; referring to the theological concept of the procession of the Trinity</note> without any beginning? 

The second appearance is of the Sardine <note>also known as a Sardius or Carnelian</note>, by which the Son is represented. This gem is red, the color of flesh, which is why it is also called *Carneolus* <note>original: "Carneolus" - Latin for "flesh-colored," from which we get the word "carnelian"</note>. It is very appropriately set in his place, for he took flesh upon himself for us and was made man like us. 

The third appearance is of the rainbow that is the color of an emerald, by which the Holy Spirit is indicated. This is he who encompasses the throne on all sides, being the one who "sits by the throne" (Wisdom of Solomon 9:4 <note>The author quotes the apocryphal Book of Wisdom: "Give me Wisdom, who sits by your throne."</note>). He surrounds the entire circuit of the Divine Majesty with an unspeakable sweetness. For the emerald shows forth such a pleasing, sweet, and shining liveliness that a person's eyes cannot look upon anything more willingly. Yet this is not the kind of rainbow that is commonly called by that name. For this is not positioned opposite the throne, but around it; neither is it a half-circle <note>original: "circle cutt in the middest"</note>, but a whole one—entire and full on every side—for it surrounds the throne. Lastly, it is not three-colored like a natural rainbow, but of one color only: a pure emerald green. Such then is this God, one in nature and three in persons, being the head and center of the Church, whom alone the faithful...

4. **And round about the throne.** So much for the head. Now he adds the body to it, as being the circumference of this Center, as we have said. This is described by the place, number of members, age, clothing, and crowns. The place is twofold: common, which is about the Highest Throne; and proper, which is the peculiar throne of every individual. The place that is common about the Throne is before it, behind it, on the right side, and on the left side, so that it intersects the rainbow at right angles (which also encompassed the Throne, but with a contrary position: above, below, and from either side). For then the rainbow would not be set in a contrary position to it, but only would be surrounded by a larger circuit, just as the circumferences that are nearer to the Center are usually contained within those that are more distant. 

This common position is given to them after the manner of the Saints, who are said to be those who stand round about him; as in the verse, *"Vow and render to the Lord your God, all you who stand round about him"* (Psalm 76:11) <note>original: "Pf.76.12." This is so that perhaps no man should complain that God deals somewhat unequally with him, as one who is set at the very back and has no open passage to God except through messengers and mediators.

# Chapter 4. A Revelation,

the same honor. This specific number of twenty-four thrones and as many elders greatly perplexes interpreters, as everyone knows. There are some who refer them to the twelve *Patriarchs* or twelve *Prophets* and as many *Apostles*, but that seems to be far from the truth. For here, the text speaks of groups that are yet to come, not those that have already passed, as we saw in the first chapter <note>original: "on the first"</note>. Furthermore, it speaks of those whose office is performed on earth, not in heaven properly so-called, as we shall see later in chapters 14:3 and 15:7.

Not to mention that these men stray quite far from the purpose of this vision. Others apply it differently, but it would be tedious to list all their opinions, let alone refute them. It will suffice simply to set down what seems most likely to me and to submit it to the judgment of the godly. The *Holy Spirit* <note>original: "Holy Ghost"</note> alludes to that distribution of holy duties and of the *king’s servants* <note>original: "Kinges seruitours"</note> into twenty-four ranks, which was appointed by *David* through the inspiration of God (1 Chronicles 24, etc.). For first of all, the high *Priests* were divided into twenty-four orders. In the same manner, the chief *Levites* who ministered to the *Priests* were also divided (in the same chapter, verses 1 and 31). The same was true for the *holy musicians* <note>original: "Holy Musitions"</note> (chapter 25) and the *gatekeepers* <note>original: "Porters"</note> (chapter 26). Of those who ministered to the *King*, there were twenty-four thousand in each of their divisions (chapter 27). 

Therefore, since the entire assembly of the children of *Israel* was organized into twenty-four orders—whether we consider the tribe of *Levi* or the rest of the people who were, in a sense, chosen for the *King's* portion to manage his affairs—these *Elders* are appropriately listed in the same number of orders. These *Elders* act as both *Priests* and *Kings* and stand in place of all the faithful who serve *Christ*. 

In addition to this, we are given to understand by this number of twenty-four how much larger the *Church of the Gentiles* is than the *Church of the Jews* was. While the Jewish church was represented by the twelve *Patriarchs* as its chief heads, the Gentile church is twice as large—that is, greater by many degrees. This fixed ratio signifies a vast increase, surpassing the former as much in its number of *citizens* as it does in the clarity of its knowledge. Because of this, the closer they drew to the times of *Christ*, the more they were—beyond all other times—full of light and magnificence. How much did *David* beautify the worship of the *Tabernacle* by describing the offices, and

All things were made of larger dimensions according to the increase of light, which grew as the Sun approached nearer. At last, when Christ was manifested in the flesh, the Sun reached its highest point <note>original: "highest climate"</note>; in respect of whose brightness, all the former light vanished away. Regarding their age, they are all Elders—not because their strength is weakened and worn out with old age, but because of their reverent gray <note>original: "hoarie"</note> hair and their mature and grave judgments with which they embrace the truth. It is also because they have a certain present possession of their dignity, such as is suitable <note>original: "meete"</note> for men of mature age and steady years. Children <note>original: "Infants"</note>, though they are honorable by right of inheritance because of their future hope, nevertheless lack the present enjoyment of things. Indeed, during the entire time of the Law, the heir was like a child: *And differed nothing from a servant, being kept in bondage under the basic principles of the world, as if under tutors and governors; but now, after the fullness of time has come, we are no longer under a schoolmaster.* Instead, we enjoy an adult <note>original: "manlike"</note> liberty, so that all the faithful are now most significantly called Elders (Galatians 3:25 and 4:1-2, etc.). 

The white clothing is the emblem <note>original: "ensigne"</note> to identify the priests, which is the office in which all believers in Christ serve, *presenting their bodies as a living, holy, and acceptable sacrifice unto God, which is their reasonable service of God* (Romans 12:1). The golden crowns on their heads declare the solemn majesty of the kingdom. For kings do not always wear their crowns, but only in solemn meetings, where they strive to make an open show of their glory as the occasion offers. But these elders always possess the ornament of their royal majesty in constant solemnity, as their crowns are never taken off, except when they give honor to their highest King. At those times, their bare heads are more honorable than when they are adorned with crowns. The *Complutensian Polyglot* <note>The first printed polyglot Bible, 1514–17</note> and the *King’s Bible* <note>The Antwerp Polyglot sponsored by Philip II of Spain, 1568–72</note> do not read "*and they had*"; neither does Aretas <note>A 10th-century Greek commentator on Revelation</note>. If those words are to be added, the usual article which is missing here should be supplied as: "*who also had.*"

so that they pay dear for their contempt, tyranny, and wrongs which they offer to—and with which they afflict—the only beloved Spouse of Christ. But He who sat on the Throne did not suffer any man to go unpunished <note>original: "scot free"</note> for oppressing His Saints. He even reproved Kings for *their sakes*, saying, *Touch not my anointed, and do my Prophets no harm* (Psalm 105:14-15). For the Lord *will roar out of Zion, and will put forth His voice out of Jerusalem* (Amos 1:2). Why then does the world not become wise at last, when it sees that this is the fountainhead <note>original: "headspring"</note> of all the evils that fall upon it? This happens because it handles the Church so contemptuously and with such indignities. 

Now, the lightnings and thunders signify the terrible punishments—those that can by no means be avoided—which rush upon men from heaven. But why are "voices" added? Voices indeed often signify the crash of thunders, as in Exodus 19:16: *And there were voices and lightnings, and a thick cloud upon that mountain, and an exceedingly powerful voice of a trumpet.* So also in Chapter 20:18: *And all the people perceived the voices, and the flashes of lightnings, and the voice of the trumpet.* 

But seeing that express mention is made in this place of the thunders, "voices" here are referred to something else: namely, to the sound of the trumpet. For here is an allusion to that dreadful blast given at the delivery of the Law, by which the Israelites were summoned <note>original: "cited"</note> to the tribunal and judgment of God. When that sound continued and grew much louder, Moses said: *I am astonished and tremble for fear* (Exodus 19:19, Hebrews 12:21). 

For the expectation of God's judgment shook his mind with fear more than the actual horror of that terrible spectacle. A mind may somehow bear the fear of a spectacle unless a conscience of sin afflicts it. When the mind is once wasted and broken by the sense of sin, it trembles at the slightest appearance <note>original: "shewe"</note> of evil, as if it were a torment prepared for it and about to be endured immediately. The "voices" here, therefore, are certain sad and sorrowful forebodings <note>original: "prognosticates"</note>, or the stings of conscience, by which they are always tormented in their minds with the expectation of some more grievous evil that is to come. This fear shall be a rack to the wicked,

The number of these Spirits is sevenfold, according to the manifold variety of the gifts with which he adorns the faithful, as we see this number used everywhere to note an indefinite number. 6. *Now there was before the throne a sea of glass.* The first outward gift, which serves to produce and increase those inward gifts as an instrumental cause, is the Sea of Glass. For how can that which is before the throne—surrounded by a company of elders standing all around it—be poured out on all sides like a sea properly so called <note>The author distinguishes between a literal ocean and the large ritual basin used in the Temple</note>? Now we must examine the descriptions <term>original: epithetes</term> given to it to see what kind of sea this is. The first of these is that he calls it a "glassy sea." Why so? Is it because of the color? There is indeed a "glassy" color, and it is one that suits the sea. This is why Virgil, in describing the goddesses and nymphs of the sea, gives them that color: *The greenish, glassy nymphs,* he says, *were carding <term>original: toze; to comb or pull apart</term> the fleeces of wool that came from Miletus, which were dyed with a deep color* (Virgil, *Georgics* book 4). And again, a little after that: *They all were astonished, sitting upon their glassy stools.* It is "glassy" indeed, but not just in color, but in its material—denoting something that shines so that one may see through it, rather than just a color without substance. The other attribute, "like crystal," serves to signify this. 

It is called a glassy sea to let us see the difference between this and the "legal sea" <note>The "legal sea" refers to the "Brazen Sea," the large bronze washbasin used by priests in Solomon's Temple under the Mosaic Law.</note>. That sea, being made of bronze—which is a thick and dark material—could not be seen through by any man’s sight (1 Kings 7:23). God's face shone upon his people, but somewhat obscurely under those rites and ceremonies; Moses also declared this *by putting a veil on his face, so that the children of Israel could not see into the end of that which is abolished* (2 Corinthians 3:13). There is indeed a certain incomprehensible majesty of God to be clearly seen in the creation, but this knowledge is common even to the reprobates <term>original: Reprobates; those rejected by God or outside of His grace</term>. God has stored such an abundant supply of both in this Sea that there is no need to fetch anything from other drains and ditches. And this ought to be the goal <term>original: scope</term> of all worship: that it may show us the face of God. The more that either doctrine or rituals hinder our eyesight in this regard, the more both of them wander from the truth.

The other epithet <term>original: Epithete; a descriptive title or adjective</term> is that it is like crystal. Why is there a need for this second description? Namely, to teach us not only that the glass is so bright that a man may see through it, but also that it is of a most pure brightness, which no other color mingled with it stains or darkens at all. For crystal is, as it were, without any color, coming very close to the purity of the air, which a man's eyes can pierce through almost as easily as the air itself. Therefore, no device of the human brain is infused into this Sea; rather, it is pure and exempt from all filth that can be added to it, just as it is also perfect and complete without any subtraction—exactly as it is commanded to be kept (Deuteronomy 4:2). Such is the worship of the saints in Christ, in whom God the Father, beholding all his faithful elect, finds no "colored" matter in them—nothing, truly, that is maimed <note>original: "mayned" (maimed); damaged, defective, or incomplete</note> and imperfect, nothing that is filthy and polluted. The whole worship of God ought to aim at this purity and perfection, and to be framed...

I will only say this—which applies to this whole book—that in every allegorical interpretation, the purpose and scope of the allegory must be respected above all else. Without this, every interpretation will be wavering, uncertain, and of no value. But if we understand that purpose thoroughly and wisely include the remaining circumstances, we can derive a meaning from an allegory that is just as consistent as one from any other clear and obvious passage.

**And between the Throne, and the things that surrounded the Throne, were four beasts.** The second outward gift is the "Beasts" <note>These are the four "living creatures" described in Revelation 4:6-8; the Greek word *zoa* implies living beings rather than "beasts" in the sense of monsters.</note>; we must first consider their qualities, which relate to their suitability for their function, once we have determined what kind of creatures they are. This is indeed difficult to determine based on the judgment of the interpreters, as they differ from one another in so many ways. Following our usual method, we will briefly state what seems closest to the truth. They are the servants and ministers of God, whose entire labor is spent in preaching the Word and in caring for those other matters belonging to church government <term>original: Ecclesiasticall government</term>. 

For first, it is plain that they are men; for they sing together with the Elders: *“You have redeemed us to God by your blood” (Chapter 5:9).* Furthermore, since there are two kinds of people who are redeemed—the general congregation and the ministers—the very place where they serve shows that they belong to this second order. For they dwell <term>original: converse</term> between the Throne and the Elders who are placed around it. Thus, they come closer to God Himself and act as ambassadors between the two. Moreover, they are the leaders of public worship <term>original: action</term>, as is clear later in verse 9.

# CHAPTER 4. A REVELATION

Lastly, they are so fashioned in their wings, eyes, and whole proportion that they are able to be most fitly prepared to discharge this function.

Neither are they some of the worthy men of the age past, but ministers <note>The author argues that these "beasts" represent future Christian clergy rather than ancient figures.</note> who are to be hereafter, to which kind of thing this whole prophecy is applied, as the first verse taught us:

...midst of the sons of Heth: Genesis 23:6. That is, "among." And so elsewhere commonly.

Therefore Theodore Beza <note>original: "Theodore Beza"; a prominent French Protestant theologian and scholar (1519–1605).</note> has translated it in a clear sense: *Between the Throne, and the things that surrounded the Throne.* By this, it is signified that the living creatures <note>original: "beastes"; referring to the *zoa* or "living creatures" of Revelation 4:6.</note> come closer to the Majesty of God than the Elders, by reason of their function, and that they do in some part touch that seat which glitters with divine glory; this is a clear argument indeed of the ministry allotted to them.

These living creatures are four in number, according to how the number of the Christian ministry is increased. For just as the Christian congregation is twice as large as that under the law—the latter consisting of twelve Patriarchs while the former consists of twenty-four Elders—so the proportion of ministers is doubled. There are four living creatures for twenty-four Elders, compared to the single tribe of Levi alone in respect to the twelve princes of Israel.

Regarding the Elders who sit in a circle around the highest throne, the living creatures are like four beams of two diameter lines dividing a circle at right angles, where the circumference is on every side and equally joined with the center of the throne. They are positioned toward all directions by the four main poles, so that they may very fitly serve to instruct the whole Church—just as the river that was divided into four heads could water Paradise. These qualities are more remote; those that are more closely joined belong to their bodies and to their wings.

To those first qualities belong the eyes with which the living creatures are filled "before and behind." This fullness signifies that singular sharpness and richness of understanding in divine things with which they are endowed by the gift of the Spirit. Christ requires this kind of minister: *That they might be the light of the world* (Matthew 5:14).

And that they might go before the blind in the right way, lest they should fall into the ditch (Matthew 15:14). They must be *apt to teach* (1 Timothy 3:2), *so that they might both exhort with sound doctrine and convince the skeptics—even stopping their mouths* (Titus 1:9, 11). *For the priest's lips ought to preserve knowledge, and the law is to be sought from his mouth, for he is the messenger of the Lord of Hosts* (Malachi 2:7).

<margin>Malachi 2:7.</margin> Therefore, those who either completely or for the most part lack eyes—what business do they have with these living creatures? 

What communion is there between blind moles and Argus <note>original: "Argos"; in Greek mythology, Argus Panoptes was a giant with a hundred eyes, representing extreme vigilance.</note> full of eyes? Let those men, therefore, who set blind and <term>beetle-eyed</term> <note>dull-sighted or near-sighted.</note> <term>lusks</term> <note>lazy, sluggish, or idle people.</note> over Christ’s people, look carefully and consider how they will answer him one day, who requires such a great abundance of eyes in the pastors.
