These ministers are as similar as can be to that householder who brings forth from his treasury things new and old (Matthew 13:52). This kind of knowledge is abundantly supplied both from the ancient scriptures—Moses, the Psalms, and the Prophets—as well as from the writings of the Evangelists and Apostles. From these fountains we must draw to the full, so that the man of God may be equipped with both these eyes behind and before. God considers all bishops in Christ to be such sharp-sighted pastors, full of eyes, who—according to the talent delivered to them in trust—faithfully teach the people committed to them, however much ignorance (natural to human nature) remains in even the best of them.

7. ***Now the first living creature was like a lion.*** So much for the property common to all the living creatures; the specific form of each one is: the first a *lion*, the second an *ox*, the third a *man*, and the fourth an *eagle*.

These four different kinds are applied by almost all interpreters to the four Evangelists. And so it is that, according to *Aretas* <note>Aretas of Caesarea, a 10th-century commentator on the Apocalypse.</note>, *John* should be the *lion* and *Mark* the *eagle*; according to others, *John* should be the *eagle* and *Mark* the *lion*. *Augustine* would have *Matthew* be the *lion* and *Mark* the *man*.

# OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chapter 4.

...master, who needed to have the name written upon every one of his pictures, as if otherwise it could not be known which were the Lion, the Eagle, and the Man. The first verse of this Chapter decides this controversy. What things (he says) must be done afterwards <note>Revelation 4:1: "Come up hither, and I will show thee things which must be hereafter."</note>. This certainly forbids us from looking back and thinking of what is past, but bids us rather to expect something yet to come. These figures seem, therefore, to belong to those gifts with which every faithful Minister was in some part to be adorned, besides those gifts of knowledge. For eyes ought to be common to them all; everyone ought to be a man capable in knowledge. The rest of the gifts are diverse, according to how God shall give them to everyone in private for the use and necessities of the Church; though no man who is truly a partaker of one of these virtues can be completely destitute of the rest. This is why Ezekiel ascribes these four proportions and visages to every one of the Beasts in Ezekiel, Chapter 1:6.

Indeed, the fortitude of a Lion, the patience of Oxen, the prudence of a man, and lastly, the Eagle-like contempt for earthly things, ought to be in force in every one of them. And yet some specific quality is applied here to each one individually, and not without cause. Perhaps by this the Holy Spirit might show in what virtues the Pastors chiefly excelled, according to the four diverse seasons in which they lived. The first age, from the time of John, brought forth men who were excellent in all these (Chapter 6, verses 1 to 7).

Their courage, nevertheless, shone forth most of all, by which they both endured and overcame the most savage cruelty of the tyrants. The age following after Constantine yielded a great store of Oxen, when the Ministers had their liberty taken away from them, and everyone—even the best of them—was oppressed under the yoke of Antichrist with the luggage and baggage of human rites <note>The author refers to the ritual requirements and ceremonies of the medieval Church, which he views as a heavy burden.</note>. # ON THE REVELATION. Chapter 5.

## Chapter 5.

### The Analysis or Breakdown.

<image-desc>An ornamental drop-cap letter 'T' featuring intricate scrollwork and floral patterns.</image-desc>

*So much has been spoken briefly about the general model <note>original: "Type." In this context, it refers to a symbolic representation or pattern.</note> of the entire Church militant <note>original: "Church militant." This refers to the church on Earth as it struggles and fights against sin and spiritual enemies, as opposed to the "Church triumphant" in heaven.</note>. The specific prophecy contains, in part, the surpassing dignity of this Revelation in this chapter, and in part, the events themselves in the remainder of the book. This is explained first in regard to the created beings, and then in respect to the Lamb. In respect to the created beings, it is completely unsearchable; this is evident partly from it being sealed up with seven seals (verse 1), and partly from the testimony of all created beings, who all acknowledge their own powerlessness <note>original: "impotencie."</note> after the matter was set forth for inquiry by the proclamation of the angel—acting, as it were, like a town crier (verse 2). It is also seen after trial was finally made to see what they could do (verse 3). The consequence of this is mournful: the weeping of John. This was wrung from him by the weakness of the creatures and his despair of enjoying such a notable benefit (verse 4). Only in respect to the Lamb is it able to be searched out; as the Elder first explains, who comforts John (verse 5). After that, the Angel <note>In the biblical text of Revelation 5:6-7, this refers to the Lamb (Jesus Christ), whom the author here identifies as the one appearing at the critical moment.</note> comes at just the right moment <note>original: "in the nicke."</note> and takes the book (verses 6–7). From this, finally, arises a singular joy and thanksgiving from all creation; specifically, first from the Church (verses 8–10), and from the angels (verses 11–12), and then from the rest of the created beings (verse 13). Last of all, they rejoice together as the Church joins in <note>original: "subscribinge to."</note> the shared joy and gladness of everyone else (verse 14).*

# THE EXPOSITION

1. *Then I saw at the right hand.* The Vulgate <note>original: "the vulgar." Referring to the common Latin translation of the Bible used in the Western Church.</note> reads, *in the right hand*; so does the interpreter of Aretas <note>an early commentator on the Book of Revelation</note> as well; but all the Greek copies agree in reading *at* or *upon the right hand*. They translated it perhaps in the ablative case <note>a Latin grammatical case often used to indicate location</note> because it follows below in the seventh verse that the Lamb took the Book out of the right hand. But this was not a sufficient cause to depart from the natural meaning <note>original: "native propriety."</note> of the words, seeing that it might be said on purpose for the better demonstrating of the weakness of created beings <note>original: "creatures." In this context, it refers to all created things (angels, humans, etc.) as distinct from the Creator.</note>: that the Book was at first, not *in* the right hand, but *at* the right hand of him who sat on the Throne. From this it would follow that if they had no ability to open it when it was offered and set forth intentionally for them to see, they would have had much less ability if he had held it in his hands. Then afterward, when the powerlessness <note>original: "impotency."</note> of the created being was proven, it is said that the Book was taken into his hand, so that the worthiness of the Lamb might be made more notable—he who did not grab at the Book as it lay right by his side, but took it into his hand, out of the hand of him who sat on the Throne. 

As for the purpose of this Vision, it seemed good to the Holy Ghost—after he had portrayed the true Church in the former chapter (which was to be laid as a foundation for all the building following, before he came to the specific predictions one by one)—to give men a watchword <note>a warning or call to attention</note> concerning the incomprehensible excellence of this prophecy. For we are accustomed (such is the dullness and perversity <note>original: "untowardness." Meaning stubbornness or inappropriateness.</note> of our nature) to pass by the greatest and most divine things negligently and carelessly, unless perhaps there is someone to pull us by the ear and to call earnestly for our efforts by telling us of the greatness of the matter we are about. Lest perhaps this very thing should happen to us in this place, he makes us see that this prophecy is such that it contains within it all the dangers and extremities which the Church is to undergo throughout its whole race upon the earth, and yet that it is wrapped in such great obscurity that no created mind can behold it, even from a distance <note>original: "aloof."</note>, much less explain it to others. This is a matter indeed most worthy to be known, and

### OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chapter 5.

This is of all others most pleasant beyond comparison, as it brings and shows us hidden mysteries—the kind that people exceedingly desire to know, and in searching for them they would otherwise torment themselves in vain. Yet it is not something to be desired for the sake of knowledge alone, but also because it contains events of such importance that it would be very sorrowful and piteous for the Church to have them completely hidden from her. 

Therefore, John wept, being aware of these dangers and considering that he and the Church were without a guide to lead them. And indeed, the Church barely functions correctly <note>original: "doth scarce run on her right wheels." This is a metaphor for the Church operating smoothly or staying on the right path.</note> even though she has this clear lamp provided for her direction. How miserable then would she have been if she had been left entirely in darkness, not knowing anything sufficiently—neither whether she should go on, nor where she should safely stop? 

John's weeping, therefore, would not have been without just cause if there had been no hope of unsealing the Book. However, the sudden passion of grief, by its violence, put the holy man out of his right mind and did not allow him to remember whose power it was to open the Book, until, at length, he became wise through the instruction <note>original: "advertisement"</note> of another. 

This prophecy, therefore, is renowned for the worth of the subject matter discussed, the eminent nature of the mystery, and the abundance of fruit it brings. But above all other respects, it is made most glorious because he alone is found worthy to open it—he who found out the way to redeem the chosen <note>original: "the elect"</note> by his own death. This is why the Church triumphs on earth, the angels in heaven, and finally all other created beings <note>original: "creatures"</note> with them. And this is not for the sake of ceremony <note>original: "pomps sake"</note> more than the truth requires—as is the habit in human writings to amplify matters for the sake of ornament—but out of a true sense and a just cause for rejoicing, as we shall see hereafter, God willing <note>original: "if God assist"</note>. 

In the meantime, shall not this exceedingly great joy of heaven and earth kindle in people's hearts a diligence in reading, a desire for understanding, and a care to observe these things? # Chapter 5. A REVELATION

...more wise than was appropriate <note>original: "meete"</note> they should be.

**A Book written within and on the backside.** The first commendation of the Prophecy comes from the Book itself: the plentiful writing within it and the seven seals mentioned in this verse. It must necessarily be a most certain thing that is set down in a Book, which is a most faithful helper of memory; whereas that which depends upon memory alone may easily, over a long passage of time, be either wholly extinguished or at least corrupted. This is why God tells Jeremiah, for the greater credit of that prophecy, to write all the words with which He speaks to him in a Book (Jeremiah 30:2). Thus He provides against our doubting, lest we should think otherwise of these things than of those matters committed to public instruments and records—indeed, things that are, as it were, engraved in brass so that they can neither be changed nor perish. 

The plentifulness of the writing is declared by the fact that the Book was **written within and on the backside**, on both pages. Here, he speaks according to the ancient manner of writing on long parchments, which were afterward rolled together around a round piece of wood; because of this, books were called volumes or scrolls, and Christ is said to have unfolded and unwrapped the Book (Luke 4:17). Now (to use the words of the most learned Theodore Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605) was a major French Protestant theologian and scholar who succeeded John Calvin as a leader in Geneva.</note>), the outside usually remained clean and unwritten, unless the inside was not able to contain the whole writing; for then they filled the outer part with letters. This kind of writing was called "backside-writings" <note>original: *opisthographi* (Greek for writing on the back of a scroll)</note>. 

This great lengthiness <note>original: "prolixness"</note>, therefore, did not only contain the chief headings of things—which might perhaps have been comprised even in a narrow space—but even all the smallest matters as well. This ensures there should be no need to seek anything from any other place, and also that we might know that nothing here happens at all without God's special providence. The Complutensian <note>The Complutensian Polyglot was the first printed polyglot edition of the entire Bible, completed in Spain in the early 16th century.</note> and some other copies read *without*, but the phrase *on the backside* is more often used in this matter, from which came the name of "backside-writings," as we said just now. To conclude, how precious are these mysteries which God keeps by Himself, sealed with so many seals? No creature could even look upon the Book (verse 4). It was so far from needing seals for the purpose of concealing matters from them; rather, in this way, He would declare with how much honor we ought to reverence His secrets.

# OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chap. 5.

2. **And I saw a strong Angel who proclaimed**: The worthiness of this prophecy is great because of its certainty, length <note>original: "prolixity"</note>, and the depth of feeling it evokes. But now it appears to be even greater, insofar as it exceeds the reach of all created understanding. For its nature is not such that the wiser sort of men may be able to comprehend it by some quick-witted foresight; rather, it is something in which all people must necessarily acknowledge their ignorance. 

For the better proving <note>original: "convincing"</note> of this, an allusion is made here to the custom of Princes. In matters of great difficulty, they are accustomed to invite their subjects—offering great rewards by the voice of a Crier—to make a trial of their strength. In such a business, there is almost no one who will not step forward to try. Even a small hope of achieving the reward is enough to motivate them; therefore, if no man dares to come forward, what is this but an open confession of their weakness and disability? 

In the same way, the Angel is sent out here to inquire, **who should be worthy to unseal the Book?** If no man offers himself, let us acknowledge our own impotence and the power of **the Mediator** <note>The "Mediator" refers to Jesus Christ, acting as the bridge between God and humanity.</note>. At the same time, let us admire these holy mysteries with due reverence. To this end, God brings us to feel our poverty and need in this way, just as He dealt with **Adam** in ancient times. God set all the creatures before Adam before He gave him a wife, so that when Adam saw he could find no fit helper for himself among them all, he might more highly value the wife who was given to him afterward.

**Who is worthy:** He does not inquire about strength and might, but about merit and worthiness. For even if all creatures conspired together, they could not avail one bit to wring matters from God by force. Whatever we obtain from Him, we enjoy by our entreaty and at His pleasure. The rightful Lord, in conferring and disposing His gifts, respects the worthiness of those on whom He bestows His benefits; unless they are commended by some due merit <note>original: "desert"</note>, either of their own or of someone else on their behalf, they can hope for no good thing from Him. But now, if the mere foreknowledge of things to come is held in such high regard, how much more should the knowledge of salvation be esteemed?

3. **And no man was able.** Here we have a frank <note>original: "ingenuous"</note> confession from the creatures that they could do nothing at all in this matter. Let them, therefore, take heed who make a creature a Patroness... <note>This is likely a critique of the practice of seeking the intercession of the Virgin Mary or saints, common in the theological debates of the era.</note>

# CHAPTER 5. A REVELATION <note>original: "A REVELATION," likely referring to the Book of Revelation/Apocalypse</note>

Why should we then wonder if no person—no matter how sharp-sighted—understands even a single jot of these holy things? This applies not only among the heathens but also in that entire Roman Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> kingdom, including the Pope himself (who blasphemously claims for himself the attribute of never erring) and the whole crowd <note>original: "rabble"</note> of his "Seraphic Doctors" <note>A title originally given to the theologian St. Bonaventure, here used to mock high-ranking Catholic scholars.</note> who claim for themselves the prize and praise of all knowledge, learning, prudence, and wisdom. The distribution of things in heaven, things on the earth, and things under the earth can be understood from the Angel's proclamation. He asked, *“Who was worthy?”* This inquiry, therefore, did not apply to the devils or the souls suffering punishment for their sins. For what hope or appearance of worthiness could there be among them? *Those in heaven, therefore, are the angels; those on earth are living men; and those under the earth are the saints, whose bodies lie asleep in their graves.* The author identifies the saints in this way using the part of them that is closer to our physical senses. For this reason, Jacob also said: *“But I will go down mourning to my son into the grave”* (Genesis 37:35). The question of worthiness could only apply to these groups. This passage, therefore, is too "cold" to ignite the fire of Purgatory <note>The author argues that because "those under the earth" refers to sleeping saints in graves, this verse cannot be used to support the existence of Purgatory.</note>.

*Neither to look into it.* This is how Theodore Beza <note>A prominent 16th-century Protestant reformer and biblical scholar.</note> reads it. The Vulgate <note>original: "the vulgar"; refers to the late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible.</note> reads: *“to look back.”* I prefer *“look upon.”* This makes the speech more impactful <note>original: "amplified"</note>, as looking upon it is a more significant matter than simply not opening it. The Book could not be looked into as long as it remained sealed, so adding that phrase would be redundant in that sense.

4. *I wept, therefore.* It is indeed a mournful thing that the Church should lack the gift of prophecy. However, John revealed his weakness here, having forgotten—or at least having little considered—that nothing is so hidden that it should be unknown to our Principal Prophet <note>Jesus Christ</note>. There is nothing He would not reveal to the Church as far as it is necessary for the good of His people. For this reason, one of the elders, while telling him not to weep, gently convicts and reproves his ignorance (or rather, his forgetfulness) at the same time. ### OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chapter 5.

...be ignorant of what even the common people among the faithful ought to know so well.

5. **Behold, he has prevailed**: It is as if many were competing, but only one obtained the prize above the rest. He seems to speak in the style of the former proclamation, by which the matter was put forward as if in a public contest <note>original: "combate"</note>, where Christ carried away the chief praise—indeed, he is all in all.

**That Lion**: An indirect <note>original: "circumlocutory"</note> description of **Christ** in his role as **King**, taken from Genesis 49:9. But what does a lion have to do with seals? Our sins kept us far away from all the mysteries of God. However, since Christ has powerfully abolished those sins and has subdued our enemies—the Devil and death—forever, he worthily comes forward with this name as a banner of victory to obtain for us that which our enemies previously prevented us from reaching.

**That stem or branch of David**: Theodore Beza <note>A major French Protestant theologian (1519–1605) who succeeded John Calvin.</note> translates it this way very well. For the Hebrew word meaning "root," to which the Greek word for "root" corresponds, is sometimes used to mean a plant or the stem of a tree; as in Isaiah, *"He grows up indeed as a tender plant before him, and as it were a root out of a dry ground"* (Chapter 53:2). Now, a root does not properly rise out of the earth, but rather the thing that grows from it—a plant from the root. Yet this plant is of such a kind that it is also the root of David—namely, the fountain itself and the headspring from which salvation and life flow to David. Nothing could be spoken more significantly, nor has there ever been any other plant of this kind. See Psalm 110:1, Matthew 22:43, etc.

6. **I looked, therefore, and behold, between the Throne**: In the midst of the Throne, as seen above in Chapter 4:4, etc. The Lamb is present in the midst of the living creatures <note>original: "Beastes"</note> and the Elders—that is, in the assembly of the faithful in the midst of the Church.

**A Lamb standing as though he had been killed**: The Lamb is described by his threefold office. His being killed refers to his **Priesthood**, which is eternal because of the everlasting power and merit of his death. **The seven horns** declare him to be a **King**. **The seven eyes** (which are the seven Spirits) and the taking of the Book show him to be the principal **Prophet**. ### Chap. 5. A REVELATION,

This indicates that he suffered death in times past, and it teaches us that the Father endows the Church with all things through the merit of, and in consideration of, his death. For this is how our **Priest**, *having once entered into the Most Holy Place <note>original: "Holy of Holyes"; the inner sanctuary of the Tabernacle or Temple.</note>, has obtained eternal redemption* (Hebrews 9:12). And since that death has once brought about <note>original: "begott"</note> redemption for the elect, will it not also obtain all things for us—whatever may serve for our benefit and advantage <note>original: "commoditie and behoofe"</note>?

The **seven horns** are that sovereign power by which Christ, sitting at the right hand of the Father, rules and governs all things, according to what he spoke to his disciples after he was raised from the dead: *All power in heaven and earth is given unto me* (Matthew 28:18).

Therefore, this most meek Lamb does not lack those weapons with which he can crush and tread down his enemies, however much he might seem—due to his great long-suffering—to ignore the injuries they offer him. Now, you may observe that it is not necessary for parables and metaphors <note>original: "similitudes"</note> to agree with nature in every detail, seeing as seven horns are given to a lamb here (contrary to its nature), as well as seven eyes.

These **eyes** are the **seven spirits of God**: that is, the gifts of the Spirit with which Christ endows the faithful. They are sent from him, since no one can share in even the smallest gift unless he gives it freely. For *God does not hear sinners*, but *from his fullness we have all received* <note>original: "vvee all drauve"; likely a reference to John 1:16, "of his fullness have all we received."</note>; and having gone to the Father, he sends the **Comforter** to his members, *who leads them into all truth* (John 16:7, 13). A visible sign <note>original: "token"</note> of this in the past was the divided <note>original: "clouen"</note> tongues sitting like fire upon the Apostles, and that miraculous gift of suddenly speaking *with other tongues* (Acts 2:3, etc.).

The Apostles excelled remarkably <note>original: "singularly"</note> with this power, as did others who later embraced the faith. They are not only sent throughout the earth to bestow the saving knowledge of salvation upon the elect, but also so that Christ might search into everything done in his Church—indeed, everything done anywhere else in the world. How great an insolence <note>original: "impudencie"</note> is it, therefore, to force a visible head <note>The author is likely referring to the Pope, arguing that Christ’s own spiritual presence and "eyes" make a human vicar unnecessary.</note> upon the Church, when the Lamb is furnished with so many eyes? He does not carry them about him idly but sends them out diligently into all the earth.

# OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chap. 5.

The care indeed which Christ takes does not take away the ministers, either ecclesiastical or civil, which he himself appointed. However, to coin and devise a new kind and order—and that under the pretense of Christ's absence—is the proper role of that man who is completely contrary <note>original: "overthwart"; meaning perverse or obstinate.</note> and an utter adversary to Christ. Regarding the words, some copies read, *which things are*, as it is noted in the Greek Bibles published recently at Frankfurt <note>original: "Franckford"</note>, so that the relative pronoun may be referred to his horns as well as his eyes. Aretas <note>Aretas of Caesarea, a 10th-century commentator on Revelation.</note> also reads it in this manner.

And the horns may well be said to be sent into all the earth, inasmuch as Christ shows and puts forth his power in the relieving of his own and the destroying of his enemies. But it more properly agrees with the eyes, which we are said to cast upon anything when we turn them toward it.

7. *He came and took the book out of the right hand of him who sat on the throne:* There is a double consideration of Christ: one as he is eternal God sitting upon the throne together with the Father (Chapter 4:3); another as he is Mediator, serving or attending at the throne, and ready and prepared <note>original: "addressed"</note> to undertake those things which work toward the salvation of his people. There is a similar consideration of the Spirit, who, as he is eternal God, is a partner in the throne, surrounding <note>original: "compassing"</note> it (Chapter 4:3). But as he sanctifies the Church with created gifts, he is the *seven Spirits before the throne, seven burning lamps, seven horns, and seven eyes.*

8. *Having each of them harps and golden vials:* Here is the celebration <note>original: "gratulation"</note> and thanksgiving of the Church for this great benefit: the Lamb's taking and unsealing of the book. They bring, therefore, instruments fit for such a work—*harps and vials*—that is to say, praises and thanksgivings. For the *vials full of odors* <note>original: "odours"; meaning incense or fragrances.</note> are the hearts of the saints, which the Spirit has filled with a burning desire to call upon God. The *harps* belong to rejoicing; and joy in prayer is the very giving of thanks. Now, here is an allusion to the custom <note>original: "manner"</note> of the Temple, where the Levites praised God with musical instruments, and the priests had pots and cups set before the altar, full of incense (Zechariah 14:20). 

*Which are the prayers of the saints:* Here there is nothing to do with offering

# Chapter 5. A REVELATION

offering of prayers for the dead which are made by those who are alive upon the earth; but as we showed in the former chapter, all that is attributed to the *Beasts* and the *Elders* shows the earnest studies and endeavors with which the Saints are occupied in the Church militant <note>The "Church militant" refers to the Christian Church on earth, which is conceived as being at war against sin and the devil.</note>. So also afterward, *verse 10: "And we shall reign (say the Elders) upon the earth."* Here they do not magnify a kingdom of departed souls, but of the Saints who are alive on the earth. These men's hearts, like golden vials, breathe out praises and thanks for those exceedingly great benefits which are purchased for us by *Christ.* If the Elders were to offer up only the prayers of others, as the *Jesuit* <note>Likely referring to a Catholic commentator like Francisco Ribera, whom Protestant authors frequently debated.</note> interprets it, then they themselves would be silent in the common joy of all the Saints. No, the benefit is theirs, for they themselves shall reign, as they say; therefore, they do not offer other men's prayers, but their own.

9. *And they sang a new song:* It is called a "new song" in respect to that more plentiful grace now administered after *Christ's* appearing <note>original: "exhibiting"; here meaning his manifestation or incarnation.</note> in the flesh, more than was given of old under the shadow of the Law. The old Fathers <note>The patriarchs and prophets of the Old Testament.</note> did not so openly and in such a clear and notable manner sound forth the praises of *the man Christ* before he took flesh, as the faithful do now at this day, celebrating him as one clothed in our nature. Therefore, this clearer preaching is not unworthily called a "new song." But he alludes to the custom of the Law, where by new forms of thanksgivings purposefully composed, they magnified God for new and extraordinary benefits; this is why there is such frequent mention of *a new song* in the Book of Psalms.

*And have redeemed us:* The *Beasts* therefore and the *Elders* are men redeemed by *Christ's* blood. They are not merely twelve principal men from the Jews and as many Christians (the twelve Apostles with the four Evangelists). For all this *choir* <note>original: "Queere"; an archaic spelling of choir.</note> was not chosen out of every tribe, and tongue, and people, and nation, but out of the nation of the Jews alone. Instead, all the faithful everywhere throughout the world are meant by the *Beasts* and *Elders*, whom this holy company—gathered <note>original: "pressed"; meaning drafted or gathered together.</note> without distinction of person from all the world—may worthily represent, as we noted at the fourth verse of the fourth chapter. Now, it is significantly said "out of" every tribe, etc., and not "all" tribes, etc., because all are not redeemed by the blood of *Christ*, but only the elect.

# REVELATION, Chapter 6

## Chapter 6

### The Logical Analysis of it <note>original: "Logicall Resolution"</note>

*So much for the worthiness of the prophecy. The events follow, which are first Seals, then Trumpets, and last of all Vials. For the rest of the prophecy is divided into three notable periods of time <note>original: "termes of time"</note>, which contain within them the principal changes that will occur in the world, even until the coming of Christ. Each of these is again divided into seven moments—the individual parts of those three periods—so that the entire following period always arises out of the last stage <note>original: "Article"</note> of the period that preceded it. Concerning the Seals, there is a certain preparation in each of them, and then a symbolic representation <note>original: "Type"</note> of things to come.*

*Now, the preparation is partly common to all, whereby the Lamb opens each of them in order, and partly specific to the first four; these, besides the opening, include an invitation from one of the four living creatures <note>original: "Beasts"</note> to "come and see." The symbols in this chapter are six, for there are six seals opened in it: the White Horse (verse 2); the Red Horse (verse 4); the Black Horse (verse 5); the Pale Horse (verse 8); the cry of the souls (verses 9, 10, 11); and a mighty earthquake continuing until the end of the chapter.*

## THE EXPOSITION.

*After that, I watched when the Lamb opened the first of the seals.* Now the Holy Spirit <note>original: "H. Ghost"</note> begins to address the events themselves. These will inform us regarding the shifting patterns <note>original: "interchangeable courses"</note> of the world as they concern the Church, specifically those events of great importance <note>original: "moment"</note> until the final end of all things. This is a significant matter and exceedingly necessary to be known, yet it is such that no mortal eye—no matter how sharp-sighted—can pierce into it.

Therefore, I call again for help upon the same God to whom I prayed in the beginning. By His grace alone, I have made good progress this far. May He who gave me the power to begin in a way that I trust agrees with His Truth also enable me to happily finish what remains. 

Therefore, You, most holy and most wise Lamb of God, who alone have merited the right to take and to unseal the Book—and did so not to keep those secrets to Yourself alone, but to communicate them to the Church as far as might be beneficial <note>original: "behoofeful"</note> for it—grant to me, Your most unworthy servant, by Your goodness, that I may clearly perceive the things which these hidden and closely guarded seals contain. May I reveal them to the world in a holy manner for the building up <note>original: "edification"</note> of the Church, the destruction of Antichrist, and the glory of Your own name, which is to be praised for all ages. Amen.

In dividing these events into three ranks, we follow the Holy Spirit himself as our guide <note>original: "Author"</note>. He joins the Trumpets to the Seals, and the Vials <note>original: "violes"</note> to the Trumpets, so that the first part of what follows always arises out of the last part of what went before. Therefore, those who lump the Seals, the Trumpets, the Vials, and the seven candlesticks all together blind themselves with confusion <note>original: "cast dark mists before their own eyes"</note>. They act as if every part of each sequence were joined to the others equally, or as if a father and his sons were the same age and lived their years simultaneously. Furthermore, while the Seals are, as it were, guarantees <note>original: "pledges"</note> of things to come, the Trumpets are evils that burst upon the world with a loud clamor, and the Vials are such evils as come sliding...

<meta>This page continues the exposition of Revelation 6, focusing on the interpretation of the first seal and the chronological starting point of the prophecy. The author critiques Jesuit interpretations and establishes that the visions represent events starting from the time of the apostle John.</meta>

<page-num>204</page-num>
<header>Chapter 6. A REVELATION.</header>

Sliding in little by little, and oppressing men unawares (as we shall see later), to mix these opposites into one—so that a matter should be both promised and performed at the same time, and the same thing should happen both openly and secretly in the exact same moment—seems to me to be inconsistent and illogical. 

But let us come to the words themselves: *when he had opened one seal*. This refers to the first seal, as Theodore Beza <note>original: "Theo. Beza"; Beza (1519–1605) was a major Protestant reformer and successor to John Calvin.</note> translates it, because the second and third follow afterward. This is the common interpretation among Hebrew scholars <note>original: "Hebricians"</note>. 

But before I proceed further, I must remove that foolish notion <note>original: "fond conceit"</note> of the Jesuit <note>Likely referring to Francisco Ribera or Luis del Alcázar, Jesuit theologians who promoted "Futurist" or "Preterist" views of Revelation to counter Protestant interpretations.</note>, in which he holds that the opening of the Book is a different matter from the unsealing of the seals. He suggests that nothing could have been read in the Book or declared to us until all the seals had been opened. This opinion truly imagines some kind of empty and blank Book brought to us, in which we have not received a single written word, nor are we given notice of anything to come. For the Book of Revelation has nothing in it besides the unsealed seals. The Trumpets come forth from these, and the Vials <note>original: "violes"</note> likewise from the Trumpets, as we mentioned in the Analysis of the whole Book. Thus, the entire remainder of the prophecy is contained within the scope of the Seals, as we shall show in the proper place with clear arguments. 

Therefore, if he has found some Book that is to be read only after all the Seals are opened, it is truly apocryphal. It is perhaps the kind of book that lies hidden within the "closet of the Pope's breast" <note>A satirical reference to the Roman Catholic claim that the Pope holds all laws and truths in the "shrine of his heart" (*in scrinio pectoris*).</note>, but it is certainly one that the Church has little need to read or know. 

Furthermore, for a clearer understanding of the periods of time and each of their parts, it is necessary to establish a starting point from which we must begin. We hold that this begins immediately from the time of John's writing. For the phrase in the first verse of Chapter 4 ("I will show you what must take place after this") calls John back to the moment when this Revelation was made and teaches us to count all the things delivered in the following Book from that point onward. Therefore, there is no need to look back to the first ages of the world, nor to the ancient monarchies, nor to the time of Christ or the Evangelists, nor any such matters of the past. We maintain that the beginning of the Seals—that is, of the first Period—is to be fixed at that time. From that point, we shall see every following event flow in a continuous and ready course, unhindered by any confusing complexities. The outcome of each period will be revealed to us in the exposition. These things being settled, let us return to explaining the text, and then we shall see the matter itself and how it fits together.

The first preparation involves the Lamb opening the first seal. For this Lamb is the Word of the Father, who provides us with the understanding of God's will; whatever we know of it comes through him. Now the events are called "Seals," both because they contain a most hidden mystery kept from the understanding of the ungodly masses <note>original: "profane multitude of men"</note> (Isaiah 8:16), and also because these first records <note>original: "documents"</note> should be like pledges of those that should come after. We do not understand them to be mere signs of things to come, or empty promises and threats that only foretell good or evil in words (with the actual execution recorded elsewhere in this book, for that is nowhere to be found). Rather, they are the kind of signs that carry their own execution along with them and provide a solid pledge of things to come. He unseals the Seals in order, one after another, not all at once with a single effort. This was done because the nature of the events required it, and because the entire prophecy was not to be uttered all at once, but was to be released little by little, so that it might serve as a daily ration <note>original: "pittance"</note> for the Church's relief.

The second preparation involves one of the four Beasts calling John to "come and see." Now, this first Beast is the Lion (Chapter 4:7). The Beasts represent the governors of the churches <note>The 'four living creatures' described in Revelation 4, often interpreted by the author as church leaders or ministers.</note>, as was noted in the previously mentioned place, whose labor God uses to instruct others. These beings call us to see and take notice, not only because it is their office to warn the Church of things that might happen, whether good or bad, but especially because the events that would happen next would be notable through their faithfulness and diligence. # Chap. 6. A REVELATION,

...the lists <note>original: "listes" – the barriers enclosing a field for a tournament or race; here referring to the start of the prophetic events</note> first of all, should be of similar power and success, no less prevailing in what they intend than lions that follow their prey. The voice is, as it were, of thunder—piercing and striking from a distance—so that it might be heard by many and from far away. "Come," he says, "and see," speaking to John, who now represented the faithful people who should likewise be stirred up to observe these marvelous events. This is also common to the three Seals following, so that this being said once may be understood for the rest.

2. **I look, therefore, and behold a white horse.** The first type <note>meaning: a prophetic symbol or figure</note> is a white horse, and its rider has a bow and a crown. As for the horse, it is a warlike and swift beast, to which God worthily compares his own actions, both here and elsewhere, because they will break through with great courage and swiftness against whatever men shall endeavor to the contrary (Zechariah 6). The white color is joyful and festive, common in any notable solemnity, as in the triumph of Diocletian and Maximian. After that, says Pomponius Laetus <note>original: "Pompon. Lætus," a 15th-century Italian humanist historian</note>, the chariot of the triumphers followed, made of gold and precious stones, which four horses drew that rivaled the snow in whiteness. 

But there is a rider attributed both to this and to the other horses, so that we may know that they do not roam abroad at random as they please, but are guided and governed by the reins of God’s providence. Now, as to what kind of rider this is, it may easily be conjectured by the analogy of the 8th verse. For there, he who sits upon the pale horse is designated by name, and his name is Death. Therefore, the name of this rider (who is so beautiful and pleasant to see) may be Life or Truth. 

Now, because he is furnished with a bow and a crown and comes forth conquering—and so that he might conquer—it signifies that an attack shall be launched from afar, and that a famous victory is to be obtained from it, such as should not vanish away with the immediate success, but should flourish equally in future happiness. For a bow is a kind of weapon with which enemies are struck both from a distance <note>original: "a loofe"</note> and at hand. The crown is a badge of victory, so that all things are joyful and prosperous, both in the horse and in the rider. Such is the interpretation of the words, with which history agrees so marvelously that no picture can more perfectly resemble its model than the symbol of this seal resembles the state of those times. # OF THE REVELATION. Chap. 6.

Under the Emperor <note>Trajan, though not named here, is implied as the successor to the era of John's return</note>, after John had returned again to Ephesus from Patmos—that is, immediately after the Book of Revelation was written—a most woeful persecution became very fierce. Raging until the fourteenth year, it was at last gradually stilled and moderated through the letters of Pliny the Younger <note>original: "Pliny the second"</note>, the Proconsul of Bithynia. 

Yet the first beast had not spoken up to this time. For Pliny was a heathen and no member of the Church, much less a ruler of it. Neither did the calamity stop by his admonition alone; it was only obtained that Christians should not be sought out for punishment, but only punished when they were accused (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* <note>original: "Euseb. Hist. Eccles."</note>, Book 3, Chapter 33). Therefore, the combat still lasted, and after Trajan was dead, within a few years it became painful again under Hadrian <note>original: "Adrian"</note>. As he proceeded outrageously even to the overthrow of the very name of "Christians," the Lion cried out—which is the first beast—as if it had been thunder. 

For God raised up Quadratus, the Bishop of Athens, as well as Aristides the philosopher, a citizen of that city. Like lions in courage, disregarding the danger of losing their lives in comparison to the welfare of the Church, they called upon Hadrian by their written Apologies <note>term: formal legal defenses of the Christian faith</note> and also pleaded the cause of the Christians openly. With this voice, the hearts of the faithful were lifted up through the expectation of the outcome, and that not in vain, seeing as a great change followed immediately upon it. 

For the **white horse** came forth and its rider with a bow and a crown; that is, the truth triumphed for joy when the Emperor, being overcome and battered down by the orations of these godly men, ordained that no Christian should be condemned unless he were found guilty of some crime punishable by civil laws. This was a manifest victory for the Truth and a great taste of the happiness that was to come (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 4, Chapter 3). 

But its felicity was even more remarkable under the next Emperor, Antoninus Pius. About the beginning of his empire, when the Christians were miserably oppressed again because of the deep-seated hatred the world held against them, at length Justin Martyr—the "Lion" preaching the word of God in the garb <note>original: "habite"</note> of a philosopher, as Eusebius says in Book 4, Chapter 11—wrote Apologies for the Christians to Antoninus, to his sons, and to the Roman Senate. By this he achieved his goal, with God working through him, so that it was decreed by public...

# ON THE REVELATION. Chapter 6. 109

...he should not carry out the matter by his own will, but at the command of another. This power is given partly by word and partly by a sign: by word, because permission was granted to him to take away peace from the earth. For the word that commonly signifies "to take" is sometimes used to mean "taking away," as we have observed before in Chapter 3, verse 11. 

Now, the "earth" is contrasted with "Heaven." Since "Heaven" in this Book signifies the true and holy Church (as will be made clear later), the "earth," by contrast, signifies the wicked world from which peace is taken—not from the Church. This may be made even more evident by the description of this power, which goes so far as to set men against each other to kill one another, as shown by the words *that they may slay one another*. The Church does not take revenge upon its enemies even when the opportunity is offered, much less is it driven by a mad fury to kill its own brothers. 

Instead, this mutual butchery arises from the fights and battles between the heathens <note>original: "Heathens"; referring here to the non-Christian peoples of the Roman Empire</note>, whereby some nations would rush toward the destruction of others. Therefore, this is not a discussion of the persecution of the Church, but of the stormy time of wars with which the whole world would be shaken and tossed together. This is shown to be a very massive conflict by the sign and by the instrument of exercising power: a great sword given to the Rider. 

This came to pass after Antoninus Pius <note>original: "Antonius Pius"</note> ended his life. For his son, Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Verus—a philosopher in name, but in deed a grievous enemy of the truth—being blinded by heathenish superstition, raised a bloody persecution against the Christians. To soothe this, the second Beast <note>term: the second of the "four living creatures" from Revelation 4, interpreted here as an Ox</note> lifted up his voice. For Justin <note>original: "Iustine"</note> presented a second Apology <note>term: a formal legal defense of the faith</note> to the Emperor (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 4, Chapter 16). 

But the Emperor, being greater in learning than his father but lesser in godliness, received the defense with deaf ears. Hereupon the voice of this Beast became the voice of an ox; it did not prevail as the voice of the Lion had before. Instead, the Beast, after its lowing <note>term: the sound an ox makes; here used metaphorically for a humble or suffering plea</note>, nevertheless continued to endure the heavy yoke of the previous calamity. Justin himself—who before was a lion in strength, but was now an ox for patience—was killed for Christ’s cause and gained the name of a Martyr (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 4, Chapter 16). <header>Chapter 6. A REVELATION,</header>

However much this voice failed to lesson the cruelty of the wicked, it served instead as an alarm to warn the faithful of how much calamity hung over the world because of their cruel stubbornness against the True Peace. Peace would be taken away from men soon enough, since it was most just that those who refused and rejected everlasting peace should enjoy neither that, nor even peace on earth—and that those who thirsted so greedily for innocent blood should eventually be satisfied with their own blood. And therefore, all things were immediately set on fire with wars. 

The Parthians now, for the first time since the reign of Trajan, revolted against the Romans. The Emperor’s brother <note>Lucius Verus, who ruled alongside Marcus Aurelius from 161–169 AD</note> went there, having been made a co-partner with him in the Empire. Finally, after he had caused a huge slaughter, he returned home with a Triumph <note>a ceremonial victory parade in Rome</note>. Yet his happiness was short-lived, for he was suddenly taken away by a stroke <note>original: "Apoplexy"</note> while sitting in a chariot with his brother. (See Eutropius, *Summary of Roman History* <note>original: "Eutrop. Brev."</note>, Book 8). 

A short time later, a war with the Marcomanni <note>a Germanic tribal confederation</note> arose in Bohemia, so great that nothing like it had occurred in living memory. As the same Eutropius says, it could worthily be compared to the Punic Wars, because it was incited by the Quadi, the Vandals, the Sarmatians, and the Suebi, as well as by the Marcomanni—indeed, by all the barbarian lands from Carnuntum in Pannonia <note>a Roman army camp on the Danube, near modern Vienna</note> even to the middle parts of Gaul <note>original: "Cyalls"; likely a corruption of "Gauls" or "Alps" in the Latin source</note>. 

How woeful the state of things was then, the same author vividly portrays in this manner: "Surely," he says, "there was no rest from weapons; and wars flared up throughout all the East, Illyricum, Italy, and Gaul. There were earthquakes that destroyed cities, floods, frequent and severe plagues, and a type of locust that ruined the fields. To speak generally, there was almost nothing that can be mentioned or imagined by which mortal men are usually consumed that did not violently plague the world while Antoninus was Emperor." 

These are his words. It was, therefore, a "great and cruel sword" which was made wet and drunk with so much blood. If anyone thinks that war was nothing unusual for the Romans, and that it is unlikely such a common and usual matter is signified here, let them compare the reign of this Antoninus with those who preceded him. He shall see that, by God’s providence, wars had been hushed for a long time before this, so that when this judgment of God occurred, it might be made so much the more [remarkable]...

# OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chap. 6.

<margin>Sextus Aurelius Victor</margin>
...remarkable. Antoninus the Father <note>referring to Emperor Antoninus Pius, who reigned 138–161 AD</note> ruled the entire world by his mere authority, waging no war for a period of 23 years. Likewise, Hadrian had peace during the whole time of his Empire, except for one time when he fought through a deputy (Eutropius, *Summary of Roman History* <note>original: "Eutrop. Brev."</note>, Book 8). Was it not a matter worthy of observation that after such a deep peace of forty-four years, all things should burst into flame with a sudden fire of wars? There is no one who does not see that there is such a great agreement of all things—of the prophecy, the time, and the event—that he cannot doubt that the Holy Spirit pointed solely at this matter. 

Tertullian tells us in his *Apology* <note>original: "Apologeticum"</note> that a notable security was finally granted to the Christians by the edict of this Emperor <note>Marcus Aurelius</note>. However, this happened after the end of the war with the Marcomanni <note>a Germanic tribal confederation</note>, during which he had experienced the singular aid that God gave him against his enemies in response to the prayers of the Christians who were soldiers in his army. After this, he could not help but provide for the welfare of those who had been the means of saving both him and the Empire. And yet, he did not live long after this war, but departed from this life the year after his triumph.

<margin>Chapter 4:7</margin>
5. *And when he had opened the third Seal.* The living creature <note>original: "Beast"</note> of the third Seal is a **Man** who excels in reason and experience of matters. This is not because the previous living creatures were thought to lack this same power and force of reason, but because this would be the principal trait for which this third creature should be esteemed. The voice of this creature is also more obscure than that of the first, yet it was sufficient to teach the faithful what revenge God would take on the world for their sake.

# Chapter 6. A REVELATION.

The balance which this rider has in his hand is, in the Greek, a word <note>original: "zygos"</note> that is properly used for a "yoke"—that is, the tongue or beam of a balance upon which the scales hang—but by a synecdoche <note>a figure of speech where a part represents the whole, or vice versa</note> it signifies the whole object. This is a truly fitting instrument for a famine, when corn is not measured by volume but weighed by the scale.

6. *And I heard a voice, etc.* This is the voice of the Lamb, dwelling in the midst of the living creatures (Chapter 5:6), whose eyes are sent out over all the earth, and to whom the entire administration of matters has been delivered. Now, seeing that this voice is heard among the living creatures—not as if coming from outside, but abiding there—it signifies that the Church shall not be free from this calamity. However, the Church alone would understand God’s counsel in inflicting this stroke. 

*A measure of wheat for a penny.* Interpreters do not agree about the exact quantity of this "measure." Some give it the value of three English measures (equal to about half a pint, three-quarters, and half a karat, plus 4 grains); others say four, and others eight. Hesychius <note>an Alexandrian grammarian, likely 5th century AD</note> describes it as a measure containing an allotted portion of food, which in one word is commonly called a *demensum* <note>original: "demensum"; a Latin term for a monthly allowance of grain or provisions given to slaves or soldiers</note>. 

Athenaeus <note>a Greek rhetorician and grammarian, c. 200 AD</note>, in his third book, teaches more distinctly how much this allowance is, calling it a "day's nourishment"—that is, as much as will serve for food for one day. Aristophanes, in his comedy *The Wasps*, brings a little more light to the subject when the character Philocleon, upbraiding his servants, says <note>OCR error: "faith" corrected to "saith/says"</note>, "whom I have taught to make four loaves out of one *choenix*." So much corn, then, does this measure (called in Greek a *choenix*) contain as would suffice to make four loaves. 

The commentator on that poet adds that four great loaves were made from a *choenix*, or eight little ones. The word "corn" in general must in this place be taken for wheat or barley meal, which is more expensive than barley (three measures of which are sold for no more than one of wheat). 

*For a penny*—understand here, "let it be sold for a penny," or some such phrase. The Latin word put for a penny <note>the *denarius*</note> is worth ten of those pieces called *asses* <note>Roman bronze coins</note>, which are pounds. The ancient writers make it equal in weight and value to an Attic *drachma*, which is of three kinds according to some: one is worth seven pence in our currency, another eight, and another ten. # ON THE APOCALYPSE. Chapter 6.

...in this way: *And do not harm the wine and the oil.* The meaning is, "yet see that you do not harm the wine and the oil," following the Hebrew style where the "and" (the conjunction) is used instead of "but" or "yet" (the disjunctive). These words—*oil* and *wine*—cannot be referred to the items mentioned previously. It is not as if he were saying, "let a measure of wheat be sold for a denarius <note>a Roman silver coin, roughly a day's wage</note>, and let three measures of barley be sold for a denarius; likewise, let oil and wine be sold for a denarius." 

For the words *oil* and *wine* are in the accusative case <note>original: "fourth case"; the grammatical case for a direct object</note> following the words "do not harm"—or as Junius <note>Francis Junius (1545–1602), a Huguenot theologian and translator of the Bible</note> translates it in this passage, "do not deal unjustly with them." They are not in the nominative case <note>the grammatical case for the subject of a verb</note> coming before a verb, as the words for "measure" and "measures" are. Therefore, not all resources for maintaining life were to be taken away; rather, only the basic necessities were to be reduced. 

The oil and the wine, which serve for pleasure and luxury, were to be preserved unharmed. This is because it seemed right to God to punish the common people <note>original: "meaner sort"</note> first, while the princes and peers were preserved like delicacies and kept away from the famine only to be saved for the plague. For those whom hunger could not waste away because of their wealth and abundance, the pestilence would feed upon them and consume them with a swift death, as we may see in the next Seal. 

So much for the explanation of the words. The historical event described here is not as clearly recorded by historians as one might wish. This is because they tend to select the most extraordinary events, while they easily overlook things that are common or ordinary, especially since this famine consisted primarily of a scarcity of grain only, rather than a shortage of all food supplies <note>original: "victuals"</note>. 

Yet God intended for some traces <note>original: "footsteps"</note> of it to remain, enough to uphold the credibility of this prophecy. Commodus succeeded his father, Antoninus Verus. During his empire, the world had some relief <note>original: "breathing"</note> from outward calamities through God's mercy. I believe this was because the world already suffered enough plague and misery simply by having such a wicked Emperor. Pertinax and Julianus succeeded him, both having short reigns and, for that reason, doing less damage. 

At last, Septimius Severus came to the throne. He was the cruel author of a most grievous massacre of Christians, whether he did it of his own will or was pressured by others. At that time, the third living creature <note>original: "Beast"</note> cried out loudly, warning the faithful that God would take revenge for their wicked rejection <note>original: "loathing"</note> of spiritual food by sending a great scarcity <note>original: "penury"</note> of food for this earthly life.

### CHAPTER 6. A REVELATION

Consider Tertullian, whom you may rightly call a man of great excellence in wit, acuteness, and learning. He has almost as many arguments as words in his writings. Even so, in a very irritable mood, he revolted to Montanism <note>a 2nd-century prophetic movement often deemed heretical for its claims of new revelation</note>. By this weakness, he showed that nothing common to human nature was foreign to him <note>original: "nothing incident to the nature of a man was disagreeable vnto him," a reference to the Roman playwright Terence’s famous line</note>. 

This Tertullian, I say, wrote a most learned *Apology* <note>a formal defense of the Christian faith</note> against the Gentiles <note>non-Christian Romans</note> and sent it to the chief governors of Rome. As Francis Zephyrus <note>a 16th-century scholar and editor of Tertullian's works</note> writes, they might through this work at least privately and secretly learn about the common cause of the Christians, since it was not lawful to do so openly. 

He did not think it sufficient to speak only to the princes of the Roman Empire in general terms, but he also called upon Scapula, the deputy of Carthage, by name, hoping perhaps to soften his savage mind. He labored to teach him the true cause of the public calamities—namely, that by persecuting the truth, the wicked world brought upon itself those barren seasons and poor soil. Consequently, after the sowing seasons, the harvest times were lost, and floods from rain and horrible storms ruined everything. As he says:

> "Yet we must needs be grieved that no city shall go scot-free for the shedding of our blood, just as it happened under Governor Hilarian. Regarding the threshing floors <note>original: "corne floores"</note> used for our burials, the people had cried out, 'Let there be no threshing floors!' Indeed, they were no threshing floors to those who owned them, for they did not bring their harvests into them."

These words clearly enough show that the barrenness was very great in those times when there were no harvests. Therefore, it seems those threshing floors were formerly granted to the Christians as places to bury their dead, because, due to the great famine, they were of no use for storing grain. 

And why should we not recognize the Black Horse <note>the Third Seal of Revelation, representing famine and scarcity</note> here, as the truth indicates? For the sun had almost entirely lost its light during the assembly at Utica, and that was not by an ordinary eclipse, but while the sun was at its full height and peak, as the same Tertullian witnesses in his letter to Scapula. 

This grain shortage did not only trouble the wicked Gentiles, but it also troubled the Christians, since God wills that benefits be shared by the profane and the godly alike, and that hardships be shared by His people and the wicked. Through this equal partnership, all men might have...

Thus, the event agrees with the prophecy by punishing the world with famine—another of God’s scourges—since the world could not be roused from its dead sleep by the great sword and the devastation of war. The Jesuit <note>likely Francisco Ribera (1537–1591), a Catholic commentator who applied much of Revelation to the early Church or the distant future</note> insists that this black horse should be understood as representing heretics. However, following his usual error, he disregards the timeline. He attributes these events to the year 40 AD, when Matthew wrote his Gospel. In doing so, he oversteps the boundaries set by the Angel: *"I will show you things which must be done hereafter"* (Chapter 4:1). 

It is true that many heretics arose during the period of peace the Church enjoyed under Emperor Commodus <note>ruled 180–192 AD</note>, such as Montanus and others of that kind. However, since the horse that came before and the one that follows after denote physical <term>corporal</term> calamities inflicted upon the world because of the injuries and violence offered to the truth, it would be absurd to interpret this horse placed in the middle as a different kind—especially since the historical evidence is so clear. Nor should we think that a typical famine is too minor a matter for men to be forewarned about. For it is the Holy Spirit’s intent to make these initial calamities serve as tokens <note>original: "pawns"</note> to confirm the prophecy that follows. This is why they are called "Seals," as if they were confirmations of the matters yet to be delivered. Once the faithful had fully perceived the truth of these predictions occurring in the immediate future, they could be equally assured of the things expected in the final ages. These seals, then, are like the three young goats, three loaves of bread, the bottle of wine, and the harp, tambourine, flute, and lyre that Saul encountered, which gave him undeniable evidence of his promised kingdom (1 Samuel 10:3–5).

**7. And when he had opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature.** The fourth creature <note>original: "beast"</note> is an eagle, soaring high and paying little attention to earthly things (Chapter 4:7). It proceeds in equal rank with the previous creature, though it does not reach the intensity of the first, whose sound of war was like thunder. Yet, it gives a sufficient warning <term>caveat</term> to the faithful with its clanging cry concerning the coming evil, inviting them to "Come and see" how great a destruction would immediately invade the world.

# CHAPTER 6. THE REVELATION.

8. **And behold, a pale Horse**. The fourth type is a pale horse, whose rider is described by his name, his companion, and the business committed to him. The color of the horse in the Greek properly signifies "green as the grass" <note>original: *chloros* ($\chi\lambda\omega\rho\text{ó}\varsigma$)</note>. Sometimes it refers to the dead color of herbs that wither and dry, which is why it is sometimes used to mean "paleness"—the hue of anything withering and fading. For example, fear is called "pale" because it makes people pale. Thus, Constans <note>The author likely means Constantius Chlorus (c. 250–306 AD), the father of Constantine the Great</note>, the father of Constantine the Great, was called *Chlorus* because of his paleness, as Zonaras <note>Joannes Zonaras, a 12th-century Byzantine historian and theologian</note> says in his *Life of Diocletian*. 

This diseased color is very fitting for this horse, on whose back Death itself sits. The rider is identified in the next words, where "he that sits" is used instead of "to him that sits"—using the first case (nominative) instead of the third (dative). This manner of speaking follows Hebrew usage, as has been observed in Chapter 2, verse 26. 

Lest anyone should think this grammar is incorrect and, through their own ignorance, accuse the Holy writer of poor writing <term>barbarism</term>, there are enough examples of this in other languages taken from the most elegant authors. Livy <note>Titus Livius (64 BC–17 AD), a famous Roman historian</note> speaks this way: "Those," he says, "who were skillful in religious matters and common law denied that—when two ordinary consuls of that year died, one by the sword and the other by disease—the consul appointed to replace either of them could call a Council." In this instance, the first case is used for the second (genitive). 

Sallust <note>Gaius Sallustius Crispus (86–34 BC), a Roman historian</note> writes similarly: "Therefore kings in the beginning (for that was the first name of an empire on the earth), they diversely exercised their wits, some their bodies." Many such figures of speech are noted by learned men, who also observe that this style of writing is very familiar to the Greeks.

First, a name is given to this rider: "Death." By the same logic, names may also be given to the previous riders: he who sits on the white horse may be called Truth; on the red horse, War; and on the black horse, Famine. I point this out because I see some commentators invent unsuitable names, such as the Devil or other riders I do not recognize. 

Now, this rider is called Death for a specific and primary reason: because the strike of this Seal brings destruction more swiftly than any other, and also because it afflicts men with many kinds of deaths. God’s third scourge is usually pestilence, as in Ezekiel: *"They shall fall by sword, famine, and pestilence"* (Chapter 6:11). Yet, pestilence is not made a "captain of a band" here, but is only pressed into...

<margin>9. *And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw souls under the altar.*</margin>
There is no living creature <note>The "Beasts" or Four Living Creatures of Revelation 4:6–8 introduce each of the first four seals, but are silent for the fifth.</note> belonging to this seal by whose voice John is invited to see. This is done for this very reason: because this seal passes by quietly <note>original: "closely"</note>. There was no public or solemn cry made to stir men up to observe the event, as there was in the previous ones; indeed, history does not relate that any man undertook such labor, for which such an office might have been worthily given to him. Besides, this seal consists partly in reporting things past, and partly in recording a future event of such a nature that it usually slips by almost without being noticed <note>original: "perceiverance"</note>. This is especially true since we are so inclined that adverse and troublesome things stick more firmly in our minds than prosperous ones. Therefore, since the seals correspond to the events, it is no wonder that no symbolic figure <note>original: "type"</note> is proposed here, as there was no external event to match it.

"I saw souls under the altar." The fifth seal consists of the souls lying under the altar in this verse, requiring vengeance upon their enemies (verse 10) and receiving an answer (verse 11). These three parts belong to three times: past, present, and future. *The souls lying under the altar* most elegantly declare, through what follows, what went before—namely, the state of the Church during the time of the previous seals and how greatly it was harassed by the cruelty of men. We have indeed heard of the Truth overcoming <note>The White Horse of the First Seal</note>; we have also had it reported that war, famine, and pestilence, with their consequences, seized and destroyed all things. But there was no mention yet made of how it fared in the meantime with the worshippers of Christ. Although their struggle <note>original: "combate"</note> might have been guessed from the victory of truth and from those calamities that plagued the world, one might have conceived that great wrong was done to the godly, for which their enemies were so sharply punished. ### Chapter 14. A REVELATION

When he cries out to him who had the sickle, we are taught that this man is described as if he were a martyr, more for the combat that was yet to come than because of a victory that was past. For a martyr who has departed from this life cannot provoke anyone to any notable undertaking. The example of his constancy may spur a man’s mind toward similar courage, but he cannot incite him by words to specific designs, such as this task of cutting the vine, unless he is living alongside him. This exhortation, therefore, gives us to understand that this man would endure martyrdom at last, and that he had not endured it before, when he persuaded others toward this work. 

All these circumstances, when joined together, lead us to Thomas Cranmer <note>original: Crammer; Thomas Cranmer (1489–1556) was the first Protestant Archbishop of Canterbury and a central figure in the English Reformation.</note>, formerly the Archbishop of Canterbury, as they call him. This man was a worthy martyr, having power over the fire, to which he gave his body to be burned for the Truth. His power over the fire was all the more glorious because, having formerly slipped through human frailty by subscribing to the wicked religion <note>Refers to Cranmer’s temporary recantation of his Protestant faith under pressure from Queen Mary I.</note>, he immediately repented. Revoking his subscription when he was brought to the fire, he made his right hand the first part of all to be burned up by the flames, because it had been so ready to be an instrument of such great wickedness. After this was consumed, he gave up his whole body to be devoured by the fire. *He cried with a loud voice to him who had the sickle, because in the days of King Henry VIII, he inflamed the mind of Thomas Cromwell <note>Thomas Cromwell (c. 1485–1540) was King Henry VIII's chief minister who led the administrative and legal efforts of the Reformation, including the Dissolution of the Monasteries.</note> with his words and a desire to perform a "vintage" <term>vintage</term> <note>Here, a metaphor for the harvesting or dismantling of the established Catholic Church structure.</note>.* For Cranmer, being remarkably well-learned and boiling with a fervent zeal, could not help but reinforce and push forward the doing of this work with all his might, setting on fire to do it the one whom he saw was endowed with the power to do it.

*Verse 19. Then the angel thrust in his sharp sickle.* Hitherto we have spoken of the preparation; now the execution is finished by cutting the vine. This vine is the glittering and princely glory of the Popish <term>Popish</term> <note>A term used by reformers to refer to the Roman Catholic Church.</note> Church, whose success was once very great in our realm, as it commonly was elsewhere. It swelled with full and ruddy grapes; it hung high and was firmly bound together upon the trellises, shadowing the whole land on every side with broad vine leaves and clusters of grapes set thick together. For it is well known (as the ruins of it still testify today) how every one of the most pleasant hills was beset with these wild vines throughout our entire island, and what deep root they had taken.

...and how they so hindered the sun's light with their far-spreading boughs that it could never shine upon the corn. And not contenting himself only with the ministry of these two angels—partly of Cromwell <note>original: Cromwel; Thomas Cromwell (c. 1485–1540), chief minister to Henry VIII and a central figure in the English Reformation.</note> with his sharp sickle, and partly of Cranmer who had power over the fire—he caused this whole vine not just to be lopped and pruned, but to be utterly rooted out in the year 1539. The lands and revenues which previously served to uphold a wicked religion were confiscated to the King's Treasury and put up for sale to the highest bidder. And this is the cutting down of the clusters and the casting of them into the winepress—an event no less admirable than it is memorable, if we consider the matter according to its great magnitude.

Verse 20. *And the winepress was trodden without the city.* The "City" is the Holy Church of God, which the Scriptures often designate by the name of a city; now the winepress was trodden outside its territory, and how marvelously does this agree? For although England deprived the "Popish crew" <note>original: Crue; a derogatory term for the Catholic clergy and their supporters.</note> of their goods and livelihood and stripped them of all their dignity (as they deserved to be dealt with), England had not yet attained that level of reformation at that time that would allow it to be rightly called a "Holy City." The Pope was banished, but "Popery" was still retained, as is evident by those Six Articles <note>The Act of Six Articles (1539) reaffirmed several traditional Catholic doctrines despite the King's break with the Roman Church.</note> which were enacted the year after the abbeys were pulled down. In these articles it was decreed: *that the true and natural body and blood of Christ were present under the form of bread and wine, and that the substance of bread and wine no longer remains after consecration <note>This describes the doctrine of Transubstantiation.</note>. That receiving the Lord's Supper in its entirety <note>original: intirely; referring to the practice of "communion in one kind," where the laity received only the bread, with the wine reserved for the priest.</note> is not necessary for salvation, and that the whole Christ is contained under either of the elements. That it is not lawful for priests to marry. That vows of chastity <note>original: Continency</note> are to be kept; that private Masses are to be retained; and that auricular <term>auricular: spoken into the ear, referring to private confession to a priest.</term> and secret confession of faults is profitable and necessary.* These filthy doctrines defiled England and prevented it from being a "Holy house of God" at that time.

# CHAPTER 14. A REVELATION

...of the grapes by an elegant metaphor, yet it comes closer than usual to expressing the juice of these grapes discussed now, through a certain property of speech. For it represents the calamity that occurred during the overthrow of the Pope, which was so great that not only was the whole country made wet with it, but it also overflowed to the bridles of the horses. 

For we have reports that those who were put in charge of destroying the stalls of these oxen <note>original: "stalls of these Oxen"; a derogatory reference to the monasteries and the monks who lived in them.</note> and confiscating their goods, rode up and down with a large troop and train of men to view all their houses throughout the entire country. While they performed this duty, such havoc was made of the Papists' goods that their horses seemed to swim in their spoils, as if in a river of pressed grapes. 

But besides this, I suppose another thing is signified here: namely, that not only the common people (who were no less courageous in managing this business than horses are in battle) grew very rich and wealthy from this, but also that the nobles and peers—who act as bridles to guide and keep the common people in check—gained very much from this bargain as well. It is well enough known that the beginning of many a man’s greatness and honor came from this; and others who were fairly well-off before were greatly increased by it. For there was scarcely any man, at least of any account, who did not get a good supply of "carpenters' chips for fuel" <note>A metaphorical way of saying everyone took a small piece of the wealth for themselves when the larger structure was destroyed.</note> when this great oak was felled.

*By the space of a thousand, six hundred furlongs.* That is, throughout the whole realm of England. A thousand, six hundred furlongs make two hundred English miles. Now, the length of this realm from the furthest part of the South to the longest reach of the North is more than this by a hundred miles. However, if we remove the vastness of the Northern parts—where the country is more deserted and uncultivated <note>original: "vnmanured"; in the 17th century, this meant land that was not tilled or worked by hand.</note> near the borders—it fits. These "grapes" (that is, this crew of religious monks, friars, and nuns) were afraid of the North because of the colder air, which they could not endure, as they delight in the most open <note>original: "champion"; referring to "champaign" land—flat, fertile, open countryside.</note> and pleasant places of the land. We shall see a marvelous agreement even in this detail as well. Thus stands the English "vintage," which is so clearly proven to be the one foretold here by the way everything aligns, that it cannot be doubted that this is the only natural application of this symbol <note>original: "Type"; a person, thing, or event believed to foreshadow another.</note>.
