# Chapter 15.

## The logical breakdown of this chapter into its parts.

Up to this point, we have heard of the past events recorded for us by the seventh trumpet, to the extent that they would be more fully known under its blast than ever before. The things yet to come follow now; a general symbolic representation <note>original: "common Type"</note> of these is found in this chapter, and their specific execution is described in the rest of the book.

This symbolic overview first summarizes that there are seven ministering angels prepared to take vengeance on the Church's enemies (verse 1). It also describes what the state of the Church should be while living among the Gentiles <note>referring to the secular or non-believing world</note> until the angels have completed their duty. We are presented with a portrait of this both in the "sea of glass mingled with fire," and in the victors and the harpers (verse 2). 

In their song—the authors of which are Moses and the Lamb—the subject is the praise of God's omnipotence and justice (verse 3), and His gathering together of all the elect (verse 4). After that, the text gives us a more specific description, focusing partly on the angels who are assigned to their office, as indicated by the place from which they emerge (verses 5 and 6), by their clothing (verse 6), and by their instruments—namely, the bowls <note>original: "Viols"; here meaning the vials or bowls of God's wrath</note> with which they are armed (verse 7). 

Finally, it describes the whole Church, both in respect to the chosen nations—to whom the glory and presence of God shines forth—and in respect to the rest of the people, for whom the way remains closed <note>original: "shut up"</note> until the appointed time.

# THE EXPOSITION.

*After that I saw another sign.* These words are used in the place of a transition <note>original: "in the Roome of a Transition"</note>, by which the following prophecy is distinguished from what was just explained in the three previous chapters. And now the third and final period remains. It is divided from the previous one by the nature of the events, which therefore use a new instrument—the bowls <note>original: "Viols"; refers to the ritual bowls used to pour out God's wrath</note>. Yet, this period still agrees with and is joined to the previous one, as it is a part of the seventh trumpet, as may easily be seen from what has been said before. 

For the tabernacle in heaven is not opened before the seventh trumpet (Chapter 11:15, 19). However, the instruments of this work—those who are commissioned to pour out the bowls—come out of the temple that is opened in heaven, as seen below in verses 5 and 6 of this chapter.

Additionally, the angel foretold that the end would come when the seventh trumpet blew (Chapter 10:7). Now, these seven bowls bring the end with them; the instruments mentioned in this verse are said to hold the seven last plagues, and therefore they necessarily belong to that same trumpet. 

But if the first bowl corresponded to the first trumpet, and the rest followed in order so that each bowl belonged to the same time as the trumpet joined with it, there would be no reason to call them the "last plagues." But that cannot be the case by any means, especially since the first bowl brings an evil upon the men who had the mark <note>original: "Character"</note> of the beast set upon them (Chapter 16:1–2). We have seen that this mark was the invention not of the first beast, but of the second (Chapter 13:16), whose "birthday" <note>referring to the emergence or origin of the second beast</note> occurred during the fifth trumpet. 

By that logic, the mark would have to exist before all the trumpets; if that were true, the first trumpet would not so much mark the men as it would torment those who were already marked. Furthermore, the triumphal song of the saints is sung in this chapter because of the victory won over the beast—and this happens before the bowls are even prepared, or the angels set themselves to the task of pouring them out (verse 2). But the beast...

[The Beast] does not die under the first trumpet, but is born then, and from that point he flourishes until the Harvest and the Vintage (Chapter 14), and until the time when the two prophets shall rise again from the dead (Chapter 11:11). We have shown that this happened around the end of the sixth trumpet. But some will say, "There is a great likeness between the trumpets and the bowls <note>original: "Viols"</note>." I answer: there is indeed, but only to show us that men are punished by the same steps and stages by which they have sinned. However, they differ both in timing and in the nature of the punishment, seeing that the bowls are punishments only, whereas the trumpets include the sins as well. It is clear, therefore, that this whole span of time from John's day to the coming of the Lord is divided into three periods, and each of those periods is again divided into seven parts. The first part of a following period begins under the last part of the previous one. Just as the seven trumpets originate from the last seal, so the seven bowls originate from the last trumpet. This way of dividing the time makes this prophecy easy for us to understand and allows it to flow clearly in our minds, whereas it would otherwise be impossible to untangle.

*In heaven.* That is, in the purer Church. For just as the Lord used to roar out of *Zion and utter his voice from Jerusalem (Amos 1:2)*, so the judgment <note>original: "euil"</note> by which all the Church's enemies shall finally perish will come out of his holy Church. In the Church, he shall show himself a revenger when he punishes all the reprobates. Now, this sign is "great and wonderful" because the transformation of things—seeing the Beast and the dragon overcome and destroyed, and everlasting happiness secured for the Church—is so amazing it would leave a person full of wonder. We shall see this in the details that are to be revealed individually.

*Seven Angels.* This follows the pattern used in the previous periods. These angels are men who are citizens of the pure Church, as is clear from the place they come from and by their clothing, which we will discuss in the appropriate section. Theodore Beza <note>A prominent 16th-century French Protestant theologian and scholar.</note> expresses it with a forceful phrasing: "those angels." However, the definite article is not in the Greek text, nor were these angels seen or even mentioned before the temple was opened.

# OF THE REVELATION. Chapter 15.

They begin together with the seventh Trumpet around the year 1560 <note>The author is identifying the sounding of the seventh trumpet with the events of the Reformation era.</note>. In this regard, we say they are "to come," not only in respect of this time in which we now live. Now he says his wrath "has been satisfied," because it *shall* be satisfied; the certainty of the prophecy makes him speak of future things in the past tense.

**Verse 2. *And I saw what looked like a glassy sea mingled with fire.***

So far we have heard in general of the matters that are to be done, and of those who are to be agents in their execution. Now he teaches us what the state of the Holy Church should be in the meantime, the matters and persons of which are described. Of these, the "Sea" is the doctrine, as mentioned before, whose diverse qualities have created different seas. One is heavenly, such as that in Chapter 4:6, which was also glassy and like crystal; another is earthly, turned into blood and void of all purity (Chapter 8). Now we have a third, which is a heavenly one indeed, as the previous verse showed, for this sign was seen in heaven.

It is also glassy, such as the first was, with which it therefore agrees in nature, however much there may be some little difference in the quality of either of them. For in the place of that crystal, fire is mingled in this passage; for he says *it was a glassy sea mingled with fire.* That first sea, therefore, was transparent as glass and very simple, void of all color, as crystal is. This other one here is transparent also as glass, but it is colored with a fiery redness, and is not as beautiful to behold because of the simplicity of crystal. Now, what other thing can fire signify but squabbles <note>original: "brabbles"</note> and contentious burning and boiling with mutual hatred of one against another? "I came to bring fire upon the earth," says Christ, "And what do I desire but that it may be kindled?" (Luke 12:49 <note>original: "Luc.12.49"</note>). The heavenly truth of the last period <note>original: "Periode"</note> would have this inseparable companion joined with it.

# Chapter 14. A REVELATION.
<note>The original header lists Chapter 14, though the content continues the commentary on Revelation 15:2 regarding the "glassy sea."</note>

Doctrine should be glassy and transparent, allowing us to behold the loving and favorable countenance of the Father in Jesus Christ. Yet, it was not pure on every side like crystal; instead, it was colored with the fire of contention. Indeed, all godly people find this to be too true by experience today, to their great grief. 

That unhappy contention regarding the Sacramental Signs <note>original: "Sacramentall Signes"; referring to the theological disputes over the nature of the bread and wine in the Lord's Supper</note>—how many troubles has it raised in the Church! This conflict was not content merely to cause a commotion everywhere and turn everything upside down; like an unlucky crow, it also had to hatch another evil, like an unlucky egg. This was that "monster of Ubiquity" <note>original: "Vbiquity"; the controversial Lutheran doctrine that Christ’s physical body is present everywhere</note>, the likes of which has never been seen or heard of before. 

The sparks of this fire were first cast into the "sea" of doctrine by Luther himself, but they were quenched again—partly by his own modesty and piety, and partly by that of Melanchthon and others who served the Church well. But finally, around the year 1561, John Brentius <note>Johannes Brenz (1499–1570), a German Reformer</note> and Andreas <note>Jakob Andreae (1528–1590), a primary architect of the Lutheran Formula of Concord</note> rekindled it with great effort, as if using bellows. 

Stirrings and strife were not raised only regarding these primary points of doctrine, but also concerning the grace of God, Predestination, Baptism, and many others. As it often happens, one error never travels alone without others to accompany it. Those churches further removed from the devastation caused by this fire burn with another equally scorching flame: ambition. From this, hot and fierce contentions arise over earthly dignities and honors, which churchmen claim and hunt after for themselves. They treat these as if they were the ornaments essential to the Church's existence, and they fight for them with all their might. 

This is despite the fact that the purer ages of the Church <note>Referring to the Early Church before the rise of the Papacy</note> teach us clearly that nothing has ever brought more certain mischief and ruin to the Church than this. It is this ambition that prevents the preaching of the Word from having the free passage it ought to have. It also prevents the wicked lives of men from being corrected and restrained by the rod and bridle of holy discipline. When that discipline is removed, men are granted—or at least they take—the liberty to be licentious and to commit all kinds of notorious crimes, or at least those that overthrow Christian piety. Such a fire as this flies up and down throughout the whole Reformed Church. It either consumes most people or troubles the rest as they strive to restrain the force

*And having their breasts girded with golden girdles.* These garments are tied to every person individually by faith, as if with a golden girdle. This was not because he had any such need, but only to teach us and to represent the Church of that time, which was greatly adorned in this regard.

*Verse 7. And one of the four Beasts.* It does not appear by name which of these it is, especially since "one of the Beasts" may refer to either an order of sequence or a general distribution. As an order of sequence, "one" signifies the first, as in Chapter 6:1: *I heard one of the four beasts*, that is, the first, which is the Lion. As a distribution, by a common manner of speaking, this word "one" may belong indifferently to any one of the four. However, it does not matter which of them it is. What applies to all of them belongs to each of them; all their four virtues joined together set such an image before us as every faithful minister ought to resemble, as we observed on the 7th verse of the 4th Chapter. 

Here the Holy Spirit intends to let us know that these seven Angels draw their strength from the precepts and instructions of some Minister of the Holy Gospel. They later convert and apply these instructions to work the destruction of the enemies of the Church. Yet, this "minister" is not to be thought of as any single individual, but many who agree in one faith and doctrine—such as Philipp Melanchthon, Martin Bucer, Peter Martyr, Heinrich Bullinger, John Calvin, and the rest of the servants of God who flourished about that time <note>These men were leading theologians and figures of the 16th-century Protestant Reformation.</note>.

From their godly and learned writings, so many men have drawn an excellent and "golden" understanding of holy things, that they have been made able to encounter the Antichrist and to thoroughly finish the remainder of that war which they began with such happy success.

# OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chapter 15.

A person may drink enough out of it at once, for it is larger than a pot. Indeed, he says it is a large and wide vessel like a kettle (Book 11 of the *Deipnosophistae* <note>original: *Dipnosophist*—a Greek work by Athenaeus describing ancient banquets and vessels</note>). This vial <note>original: "viol," referring to a shallow, broad bowl</note> then signifies the infinite wrath and vengeance of God that is ordained for the wicked in these last times. Perhaps such vessels are used now in the same way as when God opened the floodgates <note>original: "Sluces"</note> of heaven in ancient times and thereby destroyed the entire world with a flood, or when he overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah with a shower of brimstone and fire from heaven. For then he seemed to pour out destruction upon the heads of men, as if out of vials.

These are most fitting weapons to show the power of God, who does not require great force to confound his enemies, but can take them all away even with a certain gentle and quiet sprinkling of water. And now see how appropriate instruments are given to each kind of event. The seals were in the first place because the first events were certain confirmations and pledges of things to come. After them the trumpets followed, declaring evil that would rush in upon the world with a great noise, while also announcing more grievous matters that were to be expected unless they should repent. Now at last, vials are brought forth and set in readiness; these are wide vessels that are large enough to receive and to pour out God’s judgments, and are thus most fit to complete the destruction of the reprobates <note>original: "Reprobats"—those rejected by God and destined for damnation</note>. Neither is there any noise in the pouring out of the vials, as there was in the sounding of the trumpets. For the judgments of God that are to come bring terror, as he threatens so that they might be avoided; but those that are present rush in upon men secretly without being noticed. 

What, therefore, and of what sort are these vials? First, they are the holy minds of these seven Angels, which are endowed with understanding and capacity to conceive the will of God, out of which this liquid is to be poured that is so deadly to the reprobates. Second, they are such as the Living Creature <note>The text says "the Beast," but contextually refers to the four "Beasts" or Living Creatures from verse 7 who give the vials to the angels</note> gives to the Angels by instructing their minds and training them up in the holy doctrine. Thirdly, they are such as are full of the wrath of God—not the wrath with which God is angry against the Angels, but the wrath by which he will execute judgment against the wicked. Lastly, they are golden vials, because however severe God’s judgments shall be, they shall nonetheless be most just, pure, and precious. **Verse 8. And the Temple was filled with smoke.** This concludes the description of the preparation of the angels. What follows next to be revealed regarding this renewed Church is a clear sign of God’s presence, similar to what was seen in the Tabernacle of old (Exodus 40:34-35). But (you might say) the time of the Gospel requires a clearer representation. Indeed, God deals much more openly with us by many degrees than he did with those who lived under the Law <note>original: "lawe"—referring to the Old Testament era and the Mosaic Law</note>. Yet, whatever can be shared with us while we remain here on earth—even if we are enlightened with the light of the Gospel—is nothing but smoke and obscurity compared to that revelation which we shall eventually enjoy in Heaven. 

But here he teaches us that God’s presence is visible in his Church, though his enemies find it to be nothing but smoke to them. They can no more look intently upon it than men whose sight is taken from them by a misty smoke coming between them and the object. And indeed, who but a blind man would fail to perceive that God is present in our churches? He marvelously protects them against the many devilish plots of our adversaries who seek our destruction. 

But the minds of the Papists <note>original: "Papiſts"—a common 16th/17th-century term for Roman Catholics</note> cannot pierce through this smoke, which causes them to wear themselves out in vain by fighting against God. Furthermore, since smoke also signifies wrath, the phrase **the Temple was filled with smoke** teaches us that God demonstrates his presence through clear evidence of his burning-hot wrath against his enemies. He will now torment them with continuous anguish and misery, one after another, which shall fall daily upon their heads from the Temple and Church of God.

**And no man was able to enter into the Temple.** Here we have the state of the rest of the world expressed—specifically, how things will be while these plagues break the enemies of the Church into pieces. Namely, they shall remain outside of the Temple, being unable to enter because of the smoke, just as Moses could not enter the Tabernacle of the Congregation while the cloud lay upon it (Exodus 40:35). The state of the restored Church, therefore, shall be in some part like that of the lurking Church <note>original: "lurking Church"—a Protestant term for the true Church when it was hidden or persecuted during the height of Papal power</note>. ## The 16th Chapter.

### The logical analysis <note>original: "Resoluing"</note> of it.

*So far <note>original: "Hetherto"</note>, we have heard about the general symbolic vision <note>original: "common Type"</note>; the specific carrying out <note>original: "speciall execution"</note> of it now follows. This is distinguished by its various parts in this chapter and is handled in greater detail and in sequential order throughout the remaining chapters. It contains both a command (Verse 1) as well as its parts: those which are general—the carrying out of the work and the outcome <note>original: "euent"</note>—and the specific ones as well. These are the seven distinct vials <note>original: "viols"—the bowls of God's wrath</note> which signify, in keeping with the style of the previous sections <note>original: "Periodes"</note>, those seven notable defeats <note>original: "discomfitures"</note> by which the enemies of Christ are to be destroyed. The first of these is poured out upon the earth (Verse 2). The second upon the sea (Verse 3). The third upon the rivers (Verse 4), the secondary result of which is a double testimony: first, from the Angel of the Waters (Verses 5 and 6), and second, from the Angel coming out from the altar (Verse 7). The fourth is poured upon the sun (Verses 8 and 9). The fifth upon the throne of the Beast (Verses 10 and 11). The sixth upon the Euphrates, which also results in a double outcome: first, the drying up of the waters (Verse 12), and second, a preparation for a war. This war involves three principal instigators <note>original: "Authors"</note> and as many instruments—the frogs (Verses 13 and 14). Then, a warning is also given to the Elect (Verse 15).*

## THE EXPOSITION.

Verse 1. *Then I heard a great voice out of the Temple.* In this commanding voice, we are to consider from where it came, to whom, and for what purpose. It came out of the Temple, as it also came in Chapter 9:13, *out of the four horns of the Altar*, and sometimes it comes out of the Throne, as afterwards in Chapter 19:5. The difference is this: the voice comes out of the Throne when it proceeds, as it were, immediately from God; it comes out of the Temple when anything is obtained by the prayers of the Saints. To the Saints, the office of commanding is given here, so that we might know what force faithful prayers have; they should be, as it were, the first movers and the principal agents in the matter that was to be done. They so boldly command the business to be started <note>original: "set vppon"</note>. And indeed, it could not be otherwise than that such men as God had enlightened with so great knowledge of his truth should strive with all their might through prayers to God that he would, with all possible speed, destroy Antichrist. Aretas <note>An early Greek commentator on Revelation</note> does not read the words *out of the Temple*, but all our copies, as well as the Vulgate <note>original: "the vulgar"—the standard Latin Bible translation</note>, do with one consent read it thus, and the source of the voice is usually shown in other places. Those to whom the voice comes are the seven Angels. But some will say, what need is there for this, seeing they were long ago appointed and furnished for this office with all necessities in the former chapter? They stood indeed at the barriers and starting gates <note>original: "lifts"—the starting position in a race or tournament</note>, prepared and looking for their signal to begin the attack <note>original: "onsett"</note>; but a special command must be added to the general one if a man desires to have an authentic commission to warrant his actions.

...him in the doing of a matter. This is, therefore, what they expect, showing by this that they will not stir—not even the breadth of a finger—without God's command <note>original: "becke"</note> and providence, by which all things are governed. Now the commandment tends toward this end: that they should go and pour out their vials upon the earth. It is true that some of them are poured upon the sea, the rivers <note>original: "flouds"</note>, the sun, and the air, yet the force of them all rebounds upon the earth. The other elements are not changed except for the purpose of changing the earth through them—the earth being, as it were, the common washpot <note>A vessel for waste water; here, the final destination or "sink" for God’s judgment</note> into which all the liquid is poured. Why then, how can this be specific to the first vial (as it appears in the next verse) if it is common to them all? We shall see in the detailed explanation <note>original: "particular exposition"</note> that the first vial applies without distinction to the confused multitude of those who inhabit this earth, whereas the rest apply to certain specific groups of special note.

Verse 2. *And the first went and poured out his vial upon the earth.*

So much for the commandment; now the specific execution begins. The work being performed is the pouring out of a vial upon the earth. These words are not to be taken literally <note>original: "properly"</note>. For a vial is not a physical flagon, nor is it full of physical liquid; rather, it is full of the wrath of God, as stated in verse 7 of the previous chapter. Neither is "the earth" only the soil we tread upon. It refers first to men, and even then not to all men in general, but only to the branded followers <note>original: "rogues"</note> of Antichrist. The outcome immediately demonstrates this, as a "botch" <note>An old term for a boil, plague sore, or skin eruption</note> was inflicted upon the men who have the Mark of the Beast. 

The word "Earth" was often used in this sense earlier in the book. We therefore retain it consistently throughout our explanation so that we can see more clearly how the whole prophecy remains consistent with itself. The event brings an evil and harmful <note>original: "noisome"</note> ulcer with it—that is, the kind that physicians call malignant and incurable. Such an ulcer has such great sharpness and toxicity <note>original: "virulency"</note> that it will never allow a scar to form <note>original: "to be drawne together"</note>. Nor should this ulcer be thought of as a physical one in the literal sense, since we see that the causes producing it are metaphorical. Similar events are to be understood in the rest of the vials as well. To take them literally, as the Jesuit <note>Likely referring to Jesuit scholars like Francisco Ribera, whose literal interpretations of Revelation sought to deflect Protestant claims that the Papacy was the Antichrist</note> does, is not so much to explain as to confuse everything, ensuring that the light of the Truth is overwhelmed forever.

Those upon whom this ulcer seizes are *men*; a sore fell against *men*, as Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a major Protestant reformer and biblical scholar</note> translates it, or *into* men, as the Vulgate <note>The standard 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> reads—that is, *on* men, just as Antichrist is said to sit "into" the Temple, meaning *in* the Temple. This more closely agrees with these figurative sores, as if he should say that those things would be done against the slaves of Antichrist which would torment and vex them as severely as the most noisome <note>offensive, foul-smelling, or harmful</note> ulcers cause pain to the body. ### Chapter 16. A REVELATION

Both are compelled by this to stay inside and not venture out, so that they might avoid seeing those men whose prosperity makes them sick and sore. This is similar to the experience of the ancient Egyptians, who, along with their magicians, were so covered in <term>botches</term> <note>original: "botches"; inflammatory sores or boils</note> all over them at the sprinkling of the dust that they were not able to stand before Moses (Exodus 9:10-11). Additionally, every one of them is so afraid of anyone coming near to touch him that he labors by all means to keep himself from being shoved or squeezed.

This kind of evil invaded the men who carry the badge of the Beast immediately after the opening of the Temple (Chapter 11:19). We have shown that these Vials are to be joined to that event, although the repetition of past things has separated them by a long distance—specifically around the year 1560, where the previous prophecy ended. For then our most gracious Queen Elizabeth was commanded by a voice out of the Temple to pour out a Vial upon the Earth. That is, being advised by the counsel of godly men near the end of the first year of her reign, she most worthily cast out many of those men from their bishoprics, as well as from their other dignities and Church livings. These were men who, boasting only of the Beast’s <term>cognizance</term> <note>original: "cognizāce"; a heraldic badge or mark of identity, here referring to Roman Catholic loyalty</note> which they wore, denied their due allegiance to their lawful Princess.

Among these were the Archbishop of York, the Bishops of London and Ely, and fourteen others, besides men of lower rank such as Deans, Archdeacons, Parsons, Vicars, and the like. How these fellows must have been cruelly scorched with envy and spite when they saw their dignities, lands, <term>demesnes</term> <note>original: "demeanes"; landed estates</note>, goods, and honors bestowed upon their adversaries, while they saw themselves in the meantime lying despised and forlorn! Many of them could not endure the grief of it, which caused many to travel across the sea, intending to seek some relief from their sorrow by living out of the sight of this misery. Others were consumed at home in their hiding places with <term>cark</term> <note>original: "carke"; burdensome worry or anxiety</note> and pensiveness. All of them fled from the light and the sight of men, because seeing others so joyful and cheerful was as painful to them as a most cruel death.

And yet, their torment was not taken away when they changed their surroundings and their country, seeing that the Pope himself and that whole generation were so vehemently tortured by the mere report of these events. He bore sufficient witness to this through his <term>Bulls</term> <note>official edicts or decrees issued by the Pope</note> issued against our most noble Queen, in which he commanded all her subjects in the most severe manner to revolt...

### Chap. 16. A REVELATION,

...that troubled them but the grievous sore <note>original: "botch"; a boil or swelling</note>? Those in Germany had now for a long time vexed and provoked the Romanist faction. But the wounds which had been given before, being now about this same time made more full of filthy matter, were turned into ulcers. The decree of Charles V was grievous, as we said before, whereby peace and liberty were granted to the Protestant religion; but it stung them more cruelly every day, the less hope they saw there was of reversing it. For the Emperor Ferdinand, who succeeded his brother, thought it best to abide by the former decrees, to which he had given his consent at Augsburg <note>original: "Augusta"</note> before he was Emperor. Maximilian II, his son, always disliked that course of maintaining the Christian religion with force and arms and of compelling men to receive it against their wills. How intolerable did this moderation seem to the Papists, who were full of the sore of envy and a burning desire to be revenged on the Protestants? But let us now see also, in a word, how this boil cannot endure to be touched. This was declared by the Council of Trent in the second session under Pius IV in the year 1562. At that time, certain chosen men were entrusted with the business of considering and searching into various censures and books that were suspected or harmful—that is, they were to be careful by all means that nothing might be published among the common people which should give the slightest criticism, even with one little word, to the Romanist superstition.

Truly, this ulcer is very sore and venomous, so much so that it can endure no sharp or harsh word to come near it; and therefore order was taken that whatever was applied to it might be tender and soft. Therefore, Pius IV set forth an *Index of Forbidden Books*, which Sixtus V afterwards increased, and Clement VIII has recently reviewed. In this Index, it is ordained which books men should entirely abstain from, and also what books a man might use, provided they were corrected. In very deed, the Pope prescribes a diet for his diseased followers <note>original: "pocky Popelings"; a derogatory term implying the followers were infected with the "pox" of false doctrine</note>. Among other rules for correcting these books, one is that all things be carefully and attentively examined—not only those things that appear clearly in the course of the work, but also all such things as lie lurking, as if in ambush, within the explanations, summaries, marginal notes, indexes of books, and in the prefaces, together with the dedicatory letters.

# OF THE REVELATION. Chap. 16.

In this respect, the rest of the Angels may be called *the Angel of the Earth, of the Sea, and of the Sun*, because they have power given them over these things. For in saying in the next verse, *and you have given them blood to drink*, he excludes himself from their number. This Angel, therefore, is some Civil Magistrate who had power given to him, or who was rather the primary mover and persuader for this work of turning these fountains into blood—namely, the killing of the Jesuits and putting them to death.

If I were to name him specifically and say that it was *William Cecil*, that most honorable man of blessed memory who was recently the Lord High Treasurer of *England*, the next words will show that I do not state this carelessly or without good reason.

**"You are just, O Lord."** This testimony extols the Lord with praises for His justice and His truth, and then it adds a reason based on the present occasion: that the bloodthirsty killers were put to death as they deserved. Such a commendation of God’s justice as this was published for the occasion by that *William Cecil* whom I just named. For this worthy man—so that he might stop the mouths of the loud and abusive spirits of the Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> faction—revealed the reason why the Jesuits were put to death in a book compiled and published for that purpose in the year 1584. This book is titled *The Execution of Justice in England* <note>original: "The Justice of the Britains"</note>, through which it is made clear and manifest that certain wretched traitors <note>original: "cursed Vipers"</note> here in *England* were justly hanged for the foul and monstrous treasons they had committed. He published his work in almost all languages so that all men might hear the Angel magnifying God’s justice, and so that others who desire the safety of kingdoms and people might be stirred up by this most worthy example to endeavor to do the same. This book covers the very same subject matter contained in these two verses; neither can the essence of it be expressed in more suitable words.

**"Who is, and who was."** Theodore Beza adds to these, from a most ancient manuscript: *and who is to come*. Aretas, the Vulgate <note>original: "the Vulgar"</note>, and Montanus, instead of the words *and who is to come*, read *and Holy*. The former reading magnifies God for His constancy in His promises—that He is always consistent with Himself—by avenging Himself for the sins of wicked men in the same manner at this time as He punished

### Chapter 16. A REVELATION.

...them in former ages. This latter joins holiness together with constancy; as if he should say, "You cannot endure this wickedness of theirs to go unpunished any longer because of your constancy and your holiness." But where a title is taken from the distribution of time <note>Referring to the description of God as He who was, is, and is to come.</note>, the first two moments of time are not usually set down without the third; the first reading, therefore, seems to be the truer.

***Because you have judged these things.*** That is, because you have executed such a judgment by taking vengeance on the rivers and fountains of all mischief. This is a metonymy <note>A figure of speech where a thing or concept is referred to by the name of something closely associated with it.</note> of the Hebrews <note>original: "Hebricians"</note>, who often use "judging" to mean avenging and punishing. For example: *I will judge the nation whom they shall serve*, which means, "I will punish them" (*Genesis 15*). See also *Deuteronomy 32:36* and *1 Samuel 25:39*.

**Verse 6. *For they shed the blood of the Saints.*** These words give a reason for the previous praising of God. But where have the Jesuits shed any blood? As if this were a matter unknown to the world! Are these not the spies and promoters for the "Holy Fathers" of the Pope—the Inquisitors <note>The Roman Inquisition, a system of tribunals used by the Catholic Church to suppress heresy.</note>—to whose butcherly massacres they bring Christians, for the most part based on their own information? They do this so that no one, not even the innocent party, escapes their hands (as the saying goes), but is either put to death or loses all his goods. 

Furthermore, it is now well known to all the world that these are the plotters of conspiracies against Princes and the disturbers of public peace. They do not fear to lay violent hands even upon the sacred persons of Princes, whose deaths they contrive by various <note>original: "sondry"</note> crafty devices, as we have often experienced through their villainy here, to our great danger; other Princes have also learned this through their own misfortune. But even if these things were not so, since they are bound by their Oath of Allegiance to the Pope of Rome—whose strongest champions they show themselves to be—they are rightfully held guilty of the blood of all the Saints which the Pope himself has shed in such great abundance. In the same way, Christ condemned the Jews living then for killing Zacharias, whom their ancestors slew many ages before, because they approved of the same courses their fathers took who committed that wickedness (*Matthew 23:35*).

***And therefore you have given them blood to drink.*** Just as Tomyris <note>A legendary queen of the Massagetae who defeated Cyrus the Great and famously dipped his severed head in a vessel of blood.</note> gave to Cyrus: to give blood to someone is to put them to death. As it says: *I will give you the blood of zeal and wrath*, that is, "I will cause you to be..."

...slain, just as men are killed in the burning rage of anger and jealousy (*Ezekiel 16:36*). These are the ones who became the killers of the Saints; therefore, they must pay for that killing with their own blood.

**Verse 7. *And I heard another voice from the altar.*** The second testimony comes from the Angel from the Altar. The Greek word used for *Altar* properly refers to an altar where animals are sacrificed, though it is sometimes used for the Altar of Incense (as in Chapter 8:3). This also serves as a symbol of Christ’s death in a similar way. Theodore Beza <note>original: "Theod. Beza"; a prominent 16th-century French Protestant theologian and scholar.</note> translates this as *"out of the sanctuary,"* which does not sufficiently capture the force of the sentence. Perhaps he translated it this way because of the preposition *"out of,"* which usually refers to a place or container. This might seem unfitting for an altar, but there was a similar passage earlier (Chapter 14:18) where the Angel came forth from the altar, which helps explain the meaning here. We showed in that passage that this way of speaking refers to those who are killed for Christ's sake, whose place is "under the altar" (*Chapter 6:9*).

Therefore, this Angel belongs to that flock who, while enduring calamity for Christ's name, approves of the execution of the Jesuits with his support and celebrates God's justice for that reason. It is clear that this happened on April 4, 1596. At that time, the Hollanders <note>The Dutch people of the province of Holland, then fighting for independence from Spain.</note> and the governments of the other allied provinces decreed that no one from the "bloody sect" of the Jesuits—or anyone currently studying under that sect's professors—should secretly enter those provinces. This applied whether they were born in the confederated provinces or were foreigners, and whether they arrived by sea or land. The penalty for entering was being treated and killed as an enemy. By this decree, they give their voice to condemn those sinful wretches. They also subscribe to the decree made against them much earlier in England by the "Angel of the waters" <note>The author previously identified the English authorities who executed Jesuits as the "Angel of the waters" mentioned in verse 5.</note>. And who cannot see that these Hollanders are like those "lying under the altar"? They have suffered so many horrible things at the hands of the cruel Spaniards for so many years for their profession of Christ. Yet they have now learned by experience that there is more comfort to be found in these calamities than in...

# Chapter 16. A REVELATION

...all the delights that the Spaniards once enjoyed, while they remained meanwhile destitute of the most Holy Truth. It is only a short time; stand still and behold the salvation of God, which he will show you within these few years. But what am I doing? I could not help but digress a little and briefly warn my brethren who are in jeopardy. I now return to the main subject. 

About two years before the Hollanders made this decree, Henry IV, the King of France, was wounded by Jean Châtel <note>original: "Iohn Castellius"; Châtel was a student of the Jesuits who attempted to assassinate King Henry IV in 1594.</note>, the Jesuit who intended to kill him. Consequently, a most worthy judgment was passed and given in the great assembly of the Parliament <note>original: "the Chamber"</note>, both against Châtel and the entire company of the Jesuits. Specifically:

*That all the priests of the College of Clermont, and all others devoted to the aforementioned Society [of Jesus], must leave Paris and all other cities and places where they hold their colleges within three days after this proclamation is published. Furthermore, they must leave the entire kingdom within the following fifteen days. This is because they are, and are considered to be, corrupters of the youth, disturbers of the public peace, and enemies of the King and the Kingdom. Unless they comply, and if they are found there after the appointed time, they shall be punished as traitors and rebels, etc.*

->OF THE REVELATION. Chapter 16.<-

This is a holy and wholesome decree. But, O Father of mercies, I beseech you: set up your altar among them, so that they may utterly renounce the Roman Antichrist <note>The author identifies the "Antichrist" as the Pope or the Roman Catholic Church.</note> and may, by that means, enjoy the sincere worship of your name along with the rest of your chosen people <note>original: "Elect"</note>.

**Verse 8.** *After that, the fourth angel poured out his vial upon the sun.*
So far, these events correspond to the very times in which we live today. For our times have progressed as far as this vial; the other four <note>Meaning vials four through seven, which the author considers to be in the process of unfolding or yet to come.</note> are to be expected by us, and therefore searching for their meaning is all the more difficult.

And yet, relying on His guidance alone—by whose help we have come prosperously this far—and being furthered by the light of the vials that are past (which we have understood from the previous explanation), we hope to provide something that may help shed light on those that are to come. The specific power of this vial is directed at the sun. This has a twofold result: the first is *power given to the sun to scorch people with fire*, as seen in this verse. A secondary result is *a mighty boiling of people in heat, blasphemy, and obstinacy*, as described in the ninth verse. Regarding the "sun," it is a metaphorical one, just as the previous elements were.

For the same people complain of the intensity <note>original: "greiuousnes"</note> of this heat who endured the previous calamities, as it says in the following verse: *And they blasphemed the name of God, who has power over these plagues.* But if we were to understand this as a literal burning of the physical sun, how is it that it afflicts the wicked more than the good? After all, both live together on the earth, and one is no more protected <note>original: "defenced"</note> from the force of the heavenly bodies than the other.

Therefore, we should not think of any sun other than that which the vial is poured upon—which we have shown is called a "vial" more because of its likeness than because of its literal nature. Let the usual meaning of this word remain, by which it represents the Holy Scriptures. By their light, the darkness of men's minds is enlightened just as physical eyes are by the beams of the sun.

### Chapter 16. A REVELATION

The vial is to be poured out upon these [the scriptures], not to harm them as the previous vials harmed the earth, the sea, and the rivers, but to give them a certain power and to sharpen them so that they might prick more sharply and pierce more deeply. There is no one who is not ungrateful and spiteful in a foul manner who does not acknowledge how notable the goodness of God is toward these final times in this respect.

For through the help of certain worthy and excellent men—for why should I not call and account those learned men as such, who have helped forward the Christian religion so greatly with their studies and labors?—through the help, I say, of these men, most things are made very easy and plain to us, whereas those who lived in former ages wandered and were deceived by error. To speak plainly: Antichrist has been revealed marvelously for a long time now through God’s mercy. But seeing that the sycophantic followers <note>original: "hangby adherents"</note> of the Roman See <note>original: "Romish Sea"</note> have found and felt nothing more distressing to them in these very years in which we now live—and to which the sequence of time has brought us—than that the Jesuits should be put to death (which was the meaning of the previous vial), this boiling heat of the sun is now to be expected every day. That is, some clearer opening of the scriptures, by which the "man of sin" <note>A term from 2 Thessalonians 2:3, used by Protestant reformers to refer to the Pope.</note> may be more vehemently scorched. His filthiness shall be even more discovered, whereupon men shall pursue him with greater hatred. Because of this, he and his followers shall eventually be driven to such great distress that they shall fret and gnash their teeth against the sun, which has laid his hideous and ugly appearance open to the view of all men, so that he himself cannot endure to behold it. Therefore—

I must exhort and challenge you (O you godly learned men wherever you are), whom God has adorned with a singular talent above the rest to see the truth clearly and to cause it to be seen clearly by others, that you would bestow your utmost labors upon such a worthy work for the use of the Church.

Indeed, they chiefly carry away the prize and win the spurs who bring the battle to an end. This is the only combat that remains, it seems, for learned men to wage, which should stir them up all the more to study and labor hard. What remains to be done after this shall be dispatched with fire and sword, not with pen and ink.

> *And he had power given him to afflict men with heat by fire.*

The first event afflicts men with heat, but what kind of men? Why is nothing added here, such as the Mark of the Beast or some similar thing, so that we might know to what company this plague belongs? Shall others also, besides the household servants of Antichrist, be burnt up with this Sun? Truly, so it seems. Hypocrites and all the rest who are not truly religious—whatever religion they profess—cannot tolerate having their sins laid open, convicted, and reproved by the bright truth of God. Therefore, it should be no marvel if many other earthly-minded men also, who are not of the Popish religion <note>original: "Popish Religion." A common early modern Protestant term for Roman Catholicism.</note>, should be sorely troubled with the scorching heat of the Sun. But the words of the next verse (*who has power over these plagues*) seem to belong to the men who felt the former scourges also, as we have said.

But why are the next words (*by fire*) added, seeing the verb "to scorch" expresses the burning heat of the Sun sufficiently? Namely, so that we may know that the heat with which they shall boil shall not be heavenly, but earthly—such as that of fire is. That is to say: rivalry <note>original: "emulation." In this context, it refers to jealous competition or malicious envy rather than a desire to excel.</note>, contention, strife, and all bitter affections of the heart. For this "fire" here is metaphorical, which makes it plain that this is no literal Sun, as it does not work by its own force but by the force of another.

# Chapter 16: A Revelation

Such, therefore, is the first event, by which men shall boil with heat—not only with inward fretting and galling of their hearts, but also with open brawling and railing. But shall the "Angel of the Sun" <note>Referring to the ministers or scholars who reveal the light of the Scriptures.</note> be so rewarded for his efforts? It would have been a wiser and safer part for him to have stopped up his vial, so that it might not have dropped down such a mischievous trouble upon himself. 

But let not his courage fail, nor his hand slacken from working. God will provide a hiding place for him from the strife and venomousness of tongues. This is the very same thing that all the Prophets of God have ever been tried and scourged with. That Holy Book is of such a nature that when it is tasted in the mouth, it is sweet as honey, but once eaten, it brings bitterness to the belly (Chapter 10:9). Therefore, let the wicked rail on at their pleasure, while it is the discovery of their wickedness that makes them thus disgorge their rancorous stomachs <note>original: "rancorous ſtomacks." In this period, the "stomach" was considered the seat of pride, anger, and disposition.</note>.

*Verse 9. And men boiled with a great heat.* The second effect consists of the marvelous and unusual vexations that shall befall men when there shall be no shade—not even from a thick grove of trees—with which they may break and beat off the sun’s heat. They blaspheme the name of God, therefore, who has power over these plagues, even as those people did who were called the *Atlantians* <note>original: "Atlantici." A reference to the Atlantes, a tribe in Libya mentioned by the Greek historian Herodotus (Book 4.184), who were said to curse the sun for scorching them.</note>, who cursed the sun with all the execrable curses they could devise because it scorched them with excessive heat, as Herodotus reports. 

These last words seem to attribute this plague to those men whom the ulcers also annoyed and whose fountains were turned into blood. Yet we must not think that they shall blaspheme God in plain terms and with an open mouth—so that they would violate His Holy name openly after the manner of the Heathens and those who do not know God—but men commit this sin also at such times when they discredit and disgrace His truth by railing and speaking evil against it. Such an indirect kind of blasphemy as this is likely to be used by them.

*Neither did they repent to give him glory.* This is an incomplete expression <note>original: "defectiue ſpeach." A grammatical term for an ellipsis, where the author believes some words are omitted for brevity.</note>, which is set down in full in Chapter 9:20. It is as if he should say: *And they repented not of their works, that they might give [glory], etc.* And so it is also below in verse 11. Now, then, see here what this increase of light and heat will work: it will drive men to blaspheme God, and

<header>Chapter 16. A REVELATION,</header>

And yet some Jesuits, being constrained by the force of the truth, are beginning to speak now of the overthrow of Rome. But yet the Beast shall remain alive for some time after the ruin of the City, not for the recovering of his former dignity, but so that he may come to a more grievous destruction shortly after. And therefore he says *that his Kingdom shall be dark, not utterly extinguished*, but deprived of the former brightness and renown it had.

It shall be a mighty and intolerable pain, such as is described elsewhere by *weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matthew 22:13)*. Unless, perhaps, so great an anguish is signified by this proverbial manner of speaking—that they shall be compelled, whether they like it or not, to curb their impudent <note>original: "malapert"</note> and reproachful tongues. That is, to renounce their own writings and to speak more modestly forever after, which is called in common speech "biting one's tongue" and "eating one's words." But when it is said in the next words, *that they repented not of their works*, the former explanation is more simple. And yet they may pretend to stop their evil-speaking out of fear, even if they will not truly repent from their hearts. Yet I would rather follow the former meaning. That passage in Zechariah <note>original: "Zachary"</note> 14:12 seems to agree most fittingly with this: *Their tongue shall consume away in their mouth*. Now the words in the Greek are *out of the pain*, which is a Hebrew phrase that uses the preposition *from* or *out* to mean *because of*, as in *Psalm 102:6*.

# Chapter 16. A REVELATION,

...once having been done, be done again and anew? But it is that which flows through Mesopotamia at the east side of Judea, as we have seen above in Chapter 9:14. Yet this river is used here metaphorically for any obstacle by which the passage into this country may be stopped. The first result of this vial is the drying up of its waters, just as the Red Sea was dried up of old by means of the east winds that blew, and as it happened when the Jews passed over the Jordan into the land of Canaan (Exodus 14; Joshua 3). The purpose for why the waters are dried up is so that the way of the kings who come from the "rising of the sun" <note>original: "rising of the Sunne" — meaning the East</note> might be prepared. 

But who are these kings? Are they the four angels of whom we read in Chapter 9:15? The consideration of the timing will not allow this interpretation to stand. That trumpet sounded many years before this; this vial has not even begun to be poured out yet. It follows after the sacking and leveling of Rome—which still flourishes now, and which that trumpet saw flourishing for a long time. What then? Are they those "kings of the earth and of the whole world" mentioned in the 14th verse of this chapter? But these kings, for whom the Euphrates gives way, are kings of the East only, and not of the whole world.

It would be tedious to recount much more to refute the interpretations of other men. It seems to me that the people signified here by these kings are those for whose sake alone the Scriptures declare that the waters were dried up of old: namely the Jews. To them the Red Sea gave passage, and the Jordan stopped its course until they all passed over, making a way through the depths with their feet. This miracle is unique to this people alone. 

For while *Josephus* writes that the *Sea of Pamphylia* gave way to the *Macedonians* when *Alexander* led his army 그 way (*Antiquities* <note>original: "Antiquit." — referring to Josephus’s *Antiquities of the Jews*</note>, Book 2, Chapter 7), other writers show abundantly how that matter is to be understood. *Plutarch* reports in the *Life of Alexander* that the historians <note>original: "Historiographers"</note> have exaggerated the matter more than can be believed, and that *Alexander* himself never boasted of any such miraculous event <note>original: "prodigious accident"</note> in his letters <note>original: "Epistles"</note>. *Arrian* <note>original: "Arianus"</note> writes that the path does not usually lie open by the sea opposite *Phaselis* (which is a city in *Pamphylia*) except when the northern winds blow. These winds blew vehemently when *Alexander* took his journey that way, so that they seemed to make him an easy passage, and that not without a divine providence.

### OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chap. 16.

But Strabo <note>original: "strabo" — a Greek geographer and historian</note> writes most plainly that the soldiers journeyed the whole day through the water, being plunged into it up to the navel (Book 14). Therefore, Alexander the Great passed through shallow waters, not waters that were quite dried up. Nor do I think it is reported and chronicled anywhere that such a thing as this happened to any people besides the Jews. The vanity of writers may invent many things, but the Holy Scriptures claim this as a unique miracle that God performed for the nation of the Jews alone. "Who says to the deep, *'Be dry, and I will dry up your rivers,'*" says the Lord in Isaiah <note>original: "Esay"</note> when He discusses the deliverance of this people (Chapter 44:27).

And again, *"Are you not the same who has dried up the sea, even the waters of the great deep, making the waters of the great deep to be a way for the redeemed to pass over?"* (Chapter 51:10). And lest anyone should think that this miracle was performed only in times past, and that no such matter is to be expected afterward, the Prophet Isaiah adds in the next verse: *"So the redeemed of the Lord shall return and enter into Zion with a song,"* etc. So also in Chapter 63:11: *"Where is He who brought them up out of the sea with the shepherd of His sheep, who divided the waters before them, who led them through the deep as a horse through the wilderness?"*

It is no wonder, therefore, that a unique characteristic and identifying mark <term>cognizance: a heraldic badge or distinguishing mark used for identification</term> of this people alone is used here to represent the people themselves. But why do they need to have a way prepared for them? Will they return to Jerusalem again? There is nothing more certain; the Prophets everywhere directly confirm it and insist <note>original: "beate vppon it"</note> upon it. 

Yet they shall not go there to have their ceremonial worship restored, but to make the goodness of God shine forth to all the world. This will happen when the world sees God give to that nation—which is now and has been for many ages scattered throughout the whole world, living nowhere except by permission and request—their own homes where their fathers once lived. There they shall worship Christ purely and sincerely, according to His will and commandment alone. This is a matter that was commonly spoken of by the ancient Jews. They understood it from the Prophets, but only dimly—as if glimpsing it through a lattice. For this reason, the idea became corrupted with many "old wives' fables" among the ancient Jews, as it still is today. That same counterfeit Ezra <note>original: "Eldras" — referring to the apocryphal book of 2 Esdras</note> saw some small pieces of this truth, which he overwhelmed...

**Verse 15. *Behold, I come as a thief.*** These words trouble Theodore Beza <note>original: "Theod. Beza"; a major French Protestant theologian and successor to John Calvin.</note> greatly, as if they had crept into a place that was not fitting for them from some other more appropriate place. But since these times would be most woeful—as it is foretold regarding the Jews in Daniel 12:1—and it is unlikely that we of the Christian nations should be in any better state, this warning here does not need to seem superfluous or ill-timed to anyone. The greatness of these dangers might terrify even the strongest men of those days. 

But lest anyone should stumble <note>original: "dash his foote against this stone of offence"; a biblical idiom for being discouraged or led into sin by a difficult obstacle.</note> and suffer the shipwreck of his faith, Christ bids him to be of good cheer and not to forsake the righteousness of faith out of any fear. (This righteousness is the "garments" he speaks of here, which the adversaries will strive most of all to strip away from a person.) Christ promises that he will come like a thief suddenly, and that he will plague the enemies when they are least aware of it, and that he will also deliver the Church. A similar solace was given in Chapter 13:10 and 14:13. Thus we may know that such heartening sentences as this are neither strange nor fruitless, but most timely and necessary. Neither are these words brought in abruptly; but since mention was made in the preceding words of "God Almighty," they are brought in as spoken by this God Almighty himself in person, to give them greater force.

***Their Garments.*** That is, the assurance of the pardon of our sins by Jesus Christ alone, with which our sins are covered (Romans 4:6–7). Neither are there any other garments with which all our nakedness can be covered. The purity of the Saints, or of ourselves, cannot cover so much as our backs, so far is it from being able to hide our more deformed and unseemly parts. These garments are called afterwards the "righteousness of the Saints" in Chapter 19:8, where we shall see what force these words have.

Hebrew *Armageddon*. This is the third part of the second event. But who is it that shall gather them together? It is truly Christ; and therefore he does not speak in the plural number and say "they gathered them"—meaning those three spirits—but the words in the Greek are "he gathered them" in the singular number. Whatever the kings of the earth aimed at, God’s secret providence shall so guide and overrule them that whatever destruction they should devise and intend to bring upon others, it should fall upon themselves. This remains true unless perhaps the noun that governs this verb is "Spirits" (which are mentioned in verse 14 and are said there to go forth), to which these words may be joined, with verse 15 being treated as a parenthesis. 

But yet, whoever it was that took the pains to gather them together, they are governed by the hidden providence of Christ. For being led by the hand of God, they shall assemble together of their own accord into that place from which no way of escaping shall appear. This place is called in Hebrew *Armageddon*, as the editions of Montanus <note>Benito Arias Montano (1527–1598), a Spanish scholar and editor of the Antwerp Polyglot Bible.</note> and Plantin <note>Christophe Plantin (c. 1520–1589), a famous Renaissance printer.</note> read it with a single "d," just as Aretas <note>Aretas of Caesarea, an early commentator on the Book of Revelation.</note> also read it, except that he changes one letter to *Ermagedon*. These copies might have been correct if they had retained the aspiration <note>The "h" sound at the beginning of a word.</note> *Harmageddon*, which is how I truly think the word should be read, as I will demonstrate shortly when discussing this word, if I am not mistaken. 

Theodore Beza <note>A major Protestant reformer and scholar of the Greek New Testament.</note> wants the "d" to be doubled, as does the Latin Vulgate, as if the name were made of *Har* and *Megiddon*. This is the place where King Josiah was slain (2 Chronicles 35:22). But that place was sorrowful for the Church and prosperous for the wicked, whereas *Harmageddon* seems to be the opposite. Our countryman John Foxe <note>original: "Iohn Foxe of happy memory"; author of the famous 'Book of Martyrs.'</note> offers an interpretation from a more fitting allusion, in my opinion. He believes there is no reference to Josiah here, but rather to that notable victory which Deborah and Barak achieved with a small army against the massive host of Sisera at the town of Megiddo, which was situated on a mountain (Judges 5:19, etc.). 

However, as I consider the matter more diligently, no such matter seems to be alluded to in this place. Instead, there is a reference to the passage in Daniel 11:45: *And he shall pitch the tents of his palace between the seas in the glorious and holy mountains.* It may be proved by many arguments that Daniel’s prophecy and this one by John in this place

belongs to the same time—namely, to this sixth Vial—as we will one day make plain, if God gives leave. The difference is only in this: that the Turk <note>original: "Turke"; referring to the Ottoman Empire, often identified in Reformation-era commentary as a primary antagonist in end-times prophecy.</note> is spoken of there individually as he is the enemy of the Christian *Jews*, while here all the enemies of the whole Church—both Gentiles and *Jews*—are discussed together. Now, the place where the enemy of the *Jews* pitched his tents is specified by name: namely, in the mountain of the beauty of holiness. This is in the Holy Land, between the Syrian Sea and the Euphrates (which is also called a "sea" in the Scriptures).

But the Holy Spirit could not use a word specific only to the *Jews* in this prophecy, where he describes the place of the war against both *Jewish* and Gentile Christians generally. Therefore, he created a new name that might be common to both peoples and that might come closest to the original in meaning, calling it *Harmagedon*. This is compounded from *Har*, which means a *hill*, and *Megadhim*, which signifies "delights" (or, with the singular suffix, "his delight"). This name has the same sense as the one used in the other prophecy: *Har-Tsebi* <note>original: "Hartsebbi"; Hebrew for "Mountain of Beauty" or "Mountain of Delight."</note>, the hill of a kid, or a roe, or of pleasure and delight. For the word *Tsebi* <note>original: "Tsebbi"</note> signifies both of these things. It is a word used by lovers when they call their sweethearts by loving names, as in the Song of Solomon: *My beloved is like a pleasant roe*, etc. (Chapter 2:9). From all this, it appears that the place where the Turk shall fight with the *Jews* is foretold by name by the prophet Daniel. But here, the same place where the *Beast* shall encounter the Church of the Gentiles is only hinted at in general.

It is as if *Harmagedon* were a common name for both peoples, which is further distinguished into *Har-Tsebi Kodesh* <note>original: "Har-Tsebi quod seesch"; likely a corruption of the Hebrew *Har-Tsebi-Kodesh*, meaning "The Holy Mountain of Delight."</note>, the "Hill of His Holy Pleasantness"—the place for the *Jews*—and into a Western place that has no specific name at all but is included in the name of the whole. And yet this name teaches us that this battle is to take place where the Church flourishes with the greatest purity. For this is the "hill of delights" in Christ's account. We shall see this place described a little more distinctly in the larger opening of this Vial in Chapter 19. But let us observe for our comfort that the Holy Church among us Gentiles is no less a "hill of delights" to God than the Church of the *Jews* will be. God is no respecter of persons; He considers those in every nation who truly worship Him in Christ as most dear to Him.

**Verse 17.** *And the Seventh Angel poured out his Vial upon the air.* The outcome of this Vial will be universal, as it is poured upon the air which encompasses the land and sea all around. This "air," however, is not this elementary air that we breathe, but something else signified by this name, as was common in the other vials <note>The "vials" or bowls represent specific divine judgments poured out upon the earth.</note>. Now we know that the Devil is called in the Scriptures *the Prince who has power over the Air* (Ephesians 2:2), to which those "chains of darkness" belong that Peter speaks of in 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude in his epistle, verse 6. Seeing, therefore, that the air belongs to his jurisdiction, this last Vial shall bring a most grievous calamity unto the whole kingdom of the Devil. The former Vials plagued certain members of it individually; this shall destroy the whole body of the wicked with a universal destruction.

*And there came a great voice out of the Temple of heaven.* The first event is a great voice, which is described by the place from which it comes and by what it spoke. The place is not only the Temple of Heaven, but also the Throne of which we had a description in Chapter 4:2. That is the habitation of the Saints, as we have seen before; this is that Throne of highest Majesty which, being placed in the midst of the assembly of the faithful, glitters with an incomprehensible brightness and the glory of the most Holy Trinity. Therefore, this voice comes immediately from God himself, in respect to the ministry of the Church. By this, it is signified that God would provide for his servants under this Vial beyond his usual manner—and almost beyond all hope and expectation—by putting forth his power and force from heaven for the destruction <note>original: "defacing"</note> of all his enemies. We heard just now that all these enemies were gathered together into the place called Harmagedon <note>A symbolic site of the final battle between good and evil, derived from Hebrew meaning "Mountain of Megiddo."</note>, an interpretation we shall see confirmed more fully in the chapters that follow, where there is a more large explaining of this Vial. 

The word that was given forth was, *It is done*; which is a most fit word for the consummation of all things. We know this was used in the creation of them (Genesis 1). This is the meaning of it, as if he should say: "All things have now been which I have decreed should be done. Nor does any part of my promises remain, the accomplishment of which is to be looked for upon earth." For this phrase "it is done" has a relationship to Chapter 10:7: *In the days of the voice of the seventh Angel, when*

Now shall the end of all the Prophets' predictions come, both when all the enemies shall be utterly and simultaneously abolished, and when there shall be one sheepfold made upon earth, consisting of all the Elect—both Jews and Gentiles—under one shepherd, Jesus Christ <note>A reference to the unification of all believers as described in John 10:16.</note>. It shall eventually be translated from earth into heaven; but I find no mention in this Book of the specific time when this translation shall occur, which will be perfectly finished at Christ’s second coming. This prophecy proceeds no further than the final and universal slaughter of all enemies and the full restoration of the Jewish nation <note>Early Modern commentators often believed that a literal restoration and conversion of the Jewish people would precede the end of the world.</note>. However, it sets down no certain point of time in which the Church shall depart from the earth to take possession of its heavenly inheritance.

These things shall be made manifest in the interpretation that follows. Some taste of this was to be given here, lest some—perhaps being too curious in marking the order of matters—should slip into the error of setting down a specific time for the Last Day. I see certain learned and godly men being carried away by this, as if some very near moment of it could be defined by this Vial. If we examine this a little more diligently, we shall find that the timing is wholly laid up and hidden in the expectation of hope; it is not meant to come within the comprehension of our understanding at all.

Now, the agreement between the last Vial and the last Trumpet is this: the Kingdom of Christ is begun in the Trumpet, where the enemies are put down in part (as it is in Chapter 11:15), whereupon that voice was given forth saying, *“The kingdoms of this world have become the kingdoms of our Lord and of His Christ.”* In this Vial, the Kingdom of Christ is consummated, as all the enemies are quite swept away; therefore, the voice that is given forth in this instance says, *“It is done.”*

**Verse 19.** *And the great city was divided into three parts.* This is the second member of the secondary event, showing against what things this judgment shall be exercised—which are partly places and partly men. The places are cities and nations. There are three mentioned in this verse: *the Great City*, *the Cities of the Nations*, and *that great Babylon*. 

But what is this Great City? We have heard above that the "city" does not only signify some town surrounded with walls, where citizens inhabit in great numbers and are joined together by the bonds of the same laws and privileges. It also signifies the whole jurisdiction and government of a city. For example, the "tenth part of Rome" fell when Germany withdrew itself from the yoke of her bondage (Chapter 11:13). What, then? Is this city spoken of here only the jurisdiction of Rome? Indeed, it was called the "Great City" above, in Chapter 11:8.

But yet we may observe that the Holy Spirit <note>original: "Holy Ghost"</note> does not intensify the guilt of this city with as many and as intense words as he does that of her mother, Rome. This is because the sins of the heathens—however heinous they may be—are lighter than the sins of those who abuse God's grace. As for the wording, the "middle voice" is used for the passive in the verb "remembering," as it is in Acts 10:31. <note>In Greek grammar, the "middle voice" can indicate an action the subject does to or for itself; here the author explains the phrasing "she came in remembrance before God."</note> So also "to give" is used for "to be given," as in "to give her the cup," etc. The punishment shall be "the cup of the wine of the indignation of his wrath."

"Cup" signifies a part or portion, as in "the Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup" (Psalm 16:5 and 11:6). This is a metaphor taken from masters of feasts, who were accustomed to measure out to everyone as much as he should drink. Because of this, some characters in Homer (*Iliad*, Book 4) are said to drink by a "divided measure"—as if it were a cup half full—which is contrasted with a full cup, from which a man may drink as much as he wants. Such are God's judgments, which are inflicted upon men in such just measure and weight as is appropriate for each person. Now, these judgments are "cups of wine" because they shall be as pleasing and delightful to God as men's sins have been to them; that is, he shall take delight in cutting them off, as it says in Chapter 14:10. Or perhaps it is called a "cup of wine" because its severity shall take all sense away from men—just as gulping down <note>original: "gulling in"</note> too much wine is known to do—so that a man shall no more be able to escape a misfortune than one who is...

Now, this heaping up of words—"the indignation of his wrath"—signifies the most grievous and sharp punishments, though it is not declared expressly whether it shall be quite rooted out by these means, as old Rome was before. It is likely that the city itself shall be left standing after it has endured a mighty calamity, and that it shall be possessed by Christians and shall be in subjection unto them forever afterwards.

**Verse 20. *And every island fled away.*** So much for the calamity that shall befall the cities and provinces that are next adjoining unto them. These words here are to be referred to the more remote nations, which shall have no help or aid against calamity despite the distance of their location. This desolation shall pass over the sea and shall seize upon men in their furthest islands. Neither shall those places be in better condition which are protected <note>original: "fenced"</note> by the firmness of mountains; for these shall also be plucked up by the roots and shall perish forever, as was seen above in Chapter 6:14. And yet this "hurly-burly" <note>An archaic term for a violent commotion, storm, or period of confusion.</note> shall be far greater and more grievous than that one. For there, the mountains and islands were moved out of their places. Here, they shall be so utterly abolished that there shall be no footsteps of them left standing. 

But an <term>island</term> <note>original: "Isle"</note> in this place is not only meant for land which is encompassed on every side by the sea, but also for a continent, following the manner of the Hebrews, who give the name of "isles" to all the countries that are beyond the seas (Psalm 72:10). So the word "island" here may contain Egypt and Africa <note>original: "Africk"</note> also.

**Verse 21. *And there fell a great hail about the weight of a talent.*** Thus far of the calamity that shall befall places. As for men, a hail as big as a <term>talent</term> <note>A talent was an ancient unit of weight, often cited as being between 75 and 100 pounds. ## Chapter 17

### The Logical Analysis of It

And thus we have had the distinct prophecy of the last period, which has been divided into its seven parts <note>original: "members"</note> according to the manner that was used in the Seals and Trumpets. Now follows the continuous narrative <note>original: "enarration"</note> and the more detailed unfolding of the three last Vials, which are of the greatest weight and of special significance. 

The fifth of these is handled in this chapter, as well as throughout the one that follows, and in the first five verses of the nineteenth chapter. The sixth is contained in the fifteen verses next following in that nineteenth chapter, starting from the twentieth verse. The seventh continues through the twentieth and twenty-first chapters, and up to the sixth verse of the twenty-second chapter. From there follows the conclusion of the whole book. 

It is very helpful for making things clear that we should know which things agree in time and in the nature of the matter. Regarding the fifth Vial, it is directed entirely against the **Throne of the Beast** (as we have seen above in Chapter 16, verses 10–11). The explanation of it consists partly in declaring what this Throne is and what kind of place it is throughout this chapter; and partly in relating those things which accompany its ruin in the following chapter and in the beginning of the nineteenth. 

The description of the Throne begins with a preparation that invites John to come and know the condemnation <note>original: "damnation"</note> of the Whore (verses 1–2). This leads him away into the wilderness,

# THE EXPOSITION.

**Then there came one of the seven angels.** We said in the logical analysis <note>original: "Resolving"; referring to the structural breakdown of the chapter.</note> of this chapter that this continued explanation—which is contained in the chapters following, up to the conclusion of the whole book—concerns the last three vials only. How true this is, the matter itself will show. In the meantime, it may be asked: why is the explanation of the former vials omitted?

The reason for this seems to be that those earlier ones were partly already past and gone, and partly they were present at the time when the vial should be poured out upon the throne. Therefore, they have no need of any larger opening than either fresh remembrance or the present experience and state of matters provided,
