...but as for the rest that were to come, they needed a more detailed <note>original: "plentifull"</note> declaration, and for that reason all the rest of the labor is spent upon them. Therefore, concerning this one angel of the seven, it is that fifth angel who should bring calamity upon the Throne (Chapter 18:10). Of which calamity, though, there are certain degrees, so that there are certain light sprinklings of punishments made by the help of certain other angels before this whole vial is poured out by this one. And yet all these are accounted for and called this "one fifth angel" by a common name. This thing appears from this chapter, which is wholly spent in declaring the judgment <note>original: "damnation"</note> of the whore, although her final destruction is reserved for the next chapter. These things being thus established, let us now consider the matter itself.

First, the angel prepares a way for himself to that which he intends, both by inviting John to learn, and also by carrying him over to that place where he might behold the whole matter most fitly. He invites him, partly by calling upon him and saying, "come here" <note>original: "come hether"</note>, for that is the meaning of the incomplete <note>original: "defectiue"</note> speech in the Greek (as if John desired to understand the matter, but yet went not the right way to find it out. For we are accustomed to call back men who are desirous to know a matter and yet go astray, by showing them the right path to the place they are seeking to go, but all in vain). He also invites him partly by laboring to increase his diligence in seeking when he shows him the greatness of the matter, saying: *I will show you the judgment <note>original: "damnation"</note> of the great whore.* This judgment, though, is not a present destruction of her, but that which is to come shortly after. And so the word used for judgment <note>original: "damnation"</note> properly signifies "judgment," which, being pronounced solemnly in this chapter, should be executed a little later. 

But what whore is this whose judgment he speaks of? We have never had any express mention made of this whore before now; and yet she must be well known, because he calls John to know her judgment as a thing that was so exceedingly wished for. Certainly, this is that Jezebel of whom we have heard in the Church of Thyatira—that noble harlot who had lain sick in her bed for a long time, who is now, for all that, to be put to death and to be thrown <note>original: "tumbled"</note> out of the window, lest she should die of her disease before she dies of her punishment (Chapter 2:20).

This is that great Babylon spoken of in verse 5 of this chapter. We have already heard that she was made famous as the "mother of fornications and abominations of the earth" (Chapter 14:8). Therefore, this is no new prostitute recently heard of, but an old and almost withered madam <note>original: "bawde"</note>, containing within herself most concisely <note>original: "compendiously"</note> whatever Sodom and Egypt signified; she is one who easily surpassed all others <note>original: "winne the spurs"</note> in both kinds of fornication—both spiritual and physical (Chapter 11:8).

The angel gives John a short description of this whore here to provide a taste of her character, both regarding the place where she sits and "keeps shop" <note>meaning: conducts her business</note>, and regarding those with whom she has played the harlot. *Her seat is above many waters*, which means many people, multitudes, nations, and languages, as explained below in verse 15. Therefore, she is no low-class prostitute who will be hired for a pittance <term>dodkin: a Dutch coin of very small value; a trifle</term>, but a harlot <note>original: "Queane"</note> like a **Queen** in status and pomp—rightly called **Jezebel** and a "great whore" because of her vast dominion. Her fornicators are the **Kings** of the Earth, who have conspired to commit the same idolatry with her. They are called this, just as she is, by a very common metaphor in the Scriptures, because spiritual adultery equals or even surpasses physical adultery in filthiness and wickedness, as it is the means by which a person revolts against the true God. And she is not only immoral <note>original: "naught"</note> with **Kings**, but also with the rest of the inhabitants of the earth: **Nobles**, **Earls**, **Marquesses**, and **Governors of Cities** (for in her lust, she refuses no man). All of these she makes drunk with the "wine of her whoredom" by infatuating <note>original: "besotting"</note> them so completely with her enticing superstitions that, being utterly deprived of all sense of true religion, they suffer a kind of senselessness similar to what drunkards experience. These few words should be enough to show who this whore is and what the **Throne** of the **Beast** represents. For is not **Rome** that great whore? Have we not already proven <note>original: "conuinced"</note> her to be **Jezebel**? Does she not sit upon many waters? And has not **Rome** enticed the **Kings** and inhabitants of the earth into idolatry with her deceptive <note>original: "cousening"</note> tricks? No one who considers the matter truthfully and impartially can doubt it.

But as an introduction to the matter, he promises to give us even clearer signs than these. The same Prophet [Isaiah] uses the same phrase elsewhere without the preposition, as in Chapter 29:9, and the Greek translators <note>original: "Greek Interpreters"; referring to the Septuagint</note> render it similarly.

**Verse 3.** *So he carried me away.* That concludes the invitation for John to come. Now John is carried away into a place where he might see the matter most clearly: he is taken away into a desert and a wilderness. But some might ask: why did he need to go to an even more solitary place, since he was already on Patmos and living there in exile? John here represents the community of the faithful. His being carried away to a solitary place signifies an event—the same reason he previously stood upon the seashore in Chapter 12:18. Through this, we are taught that the revelation of this Throne <note>The seat of the Antichrist's power</note> must be sought by the faithful from people living in obscure places—as if in a desert or wilderness—from whom no such thing was expected.

For just as the first light that gave knowledge of Christ arose of old among a people *who sat in darkness and in the region and shadow of death* (Matthew 4:15–16), so his counterfeit Vicar <note>A polemical term for the Pope, whom the author views as a false representative of Christ.</note> should resemble our Lord in some ways regarding his seat of power. It is not that he was unknown to the world before, but that the wilderness provides a clearer light to recognize him more fully, so that he could scarcely dare to look men in the face.

We know that the "whore" <note>The Roman Church</note> has hardened her resolve <note>original: "hardened her forehead"; a biblical idiom for becoming shameless</note> again within these last few years. However, a new and strange reproach shall be cast upon her, coming out of the desert. Because of this, she will be compelled to hide her face—unless she has forgotten how to be ashamed and has learned to blush at nothing. Therefore, let me stir you up, my brothers, to attack this "whore" with a fresh and renewed assault. Let no man be terrified because he lacks fame or status in the world; God wills that some brilliance be recognized even in a man who seems like obscurity itself. And let no one wonder from now on why the Antichrist or the "whore" cannot be seen clearly at Rome; we must go into the wilderness to truly find her out.

For though you have enlarged the privilege of your Empire by land and sea, being amplified with many victories, yet that which you have subdued by the labor of war is less than what Christian peace has brought under your power."* <note>original Latin quote from Leo I's Sermon 82: "Ista est quae per sacram beati Petri sedem caput orbis effecta, latius praesidet religione divina quam dominatione terrena..."</note> Prosper <note>Prosper of Aquitaine (c. 390–455 AD), a Christian writer and disciple of St. Augustine.</note> says the same: *"Rome is the Seat of Peter; it is also the seat of his pastoral honor. And so, having been made the Head of the world, it possesses through religion that which it does not possess by force and arms."*

Therefore, this one shared symbol <note>original: "Type"</note> provides us with a necessary argument that Antichrist has both his Seat and his Kingdom at Rome. This single argument would be enough to end all controversy if men did not love themselves more than the truth, and if they would stop barking against it. However, because their mouths must be completely stopped, the Holy Spirit does not stop here but proceeds to other, clearer arguments. He does this so that those for whom the morning light is not enough to reveal the truth might have the noonday sun to help them, if perhaps they might then be brought to see it.

For this same color is used to represent the most grievous sins. *"Though your sins be as scarlet,"* says Isaiah, chapter 1, verse 18 <note>original: "Esay, Chapt. 1. 8." The text refers to Isaiah 1:18.</note>. Who does not see that this Beast is at Rome, where the Pope sits, whose feet kings kiss and who kills Christians who will not acknowledge his godhead? He does this most cruelly, both in the city and throughout the whole jurisdiction of Rome. It was not without cause that this color has pleased the Court of Rome above all others; this was indeed ordered by God’s providence, so that the "Scarlet Fathers" <note>A reference to the Cardinals of the Roman Catholic Church, who wear scarlet robes.</note> might provide a visible argument to the world that they are this Beast. Concerning this matter, see what Theodore Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605) was a French Protestant reformer and successor to John Calvin in Geneva.</note> has written in a most elegant epigram. 

Secondly, this Beast is full of the names of blasphemy. How "happy" an increase is made here of an unhappy matter! A while ago, only the heads wore the names of blasphemy (Chapter 13:1). Now the whole body is full of them. Indeed, the Pope’s supremacy was the chief blasphemy in the beginning, and therefore it was fitting to have the name of blasphemy carried on his head. However, time added new blasphemies to this every day, which grew daily in heaps, until at last the matter came into the hands of the Council of Trent <note>An ecumenical council of the Catholic Church (1545–1563) prompted by the Protestant Reformation.</note> and the "Masters of Controversies." <note>Theologians dedicated to defending Catholic doctrine against Protestantism.</note> By their help, the Beast is now entirely covered with most detestable errors (the whole "sea of doctrine" having been turned by them into deadly and filthy blood, as was said in Chapter 16:3).

# Chapter 17. A REVELATION

**Impudence.** In ancient times, harlots were covered with a veil, yet do you boast of your filthiness with an open forehead and a title written upon it? But what is this name? It is not the word *Mystery* as it seems; for *Aretas* <note>Aretas of Caesarea was a 10th-century commentator on the Book of Revelation.</note> joins it with the verb "written" without any mark of punctuation, in this manner: *and upon her forehead she had a name written Mystery, the great Babylon, etc.* It is as if *Mystery* were a noun used in place of an adjective, meaning "full of mystical significance," as if it were said: "and upon her forehead there was a mystical name written, Babylon, etc." Certainly, the grammatical structure requires that when one noun is joined with another without an article, it should serve as the <term>predicate</term> <note>original: "Predicatum"; the part of a sentence that provides information about the subject.</note>. Thus: *and she had a name written in her forehead, which is a mystery.*

From this, it appears that "mystery" is not to be written with a capital M at the beginning as if it were a part of the name or the identifying mark of the whore set on her forehead. Instead, it should be read together with the words that come before the name. However, the meaning is the same regardless of how it is placed; it teaches us that some secret lurks in this name, which must be interpreted differently than how it is commonly understood or how it appears on the surface. Therefore, the name written on the forehead is the entire connection of these words: *That great Babylon, that mother of fornication, and abominations of the earth.*

But some may say that there is no city that boasts of itself using such express words. The Holy Spirit does not say she does; rather, He teaches that this is her true name, which John saw written on her forehead in so many letters and syllables. However it may be, the true Babylon should have a name written on her which signifies this very same thing through other words by a mystery. Namely: *Rome the Empress of the world, the Pillar of truth, the mirror and pattern for all Churches to behold, from whose statutes we must not depart in any case, whatever she ordains,* Distinction 19, *Indeed.* <note>original: "Enimuero," a reference to a specific section in Gratian's *Decretum*, a foundational collection of Catholic canon law.</note> 

This is the name painted with great letters on the forehead of the whore. If a man diligently searches into its meaning, he shall see that it amounts to the same thing, through a mystery, as what John saw. For whatever ancient corruption has existed in the past or remains today in these Western and Northern churches of ours, all of it has flowed entirely from *Rome*. In this respect, she boastfully calls herself the "mother of the Churches," but she should be called a "stepmother" instead,

# OF THE REVELATION. Chapter 17.

Is not this same Rome the forge of rebellions and the slaughterhouse of Christian princes at this day? Certainly, this Council <note>Likely referring to the Council of Trent (1545–1563), which the author views as a source of anti-Protestant plots.</note> that is made of a company of furies first decrees the killing of princes, and then it sends out the Jesuits underhandedly. They are a crew of cutthroats and poisoning villains who bring their wicked decrees into execution by any means they can devise. It would be an endless labor to go through all your butcheries, O Rome. You are drunk indeed with blood, tumbling yourself in your own surfeit <note>Excessive indulgence.</note>, which you have vomited <note>original: "parbraked"</note> up after excessive drinking of blood.

Now, therefore, all these common properties being joined together show us such a whore as this: namely, one that is increased and sustained by the Beast; one that is princelike, rich, and glistening; that great Mother City and spiritual Babylon; the princess of all superstitions; yet one that deceives men cunningly with her juggling tricks; and lastly, a cruel killer of the martyrs. Since all of these can be found nowhere else together but in Rome alone, let us take notice of the city that is to be condemned. Let everyone take heed in time how they have any society with her, lest they perish together with her in her destruction, which is now shortly coming upon her.

**And I marveled.** Thus far we have dealt with the symbolic description. Now he passes over to the interpretation of it, the occasion of which is set down in these words. But how is it that John marvels, whereas this is the characteristic of cursed men, as seen below in verse 8?

This marveling is full of indignation because of the great prosperity of the wicked harlot, whose just destruction should have been seen at her first conception, or at least when she was in her cradle. But as for wicked men, they admire her with a kind of worship out of an opinion of her supposed excellence, even as they are said to "marvel after the Beast" in Chapter 13:3.

But was he ignorant of the Beast, which he saw in Chapter 13? No such thing; neither is he said to admire the Beast alone, but as he was joined with the woman. He had not beheld both of them joined before in this new portrayal, nor in this full and complete setting out of them.

# Chapter 17. THE REVELATION

And who is there that would not be astonished to see that the Throne of the Dragon <note>original: "Throne of the Dragon"; here referring to the seat of Satanic power, which the author identifies with Rome.</note> (which John saw become a sheepfold of Christ, in a sense, after the Dragon was cast out) could rise up again to such a height of impiety? But we must not linger on the person of John alone, who here represents the common experience of the faithful. We must understand that certain godly men living under the fifth Vial <note>In the author's prophetic timeline, the "Vials" represent stages of God’s judgment. The fifth vial was often interpreted by Protestants as a judgment against the throne of the Pope.</note>—considering the horrible blasphemy of Rome, which they have undoubtedly experienced and known, and thinking of her current prosperity—would wonder exceedingly how such great impiety could remain unpunished for so long. This wondering moved the Angel to take it upon himself to fully explain these things.

**Verse 7. And the Angel said to me, "Why do you marvel?"** This question contains a certain reproof of human negligence and foolishness <note>original: "sillines"</note>. It is as if he were saying that unless men had shamefully failed to observe former times, they would have no need to wonder at the Whore now, seeing her flourish with this kind of prosperity. But our merciful Father, who pardons all the faults of His children for Christ’s sake, forgives this carelessness of theirs as well. Therefore, He sends His Angel to make the whole matter plain to them. This is the purpose of the following words: ***I will tell you the mystery***, etc. By this, he suggests (and not obscurely) that the interpretation itself would not be clearly known to everyone, but would remain hidden from men with seared <note>original: "feared"; likely referring to 1 Timothy 4:2, describing those whose consciences are "seared with a hot iron."</note> consciences, as we saw above in verses 3 and 5.

**Verse 8. The Beast which you saw.** The first interpretation concerns the Beast, and first in regard to his whole person, as we have distinguished in our analysis <note>The author's systematic breakdown of the biblical text.</note>. Through this, his diverse state is declared according to four changes of time, as he should finally be most clearly recognized under this Vial. The first time is when he *was*; the second, when he *was not*; the third, when he *arose out of the bottomless pit*; and the fourth, when he shall finally *go into perdition*. Regarding the first, it is not to be understood as any time before John’s age, or before this prophecy was revealed to him.

# OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chap. 17.

For the Angel plainly affirms that this Beast had not yet come (*verse 10*). That is, he did not yet exist when *John* received this prophecy, but he would receive power at the same hour as the ten kings, who had not yet come into their kingdom in *John's* time (*verse 12*). Therefore, this Beast is not actually the Devil, as some of the ancient writers interpret it—a view which *Ribera* the *Jesuit* <note>Francisco Ribera (1537–1591) was a Spanish Jesuit whose commentary on Revelation argued that the Antichrist was a single future person, rather than the office of the Papacy.</note> greedily adopts. It cannot be said of the Devil that he had not yet come or that he had not yet received power; his kingdom flourished most of all then—indeed, it flourished even before *Christ* came in the flesh. 

We shall see later that the first "birthday" of the Beast refers to the time when the *Dragon* was cast out of heaven and gave the Beast his throne. Thus, the forty-two months during which he primarily exercised his power—which is the same span of time as the woman lurking in the wilderness and the two Prophets being clothed in sackcloth—shared the same beginning as this birthday of the Beast (*Chapter 13:5, 12:6, and 11:2*). We have shown that this occurred around the time of *Constantine's* inauguration into his kingdom, many ages after *John* departed from this life. 

From this beginning, the first point <note>original: "article"</note> notes the time when the Beast flourished for a certain time—specifically, from the end of the public persecutions by open enemies, whom the power <note>original: "puissance"</note> of *Constantine the Great* put to flight. The second point teaches us that after the long period of happy tranquility the Beast enjoyed, a new storm arose which afflicted the Beast so severely that people might well and justly say that "he once was, but now is not." They might have thought he had utterly perished in those troubles. This occurred after the period of peace and respite <note>original: "breathing"</note> he enjoyed under a few emperors (during which time the authority of the *Pope of Rome* had grown marvelously), when the invasion of the *Barbarians* <note>Referring to the various Germanic tribes, such as the Goths and Vandals, who invaded the Western Roman Empire in the 5th century.</note> miserably distressed all *Italy* and horribly laid waste to *Rome* itself—the Throne of the Beast—cutting off the *Pope's* authority (which had grown overgrown and unruly <note>original: "ranke and riotous"</note>) almost to the root. Might not people have rightly cried out at that time and said that the *Pope* "had been," but "now was not," since they might think not only his authority but his very Seat <note>The "Holy See" or the city of Rome itself.</note> was completely overthrown and beyond hope of recovery?

# CHAP. 17. A REVELATION

This second phase <note>original: "time"</note> was called *his wounded head* (Chapter 13:3). This event brought with it the knowledge of his former status <note>original: "estate"</note>, which could not have been known until this change occurred. However, the Beast did not remain in this state of defeat <note>original: "overthrow"</note> forever; he rose up out of it again. As the third point <note>original: "article"</note> teaches us, he ascended out of the bottomless pit. This happened when he extended his horns again, after the storm <note>original: "Tempest"</note> brought by the barbarian tribes <note>original: "Barbarous people"</note> had passed. 

This point covers both the healing of the wound by the Emperors Justinian and Phocas, as well as his rising up out of the Earth by Pope Gregory II. We have discussed both of these in Chapters 13:3, 11; 11:7; and 9:2, 11. This Gregory exercised the power that his predecessors had obtained from the Emperor—and indeed, much more. He became not only a "universal Bishop" but also a sovereign commander over all other leaders, like a dictator; he was someone who could grant or take away the Empire at his will. 

It is sufficient here to note the early beginnings of these matters. We have shown elsewhere who the first Pope was to bestow the title of Emperor of the West upon men. Therefore, the Beast emerged <note>original: "plunge up"</note> from the Pit when the Popes had seized this earthly power for themselves, as shown in Chapter 13:11. Here, he refers to the earth as the *bottomless Pit*, just as it is called elsewhere, such as in Psalm 71:20: *You make me rise out of the deep places <note>original: "bottomlesse places"</note> of the earth*.

So much for the third phase. The fourth is that "he shall go into destruction." This teaches that this newly revived dignity will not last forever; instead, it will be diminished bit by bit and wasted away slowly <note>original: "leisure-ly"</note> until it is finally extinguished. As we heard before in the second chapter, Jezebel—the mistress <note>original: "paramour"</note> of this Beast—lay sick and languishing with an incurable wasting disease <note>original: "consumption"</note>. We see this happening today both in Rome and to the Pope. However, their funeral and burial rites <note>original: "exequies"</note> are still to come; this Book of Revelation will teach us later when that will take place. 

These are the four notable changes. By observing them, any person who is not willfully blind can clearly recognize the Beast. These changes provide a powerful argument for identifying both the time when Rome is the "Whore" and the true identity of the Antichrist. For that City is the Whore where the Antichrist reigns—that is, the Beast who was, and is not, and has ascended out of the deep.

# Chap. 17. A REVELATION,

...by the perfect standard <note>original: "square"</note> of the truth itself, which is so manifest. Do not be so obstinate as to despise my counsel and advice. I am an adversary only to your errors; I desire from my heart to have your persons saved by Jesus Christ. Examine what I say—I desire to be believed on no other condition. And if, upon trial, you find matters to be as certain as I say, then take notice of the subtle, serpentine sophistry <term>sophistry: the use of clever but false arguments, especially with the intention of deceiving</term> of the Jesuits. Thrust out from among you these hellish furies; curse these detestable and pestiferous <note>pestiferous: bringing or spreading disease; harmful or annoying</note> fellows, and all the brood of them, to the Pit of Hell. Behold your own danger, and if you have any care for your salvation, at length and at last be wise and well-advised.

**From the foundation of the world.** This refers to the time before the eternal decree concerning the death of Christ and its force and efficacy <note>efficacy: the ability to produce a desired or intended result</note>, which was signified by these words in Chapter 13:8. Now, the same kind of phrasing points out the eternal election <term>election: in theology, the divine choice of those who will be saved</term> of those who shall be saved—these two things are most nearly joined together.

**Seeing the Beast which was, and which is not, and yet is.** These last words, *"and yet is"*, seem to be read thus: *"and he is present"*. The difference between the readings is this: the words of the common reading signify to us that the Beast remained alive during the defeat <note>original: "discomfiture"</note> he suffered. It is as if it were said: "Although he does not exist in the opinion of men, yet he is." Thus, both parts of the phrase refer to the same time, just as John previously saw one of the heads wounded, as if in a deadly manner, yet it was not quite cut off and killed (Chapter 13:3). 

The other reading points out the third period of time more clearly, in which the Beast should revive again after the calamity that fell on him had passed. This is plainly distinguished by Aretas <note>Aretas of Caesarea (c. 860–935), a commentator on the Apocalypse</note>, the Complutensian Bible <note>original: "Complutensis"; the first multi-language version of the entire Bible, printed in Spain in the early 1500s</note>, and other books, which read it this way: *"and he shall be forthcoming"*. Similarly, Primasius <note>Primasius of Hadrumetum (died c. 560), a North African bishop whose commentary on Revelation was highly influential</note> reads it as *"he shall come"* or *"he is to come"*. Yet the former reading of Theodore Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605) was a major Protestant theologian and successor to John Calvin</note> may carry this same meaning also: "Though the Beast was not present for a while <note>original: "erewhiles"</note> in men’s opinion, yet now he is." And so the words are to be taken in this sense: that they may refer to the Beast as he comes out of his calamity, not as he lies still within it. For they correspond to the third point: *"and he shall rise up out of the deep"*. This is evident by the actions of the men who admire the Beast; they would never honor him while he lies forlorn and perplexed (which they would have to do if these words referred to the same time as the preceding phrase).

But as he recovers his dignity again beyond all human expectation—and in a more ample manner than he had it before, as happened to him in his third change after he was healed of his wound (Chapter 13:3).

Therefore, the Vulgate <note>original: "vulgar Latine"</note> reading is faulty because it skips this third part <note>original: "member"</note>, making men marvel at the Beast when he "is not," which is contrary to the truth of the matter. From this we may gather what kind of "marvelling" <note>original: "admiring"</note> at the Beast serves as a clear mark of a reprobate <term>reprobate: in this context, someone predestined to damnation or rejected by God</term> in a special way: namely, that by which men honor the Beast that received life again after he had taken a fatal blow <note>original: "deadly foile"</note>, which is the second Beast (Chapter 13:11). But he afterwards reached such a height of wickedness that those who acknowledge him to be what he claims to be—by marvelling at and applauding him—must necessarily be excluded from God's Kingdom. Now, because the Angel does not continue to list his various states beyond this third point <note>original: "Article"</note>, he shows by this that the Beast would be openly known to the world before his final end should come.

<margin>Verse 9.</margin>
**Here is the mind.** So far, we have had the interpretation of the Beast regarding his whole person. Now the Holy Spirit <note>original: "Holy Ghost"</note> begins the interpretation of some of his principal parts, for which he prepares the way to gain better attention with this preface. It is yet uncertain whether this preface refers to what went before or to what follows; it seems to be placed in the middle to belong equally to both, moving men to consider diligently what has been or shall be said concerning the Beast.

It seems to be an incomplete <note>original: "defectiue"</note> way of speaking, which should be completed in the manner of Chapter 13:18: *“Here is wisdom; let him who is endowed with wisdom calculate the number,”* etc. So, in this place, it seems the full sentence should go like this: *“Here is an understanding; let him who has understanding understand.”* We have heard the conclusions of the seven Epistles to the seven Churches follow this same pattern.

**Verse 10. *And they are seven kings, of whom five have fallen.***

So much for the permanent heads; those which are temporary follow, which are the seven kings. Thus we see there is a double application of this one symbol <note>original: "Type"</note>, which teaches us that there is an inseparable connection between the hills and the kings. From this, another necessary argument is provided to us to prove that Rome is the seat of Antichrist, in this manner: the seat of the seven kings is the seat of Antichrist; Rome, the city with seven hills, is the seat of the seven kings (for the "heads" represent both the mountains and the kings); therefore, Rome is the seat of Antichrist. 

But who or what are these seven kings? They are not seven individual people, as Victorinus <note>Victorinus of Pettau (died 303/304 AD), an early Christian bishop and martyr who wrote one of the earliest commentaries on Revelation</note> would have it, but they are the seven forms of sovereignty <note>original: "Princehood"</note> or government <note>original: "Regiment"</note> that have existed in Rome. For if each of the heads were to represent individual men—five of whom fell in John’s <note>The Apostle John, the traditional author of Revelation</note> age, that is to say: Galba, Otho, Vitellius, Vespasian, and Titus—and Domitian was the sixth, who was then Emperor, and if Nerva was the seventh who was then expected (who would continue for only a short time and would have Trajan succeed him immediately, who would be both the eighth and the seventh at once)—if, I say, the heads are to be numbered this way, then it must necessarily follow that this Beast should have completely failed and perished with Trajan, who would be his last head, and that the world would have nothing more to fear from him at all. 

Unless we should perhaps think that he remains alive even when all his living heads are cut off, or that new ones sprouted up again like the heads of the Hydra <note>A multi-headed monster from Greek mythology that grew back two heads for every one that was cut off</note>, of which John made no mention. But so that we do not think those seven kings are taken figuratively <note>original: "Synechdochically"; a figure of speech where a part represents the whole</note>, where are the ten kings that arose together with Nerva? These must necessarily exist alongside the seventh head, as follows in the 12th verse. Or how could the Beast seem not to exist when Nerva was dead, especially seeing as he had adopted Trajan before his death?

For the "heads" are both the mountains and the kings. Therefore, these seven kings belong to Rome alone. In this way, we will save you the great labor of searching for the Antichrist. Now, Cornelius Tacitus <note>A famous Roman historian (c. 56 – c. 120 AD) who wrote about the early Empire</note>, the historian, lists these governments at the beginning of his *Annals* <note>original: "History"</note> in this manner:

In these words, Tacitus clearly teaches that there had been six kinds of government in force at Rome from the first building of the city until his own age: namely, Kings, Consuls, Dictators, the Ten Men, Tribunes, and Emperors. The seventh, which is that of the Popes, was unknown to him, as he died before he could see it.

These kinds of government had completely ceased and vanished away before the time of John the Apostle. ***One is:*** that is, the sixth kind of government, the Emperors, in whose power the rule of the world rested while John lived. ***And the other has not yet come:*** that is, the Pope, the seventh King, who was not yet the governor of Rome while the Apostle was living. And the adjective that serves to note the order is very significant; for he does not say, "the seventh is not yet come," but "***another***" or "***the other*** is not yet come." This suggests that this seventh ruler would be of a very different nature from all the previous kings.

However, he "is not," as his power was extinguished in the opinion of men after that time by the invasion of the Barbarians <note>The Germanic tribes, such as the Goths and Vandals, who invaded the Western Roman Empire in the 5th century</note>. This Beast (I say) is the eighth king, and yet he is one of those seven. 

We must observe that the seventh king is given the name of the whole system by himself and is called "that Beast," of which a description was made in the eighth verse through four alternating periods of time. All those changes apply to him alone. Therefore, the Holy Ghost—immediately after describing the second change of the Beast mentioned in the previous verse—now sets down his double condition in the very same words used to describe him first. By doing this, he shows that those words—*And when he comes, he must continue but for a short time*—mean the same as those: *the Beast which was, and is not.*

**Even he is the eighth.** Namely, the eighth *King*. For the word "eighth" does not agree in gender with the word used for "beast" in the original text. The Latin Vulgate <note>The late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> translates the words awkwardly as "he is the eighth Beast." This is incorrect, for there are not eight Beasts, but eight Kings, the seventh of which is the Beast. The relative pronoun "he" seems to be used as a demonstrative here; "he is the eighth King" means "the Beast is that eighth King."

The entire preceding part of the sentence also serves as the subject that governs the verb "is," as if he should say: now the Beast who "was" and "is not" is both that eighth King and is one of those seven. This eighth King is the same Pope after he had recovered his dignity from the defeat brought upon him by the Barbarians. This was when his "wounded head was healed," as described in Chapter 13:3, or when he who "is not" rose up out of the Deep <note>original: "the Deepe," referring to the bottomless pit or abyss</note>, as described in verse 8 of this chapter. 

Alternatively, this is when the "second Beast" rose up out of the earth, as described in Chapter 13:11—when Gregory II and his immediate successors emerged again and gained power with the help of their "two horns," Pepin and Charlemagne <note>Pepin the Short and Charlemagne were Frankish kings whose military support and land grants established the Papal States</note>. We have shown before that all these events belong to that third change. But now, where does this eighth King come from? 

Does the Beast have eight heads now, when there were only seven a little while ago? Not at all; this eighth king is the same as the seventh. He has the same disposition, manners, and government.

It is immediately added, *and he is one of these seven*, except he is one who surpasses the seventh in impiety, blasphemy, and sacrilege. This proof may be presented in this manner to make it even clearer:

The seventh King followed immediately after the heathen Emperors, who constituted the sixth King reigning at the time John lived; as verse 10 says, *Five have fallen, and one is*—that is, the sixth. But Antichrist is the seventh King (verses 10 and 11). Therefore, Antichrist succeeded the heathen Emperors immediately. And seeing that the Pope of Rome is this seventh King following the time of the heathen Emperors, as we have clearly shown above, it follows necessarily that the Pope of Rome is that highest and greatest Antichrist of whom the Scriptures [speak].

...Scriptures, do forewarn us so diligently, and that from the time of the heathen Emperors, and that the City of Rome is the whore from the same moment.

Now see, you Jesuits, from what necessary principles this argument proceeds. Verse 12. *And the ten horns which you saw are ten kings.* So far we have discussed the Heads; now he interprets the Horns, which provide a more full and clear opening of the time of the Beast than has yet been had. For the more details and company these matters have with them, the more clearly they are perceived and observed by the senses. To the end, therefore, that the seventh head might be made known with even more marks of identification, and so that his first origin might be more certainly found out, it is filled and furnished with these Horns, as if with a certain grand procession and troop <note>original: "pompous traine and troupe"</note>, the noise of which might stir us up to notice his coming.

The Angel interprets these Horns to be ten kings, who are afterwards described by what sort of people they are: both by their kingdom in this verse; as also by their mind and manners in verse 13; and lastly by the war which they shall wage in verse 14. Their kingdom is defined by two different periods. The first, when it was not yet received: "who" (says he) "*have not yet received a kingdom.*" The second, when it was received: "*but*" (says he) "*they shall receive power as kings at one hour with the Beast.*"

That first point addresses a doubt whereby someone might think, perhaps, that these kings reigned at the very same time when John wrote these things. No, he says, they do not reign yet, but they are about to reign shortly. For otherwise it would be a needless warning <note>original: "caveat"</note> if they should not come forth until three years and a half before the Last Day. The second period yields us yet more clear knowledge of the matter by a mutual discovery of each other, which the Beast and the horns make of themselves.

They shall (he says) *receive power as kings for one hour with the Beast*; for I translate the phrase "one hour" in the accusative case <note>original: "fourth Case"—referring to the Greek accusative case, which is often used to express the duration of time (how long something lasts)</note>, in which they are sometimes used to indicate a span of time, or "for how long." For example: *“these last men have worked only one hour,”* Matthew 20:12; *“Could you not watch one hour with me?”* Matthew 26:40. Mark 14:37 uses it in the same way. The best Greek writers also commonly use these words of time in this manner, as in: *“Do you continue at your business without sleep all night long?”* <note>original: "Xenoph. Paed. 2"—referring to Xenophon's *Cyropaedia*, Book 2</note>

Sometimes these and similar words are used for a specific point in time, or "when"; as in the Septuagint <note>original: "70. Greeke Interpretours"—the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>: *“Behold, tomorrow about this same hour, I will cause it to rain a very grievous hail,”* Exodus 9:19. So too, *“I will deliver them up all slain before Israel tomorrow about this same time,”* Joshua 11:6. In the New Testament: *“Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him,”* John 4:52, and *“at the ninth hour of the day,”* Acts 10:3, 30. Also, *“at what hour I will come,”* Revelation 3:3. It is uncertain, then, whether these words indicate the duration of their power, or the specific time when it should begin.

The first meaning includes the second. For if they receive power for one hour along with the Beast, it necessarily follows that they must also receive it at the same hour together with him. However, the reverse is not true, since the power of one might be extended to a later time than the power of the other, even if both had the exact same beginning. Furthermore, history agrees marvelously with the first meaning, which provides a more evident and plentiful knowledge of the Beast through this double and more general mark. Since there is no doubt that the Holy Spirit <note>original: "H. Ghost"</note> would want the Beast to be recognized with certainty, we may rightly conclude that this is the only meaning of the words.

Regarding the next words, *with the Beast*, the Vulgate <note>original: "the vulgar"—the standard Latin Bible translation of the time</note> translates them as *after the Beast*, which goes against the authority of all manuscripts and against the truth itself. For the Horns are mentioned first—even before the Heads or any other part of the body—where the text speaks about the rise of the Beast. This would not have been done if they had appeared after the Beast or the heads (see Chapter 13:1). Ribera <note>Francisco Ribera (1537–1591), a Spanish Jesuit who developed a futurist interpretation of Revelation to counter Protestant claims</note> tries to claim it is the same sense whether we read *with the Beast* or *after the Beast*, as if it were the same thing to begin their kingdom "together" and "after." However, he refers neither of them to the timing, but rather to their obedience.

The ten kings would fall into the same misfortune as the Beast at their very beginning, so that the true identity and nature of the Beast might be more clearly revealed to the whole world through the shared misery he and the kings endured together.

Now, to apply all of this to the matter at hand: we showed in Chapter 13 that these kings are the first Christian Emperors. But now the situation changed at the very start of Antichrist's reign; the sovereign Empire was located somewhere other than Rome. And Agatho <note>Pope Agatho, c. 577–681 AD</note> speaks thus of Rome: "*This is the city that is at the humble service of your Majesty*" (Sixth Council of Constantinople, Act 4). What, then, had become of "Constantine’s Donation" <term>Donation of Constantine: a forged Roman imperial decree by which the 4th-century emperor Constantine the Great supposedly transferred authority over Rome and the western part of the Roman Empire to the Pope</term> of Rome that the Papists talk about so much all this time?

And yet, even if the Donation itself were granted to be valid and lawful, it would sufficiently show where the Empire was based and who held power at that time. Secondly, these kings are the "Horns of the Beast," through whose help and promotion the Pope's status grew great, as they drove away all hostile violence that might have encroached upon it in the slightest. Nor did they only help the Popes grow by fighting in their defense, but also by giving them vast amounts of wealth. For although the Papists boast of "Constantine’s Donation" shamelessly, as we just mentioned, it is certain that he did grace and honor both the city and the Bishop of Rome with many privileges; and the Emperors who followed him took nothing away that he had given, but rather added even more to the pile.

But after those two last **Horns** fell, it can hardly be told how many and how great the calamities were that were heaped upon the **Beast** every day. At that time, there was no aid for him in either the West or the East that could drive back and beat down the outrage of his enemies who rushed in upon him. 

Being, therefore, destitute of his **Horns**, he came to such an extremity that men supposed him to have perished and to no longer exist, as the second stage <note>original: "Article"</note> of his condition <note>original: "estate"</note> shows in verse 8. Therefore, the **Horns** are rightly reckoned to be ten; in this number, the whole defense of the **Beast** is contained, which failed completely for a time after this number of rulers had come to an end. 

This is that "one hour" during which the **Beast** received power—and not only he, but the ten **Horns** with him. They also came to ruin together with him, seeing that there was no manner of valor or strength <note>original: "man hood"</note> left in any of the Western Emperors for a long space of time afterward that was able to resist the fierceness of the enemies. For the rest who followed after—namely Avitus, Majorian, Severianus, Anthemius, Ricimer <note>original: "Rethimer"</note>, Olybrius, Glycerius, Nepos, Orestes, and Augustulus (who was the last of the Emperors)—were no less short in their reigns <note>original: "continuance"</note> and feeble in power and strength. Indeed, they had no power at all, being as obscure as the Emperors who exist at this day, who are hardly known to anyone, either by common report <note>original: "rumour of men"</note> or the records of writers.

Fourthly, the time in which they had "not yet received their kingdom" was the time of John, when this Revelation was written. The heathen Emperors (namely the **Dragon**) were still playing their parts, while the woman was in heavy labor <note>original: "did travaile sore"</note> to bring forth her son. She was not yet strong enough, nor had her full time come to bring forth her offspring, as described in Chapter 12:2, etc. For although there were some men in the ages immediately following John's time who were somewhat better inclined toward Christians than others, yet the **Dragon** immediately devoured all hope as soon as it arose. He was most watchful to lie in wait for the woman's delivery, until at length the full time came—which God had appointed and blessed—for her to be delivered of her vigorous <note>original: "lively"</note> man-child.

Fifthly, the time of receiving their power is at the "same hour" as the **Beast**; for we have shown that the starting point <note>original: "terme of beginning"</note> is also included in the duration <note>original: "space of enduring"</note> of their power.

# Chapter 17. A REVELATION

But since this "hour" <note>referring to the "one hour" mentioned in Revelation 17:12</note> is a large period of time, at what moment within it was this power given? Namely, it was at that moment when the **Lamb** cast down **Diocletian** and **Maximian** <note>original: "Maximinian"; these were the Roman Emperors who led the Great Persecution against Christians</note> out of their Empire, as seen in Chapter 6:15. For then we shall find the **Beast** rising up, as is clear by the sealing of the Elect about that time (Chapter 7), and by that burning mountain that was cast into the sea a little after (Chapter 8). It is also shown by the Church's betaking of herself into the innermost part of the Temple, while the wicked did dominate in the outermost Court and in the Holy City (Chapter 11), for the space of forty-two months. Throughout that entire period of time, this lurking in the Temple and the wilderness lasted (Chapter 11:3 and 12:6).

Power was given to the **Beast** during that same period of time, and by the Throne which he received as a gift from the **Dragon** (Chapter 13:2, 5). But especially and above all else, it is shown by his succeeding next after the "sixth head" and King—namely, the heathen Emperors (verse 10 of this chapter). The common cause of all these things depends upon the driving of the **Dragon** out of heaven, when the Emperors gave over their Empire so marvelously. For what other thing could be the cause of why the Church lived in such a distressed fashion at that time, other than the **Beast**, who had then come into the world?

The woman <note>symbolizing the Church</note>, therefore, fearing him more terribly than she had feared the **Dragon**, brought forth her son and fled away both at once. That is, after she had brought the Christian Emperors into the world—among whom **Constantine** takes the first and principal place—she straightway mewed herself up <note>original: "mued vp"; meaning to shut oneself up or enclose in secrecy</note> in darkness and solitude. She had conceived more hatred in her heart against the ambitious and deceitful **Popes** (who brought in shadows and pictures of piety instead of the sound and clear representation <note>original: "expresse portraiture"</note> of it) than she did against the professed enemies of the faith, as described in Chapter 12:6. Therefore, these Emperors <note>the ten kings previously discussed</note> alone are the **Horns**, to whom alone all these properties most fitly agree.

The Kings that arose out of and after the wasting and overthrow of the Empire did not have their beginning and kingdoms together with the **Beast**, if we date his second uprising (as others commonly do) to around the year 606; rather, they began almost two hundred years before. <margin>Verse 16.</margin>
***And the ten horns which you saw upon the Beast.***
Now the Holy Spirit describes the afflicted state of the prostitute, teaching us by whom this affliction shall be brought upon her and in what manner. To this, he next joins the common cause of both: *the will and pleasure of God*, in the following verse. Regarding the wording: instead of the phrase *upon the Beast*, the Complutensian Edition <note>The first printed polyglot version of the entire Bible, completed in 1517</note>—which Arias Montanus <note>A Spanish scholar and editor of the Antwerp Polyglot Bible</note> and Christophe Plantin <note>A major 16th-century printer</note> follow—reads *and the Beast*. This reading implies that the Beast himself would eventually hate the prostitute. This is contrary to the reading used by Aretas <note>A 10th-century bishop and commentator on Revelation</note>, the Latin Vulgate, and Theodore Beza <note>A major Protestant reformer and successor to John Calvin</note>. Their reading is supported by the authority of many manuscripts and, indeed, aligns with the manifest truth.

Therefore, how could the Beast help forward the prostitute's disgrace and overthrow? This would be the necessary conclusion if one followed that corrupt translation. Yet the Beast shall take her fall so much to heart, and be so immoderately distressed by it, *that he shall gnaw his tongue for excessive grief and indignation*. Furthermore, John saw the woman sitting *upon* the Beast at the very time she comes forth to be condemned and executed.

What time, therefore, can they point to when this "forsaking of her" and "parting of fellowship" shall occur? They speak of a separation, yet there shall be such a great and near joining and uniting of them together, even until her final destruction. Bellarmine divides this entire question into nine points; the first of which is concerning the name of *Antichrist*; the second, *whether Antichrist is one individual man, or a succession <note>original: "kinde"</note> of men*. The third, *concerning the time of his coming, and of his death*. The fourth, *about his proper name*. The fifth, *out of what nation he shall be born, and by whom he is to be received*. The sixth, *where he should establish his place of habitation*. The seventh, *concerning his doctrine and manners*. The eighth, *about his miracles*. The ninth, *concerning his Kingdom and wars*. 

Regarding every one of these points—what ought to be believed, and how completely the cursed Catholic scholars <note>original: "Popish Doctors"</note> are deceived in each of them—it may clearly appear to everyone from those things which the Angel taught us in the former chapter concerning the condemning of the Harlot <note>The "Whore of Babylon" from Revelation 17</note>. For if Antichrist has come and has established the location of his See <note>original: "Sea"; the seat of authority</note> at Rome, and did so as soon as the Empire was taken away from the heathen Emperors, then it cannot be doubted that Antichrist is to be called by his common name "a hidden adversary" <term>close adversary</term>. He is a wicked kingdom, not a single man; the time of his coming is in the past, not the future; and his proper name is *The Latin One* <note>original: "Lateinos Lateinus"; "Lateinos" is a Greek word whose letters numerically add up to 666</note>. He is not to be born of the Jews, nor is he to reign anywhere except at Rome. His doctrine is Catholic and Christian in name only. And lastly, his miracles, kingdom, and battles are no different than those we have experienced for many ages. 

But Antichrist came at that time of which we have spoken. For the Angel has taught us that Antichrist is the Beast "which was, and is not, and was to rise up out of the bottomless pit <note>original: "deepe"</note>, and is to go into destruction" (Revelation 17:8). And we have shown that the Pope of Rome has long since undergone the first three of these four notable changes of his status, and that he began his first stage from the time that the Heathen Emperors ceased to reign, and that he is now giving the world the most certain evidence of his fourth change.

Secondly, Antichrist is the seventh head of the Beast, which succeeded next after the heathen Emperors, who made up the sixth head which was then in power <note>original: "extant"</note> when John wrote this Book (Revelation 17:10–11). As soon, therefore, as these Emperors gave way, he came forth, having been given the honor to be the next head.

Now, if anyone objects that there were some godly Bishops and Popes, or at least tolerable ones from this time onward, I answer that Antichrist is not defined by specific men, but by a certain kingdom and succession. Within that succession, God can exempt some individuals at his pleasure to show the riches of his infinite mercy. Now I only thought it good to make a brief summary of these matters. I want these things that have been spoken of in various places to be viewed all at once, so it might show us more clearly how all the Popish and Jesuit subtleties are, as it were, set on fire and come to nothing by the words of the Apostle alone, as if they had been struck by lightning from heaven. These, therefore, are common arguments to be applied to every one of the topics of the following dispute. I thought it good to advise you of this, good Reader, so that you may retrieve them from here rather than us repeating them in every question. We will introduce specific points to each place as the occasion requires. That is, one who acts in emulation of Christ, who would be considered Christ himself, and who would cast down the one who is truly Christ.*

I readily grant the first part of this interpretation: that Antichrist is someone who is contrary to Christ. But Bellarmine is not content with this; he requires a type of opposition like that between Marius and Sulla <note>original: "Sylla"; Roman generals who fought a bloody civil war.</note>, or Pompey and Caesar, who fought actual battles against each other. Could anyone be so foolish <note>original: "blockish"</note> that they would not recognize Christ’s enemy if he made open war against him? Would any man have cause to be deceived by him if he opposed Christ with open malice and force?

The great *Antichrist* shall deceive men more than compel them; he shall come with all deceptive unrighteousness in those who perish, as the Apostle says in *2 Thessalonians 2:10*. But you labor to prove the matter in three ways. First, because the word (*Antichrist*) cannot by any means signify the *Vicar of Christ*; for you say the Greek preposition *ANTI* <note>original: "ANTI," meaning "against" or "in place of"</note> never signifies any subordination in a compound word, as you claim is plainly apparent by the examples of all such words compounded with *ANTI*. But as for the word *Vicar*, that signifies no opposition, but subordination; therefore, you conclude that since the *Pope* is *Christ's Vicar*, he is not *Antichrist*.

I answer that even if I should grant that *Antichrist* cannot signify *Christ's Vicar*, the *Pope* shall not be a bit further from being *Antichrist*. For your argument is built on an equivocation <note>an ambiguity used to mislead or avoid the truth</note>, and therefore it concludes nothing. In your premise, you set down a true and proper *Vicar*, which indeed *Antichrist* cannot be. Although he is a hidden <note>original: "close"</note> enemy, he is a deadly one, just as the Scriptures describe him by the true names of an *Adversary*, of the *man of Sin*, of the *Angel of the bottomless Pit*, and of the *Beast*.

After that, in your second premise, you do not speak of a genuine and lawful Vicar, but of one who is such through his own detestable ambition, sacrilegious usurpation, and false boasting. Out of which nothing else can finally be concluded except that the *Pope* is not *Antichrist* by his own confession—which I easily grant you. For the question between us is not, I believe, what name *Antichrist* will call himself by, but what name he is worthy of, and what name the Scriptures give him. It is not to be expected that he will betray <note>original: "bewray"</note> himself and will honestly confess that he is the *man of sin*, the *Son of perdition*, the *Angel of the bottomless Pit*, the *Beast*, and such things, as his other...

<meta>This page continues the linguistic and historical debate regarding the prefix "anti" in the title "Antichrist." The author is refuting the argument that "Antichrist" only means someone "against" Christ (opposition); he argues it can also mean someone acting "in the place of" Christ (subordination), thereby identifying the Pope—who calls himself Christ's Vicar—as the Antichrist.</meta>

### CONCERNING ANTICHRIST ###

...names of this kind describe him to be. If he were to do that, he could not so fitly play the part of the false Prophet. You have, therefore, defended your Pope worthily when you attempted to prove that he is not Antichrist based on his own testimony. 

Secondly, I answer that what you claim regarding the meaning of the prefix *anti* <note>The Greek prefix "anti" can mean either "against" or "in place of."</note> in compound words is false (although it matters little to your purpose which of the two meanings it has—whether opposition or subordination). I will make this plain with examples. *Anti*, when compounded with the Greek word for a "hireling," signifies someone who takes the place of a hireling for another. *Anti*, also compounded with the word for a "King," is the same as the Latin word *Prorex* <note>original: "Prorex," meaning a viceroy or one acting in the king's stead</note>, or one who is the King's vice-regent. *Anti*, compounded with the word for an "Emperor" or "General" in war, signifies the person who is the Emperor’s or General’s vice-regent. As Henry Stephen <note>original: "Henry Stephen," referring to the famous scholar Henri Estienne (1528–1598)</note> observed in his *Treasury of the Greek Tongue*, it has the same meaning as the word in Appian's *History* <note>original: "Appiãs Anabaicks," likely referring to the Roman history by Appian of Alexandria</note> that signifies "sub-praetors" or "propraetors" in Latin. Budé <note>original: "Budeus," referring to the French scholar Guillaume Budé (1467–1540)</note> teaches the same thing regarding the word Demosthenes used for "Proconsul." In all these words, *anti* signifies subordination.

But you say that a *hypostrategus* <note>original: "hypostrategus," a Greek term for a lieutenant-general or subordinate commander</note> is an equal to the Captain, and that the Latin words *propraetor* and *proconsul* do not signify the Vicar or vice-regent of the Praetor or Consul in a city. You claim that Wolfgang Musculus <note>original: "Musculus," a prominent Protestant reformer and theologian (1497–1563)</note> was deceived because, reading that *Antistrategus* <note>original: "Antistrategus," literally "instead of the general"</note> signifies a propraetor, he thought it signified the deputy of a Praetor—which you say is false.

I answer that the first proconsuls who were ordained were indeed those who exercised the authority of a vice-regent, as Lucius Fenestella <note>original: "L. Fenestela," an ancient Roman historian and author of 'De Magistratibus Romanorum'</note> witnesses when writing about the Magistrates of Rome, Book 2, Chapter 21.

> *At that time (he says) the Proconsul exercised no ordinary jurisdiction, but only such as he held by delegation and assignment; though afterwards it became the usual custom that this kind of Magistrate had a jurisdiction of his own falling to his share.*

And this is what Dionysius of Halicarnassus <note>An influential Greek historian and teacher of rhetoric in Rome (c. 60 BC – 7 BC)</note> says in his *Roman Antiquities*, Book 11:

> *That the first proconsuls ordained were created in the third year of the eighty-fourth Olympiad, though he had mentioned before that Titus Quintius was created Proconsul in the second year of the seventy-ninth Olympiad; that is, twenty-one years earlier, Book 9.*

The reason for this statement is this: because these Proconsuls <note>A Roman provincial governor.</note>, such as Titus Quintius was, who exercised power only upon a trust committed to them, were not included in the catalog of ordinary magistrates. Only those who held an authority proper to themselves after the boundaries of the Empire were enlarged were included; then, for the first time, the dignity and name of a magistrate was worthily granted to them and taken by them. And yet those Proconsuls who held power on trust were called by that name, as is plain from what Dionysius <note>Dionysius of Halicarnassus, a Greek historian of the Roman era.</note> says when he speaks of this Titus Quintius. Therefore Musculus <note>Wolfgang Musculus (1497–1563), an influential Protestant theologian.</note> was not deceived in this as you claim, but you are egregiously deceived yourself, refusing to see a matter that is most certain because of your eager desire to fight against the truth.

I answer, first, that since there is the same equivocation <note>The use of ambiguous language to avoid a clear meaning.</note> regarding the name "Vicar" here as there was before, this argument has as much force in it as the first—that is, none at all. Secondly, I say that to be "exalted above all that *is called God*" is spoken figuratively, not literally. For the true God is never called "*all*" or "*every God*," but "*one God*," as the Apostle says in *1 Corinthians 8:5–6: For although there are those who are called gods, both in heaven and earth (for there are many gods and many lords), yet to us there is but one God the Father, and one Lord Jesus Christ.* But the rest of the gods, because they are more than one, are often called "*all the gods*," as in *Psalm 97:7: Worship him, all you gods.* 

Therefore, to be exalted above "all the gods" is not to be exalted above that one God in heaven, but above every "god" on earth—that is, above the Civil Magistrate <note>In the 16th and 17th centuries, "gods" was a common term for kings and judges, following the biblical precedent in Psalm 82:6 where God says to human rulers, "You are gods."</note>, to whom the Scriptures give the name of "God." This same thing is clear from the words that follow: *or which is worshipped*. For if the word "God" were taken literally there, why would something of lesser status be joined immediately after it? In lists, the lesser thing is usually placed first. For example, a person does not speak well who says, "*who is exalted above every king, or every subject*"; rather, he says, "*who is exalted above every subject, or king*." So that the whole sum does not differ from its parts, you conclude with the same "sweet" equivocation <note>The use of ambiguous language to conceal the truth or avoid committing oneself</note> with which you have embellished everything said so far on this matter. You argue: *The name of Antichrist signifies an enemy and a rival to Christ; but the Pope of Rome acknowledges himself to be Christ's servant and to be subject to him in all things. Therefore, he is not Antichrist.* That is to say, he is not the Antichrist by his own confession—and anyone who acknowledges that confession, let him be cursed with bell, book, and candle <note>A reference to the formal ceremony of excommunication</note>. For you might better confirm this "certain" conclusion with an Anathema <note>A formal curse or excommunication</note> at the end of it than the Fathers in the Council of Trent could back their cursed canons. But I pray you to understand, O Bellarmine, that it is intolerable trifling in a serious matter to rely on constant equivocation.

## Chapter II.

### That the Antichrist is not one specific man 
->who is yet to come.<-

The second point of controversy is whether the Antichrist, properly so-called, is one specific man or a unique throne and tyrannical kingdom. All the Roman Catholics <note>original: "Papists"</note> hold that he will be a single individual. However, those common arguments which we placed at the beginning of this debate prove the contrary. For if the Antichrist has reigned from about the year 300 AD until today—as has been sufficiently demonstrated—he is not a single person. Furthermore, if anyone were to consider the narrow constraints of time, the vastness of his jurisdiction, the multitude of tasks he is to perform, and their magnitude—all of which Catholic <note>original: "Popish"</note> writers imagine <note>original: "faine"</note> he shall do—he would marvel that men could be so foolish <note>original: "dote"</note> as to think all these things could be found in one person.

Moreover, a part of his kingdom boasts a duration of a thousand years, as we are taught later in Chapter 20:4–5. Let us see, then, what kinds of reasons you use to confirm your opinion. You cite the Scriptures and the Church Fathers to prove this point. There are five such reasons, the first of which is taken from the Gospel of John 5:43: *“I have come in my Father’s name, and you do not receive me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive.”* You say that these words are to be understood as referring to the true Antichrist, based both on the testimony of certain Fathers and the literal meaning <note>original: "propriety"</note> of the words themselves. I answer: regarding the Church Fathers, I have no desire <note>original: "list"</note> to examine their opinions. It would be a tedious and fruitless task to do so, since everyone who is not willfully blind confesses that they erred greatly from the truth concerning the Antichrist because of the darkness of the times in which they lived. Let us walk the sure path of searching for the truth, which is through the Scriptures, which can neither deceive nor be deceived.

# TOUCHING ANTICHRIST. Chap. 2.

What is then the strength of the words which forces us to hold that a single individual <note>original: "singular person"</note> is meant here? This you endeavor to show in four ways. First, because the Lord opposes *another man to himself—that is, one person against another—as it is clear by those words: "I," "another," "in my name," "in his own name," "me," "him."* Therefore, you say, as Christ was one single man, so also shall the Antichrist be.

I answer: the strength of this argument lies in three opposing words: *another, in his name, him.* The latter two of these depend upon the first; for whatever relationship the first has, the same shall those others have, since they are all referred to the same thing. But "*another*" here does not signify a single individual, as the Grammarians teach. Their rule is this: that *another (of two)* <note>original: "Eteros"</note> in Greek, and *the other* <note>original: "Alter"</note> in Latin, or "the other" in English, signify one of two. But the words *another (of many)* <note>original: "Allos"</note> in Greek, and *another* <note>original: "alius"</note> in Latin, or "another" in English, signify one among many. (Ammonius writing on similar and different words <note>Ammonius of Alexandria was a 4th-century grammarian who wrote a treatise on the differences between words with similar meanings.</note>).

Therefore, it follows necessarily out of this certain and true rule that a specific man is not understood here. Nor is this the opinion of the Grammarians only, but also the customary manner of speaking in the Scriptures confirms this. To omit infinite other examples: *There is one that sows, and another reaps* (John 4:37). Is there only one sower and one reaper meant here? No, for Christ adds: *I have sent you out to reap that which you did not labor for; other men have labored, and you have entered into their labors* (verse 38). So, *to one is given the word of knowledge, to another faith, to another the gift of healing, to another the power to work miracles, to another prophecy,* etc. (1 Corinthians 12:8-10). I believe <note>original: "trow"</note> you will not say that these gifts were specific to single individuals, but were common to more than one. In the same manner, when Saint Paul says: *if any other seems to have confidence in the flesh, I most of all* (Philippians 3:4), he does not compare himself with any specific man, but with any one among many. You provide exceedingly poorly for your cause by bringing <note>original: "fetch"</note> proofs from such places, where your argument is chiefly overthrown.

Secondly, you say that Christ affirms here that the Antichrist is to be received by the Jews; furthermore, it is evident that the Jews look for one certain and single individual. I answer that there is nothing at all to be found in this reason. For neither is that great Antichrist whom the Revelation speaks of, and of whom we discuss <note>original: "entreat"</note>, that Antichrist whom the Jews will receive...

# CHAPTER 2: AGAINST BELLARMINE

receive, as is clear by those things that have been said before, and as will be more plainly declared afterwards. Neither is the Antichrist of the Jews one specific and single man. For (as Christ says) "Many shall come in my name saying, 'I am Christ,'" where he speaks chiefly of those who shall arise among the Jews (Matthew 24:5). Jewish history also reports that there have been more than one person regarded as Christ who sacrilegiously claimed the name of the Messiah for themselves. Now, regarding the expectation of the Jews today, this no more proves that he is a single person than the expectation of the Papists proves that he shall be one specific man. We indeed hope and long for you to bring forth more solid evidence <note>original: "founder matter"</note> for proof than your own foolish expectations.

Third, you say: *“That all the false prophets came in the name of another, not in their own name. Antichrist, therefore, who shall come in a special manner in his own name, is a single person.”* I answer: Antichrist shall not come in a different manner than all the rest of the false prophets regarding what is meant by "name" here. For "name" here is not a title <note>original: "appellation"</note>, but authority, as is clear by the contrasting phrase: "in the name of the Father." Christ says, "I have come in the name of my Father" (John 5:43). That does not mean using the name of the Father as if he were the Father, but by the commission and authority of the Father. So, to come in his own name is not to boast of his own proper name, but to come by his own authority, God having given him no lawful authority.

And in this manner, all false prophets come both in the name of another and also in their own name. They come in the name of another in a faked and deceitful <note>original: "dissemblingly"</note> way, because they falsely brag that they are sent; they come in their own name very truly, because they have no authority but their own, running before they are commanded, as the Prophet says. Therefore, there shall be no difference in this respect between Antichrist and the rest of the false prophets who are of the same crew as him.

Fourth, you say: *“The Lord would not have said, 'if another shall come,' but 'many are coming,' if he had spoken of false prophets.”* I answer: Christ signifies that many should come by the word "another"; for it is a noun that signifies a division among many, as we have shown <note>referring to the Greek word 'allos' discussed on the previous page</note>. That swarm of false Christs could not be indicated <note>original: "inti- mated"</note> more briefly and significantly than by the way Christ speaks.

I answer: it is true indeed that the Greek article has the power to call back and restrict a matter that is of an indefinite and uncertain concept to some specific thing. However, this specific thing can be a certain *kind* of thing just as easily as it can be a certain individual matter, according to the nature of what is being discussed. So, we who are but beginners think this to be a new and unheard-of point of grammar and logic: that the Greek article should always point out some specific individual.

Shall *the sower* <note>original: *ho speirōn*</note> and *the reaper* in John 4:37 be one single sower and one single reaper? Shall *the sin* <note>original: *hē hamartia*</note> signify one individual sin entering into the world? And shall *the death* <note>original: *ho thanatos*</note> signify one single death in Romans 5:12? Or shall *the thief* <note>original: *ho kleptēs*</note> be one single thief in John 10:10? We have now gained one more rule for our grammar from the Jesuits' teaching than we ever learned before, or than any...

[No] Greek speaker, I believe, ever thought or once dreamed of this. Our writers have been too dull-witted to observe this.

I answer that this insult of yours is not to be endured, by which you would cast a stain of such notable ignorance upon that most learned man. Epiphanius teaches no differently in this matter than all other learned men. For "where the article," he says, "is added to some one specific thing that is most clear, there is significant emphasis because of the article; but without the article, the word is to be taken indefinitely as any common matter. Just as if we say *Basileus* <note>original: *Basilios* - Greek for king.</note>, 'a king,' we have indeed expressed a name, but yet we have not demonstrated any specific man, for we speak of the King of the Persians, and of the Medes, and of the Elamites. But if we shall say, with the addition of an article, *ho basileus* <note>original: *ò Basil.*</note>, 'the King,' it is beyond doubt that what is signified is the King who was searched for, or of whom speech was being made, or who is known to us, or he who reigns in some specific country." 

In the same manner, there is *theos* <note>original: *theòs* - God.</note> and *ho theos* <note>original: *ó theòs* - the God</note>, *anthropos* <note>original: *anthropos* - man</note> and *ho anthropos* <note>original: *ó anthropos* - the man</note>, and so on for the rest. Epiphanius, therefore, intends for something to have been spoken of before—something that is famous, well-known, or of which there is speech or a question—but it never came into his mind, much less did he commit it to writing, that every word is always tied to a single individual person simply because of this use of the article.

The Article may take every "habit" <note>The author is punning on "habit," meaning both a characteristic and a monk's robe, to mock the perceived shiftiness of the Jesuits.</note> to itself, just as a Jesuit does according to the various needs of time and place. # REGARDING ANTICHRIST. Chapter 2.

Regarding the claim that this **Antichrist** (whom the **Church Fathers** <note>The influential early Christian theologians of the first few centuries</note> would have us believe is meant by the **little horn**) is a single individual, because he is not called a kingdom, but a king, who would completely remove three of the ten kings from the world—whom he should find in the world—and should subject the other seven to himself: I answer, first, that these last words, "and he shall subdue the other seven," are very boldly forged and shoved in, seeing as there is not the slightest trace of them in the Book of **Daniel**.
