# Chapter 18. A REVELATION,

...laid open, as one who cannot be brought by any warnings <note>original: "admonitions"</note> to set aside her former wickedness. As for the words, **the wine of the wrath of her sexual immorality** <note>original: "fornication"</note>, this refers to the spiritual unfaithfulness that provokes God to anger. Yet, this sin makes wretched men so drunk for a time with the delight they take in it that it removes all sense of their own wickedness <note>original: "impiety"</note>, as described in Chapter 14:8. Montanus <note>Benito Arias Montano (1527–1598), a Spanish scholar and editor of the Antwerp Polyglot Bible</note> changes the order of the words to "of the wrath of the wine."

**All nations have drunk.** Montanus reads it transitively—meaning **she has made all nations to drink**—and so the sin is more vividly expressed and more appropriate for her who carries a golden cup in her hand. She does this so that she may provoke even those who are not thirsty to drink, as mentioned before in Chapter 14:8. It is a horrible sin to place a stumbling block before the blind; what is it, then, to push and throw people headlong into the ditch? But the way of speaking seems to have been changed on purpose, lest any wicked person should excuse her and say that she did not lead others into the snares she had laid for them. Therefore, this common reading followed by our copies is to be preferred, which the other neutral verbs that follow also seem to require—namely, **have committed sexual immorality** and **have grown rich**.

**And the merchants of the earth [have grown rich] from the abundance of her pleasures.** That is, out of her excess <note>original: "superfluity"</note> and immoderate desire to enjoy every delight. For Rome is like another Xerxes <note>Xerxes I, the Persian king famous for his legendary luxury and for supposedly offering rewards to anyone who could invent a new pleasure</note>, who provoked men to invent new kinds of pleasures by offering them rewards for their labor. How, then, could the clever inventors and providers <note>original: "instruments"</note> of such pleasures fail to gain great wealth for themselves? 

But what kind of merchants are these? It seems they are not those who make their living by exporting and importing physical goods and commodities. For they are numbered among those outcasts <note>original: "reprobates"—those rejected by God</note> who mourn the fate of Babylon, though its ruin is to be a cause of great joy for all the saints (verse 10). Neither shall the merchandise of these men be bought anymore once Rome is destroyed; yet gold, silver, and the rest of the things said to be their wares will not cease to be in demand in other places. To this we may add that among those to whom this name properly applies, the most significant are those who bring goods by sea from distant countries; but these merchants do not trade and bargain <note>original: "chaffer"</note> so much by sea as by land, which is why they are called the "merchants of the earth." # OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chapter 18.

**Princes of the earth (verse 23).** These are of a higher rank than those who sell physical goods for a living. Lastly, we see that the **souls of men** are also listed among these wares (verse 13). This prevents us from interpreting these words in a purely literal sense.

Therefore, we should not think of ordinary merchants here, as if they were the primary subjects—though they, too, will be greatly harmed. Rather, these are those magnificent lords: the Cardinals, the Popish Archbishops, and Bishops, who trade in the souls of men and flourish through this traffic like the glorious nobles and peers of the earth. For we shall see later that Rome is compared to Tyre <note>Tyre: An ancient Phoenician city-state famous for its vast wealth and maritime trade, described in Ezekiel 27–28 as a center of worldly pride.</note>, because Rome is no less famous as a marketplace for spiritual things than Tyre was of old for selling all those commodities that serve the pleasures of this life.

Who could desire a better-furnished market? # OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chapter 18.

...unless this worthy Captain of this battle against Rome, being moved by these causes, shall launch an attack in this battle at the appointed time.

**Verse 4.** ***And I heard another voice.*** This seems to be the first Angel and the principal agent in this battle. The second plays his part like one who is ready to take the first one’s place, and does so through persuasive and encouraging speeches. But there is no mention made here of who this Angel is; only a voice is said to come from heaven, as if this exhortation were "masterless"—meaning without a clear owner—because the name of the person from whom it proceeds is concealed. For this reason, we called this Angel a "nameless Angel" in the summary <term>original: "resolution"</term> of this chapter. 

The subject matter he deals with is indeed full of danger <note>original: "envye." Therefore, he perhaps keeps his name from being known, as it would be of little use to be identified, but might cause some danger if it were disclosed. This is because the adversaries are so full of deadly hatred against the subject of this speech and everyone who speaks in this manner. 

His speech continues until the 21st verse. It will be a powerful persuasion, full of clear evidence and strength, which will be delivered by some faithful man. It shall be published abroad together with the preparations for this battle. Its effect will be to warn people truly and devoutly concerning the punishment of Rome that is now coming upon it, and to urge people to avoid it. Yet, what we said regarding the concealing of this Angel’s name is not strictly necessary in every sense; a similar voice that came out of heaven had its owner's name identified—as the event has taught us in Chapter 14:13. Therefore, there are some of the Elect <term>Elect: Those chosen by God for salvation</term> who lie hidden as of yet within the cesspool of the wickedness practiced at Rome, whom God mercifully remembers during the common destruction of the wicked. ...the people of God, whose duty and characteristic <term>original: "property"; an essential quality or nature</term> it is to listen to the voice of God alone. ***Lest you be partakers of her sins.*** For men make themselves accessories to sins when they do not forsake the company and fellowship of those who commit them. He does not say, "lest you be partners with them in their punishments," but "in their sins," which is much more grievous. This fear shall be like a goad and a whip to compel men to fly away from Rome, once they are convicted in their consciences of being guilty of her wickedness.

**Verse 5. *For her sins are heaped up.*** The words in the original Greek are: "her sins have followed." That is, her sins, following one after another and knit together in a continuous order, have by this means grown into such a heap that they eventually reached all the way up to heaven. 

*But if Rome is the Holy City, the "Chair of Peter" which cannot err—and that throughout all the time that the Pope and his kingdom have flourished, as the Papists brag—then this row and rank of sins, thus chained and coupled together, would have been greatly broken up and hindered from growing into such a huge and high heap.* 

For seeing as the Papacy greatly exceeds the age of the heathen <term>Roman</term> Emperors in its long history, it could easily blot out the impiety of that "three-year reign of Antichrist" which they dream of as yet to come—even if we granted that he should reign at Rome during that time only. <note>The author is arguing against the Catholic view that "Antichrist" is a single individual who will reign for only three and a half years at the end of time, arguing instead that the Papacy has been a long-running "heap" of sin.</note> 

How can sins reach all the way to heaven if they are only committed in the very last days of the world, especially since so much would have been taken away from that heap by the supposed "holiness" of the Popes that lasted for so many centuries? But this Book of Revelation has made the matter clear: it teaches us that the Popes have kindled their firebrand of hellish wickedness from the outrage of the heathen Emperors. They have heaped up new sins in a continuous succession to fill up the dungcart <note>A vivid, derogatory metaphor for the accumulation of corruption</note>, into which each Pope as he went before cast his own shovelful. This is clearly shown by the perpetual order and succession of the Popes; indeed, the published "Catalogue of Popes" is of special use for this very purpose of showing their history. **Verse 7. *Inasmuch as she has lifted up herself.*** The words are "has glorified herself"—that is, weigh out to her a measure of torments with equal balances, according to the measure of her pride, glory, and excess in pleasure and jollity. The full speech would be: *Woe, woe be to us, because that great city Babylon, that strong city, is overturned, and because your judgment has come in one hour, or in a single instant.* So, they bewail the ruin of Rome and how suddenly it occurred.

Verse 11. *And the merchants of the earth.* The merchants join the kings in this lamentation; but they are the "merchants of the earth," just as the kings are. We showed at verse 3 that these are people who trade <note>original: "chaffer"</note> in spiritual matters rather than physical ones. This is proven by this verse, for the text says: *No man buys her wares anymore.* Therefore, this does not refer to literal gold, silver, silk, fine linen, perfumes, or anything else the words usually mean, because the value and purchase of those goods do not depend on Rome alone—unless perhaps they will be worth less at this time because such a greedy customer <note>original: "Chapman"</note> as Rome has been removed. But the words are specific, and no such thing was said of Tyre <note>original: "Tyrus"</note> (from which this whole allegory is taken in Ezekiel 27), even though that context required the point to be amplified with such words. Therefore, these "wares" are the labor, effort, and industry of men used to beautify and increase the power of the city of Rome. These will be very poorly valued and rewarded after Rome is ruined. For who will then give a man even a hollow nut <note>original: "deafe nut"; a common idiom for something worthless</note> for his labor toward Rome's advancement?

# CHAPTER 18. A REVELATION,

Verse 12. *The wares of gold and silver.* As we just mentioned, this entire allegory is taken from Ezekiel 27, where the destruction of Tyre is discussed. This is quite appropriate, as we showed in our commentary on verse 3, since Rome is no less infamous for trading in souls <note>original: "soules" (OCR error read as "foules")</note> than Tyre was famous for trading in physical goods <note>original: "Bodily Utensils"</note>. Ezekiel lists each of the nations in such a way that he also records the specific commodities of each country—both those they had in abundance themselves and those they supplied to Tyre for trade. 

Following this logic, the various kinds of wares listed in this passage seem intended to point us toward the various nations to which they either naturally belong, or by whose labor and effort they are transported to Rome. Therefore, even though the names of the countries are not explicitly stated as they are in Ezekiel, they can be easily understood by the goods themselves. 

The wares of silver, gold, and the other foreign <term>outlandish: exotic or from distant lands</term> commodities mentioned in this verse may signify Spain, which fetched these things from the furthest parts of the Indian countries, and through whose trade they are made available in our part of the world. 

*Cinnamon, scents, ointments, frankincense, and wine* point toward Italy—not because every one of these things grows there, but because just as Spain transports goods into Europe by way of the Atlantic Ocean, Italy provides Europe with plenty of these items which it fetches from Greece <note>original: "Grecia"</note>, Cilicia, Arabia, and Egypt by way of the "inward sea" <note>The Mediterranean Sea</note>. Furthermore, Italy itself abounds with more of these delightful fruits than any other country in Europe. 

*Fine flour and wheat* may indicate the islands of the Mediterranean, specifically Sicily and Sardinia, which serve as the granaries and food storehouses for Italy. *Beasts* signify Germany, which is full of them, just as *sheep* may represent our own country of England, which is more famous than any other for that kind of livestock. 

*Horses and chariots* <note>original: "charets"</note> point to the French, who have a great abundance of horses, and from whom the use of chariots and similar modes of transport has spread to other countries. 

*Bodies* refer to the Swiss <note>original: "swizers"</note>, who make a living by exercising their bodies in foreign warfare for hire and pay <note>The famous Swiss mercenaries</note>, and who are commonly employed by the Pope of Rome as his primary guard, stationed closest to his own person.

Silk is cloth made of the most slender threads which the silkworms twist out of their own bodies <note>original: "bowels"</note>, as if from a distaff <term>distaff: a tool used in spinning wool or flax</term>. It is not made of flowers, as Dionysius the Greek poet says in his book describing the world, speaking of the silkworms: *“These kinds of creatures,”* he says, *“refuse to feed upon well-fed bullocks or fat sheep, but by cropping speckled flowers from the uninhabited earth, they spin silk from there, from which fine garments are made.”* <note>original: Dionysius Periegetes</note> So says Virgil in the *Georgics*: *“And how the Seres [the Chinese] comb off and pull away finely their slender fleeces from the leaves of the flowers and trees,”* <note>original: "Velleraque ut foliis depectant tenuia Seres" (Virgil, Georgics 2.121)</note> unless perhaps they say that the silk is pulled from the trees because the worms make silk in the trees, and not because it is made of them.

**And all thyine wood**: the word *Thyine* both signifies in general every kind of sweet-smelling wood, and a specific kind of fragrant tree as well. As Eustathius notes <note>original: *Eustath. noteth*</note> when writing upon that passage by Dionysius <note>original: *Dionys.*</note> where he speaks of Arabia—which he calls marvelous because it is always sweet-smelling with "Thynes" (that is, with sweet-smelling fragrances)—it makes a dainty perfume, either from the *Thyine* tree (which is much like the Cypress) or else from myrrh, etc. In that passage, "Thyine" is used generally in the first instance for any kind of sweet odor, while in the second instance, it refers to a certain kind of fragrant tree. 

But here it is not mentioned so much because it serves for perfumes, but because it is used to make sumptuous and elegant buildings (for sweet odors are mentioned at the beginning of the next verse). For this purpose it serves chiefly as Pliny shows from Theophrastus <note>original: *Pliny sheveth out of Theophrastus*</note>, who, as he says, gives great honor to this Thyne tree especially. He tells us for that purpose of rafters in the ancient Temples that have been made memorable because they were fashioned from this wood. He also commends it to us for a certain "immortality" <term>immortality: here meaning extreme durability or resistance to decay</term> that this wood possesses when it is laid in the roofs of houses, as it is not subject to rotting or wearing away by any of those things that commonly spoil timber (*Natural History*, Book 13, Chapter 16) <note>original: *Booke. 13. Chapt 16. Histor. Natur.*</note>.

As for wine and oil, Italy has an abundance of her own, and she brings in fine flour and wheat out of Sicily.

...rustic roundelays <note>simple, traditional songs</note>. I hope that our countrymen will never go to visit Rome again, unless perhaps it is to accompany this angel to see and help forward her destruction.

**And horses and chariots, and bodies.** These first two belong to the French, who are famous for **barbed horses** <term>horses wearing protective armor for battle</term>, and for the inventing of chariots and coaches. This last item, **bodies**, is the merchandise of the **Swiss** <note>original: "Swizers"</note>, who have many towns that still persist obstinately in Roman Catholic superstition. They guard and defend the Beast's person with their huge bodies, which are fit for that service. He uses these men for his regular and household guard; he can also, at his pleasure and as often as necessity requires, levy great armies of hired soldiers from among these people. 

I would to God that these people, who are among the number of our brothers and allies <note>original: "leaguers"</note>, would at length learn not to prostitute their bodies and bow their backs to be trodden upon as this Beast desires. He is not content to make slaves of them in this way only, but he also seeks the certain destruction of their **souls**. I wish they would learn not to earn their pay so dearly by guarding and defending him, seeing they would bring the greatest possible good to all Christians by helping to destroy him utterly. 

But this trading of theirs with their bodies shall shortly come to an end. Would it not be better for them to **give this Lady of Lewdness the bag** <note>original: "geue this Ladye of Lewdnes the Bag-ge"; an idiom meaning to dismiss or abandon someone</note> and to leave her without a guard of their own accord, rather than to be forsaken by her whether they want to be or not, as they must be shortly? Sorrow taken up voluntarily for the sake of repentance is a saving sorrow; but that which comes through obstinacy, where proud hearts are broken despite their pride, is deadly and harmful.

**And the souls of men.** These wares do not belong to one country only, but are common to all countries. These are such choice merchandise <note>original: "chaffer"</note> that she does not consider any amount of gold too high a price to ask for them. We find a similar speech in Ezekiel 27:13: *They of Javan, Tubal, and Meshech were your merchants; they traded in your market with the souls of men and vessels of bronze.* For those are the words in the original. **Tremellius and Junius** <note>Two influential 16th-century Protestant biblical scholars</note> translate it as "with men," explaining the sense of the words correctly. # OF THE REVELATION. Chapter 18.

He used these words on purpose so that he might point out the difference between this merchandise and all the others, especially those of "Bodies." For these words are not put in the Genitive Case <term>a grammatical case usually indicating possession, often translated with "of"</term> like those that come before it—merchandise of horses, and of chariots, and of bodies, and of souls of men—but in these last words, he switches to the Accusative Case <term>a grammatical case indicating the direct object of an action</term> ("And the souls of men"), as is clear in the Greek text and as we have translated it in the Latin. By this, it is signified that there is a different and distinct consideration made in this place for souls and bodies, and that these words have a far different meaning than those in Ezekiel, even though there is an allusion in these words to that passage <note>original: Ezekiel 27, describing the trade of Tyre</note>.

**Verse 14. And the much-desired fruits.** And here the word (in the Greek) seems to be used for the causal conjunction "for." For the "Autumn that is much longed for"; the interpreter of Aretas <note>an early commentator on Revelation</note> reads it this way: "and the time of desire." This is a Hebrew manner of speaking, meaning "Your desired Harvest," just as "in the fire of the flame" is used for "with flaming fire" (2 Thessalonians 1:8). It is as if it should have been said: "Your harvest, which you have longed for so much, is now decayed and perished." By this proverbial form of speech, we usually signify that a man has had the power of earning a profit from his trade taken away from him.

Or else the same Hebrew manner of speaking may be understood such that what goes before should take the place of an adjective. It is as if "the harvest of desire" were put for a "harvest-desire"—that is, such a desire as men have in harvest time; just as "from before the glory of his might" is used for "from his glorious power" (2 Thessalonians 1:9). And thus, this "Harvest-Desire of the soul" may signify that luscious and greedy appetite for raw fruits which the richer and daintier sort of people are troubled with. In a fickle <note>original: "vvanton"</note> whim, they buy up the first fruits of any kind, which they afterwards loathe and disdain when there comes to be a great abundance <note>original: "gods plenty"</note> of them. 

It is as if he said: "In the past, you poured out your money prodigally to buy trifles at a high rate and a dear price, but now your fingers do not itch as they did to be buying such trash. Your former extravagance and daintiness are past and perished. The things which you previously thought were beneath you, you would be glad of now." This is according to the words of the Poet: *“A hungry man is seldom seen to look down on anything that is food for humans, no matter how base and ordinary it may be.”* Whichever way we take the words, we see that they are very well joined next after the previous verses, because the mourning of the merchants is greatly increased by this...

# OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chapter 18.

**Verse 18. *What city was like this great one?*** This is how the mariners cry out concerning **Tyre** in Ezekiel 27:32: *What city was equal to Tyre, which is cut down in the midst of the sea?* They had good reason to be so astonished by this and to ask this question, considering the former wealth of that city. It had flourished for a long time through the trade and commerce it shared with so many great nations; consequently, they thought it was unconquerable by any human strength. Think of how much trouble it caused **Nebuchadnezzar** (Ezekiel 29:18). How greatly was **Alexander the Great** challenged <note>original: "pufled" (puzzled or struggling)</note> in besieging it afterward? He was so hopeless of overcoming and overthrowing it that he regretted even beginning the siege against it—and yet he never thought anything else was too difficult for him.

But these mariners and sailors <note>original: "watermen"</note> will be even more rightly astonished when they marvel at **Rome**, which had been the queen of the entire world for many ages. She had been called the most ancient city and the "Chair of Peter" <note>original: "Chaire of Peter," referring to the *Cathedra Petri*, the symbol of papal authority</note>. It was said that *she was always too invincible to be overthrown by any calamities, and that she would continue to be exceedingly mighty and flourishing—supported by both her own wealth and the high status of her friends—even into her old age and until her dying day.* These and many similar claims will cause them to cry out and say, *"What city is like this great one?"* Who would have believed that such excellence, so eminent in all respects, would ever be subject to decay and destruction? 

How grossly have we been deceived by dreaming of her eternity! And how wickedly <note>original: "lewdly"; here meaning ignorantly or basely</note> did we deceive others when, in our preaching, we confidently claimed that "this ship of ours should never be sunk" <note>original: "drowned"</note>. How unexpected all these things have been, far beyond anything we ever believed, imagined, or boasted about! This is the force behind this question, which is so full of amazement.

**Verse 19. *And they shall cast dust on their heads.*** This is done in the manner of mourners (Job 2:12). These people will mourn all the more earnestly because they will be less able to support themselves now that their own wealth is gone. However, the Angel speaks here in the past tense: *they have cast dust, and they did cry,* and in the previous verse, *they did cry when they saw the smoke.* Yet these events actually precede the ruin of **Rome**, which follows immediately after in the sequence of events. For this reason, the author seems to change the tense—not only because the coming event is absolutely certain (as the Prophets often speak elsewhere), but to emphasize its inevitability.

**Verse 20. *O heaven, rejoice over her.*** 

Thus far the text has described the mourning of the wicked; now the Holy Spirit <note>original: "Holy Ghost"</note> shows how much great and abundant joy shall come to the godly from the fall of Rome. In this passage, "Apostles and Prophets" are not those famous ancient preachers of God's truth and founders of the Churches. ### OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chapter 18.

...showed by probable reason that it shall be besieged for some time; for so old Babylon was not subdued by Cyrus and brought into his power until after some long delay. But this is delivered in this way because the laying waste of Rome shall be ended most quickly once it is taken and its spoiling begins. It may be that this type <term>type: a symbolic representation or prophetic sign</term> may suggest to us the manner of surprising Rome, which we know was used in surprising old Babylon. It is very reasonable that both of these Babylons should have the same sign to foreshadow their destruction, seeing as both of them are equally ungodly and shall be destroyed in a similar manner (Jeremiah 51:63-64).

*So shall it be cast out with force.* The word shall be joined with the sign, without which signs are cold things—lacking life and efficacy.

**Verse 22. *And the voice of harpers:*** He describes this ruin of Rome in more words, after the manner of the Prophets, who are accustomed <note>original: "wont"</note> to describe the utter destruction of any place with these kinds of words, as in Jeremiah 25:10:

->*And I will cause the voice of joy and of gladness to perish from among them, the voice also of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the sound of the mills, and the light of the candle.*<-

He means that all things shall perish which pertain either to their present delight, or necessity, or else to their future increasing and multiplying upon earth. For this special numbering up of matters serves to teach us this much: they are called "Harpers" who sing and play on their harps; they are called "Musicians" by a common name who sing with a loud voice. The pipe and trumpet are wind instruments; the one having a softer and sweeter sound, the other having a harsher and more terrible sound, fit for war, and yet there is some use for it at solemn meetings in times of peace. 

But they are all brought in to express the joy and jollity in which Rome lived, as we learn from Jeremiah, from whom these words are taken. Therefore, it would be against learning, reason itself, and the scope of this passage to make a long discussion about pipes used at funerals, as the Jesuits do in this place. *And no craftsman.* After those things that serve to express what helps to nourish and testify to their voluptuous life, he comes to speak of those things which more closely express what helps to keep life and soul together; of which kind of matters there is a more necessary use, such as craftsmen <note>original: "artificers"</note> and mills. **Verse 21. *Then a mighty Angel took up.*** Until now, the ruin of Rome has been declared by bare words alone; now there is a sign used together with words by which it might be taught that it shall be sudden and eternal. Now this is done by the ministry of a certain third Angel, of whom it is not stated where he comes from; perhaps because it is that first Angel—whose place of origin was declared in verse 1—who is now brought in again to perform that very same thing which he proclaimed before was to be done immediately. For we shall understand that the matter is dispatched in the beginning of the next chapter; and the former Angels went before this ruin for some little space of time. Therefore, either the overthrow of Rome is spoken of now in these words, or else it is altogether buried in silence how it is to be carried out.

***There is a millstone cast into the sea.*** This is a suitable sign to declare the manner of Rome’s fall, just as the casting of a burning mountain into the sea was the beginning of Antichrist's tyranny (Chapter 8:8). But the matter is still hard to know; it shall be made manifest at last by the event. This Angel is said to be strong, taking up a stone like a millstone and casting it out of his hands into the sea. For this symbolic type <term>type: a prophetic symbol or foreshadowing</term> is set forth to us by so many degrees. And these things teach us the remarkable speed <note>original: "admirable celerity"</note> that shall be used in ruining Rome, as also that Rome, once fallen, shall never be repaired and rebuilt again. A great stone rushes down with its own weight, and that exceeding forcibly; but it is far more forceful if it is thrown down, and yet most forceful of all if it is thrown down by some mighty and strong man. Neither can it have any hope to float aloft again on the surface of the sea, which both its own weight and the force used upon it have pitched into the bottom of the sea. Thus shall Babylon be cast out with main force and shall never be found again. # OF THE APOCALYPSE. CHAPTER 18.

It has been shown by probable reasoning that it shall be besieged for some time. For just as ancient Babylon was not subdued by Cyrus and brought into his power until after some long delay, this passage is delivered in this way because the laying waste of Rome shall be brought to an end very quickly once it has been taken and its spoiling has begun. It may be that this symbolic sign <note>original: "Type"</note> may suggest to us the manner of capturing Rome, which we know was used in the capture of old Babylon. It is quite reasonable that both of these Babylons should have the same sign to represent their destruction, seeing that both of them are equally ungodly and shall be destroyed in a similar manner (Jeremiah 51:63–64).

**"So shall it be cast with force."** The word shall be joined with the sign, without which signs are cold things—without life and effectiveness <note>original: "efficacy"</note>.

**Verse 22. *And the voice of harpers:*** He describes this ruin of Rome in more detail, after the manner of the Prophets, who are accustomed <note>original: "wont"</note> to describe the utter destruction of any place with these kinds of words, as in Jeremiah 25:10: *And I will cause the voice of joy and of gladness to perish from among them, the voice also of the Bridegroom and the voice of the Bride, the sound of the mills, and the light of the candle.* He means that everything which pertains either to their present delight or necessity—or even to their future growth and multiplication upon earth—shall perish. For this specific listing of matters serves to teach us this much: they are called "harpers" who sing and play on their harps; they are called "musicians" by a common name who sing with a loud voice. The pipe and trumpet are wind instruments; the one having a softer and sweeter sound, the other having a harsher and more terrible sound fit for war, yet it also has some use at solemn meetings in times of peace. 

But all of these are brought in to express the joy and jollity in which Rome lived, as we learn from Jeremiah, from whom these words are taken. Therefore, it would be against learning—even against reason itself and the purpose of this passage—to engage in long talk about pipes used at funerals, as the Jesuits do in this place. 

***And no craftsman.*** After those things that serve to express what helps to nourish and testify to their luxurious <note>original: "voluptuous"</note> life, he comes to speak of those things which more closely express what helps to "keep life and soul together." These types of matters have a more necessary use, such as <term>artificers</term> <note>meaning skilled craftsmen or tradesmen</note> and mills. Wherever there is any society among men, there must necessarily be craftsmen; but yet these men cannot work

Such insignificant <note>original: "pelting"</note> commodities as these are most appropriately mentioned here to display the severity <note>original: "grievousness"</note> of this destruction. 

For if there is no supply of such matters as these—which are of ordinary and humble value and most commonly used among people—we should not expect that people will easily, or at all, obtain things of any special importance. Perhaps, however, "lights" refers to the bridegroom and the bride mentioned afterward. Lights were traditionally used solemnly in marriages. For this reason, our Savior created the parable of the ten virgins, who *went out with their lamps to meet the bridegroom* (Matthew 25:1). Undoubtedly, Christ borrowed this comparison <note>original: "similitude"</note> from a custom that was commonly used in such cases at that time. 

Among the Greeks <note>original: "Grecians"</note>, children were often called "children of darkness"—or children begotten in the dark and in secret <note>original: "hugger mugger"</note>—if their parents did not have a torchlight carried before them at their marriage, as the interpreters of Homer have observed regarding the fifth book of the *Iliad*. It was likewise the custom of the Romans that a boy whose father and mother were both still living would carry a burning torch <note>original: "fire brand"</note> made of whitethorn before the couple being married, because they used to marry at night, as Plutarch says in his *Roman Questions* <note>original: "Problemes"; referring to Plutarch's *Quaestiones Romanae*</note>. ## *The 19th Chapter.*

### The Resolution of this Chapter into its Several Contents.

So far, those things have been handled which precede or are joined together with the ruin of Rome. Now follows that which comes after it. This begins with a thanksgiving to God in the first four verses, which is twofold: first, from the vast crowd <note>original: "confused multitude"; here meaning an immense, undifferentiated assembly</note> initially giving praise to God for taking just vengeance upon the whore (verses 1–2), which is then repeated again because of the eternal nature of that same punishment (verse 3). The second part of the thanksgiving is offered by the Elders and the Living Creatures <note>original: "Beasts"; referring to the four living creatures of Revelation 4</note> (verse 4). This concludes the more complete explanation of the fifth vial.

There are two vials yet remaining: the sixth to be poured out upon the Euphrates, and the seventh upon the air. That former vial is discussed in the rest of this chapter, up to the 20th verse. The seventh is continued from there to the conclusion of the whole book. 

There were two parts of that former vial set down in Chapter 16: the drying up of the Euphrates and the preparation for a battle. In the same way, we have two parts of the explanation of it laid down here. ## THE EXPOSITION.

**After these things I heard a voice.** In interpreting <note>original: "resolving"</note> this chapter, we refer these first four verses to the Fifth Vial, that is, to the Fall of Rome. In these verses, we are taught what joyful reasons for praising God the destruction of Rome shall provide <note>original: "afford"</note> to the saints. The Angel exhorted them to rejoice previously in chapter 18, verse 20. Now, therefore, when the matter is finally accomplished, all the godly shall triumph in good earnest and with all their hearts. 

But seeing as this exceeding joy of theirs follows the fall of Rome, it must be that either the casting of the millstone into the sea is the destruction of the city, or else the manner of its destruction is altogether concealed—which shall nevertheless happen between that sign and this thanksgiving. 

The first thanksgiving <note>original: "gratulation"</note> is *of a great multitude in heaven*; that is, of a diverse <note>original: "confused"</note> company of all sorts of people who shall then be living <note>original: "conversing"</note> in the Church upon Earth. For we still maintain <note>original: "abide still in"</note> the meaning of this word that is common <note>original: "usual"</note> in this book, which will not allow us to refer these things spoken of here to any knowledge that the souls in heaven have of matters done upon earth. The citizens, therefore, of the Church Militant <term>the Christian church on earth, considered as struggling against sin and the devil</term> who are living in any place in the world where the report of Rome's ruin shall be heard, shall leap for the excessive joy they feel. By means of that joy, they shall break forth into this thankful acknowledgment of God's goodness to his Church in punishing Rome.

**Hallelujah.** This is a Hebrew <note>original: "Hebrue"</note> word, signifying *Praise the Lord*, by which the faithful urge <note>original: "provoke"</note> one another to give thanks to God. They cheer up their hearts and tune their spirits to perform this duty in the best manner by using this word as a preface to it. True joy of the Holy Ghost will not endure being kept and cooped up in any one man’s breast and bosom, but it strives to find companions—both for the pouring out and sharing of itself with them, so that they may be filled and refreshed from this spring of joy, and also so that the joy itself may be further increased and inflamed by this joint rejoicing of many good hearts together, who are all baptized into one Spirit.

But why does this heavenly host speak Hebrew at this time? What? Is there some greater holiness and mystery lying beneath the shapes <note>original: "concavities"</note> of these letters and syllables than if they were words of another tongue? These are the trifles <note>original: "toys"</note> and devices of our Rhemish translators. <note>The Rhemish translators were the Catholic scholars who produced the Douay-Rheims Bible; the author here critiques their preference for retaining certain Latin or Hebrew forms.</note> Are these and similar Hebrew words—such as *Hosanna*, *Amen*, *Abba*, and the like—retained in the Greek and other translations for this end: so that we might use them as signs and reminders of our connection <note>original: "conjunction"</note> with the Holy Church that existed under the Old Law before Christ? Namely, that we both believe in one and the same God, and that we call upon Him alone? 

This is indeed a profitable use that we may make of these retained words, and a good reason why they are kept. But it seems that the chief cause why they are retained in this place is because the Church of the Gentiles shall provoke their brothers the Jews to embrace the faith of Christ once Rome is destroyed. For then, the main obstacle <note>original: "impediment"</note> which most mightily blocked the way to their conversion shall be taken away. For it was not possible that the people who crucified the Lord should acknowledge Him to be their Lord as long as Rome flourished, or even existed in the world—since Rome was the place that gave them the power and authority to crucify Him. 

This is why this Hebrew word [Hallelujah] is so often resounded and rung out again and again in this passage. The praises previously given to God in this book were not expressed in these words; but since the conversion of the Jews is joined next to this celebration <note>original: "gratulation"</note>, the saints now speak in the language of the Jews for good reason, as they desire to be made into one sheepfold with them and to speak the language of Canaan <term>a biblical metaphor for the language of the people of God</term>.

Therefore, in this destruction of Rome, such a bright beam of God’s goodness and power shall shine forth that all faithful men shall marvel and be amazed by it. **Verse 2.** *For true and righteous.* This "truth" in his judgments refers to the promise of God; "justice" refers to the punishing of His enemies according to His promise and their own deserts. Because of this, God is now worthily magnified by His people for both reasons, seeing that He would now make the world know through sufficient experience—and more than enough, as they would now think—that God is an avenger of wickedness, and that He does not always overlook <note>original: "winke at"</note> the wrongs that are done to His people.

**Verse 3.** *And again they said.* Here a second thanksgiving is expressed, which shall be made after the matter is more certainly known to be true and definite. The first messenger who brings the initial news that the city is taken shall pour forth the first praises of God. But once the faithful have heard that Rome is utterly razed to the ground, without any hope of restoration or renewal, they shall renew their joy. Together, they shall sing new songs of praise to God, which they shall pour out from the fresh springs of their heartfelt joy. This second expression of gratitude <note>original: "Gratulation"</note> is expressed in fewer words than the former; perhaps it is recorded so briefly to make us see the dull disposition of our nature, which at the first onset of a matter is like "fire and tinder" <note>original: "fire and towe," an idiom for something that ignites quickly</note>, but we grow cool enough—and too much so—afterward.

*And the smoke thereof rose up.* That is, now Rome is delivered up to be tormented everlastingly. For everlasting fire and torments are signified by the smoke rising up forevermore. By this kind of speech, we are taught that the perpetual remembrance of that punishment shall always be worthily magnified by all the godly, as those who shall have the sign of it (this smoke always ascending) constantly exposed to their sight, lest perhaps it might be buried in forgetfulness. Here is an allusion made to the everlasting torments which the wicked shall endure. Therefore, this eternity of punishment that shall fall upon...

For this assembly of the Elders and Living Creatures <note>original: "Beasts"</note> sitting together represents the solemn meeting of the whole Church. God the Father considers this meeting to be so glorious for His Son's sake, as this most holy and glorious choir represents to us. Therefore, whenever anything is performed in the name and with the consent of the whole Church, it is expressed by this sacred senate of Elders and Living Creatures, as we showed in Chapter 4. This, then, shall be the order of giving thanks to God: the final section and epilogue of the general thanksgiving shall be reserved for the public congregation. This is the usual practice of the Church—private joy always precedes that which is communal and public.

Private joy is often sparked by the slightest rumor of a desired report. Public thanksgiving, however, is not undertaken until matters are thoroughly known and proven to be true. Now, the twenty-four Elders fall down when the Living Creatures give glory and thanks to Him who sits on the throne. It is part of their function to moderate and govern the entire proceeding in the public assembly. The rest of the congregation ought to join their hearts with them and testify to their consent by adding their common voice <note>original: "suffrage," meaning collective agreement or prayer</note> at the end. According to this custom, only two words are recorded in the entire public thanksgiving: *Amen* and *Hallelujah*. It is as if the first word were placed here to express the consent of the Elders, and the second word were placed in this order to be the result of the entire thanksgiving which the Living Creatures conceive in their prayers. But this order was explained more fully in Chapter 4. From that, we may see that the same order should be understood here, though it is only briefly mentioned at this time. *That she should be arrayed with fine linen.* He does not say, "*Fine linen was given to her*," but rather, "*it was granted to her that she should be clothed with fine linen, etc.*" The difference is this: the former words would signify that fine linen is given to her by God directly <note>original: "immediatly"</note>, while these words signify that it is given indirectly <note>original: "mediatly"</note>—that is, by means of faith. This fine linen is both pure and bright. It is pure in regard to justification, because it presents us as blameless and irreproachable before God, free from any spots or stains. It is bright in respect to the glory which it brings to a person, both before God—who makes us heirs of his eternal kingdom because of his Son's purity, which is made ours—and also before men. To them, it shows our adoption through those most excellent and glittering fruits of faith, which it causes to appear readily to the view of men by means of the Holy Spirit <note>original: "Holy Ghost"</note> working together with us and within us.

<meta>This page continues the interpretation of Revelation 19:8, focusing on the symbolic meaning of the "fine linen" given to the Church of the Jews upon their conversion. It transitions from the previous page's discussion of the Jews being "grafted" into Christ to a specific defense of the doctrine of justification by faith alone.</meta>

<page-num>815</page-num>
<header>OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chapter 19.</header>

> *For the fine linen is the righteousness, or justifications, of the Saints.*

See how distinctly and exquisitely the Holy Spirit <note>original: "Holy Ghost"</note> speaks in this place; for he does not say that the justifications of the saints are fine linen, but on the contrary, that fine linen is the justifications. Furthermore, this refers not to the wicked—as a person is when they are first converted to God—but to the saints. This means that all justification, even for those in whom piety shines forth most greatly, does not flow from a person's self or from their own inherent qualities. Instead, it resides in the outward garment that comes to them from the outside, namely in Christ and his righteousness, whom we put on by faith alone. 

It is a most plain and unanswerable passage <note>original: "place"</note> of Scripture to confirm the doctrine of justification by faith alone. I would have all of you—you Catholic people <note>original: "Popish People"</note>—consider this diligently, so that you might at last renounce your blasphemous pride of heart and find true salvation where it can only be obtained. What? Will you thrust the merits of the saints upon God and think you can silence him that way? Away with <note>original: "Out vppon"</note> these filthy, monstrous garments! 

This fine linen spoken of here is given to us to be our justification. This clothing, which will make us stand with boldness before God, is not woven from our own virtues. No comparison can more clearly set before our eyes the imputation of righteousness <term>The theological concept that Christ's righteousness is credited to the believer's account through faith</term> by faith than this metaphor of a garment, which is so often used in the Scriptures. 

But some will say, "Why does he say 'justifications' rather than 'justification'?" It is not at all to destroy the unique righteousness of faith. Rather, the word used here for "righteousness" serves as an argument by which a person proves himself to be righteous, as it is used in Chapter 15:4. And there is a double argument for this: one is before God through faith—in which respect Christ is this "white linen" of the saints (Chapter 3:4 and 7:13–14)—and the other is before men through the works of sanctification. 

Because of this double proof and evidence of our justification, the Holy Spirit used the word "justifications" in the plural number. He did this so he might include within this one word what he declared in the previous verse using the two words "pure" and "bright." For works of holiness, if they are taken as being separate from the righteousness of faith, are not "pure." Conversely, if the righteousness of faith is considered apart from works of holiness, it is not "bright" and shining forth, for it lies hidden within, far from the eyes of men. Neither of them, therefore, can be called "justifications" separately, but both of them are to be joined together...

...therefore, for expressing the force of this word that is put in the plural number; and indeed, those who have this fine linen clothing given to them are found to have both of these justifications in them.

**Verse 9. Then he said unto me, Write.** Who is this that said this? Not he that sits upon the throne; for the elders worshiped him in verse 4. But it was not lawful to worship the one who speaks here, as he is the fellow servant of John. It is, therefore, some angel who has this office committed to him: to seal and confirm this prophecy. First, therefore, he tells John to write; by such a solemn command, he teaches him that it is some great and unusual <note>original: "unwonted"</note> matter which he is informed of now. We commonly commit matters to writing when we want their authority and credit to be confirmed for all posterity; in this regard, laws were once engraved in brass and fixed in some public place in ancient times. 

As also God himself, speaking to Jeremiah regarding this very same matter, says, *“Write for yourself all the words which I speak to you in a book”* (Jeremiah 30:2). It is as if God, providing for our weakness <note>original: "infirmity"</note>, should give us, as it were, registers and books of remembrance, from which we might more confidently claim matters at his hands <note>original: "challenge him"</note> if he should seem to forget his promise. But yet John is not only confirmed by this, but the outcome <note>original: "event"</note> is also respected, as we have seen before in similar passages; it is as if it should come to pass that some public writing should be set forth by the authority of some holy man, which would most plainly prove that this is no new matter, but something that has been foretold by God ever since the earliest ages. Therefore, the goodness and truth of God are to be acknowledged and magnified in it. 

But what is it that he is commanded to write? *“That they are blessed who are called to the marriage supper of the Lamb.”* This is a marvelous matter, and something never heard of before—that they are all blessed who are called. In the past, this rule took place: “Many are called, but few are chosen,” a truth which the examples of former ages have taught us; for the outward calling did not succeed so happily among the guests who were invited of old, who refused to come when they were called. But now, there is to be a different <note>original: "diverse"</note> manner of calling from that. All who are called now shall come willingly; neither shall they offer trivial excuses as those men did who were invited formerly in Matthew 22. But now—

# OF THE APOCALYPSE. chap. 19.

Now there shall be such great efficacy and grace of the Spirit, that they shall obey at the first hearing. For so says the Prophet Isaiah: *“Before she labored, she brought forth; and before her pain came, she was delivered of a male child. Who has heard such a thing? Who has seen such things? Shall the earth be made to bring forth in one day? Or shall a nation be born at once? For as soon as Zion labored, she brought forth her children”* (Chapter 66:7–8). So also Psalm 110:3: *“Your people shall come most willingly of all others in the day of your armies, with holy beauties; out of the womb of the morning, the dew of your youth shall come to you.”* Many such places of Scripture might be brought to this purpose, and perhaps it would be profitable to bring them, at least for this end: that our writers might have occasion given them to consider these places more diligently. I fear that we wander from the right interpretation when we make them speak of things that are past, whereas they actually foretell things yet to come. This sentence, therefore, which is commanded to be written, takes away all doubt <note>original: "Scruple"</note> from John; he might have thought on the former stubbornness <note>original: "obstinacy"</note> of this Jewish nation and might have doubted their conversion in that regard.

But the angel bids him cast away this care and fear, and tells him that this people shall be so greatly willing and desirous to come, that it shall be enough only to have called them. It is to be observed that the Jews are here, and elsewhere commonly, said to be men who have been called; for the participle here is used in the past perfect tense <note>original: "preter perfect tense"</note>, as also in Matthew 22:3, 4, 8 when it is applied to the Jews. By this, a certain prerogative seems to be noted which the Jews have before others in their calling, as those who have been called from the first beginning of the world. But the Gentiles are said to be men who *are called*, in the present tense, because they were first called at the coming of Christ, or rather from the time of his death. And this difference seems to be observed in this Revelation also, whereupon those who are said to subdue the ten kings, having the Lamb for their Captain, are called those who are "called and chosen," who (as is certain) are the faithful among the Gentiles.

***These words are true.*** This is the second confirmation of this matter, taken from the principal author of it. It is as if it were said: "Do not look at me as one who reports something from my own head, but know that it is the decree of the Most High God, as you have just heard with..."

# CHAPTER 19. A REVELATION

...with your own ears, verse 5. But the natural arrangement of the words as they lie in the Greek has great force in it, which is lost if they are transposed, like this: *These true words are the words even of God himself*. That is, they contain in them a most divine, excellent, and certain truth. For some words of a man are also true, but even the truest words we speak have some weaknesses <note>original: "infirmities"</note> lying beneath them. "We always speak from the earth" (John 3:31). There is, therefore, a kind of excellence given to this truth which does not appear if we change the order of the words. It is no strange matter to say that the words of God are true.

**Verse 10. And I fell before his feet.** Why does he fall down now, more than before? Was he struck with the majesty of the angel? But he had been by now for a long time acquainted with strange and marvelous sights. Is it perhaps because of the joy that he took in hearing about the conversion of his own nation? It indeed seems to be so. For John, being enraptured with the pleasantness of this prophecy—as is clear he was, by the answer of the angel—and regarding the sudden joy with which he was carried away, he would have given greater worship to the messenger of such welcome news than was appropriate <note>original: "meete"</note>.

**See that you [do it not].** It is an incomplete <note>original: "defectiue"</note> speech, meaning: "See that you do not worship me." By this, the seriousness of his sin is signified. For he makes such haste that he does not even finish the sentence because of his hurry. Just as we are accustomed to stop a matter from proceeding with some sudden cry and noise, or else with the hand, when the matter will not tolerate delay in speaking. He confirms his prohibition by a double reason. First, because the ministers of Christ have equal dignity among themselves: "I am," says he, "your fellow-servant," and not yours only, and of the other Apostles, but of your brothers also, who have the testimony of Jesus. The function of every one of us who are in the ministry is equal. Those who preach Christ and salvation through him are of equal dignity with those who foretell things to come. The office of preaching is to be compared in worth with the office of prophesying; this is the meaning of those words at the end of the verse: *For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.* 

The second reason is because adoration belongs to God alone. "Worship him," he says, to whom alone such worship is due. Oh, why do you not tremble at the hearing of these words, you Popish <note>A derogatory term for Roman Catholics used by Protestant reformers to criticize the veneration of saints and angels.</note> idolaters who teach...

### Chapter 19: A REVELATION

...to the very moment of time, to the end of things. It is no new method that the Holy Spirit takes to deliver to us a short and concise <note>original: "compendious"</note> prophecy of the entire state of his spouse [the Church] in the person of Christ alone. He has not changed, except so far as it is necessary for his Church to have him appear changed. Therefore, in this new representation, as if in a mirror <note>original: "looking glasse"</note>, we ought to behold the face of Christ’s spouse, and we should consider it all the more diligently. 

This marvelous vision is seen in "heaven that is opened"—that is, in the holy Church, whose most renowned and shining glory shall now be made manifest to all men. This surpasses the notable dignity and excellence of the first Church of the Gentiles (such as it was seen in the times of the Apostles and shortly after), which was signified by the "door opened in heaven" in Chapter 4:1. But this is a more extensive glory than 그at, as heaven is set open here not just by some little door that leads into it, but by wide gates—or rather, by the whole walls being removed, so to speak—there being nothing to hinder men from beholding the full majesty of it, as far as it can be seen on earth.

**And behold a white horse.** 
We should not think that Christ will appear in any visible form. The events currently being described are far from the final coming of Christ, as will be made manifest by the explanation following; instead, he shall openly display and exercise such great power in the administration of his kingdom as this representation describes him to have. The entire description consists of four parts <note>original: "members"</note>. In each of these, we have both his equipment <note>original: "furniture"</note> and his name given to us to consider. 

In this first part, his equipment is a **white horse**, and his name is **Faithful and True** in his sayings. Because this vision is similar to the one in Chapter 6:2, some people have supposed that this is the same vision. Because of this error, they confuse everything <note>original: "shuffle all together"</note>. However, these two visions differ greatly in both their timing and their meaning. That white horse was set out when the Church was at the beginning of her race and at the starting gates <note>original: "varriers"; the barriers or starting stalls in a race</note>. This one comes when she is toward the end of it, at the finish line <note>original: "Goale"</note>, as it were. That one appeared shortly after John’s time, when Trajan <note>Roman Emperor from 98–117 AD</note> and his immediate successors flourished; this one is not seen until after the overthrow of Rome. In that earlier vision, the diverse multitude of all the faithful was considered; here, only the conversion of the nation of the Jews is handled. In this they agree: that the white horse does...

> *And who judges and fights righteously.*

This is how Theodore Beza <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605) was a major Protestant reformer and scholar who succeeded John Calvin in Geneva</note> translates the words, interposing the relative pronoun "who" as if all these words served to make up his name together with the former. The words properly have this force: *and he judges and fights in righteousness*. Here the conjunction "and" <note>original: "coniunction Copulatiue"</note> may be causal; it is as if these words gave a reason for both the white horse and his name, and were set next after them as an interpretation. Thus: he sits on a white horse because he fights righteously, and his name is Faithful and True because he judges righteously. And these words are spoken in respect to his own people, and are taken, it seems, out of Psalm 96:10, 13. In that context, to judge in righteousness and in justice signifies to rule and govern his people by framing and composing their lives to righteousness and justice. Yes, even the citizens of the Church began to be in a state of hesitation <note>original: "mammering"; meaning a state of hesitation or wavering uncertainty</note> and to doubt its credibility; whereupon that complaint is made in the Prophet, *The Lord has forsaken me, and God has forgotten me* (Isaiah 49:14). Until that time, the perfect accomplishing of things that are foretold is reserved; and then shall the authority of the word of God flourish in its greatest glory in this world, when its most constant truth shall be plainly perceived in everything.

In like manner, they shall be cast like clusters of grapes into the winepress of his wrath, and there they shall be trodden in pieces. Therefore, his enemies shall never again have any power to rise up <note>original: "to gett head"</note> and come against him; they must now necessarily be held under the yoke as long as the world lasts. The Complutensian Polyglot <note>original: "Complutensis"; the first printed polyglot edition of the entire Bible, completed in 1517</note> and the King’s Bible <note>The Authorized Version or similar royal patronage edition</note> read, *A sharp two-edged sword goes out*, and *he treads* in the present tense. This teaches us that the punishment of wicked men shall not be deferred any longer, as it has been before this, but they shall immediately pay for their wickedness, seeing they shall be presently trodden down with great fury like grapes in the winepress; see Isaiah 63:3 and Lamentations 1:15.

*The winepress of the wine of his wrath.* This is because the punishment of the wicked shall be no less pleasing to God than the drinking of pleasant wine is to those who are thirsty. That must necessarily be performed firmly and thoroughly which a man takes great pleasure in doing. The punishment, therefore, of wicked men shall be grievous and horrible, so that they are made to pay dearly to the uttermost for their duties <note>original: "d-tyes," likely "deities" or "duties" in the sense of obligations or pleasures</note> wherewith they have been glutted in former times; see Deuteronomy 28:63.

**Verse 16. *And he had upon his garment, and upon his thigh.***
A name is written upon his garment because it shall be manifest to all men at that time that Christ is the supreme king, a fact that was not so evident to the world in former ages. The Christian profession was spread abroad long ago into all the world; yet how miserably did the Heathen Emperors nip it in the head and pinch it in the birth when it first began to spring forth? From that time, how many mischievous ways did the Pope of Rome endeavor to destroy it utterly? Neither has he given over his old malicious course at this day. For now he has gotten the "Great Turk" <note>The Sultan of the Ottoman Empire</note> to join forces and to be a coworker with him in this cursed enterprise, though each of them goes about his work and aims at the same main end by different means. Certainly, ever since the time that Christ has been made known unto us Gentiles, he has seemed not so much to reign as to live in a miserable bondage throughout the world. And yet he has always given us some good proof and argument of this kingdom of his, even in the midst of all these miseries that the Church has endured, in that he has preserved the Church from perishing in spite of all enemies—even though he has suffered it in the meanwhile...

### Verse 17. *Then I saw a certain Angel standing in the Sun.* 

So far the description of the Captain goes; now the Holy Spirit comes to describe certain soldiers who must encounter the Beast. These are mustered by the voice of a herald standing in the Sun, who is a different Angel from the one who poured out the Bowl <note>original: "Vial"</note> upon the Sun. For this is he who shall plague the Antichristian assembly <note>original: "Synagogue"</note> by interpreting the Scriptures. That other Angel shall sound a summons to battle by stirring up the Saints for it. 

Neither shall the one who pours out the Bowl stand in the Sun itself; instead, being seated somewhere else, he shall cast his liquid upon it. This Angel, as it were sitting down in the chariot of Phoebus <note>original: "Phæbus," the Greco-Roman personification of the Sun</note>, takes his position within the compass of that great light. 

But someone might ask, how shall we be able to conceive of such a thing even in our thoughts? I think we may find a light to discover this "Sun" mentioned here from Chapter 12, verse 1, where we heard that the woman was clothed with the Sun. That is, she glittered on every side with the most clear light of the Scriptures. Adorned with the clear knowledge of these as if with a beautiful garment, she came forth and revealed herself to the view of the world. 

Now, one may be said to "stand" in their clothing, just as the Spouse stands at the King’s right hand in the Gold of Ophir (*Psalm 45:10*). Therefore, this Angel shall be some citizen of that particular Church which shall shine forth most gloriously with honor and renown above the rest, by means of her witnessing to and maintaining the most Holy Truth in a special manner. In this way, she shall prove herself to be the natural daughter of that woman who is "clothed with the Sun." 

We know that there is not the same purity in all the particular Churches that profess Christ, but that one drinks in more dregs and drags more excess baggage <note>original: "baggage stuffe"</note> after it than another. But this Angel shall be a member of that most sound <note>original: "intire"</note> and most chaste congregation of all, which shall be the most glistening and gorgeous by means of this glorious clothing. 

And he is not one of the converted Jews of whom we just began to speak, but he is a western Angel, sounding a summons to battle against the Beast and the false Prophet, who are the plague and the ruin of this part of the world where we live. And it seems that all the chief stress and violence...

Clouds and mists and whatever else does or may hinder this, your sunshine; either from shining out there with you, or from breaking out from there toward us in a glorious manner.

**Saying to all the birds that flew through the midst of heaven.** We have observed before (in Chapters 8:13 and 14:6) that the word in the Greek translated as "the middle of heaven" signifies a place between heaven and earth, like the middle region of the air where meteors are formed. It does not signify the "midst of heaven" in terms of its length, which astronomers call the *meridies* <note>original: "Meridies," the Latin term for noon or the southern point where the sun is highest</note>, the point where the sun is at noon. Therefore, this word serves to reveal to us the "imperfect perfection" and the "impure purity" of those men who have escaped the horrible filthiness of gross superstition through the knowledge and acknowledgment of the truth, yet have not attained the level of purity fitting for those who dwell in heaven. 

The Angel of the Sun calls all of these to take part in dividing the spoils, as they are all students and foster-children of the same truth, even though it does not flourish equally among them all in holiness and integrity. From this, we understand that although one or two, or a few congregations, shall profess and practice sincere piety at the time when this war is waged against the Beast, most of them—even those of the Reformed religion—will be found either never to have attained a full correction of things that are wrong, or else to have fallen back so far through their own negligence and carelessness that they fall far short of the holiness of a pure and undefiled spouse.

And who does not see that this decline and decay takes place more and more every day throughout the churches? There are some perverse and stubborn <note>original: "refratary," likely a typo for refractory, meaning stubborn or unmanageable</note> men who will not be persuaded—even if they are convinced—that there is any such difference between churches today as the one we speak of and find in this passage and others. But there are those to whom God gives the grace to deny their own wicked lusts and imaginations, and to subject themselves—with all their thoughts and judgments—to be measured and directed by the only standard and foundation <note>original: "square and Platforme"</note> of all truth, the perfect law of God. These humble and gracious men (I say) who thus prove they truly fear God, both see and, with grief of heart, bewail that there are many who should stand in the sun...

Nor shall he be destitute of all aid from the kings, even when he shall be quite bereaved of his Princely Chair <note>original: "Chaire," referring to his throne or seat of authority</note>; rather, some kings—namely those of the earth, who are worshippers of wicked superstition—shall still take his part. **But the Beast was taken.** So far goes the explanation of the Sixth Vial. The Seventh and last vial now comes to be unfolded and opened more fully. This first delivers to us the destruction of the enemies of Christ and of his Church; and first of the Beast and of his armies. The False Prophet is taken together with this Beast. These two being joined together teach us that the Pope at Rome (for so perhaps he will still be called after the City of Rome shall be laid waste) shall now at length be utterly destroyed, both in respect of his civil power (which causes him to be called the Beast) and also in respect of his spiritual power (because of which he is called the False Prophet). The Holy Spirit speaks of him as if he were two distinct persons because of that double wickedness of his, for which this "man of sin" is famous in all the world. But when I say the "Pope of Rome," I do not only understand that particular man who shall sit in that Chair of Pestilence <note>original: "Chaire of Peftilence," a phrase often used by Reformers to describe the Papal throne as a source of moral contagion</note> at that time, but the state itself and the order of Popes, which shall then so completely and forever perish that there shall be no remainders of it left standing. ### CHAPTER 20. A REVELATION

To these names, the definite articles are also joined <note>The author refers to the original Greek text here, where the use of the definite article emphasizes that these emperors were *the* specific agents of the Devil.</note>, because they were the leaders and principal instruments of the Devil's wickedness. A man worthily bears the name of the one whose manners and disposition he resembles and imitates.

This arrest <note>original: "apprehending"</note> of the Dragon indicates to us the entire first period of time, which reached from the days of John—and somewhat before—until the reign of Constantine the Great. The last part of this period is used here to represent the whole timeframe. For in speaking now of the capture of the Dragon, the author wants it to be understood that the Dragon ranged and rampaged freely and at his pleasure before this, plotting and practicing as much mischief as he could, as we have heard in the opening of the Seals in **Chapter 6**.

***And he bound him a thousand years.*** That is, he established and introduced such a manner of government as left the open enemies no power to dominate and tyrannize in and over the Church, as they had been accustomed to do in former times. This government, having been begun by him, was extended and did continue for a thousand years afterward.

And this is that second period, in which the Dragon was bound—that is, the heathen Emperors were suppressed and kept from reigning—even until the year 1300. But I call this the "Period of the Dragon," because it is not exactly that same second period of the whole prophecy (specifically the period of the Trumpets) which the Holy Spirit assigned and established previously. This period is of a longer duration and exceeds that of the Dragon by two hundred and sixty years or more. 

The history of the Dragon has some elements that are unique to itself and is not to be tied strictly to that other rule. His binding is more ancient than the time when the Trumpets began to be sounded, as his binding took place under the sixth Seal around the year 304 AD, as has been said in **Chapter 6:12** and **Chapter 12:7–9**. But why did they not consider that the Beast—who is Antichrist himself—reigned during this entire time of the thousand years while the Dragon was bound? Furthermore, the way all parts of this prophecy hang together—as we have seen so far—will not allow us to make that the beginning. To do so would cause such confusion that there would be no way to untangle ourselves from it. Should we really think that the Devil was bound at that time when he raged most cruelly through the persons of the first heathen Emperors? If he lay then shackled in prison, when shall we say that he was loosed?

...conjecture. While these men prefer such theories over the most certain events, they not only act foolishly, but also go entirely against the intentions of the very authors they cite. Those authors, by everywhere confessing their own ignorance, urged people to search for the truth—which time eventually reveals—rather than to rely on their conjectural suspicions. Indeed, those authors even condemned their own theories because of the ignorance that was revealed <note>original: "bewrayed"</note> when they set them down. Therefore, those who still eagerly cling to errors that have been proven false are deprived of all common sense by the just judgment of God. They do this so that they might comfort and flatter themselves gently and tenderly, until they at last plunge themselves headlong into everlasting and unavoidable destruction.

Moreover, one may observe from this passage that those forty-two months spoken of in Chapter 11:2 and 13:5 are not to be counted in a standard way <note>The author is arguing against a literal 3.5-year reign, suggesting "months" represent a much longer period of time</note>. This is clear because the Beast, to whom these months belong, is active for a thousand years in the light and view of the world. This is proven by the existence of those who were his adversaries for such a long time; they would not have been his enemies at all if the Beast had not existed.

This does not mean that any one individual lived so long, but rather that there was never a lack of a succession of godly people who embraced the Truth, even as Antichrist caused havoc here, there, and everywhere. To acknowledge the truth is indeed to live and to reign with Christ. Conversely, either to be ignorant of or to despise the truth is to be dead while one is alive; even if a man is at the highest peak of royal dignity, he is in a more base condition than the most lowly slave. 

Now, he mentions these years of the Kingdom not because the Saints would cease to reign when those years were ended (for we see that the "first resurrection" follows immediately afterward, which would make the former glory even more abundant), but because the Church during this time appeared to have completely vanished from the world while it lived in the wilderness and lay hidden in the sanctuary <note>original: "hiding place"</note> of the Temple (Chapter 11:1 and 12:14). The Holy Spirit, therefore, teaches us that she lived and reigned with Christ throughout all this most sorrowful time. This specific doubt could not arise concerning the Saints in heaven, whom we know enjoy everlasting blessedness as soon as they have departed from this Valley of Tears.

# Chapter 20. A REVELATION.

This kingdom of most valiant champions was described earlier by that holy army of 144,000 who pitched their tents on Mount Zion and followed the Lamb wherever he went (Chapter 14:1–2). This verse is a repetition of that idea.

**Verse 5. *But the rest of the dead men.*** So much for the condition of the Saints during those thousand years of the Dragon’s binding. Now, the condition of the multitude of men who lived during that period is briefly addressed. These men refused the truth and slept a long night's sleep, not waking again during all those thousand years so that the beam of saving doctrine might shine upon them. This is the apostasy which Paul said was to come before the appearing of the Lord (2 Thessalonians 2:3), and which John expressed earlier by describing *the whole earth wondering after the Beast* (Chapter 13:3 and 17:8).

***This is the first resurrection.*** Here we are taught what the condition of the Church would be during the "third period"—that is, immediately after the end of those thousand years. The truth would return into the world more fully and would finally make a glorious appearance, and the elect would quickly flock from everywhere to its light when it broke forth. This eager desire and effort of theirs is called the "first resurrection," specifically in contrast to a "second" resurrection mentioned in verse 12, as we shall see there. 

Now, there would be a greater abundance of those converted to the Gospel, and they would come flying to it with more ardent affections than before. This happened at the expiration of those thousand years—namely, around the year 1300—when many who had been dead and buried in Roman Catholic superstitions <note>original: "Romish superstitions"</note> opened their eyes to see the Truth as it began to arise and the "daystar" began to dawn. Thus, they rose up again to a life from which they were formerly strangers. 

Among these, Marsilius of Padua <note>original: "Marsilius Patavinus," a 14th-century scholar who challenged the Pope's worldly power</note>, Jean de Jandun <note>original: "Iohannes de Ganduno," a collaborator of Marsilius</note>, and John Wycliffe <note>an English theologian and early reformer often called the "Morning Star of the Reformation"</note> are counted, along with many other worthy men of as sincere piety and as great learning as that time could afford. Through the diligence of these men, many others were also raised up in great numbers <note>original: "by flockes"</note> and called back to the Truth from their errors—as if from death to life—as we have said before (Chapter 14:16). This marvelous conversion is called the "first resurrection," a name under which John repeats and explains the history of these former times. ***Who has a part.*** This is metaphorical speech borrowed from those portions of land which were divided of old by lot in the land of Canaan.
