<meta>This page continues the investigation into the identity of Gog and Magog, exploring the etymological origins and geographical locations associated with the name "Gog" in biblical and classical history.</meta>

# OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chap. 20.

->855<-

There is one of the sons of Reuben recorded with the name of **Gog** in 1 Chronicles 5:4. But he has nothing else in common with this *Gog* spoken of here, as is clear by those passages in Ezekiel and the *Revelation*, which are the only places (besides the one we just mentioned) where mention of *Gog* is found. The most learned interpreters *Tremellius* and *Junius* <note>Immanuel Tremellius and Franciscus Junius were influential 16th-century Protestant biblical scholars known for their Latin translation of the Bible</note> suppose that this name came from *Gyges*, who killed *Candaules*, the king of *Lydia*, and took possession of his kingdom in his place. Because of this, Lesser *Asia* was called *Gog*, just as later, when *Croesus* enlarged the borders of his kingdom into *Syria*, a certain town near *Libanus* <note>Lebanon</note> was called *Gygarta*, instead of *Gog-karta*, which means "the City of *Gog*." Certainly, at the time when Ezekiel prophesied, either *Alyattes* or *Croesus*—both of whom were of the posterity of *Gyges*—reigned in Lesser *Asia*. And it is no strange matter that countries are called by the names of their chief governors, especially in the Scriptures, which teach us that each of the nations took their names this way in the beginning. Yet this perhaps applies more to the first princes than to those who succeed them; nonetheless, these successors have also imposed names upon countries.

It was enough for the Prophet to identify the nation by the name of its first ancestor from whom it originated, who reigned there at that time, even if perhaps that country was not commonly called by that name. These things make this opinion probable. Notwithstanding, Ezekiel—with whose prophecy this whole passage, which was entirely taken from there, agrees perfectly—makes this *Gog* the chief prince and commander of *Meshech* and *Tubal* in Chapter 38:3. That is, of the *Cappadocians* and the *Iberians* in *Asia*, as *Josephus* says in the first book of the *Antiquities of the Jews*, Chapter 7. And there was none of *Gyges’* posterity—not even *Croesus*, who reigned last and furthest of them all—who was ever prince of these nations, as his dominion was bounded within the borders of the River *Halys*, as *Herodotus* writes in *Clio* <note>original: "Clio"; the first book of Herodotus’s Histories</note>. There is, therefore, perhaps some other reason for this name. And it seems to be this: that *Gog* should not be the usual name of any country, but a name derived from *Magog*, both so that it might note the exceedingly close concord and friendship of both these nations, and also that it might appear that *Gog* had his origin from *Magog*.

# A REVELATION, Chap. 20.

->856<-

For *Magog* is the ancient and primary name of one of the sons of *Japheth*, who are listed as *Gomer*, *Magog*, *Madai*, *Javan*, and others (Genesis 10:2). Now, the name *Gog* is derived from that name by removing the first syllable, intended to show us that he is an offshoot of that lineage. However, the countries that *Ezekiel* assigns to him did not submit to any such prince at that time; instead, they were destined to come under the power of such a man when that prophecy was eventually fulfilled. This *Gog*, breaking out from these regions as if from a starting gate, would make his first assault to conquer the rest of the world. It is as if it were said: "Behold, I come against you, O people who originated from *Magog*, but now live in the regions of *Meshech* and *Tubal*."

In these words, the prophet identifies the *Turks* in their early history most accurately. For these people were originally *Scythians* who inhabited the northern side of the Caucasus Mountains, as *Zonaras* <note>Joannes Zonaras was a 12th-century Byzantine historian and theologian</note> says in his third volume addressed to *Constantine Pogonatus*. After these men were called into *Persia* to fight against the *Saracens*, they eventually revolted against the *Persians* and brought the *Babylonians* and nearly the entire East—including *Armenia*, *Iberia* <note>original: "Iberia"; a historical region in the Caucasus, roughly modern-day Georgia</note>, and *Cappadocia*—under their power.

The *Turk*, therefore, represents the *Scythian Nation*, which eventually became the ruler of *Meshech* and *Tubal* (that is, of the *Cappadocians* and *Iberians*). He remained in these places, resting, until the Devil was released in the year 1300, seducing and provoking this nation to wage open war against the Church. At that time, during the reign of *Andronicus Palaeologus*, he utterly defeated and destroyed the army of the *Romans* <note>meaning the Byzantine or Eastern Roman Empire</note> in *Paphlagonia*. With this gateway opened to him, he launched an invasion as far as the River *Sagaris* (which flows from *Galatia* into the *Euxine* Sea <note>The Black Sea</note>) and into all the provinces stretching from the Sea of *Pontus* and *Galatia* to the Sea of *Lycia* and *Caria*. He even brought the River *Eurymedon* under his jurisdiction (*Nicephorus Gregoras, Byzantine History, Book 5*).

This was the beginning of all these misfortunes. For immediately after this, *Ottoman* <note>Osman I, the founder of the Ottoman Empire</note> rose to power, and the calamity that has afflicted our part of the world has descended from him through a long line of successors. Thus has *Gog* been seduced. He was indeed only the prince of *Meshech* and *Tubal* when he first began to raid and assault the world; but now, all of Asia Minor, *Syria*, *Mesopotamia*, *Arabia*, *India*, *Palestine*, *Egypt*, the islands, *Greece*, *Macedonia*, *Thrace*, and more are provinces subject to him. As his tyranny grew across all these provinces...

# OF REVELATION, Chapter 20.

->857<-

...to its full and broad extent, they are called by the Prophet by the common name of Gog. But someone might ask: what closeness or connection does Gog have with Magog, if we acknowledge him to be a Scythian in his origin? It is very significant, both in lineage and in nature. For Magog is a Scythian, and the prince of that nation, as Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus was a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note> says in *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 1, Chapter 6. Magog (he says) was the founder of the Magogites, who took their name from him and are called Scythians by the Greek writers. Yet the Sibyl <note>The Sibylline Oracles, a collection of prophetic utterances</note> seems to sing us a different kind of song in her description of the place where Magog was located, when she says:

> *Woe, woe to you, O country of Gog, and you, Magog, who are situated in the midst of the rivers of the Ethiopians.*
<note>original: "vvoe vvoe vnto thee o cuntry of Gog, and thou Magog that are seated in the middest of the riuers of the æthiopians."</note>

Is Magog then among the rivers of the Ethiopians? We know that these southern people live near the seaside, and that this name does not apply to any nation further north than Egypt—which is often called Ethiopia, as Eustathius <note>A 12th-century scholar and Archbishop of Thessalonica</note> teaches in his commentary on Dionysius <note>Dionysius Periegetes, an ancient geographer</note>. And this is undoubtedly the Ethiopia that the Sibyl refers to, which she rightfully attributes to Magog. For who does not know that the Circassian Scythians <note>Scythian tribes from the Caucasus region</note> were sent to live in Egypt, where there is also a town named after them, Cercasorum? Besides, Ezekiel lists the Persians, Ethiopians, and the men of Africa (whom he calls Put <term>Put: a biblical name for the regions of North Africa, often associated with Libya</term>) among the armies of Gog in chapter 38:5. 

The Sibyl, therefore, does not describe Magog by his own native country, but by the colony where he was sent; she mentions this specifically because the disaster of Magog would fall most heavily upon that part of his dominions. But even if Magog is a Scythian, how did the Devil seduce him? By inciting him to join forces with the Turks and to attempt to destroy the Christians along with them. 

When new troops of the Scythians first broke through the passes of the Caspian Sea into that part of Asia nearest to them (which was around the year 1250, when John Doukas <note>original: "Iohn Duca"; John III Doukas Vatatzes, Emperor of Nicaea</note> reigned at Nicaea), they harassed the Turks, who were of the same blood as them and had entered those countries several centuries earlier. They drove the Turks out of those regions, beyond the Euphrates, into those narrow passes of Lesser Armenia and Cappadocia that we just mentioned. Consequently, the Turks were forced to seek peace with the Roman Emperor so that they could resist the Scythian invasions pressing hard upon them from behind.

This was the state of affairs with the Turks until the appointed time came when the Devil should be loosed from his chains. The number of this army is almost infinite. *For it is like the sand by the seashore; that is, very huge and innumerable.* It was described before by a specific number: *two hundred million* <note>original: "tvvo thousand times an hundred thousand"</note> (Chapter 9:16). In both places, an infinite multitude is signified. And what Emperor is there who takes the field with an army as mighty and numerous as the Turk does? The forces of the Christians, when they are all put together, scarcely equal the fourth part of his army in any battle that is fought between them.

For the Devil, by whose means they are raised up, shall not be confined again in prison for a certain time, but he shall be cast forever into the lake of fire, never to go out again to raise up any such new troubles and tumults.

But observe that the Beast and the false prophet shall be destroyed before the Turk—just as his destruction has been revealed and opened before—and then finally this devilish Turk follows after him as a partner in the same punishment.

# OF THE APOCALYPSE. CHAPTER 20.

*And shall be tormented.* The Latin Vulgate <note>original: "vulgar Latin"</note> omits the coordinating conjunction "and," joining the verb *shall be tormented* directly with the Beast and the false prophet. But this is awkwardly done, seeing that it is no less necessary for us to understand that their common punishment shall be eternal, just as they shall all share one and the same punishment.

Verse 11. *And I saw a great white Throne.* Up to this point, the Holy Spirit has declared the final destruction of the enemies of the Church. The happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note> of the Church now follows, to be laid open and enjoyed after all these storms of calamities have been driven away. The first part of this is the gathering of the saints, described in the rest of this chapter. This gathering is foreshadowed by the *resurrection from the dead* and the last judgment that shall be given to those who have been raised up again. 

For, with all due respect to the learned, I am of the judgment that this resurrection spoken of in this place—which has been commonly held and believed by all men (as far as I know) to be that final rising of the bodies of all men for judgment who have been lying asleep in their graves since the death of the first man, Adam—I say, I think that this resurrection is nothing else but the full restoration of the Jewish nation. Furthermore, I believe it is not brought in and described here for any other purpose than for a more complete opening and declaring of that restoration. 

I hold this view not because I desire to be the first dispenser <note>original: "skinker"; a tapster or someone who pours drinks, used here metaphorically for one who provides new ideas</note> of newly discovered and strange <note>original: "unketh"</note> opinions to the world, or as if I took pride and pleasure in going against the consensus of all writers. I hope those who know me will consider me far from being so proud, dogmatic, audacious, or foolhardy. Indeed, God is my witness how greatly I detest and abhor that restless desire for hunting after and inventing <note>original: "minting"</note> new and monstrous errors out of a profane loathing for the long-accepted truth. Rather, I follow this interpretation only because the entire order of these matters and the marvelous agreement of the rest of the Scriptures compel me to do so. 

I have thought it good to set these things down briefly so that it might appear to all men what reasons draw me to this judgment. If these reasons have any weight <note>original: "moment"</note> in them to reveal and confirm the truth, we might gain for ourselves the knowledge of a matter that has not been thoroughly searched out or certainly known before. But if they are found to be too weak or unsound to build such a significant point upon, they might be erased and scratched out.

I take no pleasure in catching butterflies like children—that is, to drive at feeble <note>original: "sillye," which in this period meant weak or insignificant rather than foolish.</note> subtleties that have no substance in them—but only I desire to set before our eyes the truth, as it seems to me, of that portraiture of a serpent which the Holy Ghost has devised and described to us.

To this we may add his dwelling in the sea, for which cause he is also called Leviathan, or a great whale. How marvelously does this agree to the Turk <note>The author uses "the Turk" to refer to the Ottoman Empire.</note>, who has fixed the seat of his Empire within the very mouth of the sea of Pontus and Propontis <note>The Black Sea and the Sea of Marmara.</note>, namely at Constantinople? Therefore, when God shall visit this serpent and Leviathan in his wrath—that is, when he shall utterly destroy the name and nation of the Turks—then shall this resurrection here spoken of come to pass. For the Prophet Isaiah <note>original: "Esay"</note> joins these two things together, saying, *Your dead men shall live again,* and, *In that day the Lord shall visit that Leviathan with his most cruel sword.* And thus he begins the next chapter by setting the time in which this shall be effected, against that in which the Lord shall bestow that benefit upon his people of which he made mention at the end of the former chapter. So does Saint John in this place join this resurrection immediately after the prophecy of the Turk's destruction.

The third place is Ezekiel 37. Where, what other things are the dry bones, the slain men, and the graves, but the Jews? They are afflicted and overwhelmed with all kinds of miseries and calamities, and they should have no more power to deliver themselves from that destruction than those men have who are dead and buried to rise up out of their graves. What also do those sinews, flesh, skin, and breath signify, but the restoring of that people? This shall be fulfilled at length, and it shall be almost as acceptable and wished-for a matter to them as a new life would be to a man after he has been lying asleep in his grave. *Behold, I am he,* says the Lord God, *who will open your graves, and who will cause you...*

# ON THE APOCALYPSE. Chapter 20.

"...you to come out of your graves <note>original: "Sepulchres"</note>, and that will bring you into the Land of Israel, and you shall know that I am the Lord when I have opened your graves, and brought you up out of your graves, oh my people" (Ezekiel 37:12-13). For what purpose should they be brought into the Land of Israel again after the last resurrection? For we shall then, all who belong to Christ, have our dwelling in the heavens, not on the earth. Besides, that resurrection which Ezekiel speaks of shall be accomplished little by little, gradually <note>original: "leasurely"</note> (Ezekiel 37:8-10). But the general resurrection shall take effect in a *moment*, in the *twinkling of an eye* (1 Corinthians 15:52). Besides, these bones are the "whole house of Israel" (verse 11), and now there shall be a uniting of Judah and Ephraim into one, which is demonstrated by those two pieces of wood that are joined together into one. Now these things are specific to the Israelites—and not things already past, but things to come, as that happiness shows which is spoken of at the end of the chapter, which is greater than any past time can claim for itself. How fitting is it also that the vanquishing and confounding of Gog and Magog is coupled together with this resurrection in the 38th and 39th chapters? Except that the resurrection goes before it in Ezekiel, but it follows it here in John's Revelation; we will speak of the cause of this immediately <note>original: "straight wayes"</note>.

And I do not doubt that the Prophet Daniel also intended to teach us as much by those *many who sleep in the dust of the earth, who shall awake, some to everlasting life, others to shame, and to perpetual contempt* (Daniel 12:2-3). For "many" are not "all"; but this word seems to be used on purpose so that a difference might be put between the General Resurrection and this one spoken of here. He also gives the chief honor to those who teach and turn others toward righteousness, not because of their labors which were completed before in their lifetime, but because of their present labor and diligence. For those who make others wise by instruction shall shine; not just those who have made others wise in the past. We know that none of these things are to come to pass after the last resurrection. For the sake of brevity, I will not now examine how that passage of Hosea 13:14 also belongs to this purpose. Since the Scriptures, therefore, so willingly use this very clear metaphor of the Resurrection to signify the restoration of the Jews, and we do not find this matter—which is of so great importance <note>original: "momēt"</note>—fully declared elsewhere in this book, we hope that we offer the truth no violence...

### Chapter 20. A REVELATION

It is true; but that which belonged to the sixth Vial <note>original: "vial"; in Revelation, the "vials" or "bowls" represent successive stages of God's judgment.</note> was only begun, not full and absolute, such as this is to be which shall belong to the last Vial, when all the enemies shall be destroyed. The previous words sufficiently declare this distinction of "calling," seeing that in that first calling John was bidden to write, *that they were blessed who should be called to the Marriage Supper of the Lamb* (Chapter 19:9). In which words we were taught that that first calling was not full, where there was need of such confirming of the matter—which serves to seal a matter that is not yet sufficiently made known and certain, and that is also yet to come—which would be superfluous when all who shall be called are already called. 

But Daniel shows this most plainly, as he has distinguished both callings by their individual times. He makes the first to *be at the end of one thousand two hundred and ninety days*; the second, *at the end of one thousand three hundred thirty-five days*. Afterwards, when some time has passed in which they were destitute of the breath of life, we shall see them at length to be quickened with breath and to live a true life, performing all those works of life which are usually acted out by bodies that are endowed with souls. That approaching of the dry bones to one another is that first calling that is spoken of in the previous chapter.

This coming of breath unto them, which gives them full life, is this latter calling, this resurrection, which shall have nothing lacking that may bring them a perfect restoration to the saving knowledge of God in Christ. Both of these callings, though Ezekiel comprehends them in the same chapter, he nevertheless handled more distinctly afterward. # OF THE APOCALYPSE. chap. 20.

The Resurrection mentioned in verse 5 of this Chapter belongs to the Gentiles; though this first resurrection of the Jews shall fall within that same time, towards the end of it—so that it may be the "first" in every way—it shall happen presently after the overthrow of Rome. The second shall follow straight away after the destruction of the Pope of Rome and of the Turk <note>original: "Turke"; in the 16th and 17th centuries, the Ottoman Empire was frequently identified in Protestant theology as a primary enemy of the Church alongside the Papacy.</note>. This resurrection is that power to enter into the Temple, which the smoke took away from all men until the seventh and last plague should be accomplished (Chapter 15); and this time is entirely spent in destroying the Pope of Rome and the Turk, as we have sufficiently shown before.

Now, if I shall seem to any man to weaken the doctrine of the General Resurrection <note>The final bodily resurrection of all people at the end of the world.</note> by this interpretation—in that I thus take from under it this so excellent a foundation, which this passage seems to support—let such a man know that that Article of our faith receives no damage or impeachment at all from this. This Scripture still has within it a most invincible and indefeasible bulwark for the upholding and confirming thereof; for the Holy Ghost does not deceive us by bringing in a feigned and counterfeit similitude <note>A comparison or symbolic representation.</note>, but such a one as ought to have the most certain credit among all Christians. Otherwise, he would have lost his labor and proved nothing, if he had illustrated his matter with a comparison of no substance nor truth. Indeed, he would have driven me to desperation by proposing such a matter as should have never taken effect. For both the Jews and the Christians would have thought themselves undone and past hope alike; but seeing he brings a type <note>A symbolic foreshadowing.</note> of a matter that shall most certainly come to pass in its due time, he both puts the calling of the Jews out of doubt and makes it to be past all controversy, as he also reveals the manner after which the Resurrection shall be at last accomplished. And thus much touching the true meaning of this passage of Holy Scripture. Now let us prosecute the things that remain to be handled.

*And I saw a great white Throne*, Here we have the preparation of God the Judge restoring his people to liberty, which is taken from the similitude of the General Resurrection. It is commonly taken by many to mean the place of the damned, but yet it usually signifies nothing but the grave and the common state of the dead, as may be learned from this place and others found in this book.

Verse 15. *And whoever was not found.* No one shall be gathered into this Church except those who have been chosen from eternity for eternal life. How remarkable the glory of this Church will be! It will not be defiled at all by hypocrites and counterfeit <note>original: "counfaite"</note> Christians, as used to happen with the Church in the past. What a beautiful field this will be to behold, laden with a most plentiful crop of good corn, completely cleared of all tares, cockle, and darnel <note>original: "Tares, Cockell and darnell"; common weeds that resemble wheat, often used in biblical metaphors for hypocrites among believers</note>. Whatever is found in this dragnet may be stored away safely in a vessel. Therefore, words cannot express or declare how lovely this most glorious spouse <note>The "spouse" refers to the Church, often described as the Bride of Christ</note> shall be.

Therefore, the bounty and power of God will be most wonderful and greatly magnified throughout all the world by means of this renewal and restoration of the Jewish nation. 

We see this because He will so marvelously restore to life and to the saving knowledge of His Son those people who were beyond recovery in themselves—and who seemed to be so both in their own eyes and in the eyes of the whole world—and because He will also make such a unique choice of those whom He will redeem. But also, see how the godly may derive unique comfort from this. For since every person—even the holy men who are or shall be in this world—might justly tremble and quake for fear because of their sins, of which they know they are guilty in their own consciences, we have here a notable source of comfort to arm us against this fear: that our election <note>original: "Election"; the theological doctrine that God chooses specific individuals for salvation</note> through Christ shall set us free from all guilt of sin and liability to the punishments of sin.

Chapter 21. A REVELATION.

## Chapter 21.

### A <term>Logical Resolving</term> of the Chapter into its Various Contents.
<note>original: "Logicall Resoluing"; this refers to the process of breaking down a complex text or argument into its logical components or sections to better understand its structure.</note>

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial H featuring symmetrical botanical scrollwork and leafy motifs within a square border.</image-desc>

*So far, the Holy Spirit <note>original: "Holy Ghost"</note> has explained the manner of gathering the Church together; after this, its condition is explained once it has been gathered. This state is declared to be most joyful: first, generally, through the things seen by John—the new heaven and earth (verse 1) and the Holy City (verse 2)—as well as through the things he heard. This is partly in common, regarding the presence of God with men (verse 3), the removal of calamities (verse 4), and a new restoration of all things (verse 5). It is also partly in private, concerning the certainty of the prophecy (verse 5), the mystery that was now fulfilled (verse 6), and the rewarding of both the godly (verses 6–7) and the wicked (verse 8). This concludes the general explanation of the Church's happy state.*

*The detailed explanation names the one who reveals it—the angel (verses 9–10)—and the matter that is revealed universally (verses 10–11). It also details the wall, the city, and their essential parts: the form of the wall (verses 12, 13, 14) and the form of the city (verses 15, 16, 17). Then it describes the materials: common materials (verse 18), and specific ones for the wall (verses 19, 20, 21) and the city (verse 21). External <note>original: "Eternall"; the author likely intended "External," meaning outward proofs or features that demonstrate the city's glory</note> arguments used to showcase the glory of this city are: first, God himself, who is both the Temple (verse 22) and the light of the city (verse 23). Second, the nations, who shall bring their glory here (verse 24); they will be free from all fear and suspicion (verse 25), and will not defile the city with any contamination (verse 27). Third, the marvelous abundance of necessary things and the permanence of this glory, which will be covered in the following chapter.*

## THE EXPOSITION.

*And I saw a new heaven.* The opinion regarding the resurrection which was grounded upon the end of the previous chapter has persuaded very many men to interpret all these things as referring to the Church as it is to be eventually in the heavens. But we have shown that there is neither any discussion in that place concerning the final resurrection, nor does the Holy Spirit <note>original: "Holy Ghost"</note> depict for us here the angel-like happiness of the Saints after this life. Instead, he is still treating <note>original: "entreating"; here meaning to deal with or discuss a subject</note> of matters to be done upon earth, as the very matters being discussed will make manifest in their proper places. 

And perhaps we might think it unnecessary for us to have the heavenly inheritance described in words, since everyone knows well enough that it is beyond all the praise that any man can give it. Indeed, even those men know this much who are otherwise accustomed to thinking lowly of the Church on earth, as if it were a vile and contemptible thing. But the estimation of the Church while it is a pilgrim on earth is less than it ought to be among mortal men; so there may be a necessary reason why its glory and dignity should be more fully commended. 

And yet this description gives us a good starting point <note>original: "Rise"</note> to help us conceive of that heavenly felicity in our minds. For if the magnificence of the bride <note>original: "spouse"</note> is so great upon earth, what kind of things and how excellent are those which God has prepared for his Saints in his own presence? But our minds are too dim and dull to meditate on these things as they are in themselves; let us, therefore, turn our eyes to contemplate this earthly Paradise. Although it is greater than can be praised with any eloquence of words, yet it is closer and more agreeable to our senses, and shall be seen openly in the world within these few years. 

The interpretation of the *new heaven and earth* may be taken from that passage, Hebrews 12:26: <note>The original text cites "12. 26."</note> *“Whose voice then shook the earth; but now he has promised, saying, ‘Yet once more I shake not the earth only, but also heaven.’”* Where "to shake heaven and earth" is, according to the interpretation of the Apostle himself, to *abrogate the old manner of* worship <note>catchword: "vvorfhipping"</note>

<summary>The author argues that the "new heaven and new earth" in Revelation 21 refers to a future, glorious state of the Church on earth rather than the final state in heaven. He explains that this earthly "Paradise" serves as a more accessible way for humans to understand the even greater, incomprehensible glory of the afterlife.</summary>

Just as, therefore, God shook heaven and earth during the first coming of His Son by rejecting the old worship and people, and by ordaining and choosing a new one; so again, when it shall seem good to Him to have mercy upon that forlorn and forsaken nation, and to make them partakers of salvation by Christ, He shall darken the former glory of heaven and earth by making the dignity and honor of the new people to be so glorious, as if He had created all things new again. This effectively means the same as if he were to say: what shall their reception into grace and favor be, but as it were a general resurrection? Rather, there shall be a more plentiful coming-in of all the nations of the earth that shall obey the kingdom of Christ, whichever way their countries lie and reach, according to the scripture: *"The Lord shall be king over all the earth; in that day there shall be one Lord, and his name shall be one"* (*Zechariah 14:9*).

...the word of God is despised everywhere; new errors spring up and are broached every day, and old ones are called back from Hell. This might be because the passing away of "the first heaven and earth" may be understood not as the final perishing of the truth among the inhabitants of Europe, but as such a renewing of all things among the Jews that—in respect to its glory and brilliance—whatever was excellent before may be said to have passed and vanished away. One might rightly call this the "first heaven," as it was instituted by God himself in the first place, and almost at the beginning of the world. But the Christian people among the Gentiles were neither the first people, nor were the rites they observed the first ordinances delivered from heaven to the Church. 

So, after all this examination of these words, they seem to be understood in this sense: although the Jewish people thirsted after their old rites and worship during all the time of their rejection, and boasted openly that the time would one day come when they would be given power to practice their former worship freely in the old manner (which we know they still boast of today), yet in this restoration of theirs, they shall so completely align and apply themselves to the will of God that they shall willingly renounce their ancient customs used in the service of God. It comes down from God, therefore, because His singular power and mercy shall appear in building this new city. The rising up of the whole building shall be so swift, and the brightness and dignity of it shall be so great, that all men shall acknowledge the hand of God to be in it, and shall magnify Him alone for the workmanlike builder of it with one consent. *Prepared as a spouse.* To be delivered over to her husband, not delivered already as she shall be when the marriage is once finished. After the last resurrection, the marriage shall be fully solemnized, not merely set in readiness for a time to come. The members of the body are often used to express the same thing, but the likeness <note>original: "similitude"</note> of a city sets a more lively portrait <note>original: "portraiture"</note> of it before our eyes. There is a greater variety of matters and a further separation <note>original: "disjoining"</note> of offices and duties in a city, which yet are coupled and held together by one and the same law, and they look toward <note>original: "respect"</note> the one chief good of the whole. This city, therefore, notably represents to us how the faithful—who are most diverse in their function, duties, and course of life—grow up together into one holy body.

**Verse 3.** *And I heard a great voice saying from heaven: behold the tabernacle of God.* The Holy Spirit <note>original: "Holy Ghost"</note> comes here to that part of this city's glory which is declared by the things that are heard. The Tabernacle belonged properly to the Jews and to the old form of worship, so he intimates here the whole divine worship of this people, to whom the Tabernacle belonged <note>original: "was proper"</note> before. Furthermore <note>original: "Withal"</note>, he declares that there is not yet any such full manifestation of the glory of God to come as the saints shall enjoy after the last judgment. But however much more plentiful it shall be than ever before, yet *men shall see God through a glass darkly, not face to face; they shall know only in part, not as they have been known,* as the Apostle speaks in 1 Corinthians 13:12. The tabernacle is fit to symbolize <note>original: "shadow out"</note> the Church that is on her pilgrimage, not that which has attained a permanent dwelling in her own country <note>meaning heaven</note>.

*And he shall dwell with them, and they shall be his people.* Both God himself shall take care <note>original: "tuition"; meaning protection or guardianship</note> of the saints according to the form of his covenant made with them in Genesis 17:1, and the saints shall also willingly subject themselves to God to be ruled by him. So does Jeremiah <note>original: "Jeremy"</note> interpret these words from which they are taken: *I will put my law into their minds and write it in their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.*

**Verse 4.** *And God shall wipe away.* So much for the presence of God; now, regarding the removal of calamities, the true Church shall not be vexed and grieved anymore. These words are borrowed from Isaiah <note>original: "Esay"</note> 25:8. *Neither mourning nor crying, nor labor.* These words teach us how far death shall be taken away—namely, as it is a punishment, not as it is a means to translate men to everlasting life. So shall the attendants and officers <note>original: "seruitours, and Sergeants"</note> attending upon it be taken away also. For what right have servants where there is no power in their master? O most happy Bride <note>original: "Spouse"; referring to the Church</note>, who shall never be molested with such disturbers of her happiness as these! A visible image of the happy Kingdom in heaven shall live <note>original: "conuerse"</note> now among men upon earth.

***And he said to me, "Write."*** John now addresses those things which were spoken specifically <note>original: "by name"</note> to himself. ***Verse 6. And he said to me, "It is done."*** This is the second thing that was told to John in private: namely, that the mystery was fulfilled, reaching its end in the restoration of the Jews. The same word is used here as is used there to express this accomplishment: *It is done.* If the accomplishing of some other matter were meant here that should occur after what is said to be accomplished there, the words *It is done* could not be correctly spoken in that place, as there would still be something remaining after it that has not yet reached its proper outcome. Therefore, seeing as some things are said to be done after the fulfillment of the mystery—things which are proper to this earthly life and which cannot be applied to that which is to come after the Last Judgment, as we have observed in Chapter 16:21—this fulfillment spoken of here shall not belong to any other time than this present life. *Aretas <note>an 8th-9th century bishop and commentator</note> and Montanus <note>Benito Arias Montano, a 16th-century Spanish Orientalist</note> read this differently: "And he said to me, 'I have become the first and the last, the beginning and the end.'" ...unto me, ***"It is done, I am the beginning and the end."*** But Aretas <note>original: "Aretas"—Aretas of Caesarea, a 10th-century commentator on Revelation</note> and Montanus <note>original: "Montans"—likely referring to the scholar Benito Arias Montanus</note> are mistaken to omit the words, *"It is done,"* seeing that this pertains to the explaining of the seventh vial. A chief part of that vial concerns the fulfillment <note>original: "consummating"</note> of the mystery, which is not perfected merely in the destroying of enemies (of whom alone mention was made in Chapters 16, 17, etc.). Rather, it is perfected in this calling of the Jews, the accomplishment of which is laid forth here. The words ***"It is done"*** are given for this reason: because all the prophecies reach their final conclusion at this point. ***"I am the beginning and the end"***; that is, I am he who both at first decreed that these things should be done, and who has also finally brought these same things to a conclusion now at last.

***"I will give unto him that thirsteth."*** These words contain the rewarding of the godly, who are called "those who thirst"—that is, those who have an ardent desire for these things. All people who have a taste for heavenly good things are of this sort. "Blessed are they," says Christ, *"who hunger and thirst after righteousness, for they shall be satisfied"* (Matthew 5:6). But the Jews shall then be the primary "thirsters," as they will not be satisfied with any amount of desire and care until they may perceive a fuller sweetness in Christ. And yet, even to these people, who shall burn with a most fervent desire, grace shall be given out of the fountain of living water. This is not because of the merit of any diligence or desire of theirs (though such desire is excellent among the gifts given to men), but for the sake of the mere mercy of God. This is a notable passage to overthrow the blasphemous doctrine of the Catholics <note>original: "Papists"</note> regarding Merit <note>term: Merit—the theological idea that human works can earn a reward or salvation from God</note>.

The Jesuit <note>likely referring to the Spanish Jesuit Francisco Ribera (1537–1591), a prominent commentator on Revelation</note> endeavors to take this passage from us with his cursed commentary <note>original: "glossing"</note>, holding it to have the same meaning as Romans 8:18: *"The sufferings of this life are not worthy of the glory which shall be revealed."* In those words, as he says, our good deserts are not to be compared with future blessedness, but the sufferings (that is, the afflictions which we suffer for God) are not. It is as if it were said: "Our griefs and pains which we suffer here cannot be compared with the joys of the blessed saints." However, he argues that their patient enduring of those griefs—as they are endured by the help of God's grace in them—is, without all doubt, worthy of everlasting life. Notice here, I pray you, the fraudulent device of an evasive Jesuit. Having nothing to say by way of answer to this passage we are now handling (which we object against them), he flies to another passage so that from there he...

<header>chap. 21. A REVELATION,</header>

...might provide some appearance of an answer to this passage. But without dwelling now upon the examining and sifting of that passage in the Epistle to the Romans, why does he even speak now and tell us (as he thinks) strange tales about the sorrows and afflictions of this life? These are not to be compared with the joys of the blessed ones in heaven, yet he can plainly see that here we have nothing at all to do with any of these sorrows. All tears, mourning, crying, labor, and death itself are said to be banished away from this city, which is described here in verse 4. So, nothing could be done by him more against the grain <note>original: "against the haire"—meaning contrary to the natural direction or intent</note> and the drift of this passage than to spend time commenting and debating about any such comparison.

For it is affirmed in these words, ***that not only are the sorrows of this life inferior to the joys of the Saints in heaven, but that thirst and hunger also—that is, the most ardent desire for and pursuit of godliness (than which there can be nothing in a person of greater worth and estimation)—do not obtain eternal life by their own merit and desert, but only by the mere grace and mercy of God.***

Neither is that any less frivolous which their pseudo-Ambrose <note>original: "counterfait Ambrose"—referring to the author of works once attributed to St. Ambrose, now known to scholars as Ambrosiaster</note>, Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century Scholastic theologian</note>, and Rupertus <note>Rupert of Deutz, a 12th-century Benedictine theologian</note> say. They argue that this water of life is said to be given "freely" here because, although they wickedly dream that eternal life is a debt due by right to the merits of righteous men by their very <term>condignity</term> <note>condignity: a theological term for merit that is inherently equal in value to the reward received</note>, yet even these merits themselves could not be merits at all without the help of grace, which they say is given to them freely. Thus they speak foolishly, and yet they think they have commented worthily upon this passage and similar ones. They believe they have turned the edge of this word "freely" so it does not hurt their devilish doctrine of mangy <note>original: "maungy"—scabby, contemptible, or worthless; here used as a derogatory term for the Catholic doctrine of human merit</note> merits.

For if they had been pleased to speak without such barbarous and profane reasoning from their own perverse brains and hearts—full of the poison of the old subtle serpent, the father of such lying sophists as these—they would never have said that any grace is given to men through which they might perform works that are equivalent in worth and value to everlasting life. For they might hear the Holy Spirit speaking here expressly to the contrary: namely, that the reward for the most excellent works that can be done in this world by mortal men is bestowed altogether freely upon the worker. It is not given for the dignity of his work, but for the merciful acceptance of his person, and of his work for the sake of his person.

# OF THE APOCALYPSE. chap. 21.

<margin>verse 9.</margin>*Come, I will show you the spouse.* Did John not see her before yet? He saw her there as if through a lattice, and in a more confused manner; now he sees her more distinctly and exactly. The first sight and appearance of the New Jerusalem, as she comes down, shall seem to be goodly and delightful; but yet, after she has stayed for a long time upon earth, she shall then be far more majestic to look upon. For we gather from things previously delivered that these words point to the actual event. This is also shown by the fact that the Angel invites him to "come and see," from which we learn—by comparing these to things said before—that some holy man shall publish a book in which he shall make it plain to all the faithful that the majesty and glory of this Church shall be most divine and heavenly. But we see these things from afar and darkly as yet; time shall make the matter most clear at length.

Verse 10. *And he took me up in the spirit to a great and high hill.* Here he begins the description of the city—an even fuller description than the previous one—presented in a more concise <term>original: "commodious"—meaning advantageous or efficient</term> manner in these following two verses, after which he describes it most extensively of all. Therefore, so that John might know this spouse thoroughly and certainly, he is taken up to a high and lofty mountain. The first condemnation of the whore <note>A reference to the "Whore of Babylon" described in Revelation 17</note> was seen in the wilderness, <margin>Chapter 17:3.</margin> but the glory of the spouse shall be revealed on a high mountain, in the eyes and sight of all the world. This mountain seems to be that of which Isaiah <note>original: "Esay"</note> speaks: *In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of other mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills; and all nations shall flow unto it* (Isaiah <margin>Chapter 2:2.</margin> 2:2). This mountain is rightfully called "great and high," as it is set on the ridge and the top of other mountains. Whatever excels in dignity upon earth, therefore, shall be surpassed by the prominence of this Church. The beauty of this city shall appear on this mountain, as if its venerable and divine excellence should be most clearly seen by its citizens who dwell within its walls; yet this cannot be so obvious to those who stay further away in remote places. And indeed, there shall be many "Johns"—that is, godly and holy men—who shall leave all their own homes to flock to this mountain. They do this not to view "holy places" as superstitious pilgrims are accustomed to do, but so that they may behold the glory of the Lord.

### CHAPTER 21: A REVELATION

For could anything be more desirable than to live together with those who worship Christ in the purest and holiest way, according to His ordinance and appointment alone, and to do so with the most burning desires and efforts? Here, certainly, men shall have a most sweet taste of the close fellowship between the saints and the holy angels. However, it is enough to briefly mention <note>original: "give a touch of"</note> these matters, lest I should seem to some people to be comforting and flattering myself with a sweet dream. But let us observe that if these things were spoken regarding the heavenly country where the saints shall live gloriously after the Last Judgment, no Olympus <note>A mountain in Greece, legendary home of the gods; used here to represent the highest possible earthly vantage point.</note> would be a mountain high enough to demonstrate this to us.

**Verse 11.** *And he showed me that great city.* This city is "great" because it is filled with a multitude of citizens. Until now, it has always been small and narrow <note>original: "straite"</note>, being content with a very small company of people; now it begins to be called great because its borders are enlarged, and the number of its citizens has grown to its full size. It shall be all the more glorious in this respect, seeing that the more widely shared a good thing is, the greater its goodness becomes. But it is also "holy" and "coming down from God," the reasons for which we have seen before. This detail is newly added to its description: it is said to be "adorned with the glory of God." This means it has the presence of God manifested by a certain glorious brightness which God gives to it, as is explained to us in the verses that follow. For this purpose, the Temple was once filled with smoke, according to the ancient manner of God’s appearing in the Tabernacle and the Temple; but there shall be a different manner of His appearance at this time. God will give a more glorious show and sign of His Majesty and glorious presence than He has ever done before—either among the Jews or among the Christian people. 

And then it is also said *that it has a shining light, like a most precious stone, etc.* What light is this? It is not a brightness originating from the city’s own purity—though it is indeed bright and radiant in itself—but a light which is transfused into it from another light. For the Greek word <note>original: *phōstēr* (φωστήρ), meaning a luminary or light-bearer.</note> translated here as "shining" signifies something that sends forth light from itself, such as the sun, the moon, the stars, a candle, or a torch. # ON THE REVELATION. Chapter 21.

word, when they translate those words, *the two great lights (Genesis 1:16)* and Paul, when he says, *you shine as lights (Philippians 2:15).* The light of the City, then, is that which gives light to the city; it receives this light from the Light itself, but does not possess it inherently. From where, then<gloss>n</gloss>, is it provided? From the very glory of God. For these things depend upon those words that came just before, as if it were said: *I saw a city having the glory of God, and this glory of God—that is, its light—was like a most precious stone,* etc. And verse 23 below helps us with this interpretation, where enlightening<gloss>n</gloss> this City is described as the work of God. 

But why is the light compared to a most precious stone, and not rather to the sun or the stars? Perhaps because the light of the sun burns and blinds the eyes; it is more delightful when viewed indirectly than when a person looks intently <note>original: "wishly"</note> and gazes upon it. However, the brightness of a stone causes no harm, yet provides much delight—the more so the longer a person continues viewing it. This notably resembles the pleasantness of divine knowledge.

For when divine knowledge is looked upon even once as it appears in its beauty, it refreshes a person's mind when it grows faint or is oppressed with grief. But it brings even more refreshment the more earnestly and intently a person applies their mind <note>original: "bend his wits"</note> to consider it. Also, the brightness of other things, such as the moon and the stars, is overwhelmed by the beams of a more abundant light. The glistening of a precious stone competes with the sun for brightness; its light is not diminished by the sun's beams but rather increased—just as there is no greater glory that can obscure the glory of God's majesty. 

Those things which shine among us—such as torches <note>original: "firebrands"</note>, lamps, and candles—always require fuel <note>original: "matter"</note> to nourish their light; otherwise, they will immediately go out and turn to darkness. The sparkling luster of a gem is natural; it has no need for external supply or help, but always shines with its own flame. In this regard also, it sets before our eyes the everlasting brightness and glory of the most high God. The specific kind of stone is also mentioned: for it is like a jasper stone that is as clear as crystal. The jasper is a most noble gem, both for its ancient history and its variety. **Verse 12.** *And it had a great wall high.* Now the Holy Ghost opens the matter particularly. But the heavenly Jerusalem that is upon the earth—which we have seen to be tossed and vexed with very many and mighty storms from its first beginning until this day—had need of this fortress and defense of walls, lest a person should fear the same thing happening to this City which he knew had always befallen it in former times. **Verse 15.** The minister is the same one who spoke with John—the seventh of those angels to whom the bowls <note>original: "vials"</note> were delivered (verse 9). **Verse 16. *And the city lay foursquare.*** Now the Holy Spirit speaks of the form of the city regarding its size. It is foursquare, being as long as it is broad. Therefore, this city shall be most stable, prepared for every change so that, however things go, it shall always maintain a firm foundation. This Jerusalem is of a different nature than the one that was among us Gentiles, which lay hidden for one thousand two hundred and sixty years. That version also had a foursquare figure, but it had unequal sides of length and breadth as we have shown in the seventh Chapter—having twelve thousand in its length, but only twelve in its breadth. From both of those numbers, the total number of those who were sealed was gathered, namely one hundred and forty-four thousand. The reason for this was that there was a multitude of the godly at that time in "length" (referring to the continuation and process of time), but they did not flourish with any "breadth" (meaning a present abundance of believers in any specific age of those 1,260 years). But it shall happen differently in this city. It shall be made no less noble and famous by an infinite company of faithful people through every present age than by a most happy propagation of the Church over a long duration of time. This is what the equal length and breadth declare.

# CHAPTER 21. A REVELATION.

> *And he measured the city with a reed, twelve thousand furlongs.*

So much for the size <note>original: "quantity"</note> of the city; now he speaks of the description of the number. First, regarding the city, its measurement is 12,000 furlongs. It is uncertain whether this refers to the entire plot and floor of the city, or only to its circumference. We can find nothing that can be stated with absolute certainty regarding this matter. If we assume the former (the area), it is a mighty city, where every side would be 109 furlongs and more—falling somewhat short of ancient Babylon, which was 120 furlongs on each side, according to Herodotus in his book *Clio* <note>Herodotus, often called the "Father of History," wrote *The Histories*; "Clio" is the title of the first book.</note>. But if the circumference alone of the city receives this measure, there was never any city to be compared with this greatness; every side would be 3,000 furlongs, and the entire floor would be 1,900,000 furlongs. 

The *Complutensian Polyglot* <note>The first printed polyglot edition of the entire Bible, completed in 1517.</note>, which Arias Montanus and the Plantin edition follow, read these words differently: "twelve furlongs of twelve thousand." This means, as I suppose they intend, 12 times 12,000 furlongs—as if the entire capacity of the city had as many furlongs as there were sealed saints out of every tribe in Chapter 7, namely, 144,000 furlongs. This consistency <note>original: "conveniency"</note> makes me suspect that this reading is more accurate. It both strongly declares the exceeding great connection between the Church of the Jews and that of the Gentiles, and it also maintains a proportion in number exactly matching that of the wall in the following verse. 

According to this interpretation, the dimensions of the city are created by the mutual multiplication of the citizens and the ministers, just as the dimensions of the wall are created by the number of the ministers squared <note>original: "redoubled within itself"</note>. For 12 times 12,000 equals this number. In these numbers, the multiplier (12) signifies the ministers, and the number to be multiplied (12,000) signifies the citizens. In this case, every side of the city would be 379 furlongs and somewhat more. 

But here it may be asked: why does John make this city far more large and spacious than Ezekiel does, when both of them are undoubtedly describing the same city? For Ezekiel makes the measure of every side of it to be 4,500 cubits (Ezekiel 48:30), which is only 12 furlongs and a little more. For this reason, Solomon’s Temple was built with more ample dimensions than the Tabernacle was, and Ezekiel’s Temple had larger dimensions than Solomon’s; and now this city described by John has larger dimensions than Ezekiel’s. For after the coming of Christ, the greatest clarity <note>original: "perspicuity"</note> of matters has occurred; and so, according to this increase of knowledge, a corresponding magnificence is used in the framing of the Church.

**And the length and the breadth and the height thereof are equal.** We said just now that the length is the duration of time in which the Church should endure; breadth is the present period of every time, which shall be no less beautiful and goodly to behold than the glory of its duration. Here, for the first time, mention is made of its height: and this seems to signify the excellent glory of this city, which is so extolled with the speech and praise of all men. Matters are set "on high" when they are commended and magnified. So it is the common manner of speaking to say that things are "lifted up to heaven with praises" when they are extolled greatly. This city, therefore, shall be no less famous and renowned among all men than it shall be durable and flourishing, always having an exceedingly great and abundant company of citizens. For this city is solid, not superficial—square altogether like a die <note>meaning a gaming die or cube</note>, and a perfect square <note>original: "squadron"</note> on every side, as it consists of all dimensions and those are equal. It is perfect and <term>point-device</term> <note>original: "point uice"; meaning perfectly exact or precise</note>, so that nothing can be added to it. The former cities lacked solidity, and besides, their breadth was so narrow that it could not be seen by men. What marvel is it then if they were shaken with every stormy wind and tempest? This city shall stand more firm and stable, and with such great strength on every side that it fears no tempests.

It has a variety of sweetness in it, such as none of the most clever minds or sharpest eyes are able to fully distinguish. It may signify, therefore, that rich treasure of gifts that shall be heaped up within the minds of some men, wherein one may recognize a manifold excellence, yet cannot easily tell which quality excels above the rest. In this respect, it was used previously to express the divine nature of the Father in Chapter 4:3 <note>The original text says Chapter 14:3, but this is likely a printer's error for Revelation 4:3, where God on the throne is compared to a Jasper stone.</note>. This is because such a blended beauty suggests and represents, in some way, the incomprehensible depth of God’s majesty and excellence. 

The **Sapphire** glitters with golden points and is a gem of very great excellence among the Medes; this shows a certain and distinct kind of pleasantness. Similar to this, some teachers are to come in the next place after that first kind, whom a singular excellence in some one rare gift shall bring into honorable estimation.

The **Chalcedony** is of a solid color, like a carbuncle <note>A "carbuncle" was a general term for any deep-red gemstone, like a garnet or ruby, thought to glow like a coal.</note>, glistening with a fiery brightness. It is a gem that grows in the northern parts and is found near the straits of the Sea of Chalcedon, above Chrysopolis—both of which are located in Bithynia, close to the rocks called the Symplegades, as Aretas <note>Aretas of Caesarea, a 10th-century Bishop and commentator on the Book of Revelation.</note> records, which is where it gets its name. This stone may signify the zeal and fervency of the teachers who shall succeed the former ones. 

The **Emerald** is a most noble stone growing in Scythia; it has a most pleasant greenness, so much so that nothing can delight the eyes more. But since the description of inward graces is more the aim in this place than any outward ornaments, this greenness represents the most divine knowledge of matters upon which the mind of a man desires to be fixed more than upon anything else. It is placed next after the chalcedony so that knowledge may accompany zeal.

The **Sardonyx** <note>original: "Sardonix"</note> has a likeness of humanity and natural goodness, as it has whiteness mingled with redness. The **Sardius** <note>original: "Sarduis"; usually identified as carnelian</note> is found among the Sardians; it is red all over with a bloody color, and so it may signify a certain severity. It is joined with the sardonyx for a very good purpose, lest perhaps gentleness should become worthless and contemptible for want of such a companion as this. And these first six stones are Eastern and Northern, which declare to us this happy and abundant increase of teachers that should come out of these regions. In this, we may see how the Holy Ghost makes things agree sweetly together, as this does with the former points; for the first people and the first teachers shall be revived to profess and to preach the Gospel with a saving desire and endeavor out of those same parts of the world.

The seventh foundation is a **Chrysolite** <note>original: "Chrysolith"</note>, which shines throughout with a golden color; it is a gem full of dignity and majesty, and Ethiopia produces it. As for the **Beryl**, *Pliny* <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and natural philosopher</note> says, *It is an Indian stone*. *Dionysius* <note>likely Dionysius Periegetes, a Greek geographer</note> says it also grows in Babylon; and as the same author says in his verses, it is sky-colored and somewhat dark like water. The watery color betokens leniency and humility, such as water itself is, which will easily give way to everyone. So it is a most suitable companion to follow next after the majestic Chrysolite, so that it may keep that stateliness within measure and proportion.

The ninth foundation is a **Topaz** <note>original: "Topaze"</note>, which is a gem of a green color and is found (as *Pliny* writes) among the Troglodytes <note>literally "cave-dwellers," a people the ancients located near the Red Sea</note>, a people that dwell by the Red Sea. *Dionysius* says, *it is an Indian gem*, and he gives it a pure sea-green color. But it is not of a simple and pure green color, but rather it shines yellow and ruddy like gold. Whereupon *Eustathius* <note>a 12th-century Greek scholar and commentator</note> gives it *a golden color, and he says that it shines like gold*. He borrowed this from *Strabo* <note>a Greek geographer and historian</note>, who writes many more things about this stone in his sixteenth book. There are some who conjecture that this word took its beginning from the Hebrew *Pazaz* <note>referring to refined or pure gold</note>, as if it had been written at first in Greek as *To Pas* <note>original: "To Pas"; meaning "the whole" or "the all"</note> or *To Pasiou*, which afterward grew together into one word, *Topas*, through the lack of skill of the printers.

A **Chrysoprase** <note>original: "Chryfoprafe"</note> also resembles gold in some way, as its name shows, but yet as if it were gold that has had the juice of a leek sprinkled upon it. The eleventh and twelfth foundations are the...

The **Hyacinth** <note>original: "Hyacinth"; likely a sapphire or zircon in ancient texts</note> and the **Amethyst** are both of a purple color, the former shining more brightly, the latter of a more wan and weak color, as Dionysius <note>likely Dionysius Periegetes, a Greek geographer</note> says of it. India and Ethiopia furnish us with these two stones. These last six stones, therefore, come out of the East and the South. Our western coast, it seems, shall provide citizens in the same manner as other countries do, but it shall contribute few or no gems at all to build up the wall. It may be that Gog <note>A symbolic enemy of God's people in the Bible; here used to suggest that great teachers will emerge from even the most hostile or "repugnant" regions</note> will, by this means, make his power more glorious by raising up such worthy teachers out of those places which are most opposed to the Truth. 

The last four gems are of golden and purple colors, which are the colors of greatest value and estimation. The Holy Ghost seems to have placed these in the final positions on purpose, and mentions them twice over, as if he would teach us by this that these teachers should never be out of favor, but that they should flourish always with the greatest authority possible. Truth is usually acceptable at first, and its ministers are judged worthy of all honor, but the eager desire of men usually grows cold in time, and then the authority of the teachers begins to decline <note>original: "quaile"</note> once men become familiar with them. But no such thing shall happen here. The final end shall match the beginning; the ministers <note>original: "dispensers"</note> of the Word shall be no less honorably esteemed after the Truth has persisted for many ages than they were at the time when it first sprang up. And this, I think, is the reason why such a great abundance of golden and purple color is placed at the end. 

I know that others seek out a correspondence of other properties in these stones; but seeing that writers have such different judgments about the specific virtue of each stone, and the certain truth of it is not sufficiently cleared to this day, I chose rather to insist upon matters that are plain and of a known meaning—those that agree with the logic <note>original: "analogy"</note> of the prophecy—rather than to spend my labor in vain seeking out doubtful matters. And thus we have that thing explained to us more particularly and abundantly by these various kinds of gems in this place, which the Angel summarized in one word in the Prophecy of Daniel when he says:

<margin>Stars forever and ever. Chapter 12:3. <note>likely a cross-reference to Daniel 12:3 regarding the brightness of the righteous</note></margin>

**Verse 21. And the twelve gates were twelve pearls.** So much for the material of the walls. The gates are made of pearls, and these signify Christ, who is the way and the door unto life. "If any man shall enter in by him, he shall be saved, and he shall go in and out, and find pasture." John 10:9. Now, how notably do pearls resemble the Son of God, who was conceived in the womb of the virgin? For they are not made through any earthly copulation, but are begotten of the celestial dew, as if by a husband. It is said that shellfish draw into themselves some of the dew from heaven at a certain time of the year, and that they conceive and are, as it were, "with child" from this, and that they bring forth a more noble <note>original: "generose," meaning high-born or of excellent quality</note> offspring the more they have been tossed up and down by troublesome storms after conceiving the dew. 

In the same way, the Holy Ghost came upon Mary, and the power of the Most High overshadowed her; Christ was scarcely born into the world before people sought to kill him, and he was driven into Egypt by a horrible tempest. After a similar manner, the first entrance into this City shall be very toilsome and troublesome; but men shall have a much greater store of commendation and esteem once they have entered. The gates are twelve, yet all of them are made of one pearl because Christ is one, *and there is only one name given unto men under heaven by which they must be saved.* Acts 4:12.

**And the streets of the City were pure gold.** The Holy Ghost sets down the material of the city in the last place. He spoke of gold above regarding the material of the whole City generally; here he mentions the streets specifically. These are the highways where the citizens meet together when they have anything to do with one another. Therefore, just as the "ways" of a man are the actions in which he is occupied, so those streets of the city are those public duties and trades in which the citizens are diligently employed for the maintaining of this physical life. The Holy Ghost says that all these shall be holy, pure, clean, and precious; for the place where men shall meet to conduct these affairs is made of pure and glittering gold, as mentioned above in verse 18. How holy and blameless shall this City be, where the common conduct <note>original: "conversation," referring to social interaction and lifestyle</note> of men—which is usually nothing but filthy and defiled—shall be free from all wicked corruption?

**Verse 22. And I saw no temple there.**

So far <note>original: "Hitherto"</note> we have seen the inward and essential beauty of this city, as much as it can be seen by us. We do not behold it from the top of a high mountain, but from a distance on a low and level piece of ground, where hills and trees greatly obstruct our eyesight and keep us from beholding the matter clearly and plainly as of yet. And yet it did my heart good to open my windows toward this Jerusalem, as it delighted Daniel to do long ago, so that I might create a view <note>original: "prospect"</note> for myself to behold this holy city from afar. Even seen from this distance, the cloudy and sky-colored tops of the city greatly comfort my soul. 

Now the Holy Spirit <note>original: "H. Ghost"</note> teaches us how much dignity shall come to the city from the things that are outside of it. First, God the Father and the Lamb, His Son, shall be in place of <note>original: "in steed of"</note> a temple for it. That is, the worship that shall then be practiced will be most simple and most pure. It will not be obscured with any of those legal rites which God instituted of old to continue until the "Time of Reformation," much less with any human inventions or patched-together rituals <note>original: "pacheries of humane Rites"</note>. Instead, it will be such that through it, God shall show Himself present among men in a most simple and familiar manner. 

How then does John, in this description of the New Jerusalem, agree with Ezekiel? Ezekiel discussed this very same time and matter in eight whole chapters—specifically from the fortieth chapter to the end of his prophecy—where he describes the temple, the city, and the whole legal worship so exactly. 

They agree very well, as it happens. For all that description serves this purpose: not to teach us that the old ceremonies are to be brought back, but that when those are finally abolished at length, Christ is to be worshipped most purely and precisely according to His own ordinances alone. For what else do those new dimensions mean—of the walls, gates, courts, and so on—of the whole building, the new division of the Holy Land, and the new portions given to the tribes, the priests, the Levites, and the prince, but a complete overturning <note>original: "utter abrogating"</note> of Moses and of all the legal ceremonies ordained by him? But the people of the time in which the Prophet wrote were not able to understand what a spiritual worship of God meant, except by having it described under those symbolic shadows. # OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chap. 21.

From this we may observe that the Church is most glorious when the Sun of Righteousness <note>Christ; see Malachi 4:2</note> shines most brightly and openly, rather than being covered over by the clouds of misty and mystical ceremonies. Therefore, let those who introduce pompous and garish <note>original: "carish," meaning gaudy or overly-decorated</note> ceremonies of their own invention see what a foul error they live and wallow in. They do this, they claim, so that they may procure more authority and reverence for the service of God among the people. 

Besides this, let us consider to what times John applies the passages of the old Prophets. By doing so, we may know that those things are yet to come which we commonly interpret as things that are already past and gone. Furthermore, these events are to occur not only in our heavenly Country <note>the afterlife</note>—the happiness of which needs no human words to amplify it—but also here upon earth in that restoration of the Jews <note>a reference to the historical belief in a future mass conversion of Jewish people to Christianity</note> of which we have spoken.

**And the Lamb shall be the light thereof.** Therefore, this light—which shall be the clearest and brightest of all that has been in former times—shall not be full and perfect, such as it shall be after this life. It is only like candlelight in comparison to that future glory. This is to be noted lest we should perhaps rest and sit ourselves down while we are still traveling homeward on our journey, as if we had reached our final goal <note>original: "upshot"</note>, even the highest heaven of heavens.

**Verse 24. And the nations <note>original: "People"</note> of those who are saved.** This verse contains the second outward matter that argues for and sets forth the excellence of this glorious Church of the Jews: namely, the glory that shall come to it from the Gentiles <term>Gentiles: non-Jewish people</term>. In former ages, the Jews were always used to finding the Gentiles most hateful and spiteful against them; they labored by all possible means to annoy and harm them. But now the case shall be quite altered. The Jews shall have no cause to fear any harm or wrong at the hands of the Gentiles. Indeed, they may henceforth look for all possible good from them, as the Gentiles shall employ all the power they have to increase, advance, and extol them. 

However, these nations are not all people universally, but they are defined as a certain kind of people; for he says **those nations which shall be saved**. This word is put in to explain what kind of people shall walk in the light of the Jewish Church. These words are taken out of Isaiah 60:3 <note>original: "Esa. 60. 3."</note>, where the Prophet speaks thus: *And the Gentiles shall walk in your light.* Now John applies this to the Elect <note>those chosen by God for salvation</note> among the

# OF THE APOCALYPSE. CHAPTER 21.

Antichrist, who has been revealed to us in the former chapters, manages all matters throughout the whole world, and this power shall be in the hands of a woman. But what kind of woman? Shall she be a literal woman? Not at all. This woman, then, is the Church, the spouse of Christ, whom the text calls a widow—not because her husband is dead and she is therefore deprived of him, as this word is usually meant to signify, but because she is absent from him during the time of her pilgrimage upon earth. For a woman may also be called a widow if she does not live in the same place as her husband, whatever the cause may be; or she may be called a widow because she remained desolate for so long before her restoration, as it says in *Hosea*: *“You shall remain alone for many days and shall not marry another man for my sake; for the people of Israel shall remain desolate many days, without a king, without an offering, without an image, without an Ephod, and without Teraphim; afterward they shall convert, etc.” (Hosea 3:3–5)*.

So *Isaiah* says: *“Then you will say in your heart, 'Who has begotten these for me, seeing I have been bereaved and solitary, a captive and a wanderer to and fro?'" (Isaiah 49:21)*. This is, therefore, that widow who, after she has reigned like a mighty empress on earth for a time, shall at length give up her subjects to be transported <note>original: "translated"</note> into heaven, where they shall at last be moved when all this world shall be consumed by fire. 

Since things are so, these words of St. John are not to be understood as referring to the state of the Church after the resurrection. For how can kings bring their glory there, unless perhaps it shall be by building and enriching temples, by sending out preachers into various regions, and by suppressing the nations that are enemies to the faith? The Jesuit <note>Likely referring to a Catholic commentator like Francisco Ribera, whose futurist interpretations often clashed with Protestant historicist views.</note> writes about all of these things ridiculously. But do you think the man was daydreaming while awake when he set down such stuff as this? Would he have us look for and long for such activities as these after this life? But I will not disquiet the man too much, as he seems to be sick with a dunsical <term>dunsical: foolish or intellectually dull, derived from the followers of Duns Scotus who were mocked by later scholars</term> fever.

**Verse 25. And the gates thereof shall not be shut.** All danger shall be so far removed that no man shall be troubled with any fear of it. There shall be no enemy to invade the city, but the gates shall lie open always to welcome the new citizens, who shall come flowing there continually in great troops. *Isaiah 60:11: "O happy city, that shall enjoy such a happy, deep, and secure peace."*

### CHAPTER 21. A REVELATION

<margin>Isaiah 60:11</margin>
Isaiah, who speaks thus: *“And they shall open your gates continually, which shall not be shut by day or by night, etc.”* <note>original: "Esa," referring to Isaiah 60:11</note>. The Holy Spirit has the same meaning in this place, only he omits the mention of the night, which signifies adversity. Therefore, it is appropriate to mention it here in the description of the Church’s happiness <note>original: "Felicity"</note>, as if he were to say: "The gates shall never be shut." For they are not usually shut in the daytime, and there was no need to add, "nor in the nighttime," because there shall be no night there.

Verse 26. *And the glory of the Gentiles, etc.* We have spoken of this matter before in verse 24. Yet there is no useless repetition in this verse, as it teaches us that it shall be the constant desire and care of the Gentiles to enrich and expand this city. This is not because they shall focus all their efforts on piling up riches and worldly advancements, but because their goodwill shall be most acceptable, as they will always desire the best for it. Or else, we may read the words as they sound:

> And they shall bring the glory and the honor of the Gentiles into it. That is, the Jews themselves, as if we were now to be informed <note>original: "advertised"</note> how much they should prevail by their own strength after it had been sufficiently shown what strength should come to them by the generosity <note>original: "beneficence"</note> of others. So they shall not only be increased by others, but they shall also be filled with great glory by means of their own riches and abundance.

Verse 27. *Nothing that defiles shall enter, etc.* By this we learn that this glory of the Jews shall remain as entirely pure and undefiled as it shall be secure and free from the fear of enemies. It commonly happens that when rivers overflow their banks, they carry much muddy <note>original: "mirye"</note> filth with them, which makes the whole water become clouded. Similarly, it might perhaps be feared that in such a great flocking and flowing together of the Gentiles, many wicked men might flow in with them for company, causing the clearest truth to eventually be defiled by their bad influence <note>original: "contagion"</note>. But the Holy Spirit tells them not to fear in this regard; God will provide that no filthy or impure thing shall enter, so that the excellence of such great dignity should not be impaired in the slightest way.

*But those who are written.* But now the elect are not counted among those who are unclean, for through Christ they have no blemish, or <meta>catchword: wrinkle,</meta>
