It is as if it were said: no unclean person shall enter into the City, unless it be those who are written in the book of life, who before their calling were unclean, but being now sanctified by faith in Christ, have ceased to be so.

## Chapter 22

### The Logical Analysis of the Chapter

Up to this point, we have dealt with the first two external arguments by which the glory of this City is illustrated. Now follow the last two arguments: the abundance of necessary things, and their eternity <note>original: "perpetuity"</note>. That abundance consists in two things which encompass everything else: the most pure water that proceeds out of the Throne (verse 1), and the Tree of Life (verse 2). The fruit of this tree is described both by its quantity—in its types, for there are twelve fruits, and in its timing, for it is brought forth every month—and by its usefulness, which appears in that even its leaves are good for medicine for the Gentiles <note>The nations</note> (verse 2). This concludes the section on abundance.

The eternity of the city is declared by removing those things that might cause corruption (verse 3) and by establishing those things that cause preservation (verses 3, 4, 5). And thus far the prophetic narrative has reached, covering both matters belonging to particular Churches and matters common to the whole Church.

Now follows the Epilogue, which closes the entire Revelation and Epistle; it consists partly of a confirmation and partly of a salutation. The confirmation first makes a rehearsal and collection of matters spoken of before, so that being presented like a rough sketch, all at once <note>original: "vnder one vewe"</note>, they might have more force to win credit. This rehearsal continues until verse 18, identifying for us:
* The Author of the Revelation (verse 6).
* The happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note> of those who obey <note>original: "obserue"</note> it (verse 7).
* The Ministers (verses 8, 9).
* The command to publish it for the free examination of the things contained within (verse 10).
* An added answer to a hidden objection (verse 11).
* The nature of Him who reveals this prophecy: He is just (verse 12) and Eternal (verse 13).
* The thing revealed (verses 14, 15).
* The testimony of Jesus, openly manifested (verse 16).
* And lastly, the desire of the Spirit and of the Bride <note>The Church</note> (verse 17).

Every one of these is of great force individually to establish the authority of this prophecy, but all of them joined together are indeed of the greatest force. In the second place, John introduces some new matter on his own part: both pronouncing certain destruction against those who shall corrupt <note>original: "depraue"</note> this prophecy in the slightest way (verses 18, 19), and witnessing his own most fervent desire to have it accomplished speedily (verse 20). The Salutation at length concludes the whole Epistle with a prayer (verse 21).

### THE EXPOSITION.

**Verse 1. *After that he showed me.*** The immensely great glory of this City is further declared by its wholesome fruit, which not only the citizens but also the foreigners enjoy. To this end, both this River and this Tree are established, by which they obtain both food and drink for life. The Angel shows both of these to John, for it says: *he showed me.* But who showed it? That Seventh Angel who made the City clear to him in the previous chapter (verses 9–10). Therefore, we have not yet reached the heavenly happiness of the saints after the final resurrection, because at that time we will not need the help of Angels or any other teachers. 

Concerning this water, it is not some small brook but a river, and one that is not polluted and murky like the Nile <note>original: "Nilus"</note>, but flowing with most pure waters, like the Kidron <note>A stream in Jerusalem</note> and Callirrhoe <note>A famous thermal spring near the Dead Sea; the name in Greek means "beautiful flow"</note>, which makes the City of God glad (*Psalm 46:4*). Besides, it is a River of the water of life, not only because of its perpetuity—as it flows continually with new and fresh waters, the kind called "living" in the Scripture—but also because it brings life to those who drink it (*John 4:14*). *The River is clear as crystal*, far surpassing the clarity of other springs. Lastly, it comes from the *Throne of God and of the Lamb*, who are its primary sources <note>original: "head-springs"</note>; it also leads people back to them like a companion, or rather it goes before them like a leader <note>original: "Captaine"</note>, just as a river leads people to the sea. 

In Ezekiel, this same river flows out of the Temple and the Altar (*Ezekiel 47:1*). But there is no Temple in this new Jerusalem, as has been said (*Chapter 21:22*). Therefore, the Holy Spirit places the Throne of God in its stead. It is not expressed here where it flows, but the Prophets teach this abundantly: namely, *toward the East, from the South side of the Altar, first into Galilee and into the plain; then the waters go into the sea, where they are healed by the waters that are emptied into the sea* (*Ezekiel 47:1, 8*). So says Joel: *also a fountain shall go out of the house of the Lord, and shall water the valley of Shittim* <note>original: "shitten," referring to the Valley of Acacias where the Israelites camped before entering Canaan</note> (*Joel 3:18*). This refers to the plain of Moab where the Israelites committed sexual immorality <note>original: "whoredome"</note> with the Moabite women (*Numbers 25:1*). Zechariah also says: *It shall be in that day, that the waters of life shall go out of Jerusalem, half of them toward the East Sea, and half of them toward the Western Sea* <note>original: "vttermost Sea"</note>, *and shall be both in summer...*

**Verse 2. *And in the midst of the street thereof.*** That is, the place where the whole multitude of the citizens gather. For this is no fountain sealed up, but one that everyone who has a part in the city has free and full power to partake of. In this place also does the tree of life grow and flourish. Ezekiel mentions many trees. *“Behold,”* he says, *“I saw many trees here and there, on the bank of the River.”* Tremellius <note>original: "Trem."; referring to Immanuel Tremellius, a 16th-century Hebraist and Bible translator</note> translates it "great trees," but their greatness is not as noted as their number, as appears from verse 12. Thus: *in the midst of the street thereof, and of the River that flows on this side and beyond, was the tree of life.* It is as if the tree were placed in the middle, so that the River, divided into two arms, should embrace it on both sides. And so it is one tree, by which there is a more manifest allusion to the tree of life in Genesis 3:22, which he mentioned before in chapter 2:7: *“To him that overcomes I will give to eat of that tree of life, which is in the midst of the Paradise of God.”* John saw one tree because all the elect have one common food <note>original: "meate"; in this period, "meat" referred to any solid food, not specifically animal flesh</note> of life (1 Corinthians 10:4). Ezekiel saw many to signify to us the plentiful store of food which this one tree provides <note>original: "ministreth"</note>. This tree is Christ, who is both food and drink to his people; that is, a most rich storehouse of all things which are necessary to salvation.

He shall also claim them openly as his own servants, honored with his own name. And not only men, but "holiness to the Lord" shall be written even upon the horse bells, and the pots in the Lord’s house shall be like the bowls before the altar (Zechariah 14:20). He shall take upon himself the patronage and protection <note>original: "Tuicion"</note> of all matters that belong to him, even the very least of them.

**Verse 5. *And there shall be no night there.*** They shall not be afflicted as in former ages, neither shall they have need of the lighter comforts of candlelight and similar matters which they were accustomed to use before. Instead, they shall be filled with exceeding great joy from God Himself. They shall neither seek nor care for any other means of lightening and lessening the troublesome affairs of this life (Isaiah 60:19–20). But how does he say that there shall be no need of a candle, when he said before *that the Lamb should be the light* (Chapter 21:23)? He does not absolutely deny that there shall be any need of light, but rather that they shall need any other light besides the Lamb.

***For the Lord God enlightens them.*** That is, God’s bounty shall be more plentifully and clearly shown than if it were attributed to any outward means. There shall be such a great increase of knowledge that men shall seem to come to understanding not so much by hearing the Word as by being taught and inspired by God immediately. The nature of all other gifts of God shall be similar; their excellence shall far surpass all means which men could use in achieving them. At the end of the verse, a summary of these three preceding verses is proposed in plain words: namely, that this Kingdom of the Saints shall be eternal, that it shall be begun upon earth, and shall never be interrupted until it is at length translated into Heaven.

**Verse 6. *And he said unto me, etc.*** Hitherto we have had the prophetic narration; now follows the concluding of the Epistle, the conclusion of the whole Revelation. This briefly rehearses some chief heads of arguments whereby everyone may strengthen his mind in giving credit to this prophecy, the authority of which he finds so well established. Indeed, it is a most beneficial <note>original: "behooveful"</note> epilogue and full of divine majesty. The Holy Spirit <note>original: "Holy Ghost"</note> knew how much this Revelation would be neglected among men, and that there would be some so bold <note>original: "audacious"</note> as to call its credit into question; therefore, he uses more words than he is accustomed to, in order to pull this doubt <note>original: "scruple"</note> and every part of it out of the minds of men. But who is this Angel who speaks with John now? It seems he is someone other than the one who showed him the river of water of life in the beginning of the chapter, or who brought the City into his view. For this is the seventh Angel—namely, one of those who had the business committed to them of executing the seven last plagues (Chapter 21:9). Whose charge was certain and comprehended...

# ON THE REVELATION. Chapter 22.

...comprehended <note>original: "prehended"</note> within the bounds of any single part, and had not power given over the whole Revelation. Now this confirmation is common to the whole book, and therefore seems to belong to that angel who was sent in the beginning to make these things known to John. Besides, it is also likely that the angel does not speak here again with his own voice, but that John relates those words in the person of the angel, which he had received from him previously by his own voice. Certainly, the accumulation of subjects joined together without any connecting conjunctions <note>original: "conjunctions copulative"; these are words like "and" or "but" that link parts of a sentence</note>, or any necessary coherence between themselves, seems to prove such a list.

If we follow this opinion, the words are not to be read as, "*Then he said unto me*," which would indicate the time of a new speech beginning after John had seen the city, but rather as, "*And he said unto me*." It is as if it were said: "Since I have now fully delivered all things to you which have been revealed to me as things to come and to be accomplished hereafter, nothing remains now but for you to embrace them, giving them most certain credit in your hearts. So that you may do this more easily, consider how holily and religiously the angel has affirmed to me that *these words are faithful and true*."

Therefore, this confirmation by the angel does not only belong to those things which went immediately before concerning the *New Jerusalem*—though the demonstrative pronoun <note>original: "pronoune demonstratiue"; a word like "this" or "these" used to point to something specific</note> is often used that way—but it also applies equally to the whole book. Likewise, that denouncing of judgments which follows in verse 18 claims authority for the whole prophecy universally, and does not labor only for the authority of any one specific part. These words are repeated from Chapter 19:9 and are applied to the words of John, relating what the angel had spoken before, to make the whole Revelation more fully approved.

**Verse 6. *And the Lord God of the holy Prophets.*** The angel did not declare "*that these words are faithful and true*" of his own mind, but by the commandment and authority of God who sent him. The same God who inspired the old prophets so that they might be able to foretell future things most certainly, sent this angel to reveal these things to John for the benefit <note>original: "behoofe"</note> of the Church. These words are repeated from Chapter 1:1: "*which revelation He gave to him to show to His servants*," when He sent it by His angel and showed it to His servant John. But you may observe that this latter part of the verse is so...

**Verse 7. *Behold, I come quickly.*** These words are the testimony of Jesus regarding the speedy execution of these things, taken from Chapter 1:1: *Which must be done shortly*; and again, verse 3: *The time is at hand*. The fulfillment <note>original: "Euent"</note> of things immediately to be done should bring credibility to those that were to follow after; and therefore he mentions a speedy execution. It is as if it were said: "Let everyone take, in each of their own ages, a pledge and, as it were, a security of things to come, from the things which he sees happening presently." For these will guarantee that the things to come are no less certain. But as for us, who have seen the agreement between the event and the prophecy for the space of fifteen hundred years—that is, ever since the days of John—we cannot possibly doubt any longer regarding those few events which yet remain to be accomplished. And observe, I pray you, how these things are heaped up one upon another without any connecting words <note>original: "bonds of speach"; referring to a lack of conjunctions like "and" or "then"</note>, as is the custom when rehearsing a list of matters, which is the point we mentioned just now.

**Blessed is he that observes.** Here we have a confirmation of this prophecy, taken from the happiness <note>original: "felicity"</note> of those who observe this prophecy. Nothing can lead a person to this happiness except the truth which is inspired by God, as we heard before in Chapter 1:3, from which these words are repeated.

**Verse 8. *And I, John.*** Here we have a confirmation of the prophecy from the ministers. It must be a most certain prophecy if an angel is the minister—one who was so full of glory and majesty that the Apostle John thought himself bound to adore him; and yet he was so full of holiness that he refused and forbade the divine worship which John offered him. John here relates what had happened before in Chapter 19:10, but he does not fall down again to adore him, which was forbidden before.

**Verse 9. *And he said to me.*** The words are "he says" for "he said," for he does not record a new matter, but that which was past. But it is to be observed that what he said before—*and of your brothers who have the testimony of Jesus* (Chapter 19:10)—is brought in here with different words: *and of your brothers the prophets, and of those who observe the words of this book.* Therefore, to observe the words of this book is to have the testimony of Jesus.

# OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chapter 22. 917

**Verse 10. *Seal not.*** Here we have a command to publish this book, whereby everyone has the free power to examine and to judge this prophecy by its fulfillment <note>original: "event"</note>. John was not to keep this prophecy for his own use alone, but he was to offer it for public inquiry, whatever danger might come of it, as he was commanded shortly after the beginning: *What you see, write it in a book, and send it to the seven churches* (Chapter 1:11); and again, *Write what things you have seen, and which are, and which are to be* (Chapter 1:19). That is: do not conceal them from others, but make them openly known to the people. 

Now, if the public setting forth of these things in writing is all that is meant here, why was Daniel commanded *to shut up his words, and to seal the book* (Daniel 12:4), since he also committed his prophecy to writing just as John did? This prohibition against sealing, therefore, intends some further matter than that: namely, that future matters should be so described that men might be led by current and immediate events, as if by the hand, to a plain understanding of the prophecy. This was not the case with Daniel, whose meaning would not be plain and evident to every age; he only lightly touched on the matters that occur in the meantime and was chiefly occupied with laying out things that were to happen at the very end. Therefore, the determined time had to be waited for, before which it could not be explained. 

And what I say of Daniel is to be understood partly regarding those harder visions, and partly regarding the Jewish people, whom that prophecy chiefly concerns. The words that follow confirm this interpretation: *for the time is near*. It is as if it were said: "Do not seal the prophecy, for the time that approaches shall reveal it." But Daniel's was sealed because its fulfillment, being a long time off, caused it to lie in obscurity for a long time. These words then have the same force as those earlier: *Behold, I come quickly.*

**Verse 11. *He that is unjust, let him be unjust still.*** In these words, John anticipates and removes a secret doubt <note>original: "scruple"</note> by which the minds of weak Christians might be shaken and made more feeble. For they see wicked men persevere in their wickedness, and that God's vengeance lingers for many ages. They might, therefore, ask this doubtful question: how can he be said to come quickly, when he tolerates wicked men for such a long time? Here, then, he addresses this objection and gives a warning <note>original: "caveat"</note> that none of the faithful should be troubled by this, but should understand instead that wicked men shall persist in their ungodly practices, and

It is not to be wondered at if God permits a certain increase in wickedness for a set time, leading to the more just and fearful condemnation of the wicked. At the same time, he warns the faithful to leave these men alone in their own desperate ways and not to be offended by them. Instead, they should look toward the Elect <note>Elect: in Christian theology, those chosen by God for salvation</note>, whose constant love and pursuit of godliness ought to strengthen their weak and wavering minds against the stubbornness of the reprobates <note>reprobates: those rejected by God and destined for damnation</note>. These words, then, are not meant as an exhortation but for comfort and warning, so that our joyful expectation should not be lessened by these scandals, seeing as this will be how things go in the world until the very end.

*And he who is righteous, let him be more righteous still; that is, let him diligently engage in such works by which he may prove himself to be a righteous man, both to himself and to others. However, he does not so much urge the Saints to persevere as he foretells that they will persevere, as those who, being planted in the house of God, bring forth more plentiful fruit in their old age.*

**Verse 12. *And behold, I come quickly.*** Although this was repeated before in verse 7, it is now driven into our memory again by a new repetition. This is because it is a remarkable remedy against the offense that the godly might take at the callous <note>original: "brawny"</note> hardness of heart to which God abandons the reprobates. It is as if he were speaking to them: "Whenever the wickedness of men confuses your minds, remember that the coming of the Lord will be soon." He who cannot deceive has promised it; do not judge his long delay by your own feelings, but believe most certainly that it will not be very long before he fulfills his promise. Indeed, consider rather that the Lord is already present in those things which are done daily in the world. See him even now as busy as can be in fulfilling his promises, so that you do not complain about his supposed slowness or have the slightest thought that what he foretold might not happen at all. These words, then, have an excellent connection with those that came before and should not by any means be moved elsewhere. Yet, if this interpretation of matters is not considered correct, we should not be troubled or make a great fuss about the outcome <note>original: "consequence"</note>; the

# OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chapter 22.

Bbbbbb 3

The list of matters which the Holy Spirit intends here may (as we have said) contain various things and different people within one period, without any obvious connections or transitions.

*And my reward is with me.* These words belong to the same consolation as the previous ones, and they set before us the reward which shall be given to the faithful. This may hearten us against the scandal <note>scandal: here meaning a "stumbling block" or cause of moral offense</note> of both the prosperity <note>original: "felicity"</note> of the wicked and the troubles which the Saints feel through painful experience in the meantime. God is just, and it cannot be but that it must go well with the good and ill with the wicked in the end, as has been expressly shown in this same book (Chapter 13:10 and 14:13), as well as by the events described throughout the book. These words are spoken by his own mouth.

*I am Alpha and Omega* <note>original: "A, & O." The first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, representing Christ as the beginning and the end of all things.</note>. These are the words of Christ, not spoken by his own person in this place, but reported by John. They serve to confirm this prophecy based on the eternity of Christ, or rather from his power, as we have interpreted them before. Since he is eternal, or he who gave a beginning to all things and therefore can set an end to them again at his pleasure, why should we not believe him when he pronounces anything about things to come, just as if they were already past? (Chapter 1:8).

*Verse 14. Blessed are they which keep his commandments.* These words pertain to the authority of Christ, who gives witness and makes those people blessed who believe his testimony. This is he who has power over the tree of life, of which he makes those men happy participants who obey him (Chapter 2:7 and the second verse of this chapter). He grants them a right to enter into the City through the gates, which are the only way in, seeing the wall is so high that it cuts off all hope of climbing over it (Chapter 21:17).

*Verse 15. But without shall be dogs.* That is, men of a "dogged" impudence and maliciousness, who love to be forever barking and venting their bitterness <note>original: "rancour"</note> against the best things. It shall be a great part of our happiness to be exempt from all interaction with these "dogged" wretches. Regarding the rest of this cursed crew who shall be shut out, see Chapter 21:8.

*Verse 16. I Jesus have sent my Angel.* Here we have a confirmation from the open testimony of Jesus himself. This is not, however, uttered in this place with his own voice, but through John's, and is repeated from Chapter 1:1. Christ never gives a speech throughout this book in his own person without some sign of his glorious Majesty...

### Chapter 22. A REVELATION

Majesty, by which he testifies to his glorious presence.

*That bright morning star.* The morning star is the most luminous <note>original: "lightfome"</note>, and shows that the day follows immediately after. In the same way, Christ shines out most brightly to the faithful in this life. He is also, to those who behold and enjoy him, a pledge of a greater and more glorious brightness, which they shall be made partakers of by him and with him, and that right away. But besides this, he also shines to them at first through some "first fruits" of his truth which he reveals to them, being ready to bestow upon them a plentiful measure of it immediately. This commendation of Christ is repeated from Chapter 2:28, where you may see these words explained more fully.

**Verse 17.** *And the Spirit and the Bride say, etc.* These words contain a confirmation taken from the wish and desire of those who are sanctified. They long for nothing in this world more eagerly than to see these things completed <note>original: "confummated"</note> which this Book gives them hope for. For just as the souls under the Altar cried with a loud voice, desiring their deliverance (Chapter 6:10), so the faithful leap for joy because God has given them hope of their future marriage, and that makes them desire so exceedingly for that day to be hastened (Chapter 19:7). For the "Spirit" here signifies each of the faithful in whom the Spirit dwells; the "Bride" signifies the whole Church and the multitude of the faithful. The longing desires of all the faithful, both individually <note>original: "feuerally"</note> and collectively, strive together through prayer with the Lord to accomplish this one thing only. And that earnest desire and request which is kindled by God's Spirit cannot be frustrated.

*And let him that hears say, "Come."* This is as if he should say that this is not only the request of the present Church, but also of that which shall be spread <note>original: "propagated"</note> every day until the very end. Every one of the elect, as soon as he comes to the knowledge of these things, shall be set on fire with the self-same desire which his forefathers expressed in their time.

*And let him who is thirsty come.* These words show that this prophecy does not only serve to fire up our minds, but to fill them with joy to their full contentment, which is the unique property of the word of God. And so that nothing might be lacking to establish the certainty of this Book, you may understand by the words that follow at the end of the verse that this prophecy puts men in

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Revelation 22:17, explaining that salvation is a gift of grace rather than a reward for works.</meta>

# OF THE APOCALYPSE. Chapter 22.

...hope of salvation, by making them expect it not as the just wages of their works, but through the mere grace and mercy of God. He proclaims life and salvation freely, and not as a debt owed to the merits of our works, in the same way as the rest of Holy Scripture does. This is a worthy and excellent touchstone by which to test and discover heavenly truth.

**Verses 18–19.** *I warn everyone, etc.* <note>original: "Doubtlesse I proteste"</note> Up to this point, we have had a repetition of the former testimonies and arguments which were laid down sporadically <note>original: "scatteringly"</note> throughout the whole book preceding this. Now John brings in some new material, yet it is of the same divine authority as the previous parts—namely, that this prophecy is most certain and holy, and no one must dare to violate it in the slightest manner, either by adding to it or taking away from it, unless they want to desperately rush toward extreme punishments. Since this threat is attached only to the Word which comes from heaven, this Book of Revelation must be placed in the same rank as the books of the Law (Deuteronomy 4:2 and 12:32).

**Verse 20.** *He who testifies to these things says:* That is, Christ himself, who is called the witness both in respect to the Gospel which he brought into the world and also this prophecy, which relies upon his authority alone. And finally, the whole matter is sealed both by his repeated testimony and by John’s fervent request.

**Verse 21.** *The grace of our Lord.* This is the usual way of closing the holy Epistles of the Apostles. This entire prophecy is of that nature, as it was sent to the seven churches by the commandment of Christ himself (Chapter 1:11).

<meta>This page serves as the formal conclusion and concluding prayer to the author's commentary on the Book of Revelation (Apocalypse), Chapter 22.</meta>

->Glory and thanks be given to God forevermore, Amen.<-

> I give you thanks, (O almighty and everlasting God) that though I am a blind, unskillful, and wretched man, who has no judgment or wit <note>original: "vvit"; meaning intelligence or reason</note> at all, yet you have out of your pure <note>original: "meere"</note> mercy for Christ’s sake, conducted me through this impassable wilderness. You have enabled me to view many hidden corners closely on every side, and have made me travel safely through the dens of the Dragon and wild beasts. Even so, O Father, for such is your good will. You choose the ignoble and obscure people of the world, and have established strength out of the mouths of babes and infants, so that no person <note>original: "flesh"</note> might boast. How incomprehensible is your wisdom, how admirable is your truth! How just and holy are all your ways? Who would not fear you? I would willingly speak your praises, but my tongue lacks words, and my words lack understanding. Whichever way my mind turns, it is swallowed up by your infinity. If it ascends into heaven, you are higher than it; if it thinks upon your works, you are greater than they; if it meditates on your holiness, you are purer than the sun itself. O huge depth and unmeasurable gulf without bottom, how do you surround us on every side, and yet you are nowhere contained yourself? What mortal eye is there that can avoid being overwhelmed by your infinite brightness? Therefore my dim sight turns away from this light that cannot be approached, so that it may behold you through the "cloud" of your creation <note>original: "Cloud of the Creatures"</note>. Above all, it delights me to contemplate your most lovely <note>original: "amiable"</note> countenance in your blessed Son. Yet as you are most visible in this mirror <note>original: "glasse"</note>, so you are most admirable—as far exceeding all our understanding as you submit yourself lowest and nearest to our senses. You are great, O Lord, above all that can be either spoken or thought. Make us reverence your infinity, which the world cannot contain; to fear your presence, which our eyes cannot behold; to adore your Majesty, in respect of which the entire world, with all creatures here below, are less than nothing; and to magnify your bounty, which you show plentifully upon us, who are most unworthy men. Accomplish at length your great mystery, and let the world acknowledge that your long delay <note>original: "tariance"</note> has proceeded from your mercy only, and not from any forgetfulness or carelessness of your promise. Destroy that Beast of Rome <note>The author refers here to the Papacy.</note> and the dragon of Constantinople <note>The author refers here to the Ottoman Empire, which controlled Constantinople at this time.</note>. Build up your New Jerusalem, in which Christ shall reign, and where the Saints shall have dominion together with him, so that they may enjoy a blessed kingdom for a time upon earth and a most happy and eternal one with you in the heavens. Hear us graciously, O Father, from whom no thought of our heart can be hidden. Draw near with your presence—you who are absent from nowhere—and grant our holy desires, for which you have prepared the way with your decree and set aflame with this revealed Revelation. Then we shall prepare our harps and sing praises to you, magnifying you as one God in three Persons: Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. To whom be all honor, praise, and glory throughout all ages, and forevermore, Amen.

<summary>This concluding prayer offers thanks to God for guiding the author through the difficult interpretation of the Book of Revelation. It calls for the ultimate fulfillment of prophecy, the destruction of the Church's enemies, and the establishment of Christ's kingdom on earth and in heaven.</summary>
